IPO-bound Zetwerk and US-based transformer startup Ayr Energy have reached a settlement by agreeing to dismiss all claims in lawsuits pending before the Texas Business Court and a separate case involving Zetwerk Manufacturing Businesses and Ayr Energy’s founder Anirudh Reddy before a Bengaluru court. "The companies have dismissed all claims asserted in the lawsuits pending in the Texas Business Court and those asserted in the case involving Zetwerk Manufacturing Businesses Limited and Anirudh Reddy in XXXV Additional City Civil and Sessions Judge in Bengaluru, India, and they have jointly sought termination of the related US International Trade Commission investigation," the statement read. The settlement comes more than a year after the dispute began. At the heart of the dispute is Zetwerk’s allegation that Reddy incorporated Ayr Energy while still serving as a senior executive at Zetwerk. Reddy resigned from Zetwerk in January 2025, months after incorporating Ayr, the manufacturing company had alleged. The company claimed Reddy had downloaded hundreds of internal documents before leaving, including customer lists, pricing information and strategic plans. Zetwerk also alleged that Ayr used the information and relationships to secure contracts from customers in its sales pipeline. In May 2025, Zetwerk initiated a discovery proceeding against Ayr Energy in Delaware, which was denied in August 2025. The dispute escalated in October 2025 when Zetwerk and its US subsidiary filed a lawsuit in Texas against Ayr Energy and Reddy, alleging misuse of confidential information and trade secrets. Ayr Energy filed counterclaims against Zetwerk, accusing the company of trade secret theft, trademark infringement, false advertising, fraud and unfair competition. It sought at least $1 Bn in damages and approached the USITC over alleged trade-secret and other violations. Zetwerk disputed the allegations. In May 2026, the Texas Business Court allowed Zetwerk's claims to proceed after declining Ayr Energy's motion to dismiss. For context, Ayr Energy builds high-voltage and medium-voltage equipment, including transformers and switchgear, for data centre developers, utilities and power producers. The California-based startup was founded by Reddy after his stint at Zetwerk and has raised $3.5 Mn in a seed round led by General Catalyst. Meanwhile, Zetwerk was founded in 2018. It operates a manufacturing and supply chain platform serving sectors including energy, renewables, aerospace, defence, automotive and electronics. The company has raised funding from investors including Peak XV Partners and Lightspeed and is preparing for a public-market debut. Zetwerk is currently in the run up to making its public markets debut. After receiving the regulator’s approval for its confidential filing, Zetwerk filed its updated IPO papers in August. Its public issue is expected to comprise a fresh issue of shares worth ₹2,600 Cr and an offer-for-sale (OFS) component of up to 9.6 Cr equity shares. On the financial front, its net loss climbed 333% to ₹1,606.1 Cr during the fiscal under review from ₹370.7 Cr in FY25. The surging loss came at the behest of a ₹450 Cr provision related to the discontinued civil infrastructure business and around ₹800 Cr accounting charge related to the founders increasing their ownership from 15% to about 20%. The manufacturing company’s operating revenue jumped over 40% to ₹15,913.3 Cr in FY26 from ₹11,300 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Of this, approximately ₹9,300 Cr came from manufacturing, while the remainder from its ecosystem/raw-material business.

The graphic presented an unfair comparison of changes to the inflation rate for 12 household goods and utilities during the Biden and second Trump administrations. The graphic's comparison wasn't accurate because it compared Biden's full 48-month term to only 20 months of Trump's. Additionally, Snopes could not replicate the figures the graphic presented using the database it listed as a source.
In September 2026, a Facebook graphic (archived) circulated online that social media users claimed authentically showed that the price of some household goods and utilities rose more during the U.S. President Joe Biden's administration than during President Donald Trump's second term.
In other words, social media users claimed the graphic showed that the rate of inflation, meaning the increase in prices over time, was higher during Biden's presidency than during Trump's second term.
For example, one Facebook user shared the graphic and wrote, "Inflation hit American families hard under Biden."
The graphic also circulated elsewhere on Facebook, including on the page of the Denton County Republican Party in Texas (archived, archived). Social media users on Instagram, Threads and TikTok also shared the post (archived, archived, archived). Snopes readers contacted us to ask whether the numbers on the graphic were real.
While the graphics did purport to show that the price of some household goods and utilities rose less during the second Trump administration than during Biden's presidential term, its figures appeared to be false (wrong), fake (fabricated) or both, and the comparison it made wasn't accurate or fair.
We could not replicate any of the rate-of-inflation changes the graphic indicated took place between January 2021 and January 2025 or between January 2025 and August 2026 using the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) database. Importantly, it's the same database the graphic said it pulled its data from.
The graphic also made an unfair comparison by directly comparing Biden's 48-month presidency to the 20 months between January 2025 and August 2026 (both included) of Trump's second term. Because inflation is measured over time, direct comparisons should use time periods of the same length. A "fair" comparison in this case might have compared either the first 20 months of Biden's presidency to the first 20 months of Trump's or Biden's full term to Trump's full first term.
The source of the graphic was unclear. We contacted the Denton County Republican Party, which posted an early version of the graphic, to ask where they got their data from and await a reply.
It's worth noting that Pangram, a highly regarded artificial intelligence detector for images and text, found two versions of the graphic to be fully AI. Facebook also marked the Denton County Republican Party's posting of the graphic as AI content. (It's important to note that currently, no AI detection tool is regarded as 100% reliable.)
It's unclear what the sources of the images we scanned might have used AI for. They could have used AI tools to find or conjure the data or merely to present it.
What is the CPI?
The graphic listed the BLS' CPI-U database as its source. According to the BLS, the CPI tracks "changes in prices of all goods and services purchased for consumption by urban households" — in other words, inflation. CPI-U covers urban consumers, which the BLS says accounts for 90% of the total population of the U.S.
Because the CPI tracks price changes over time, it makes the most sense to use the index when comparing one point in time to another. According to the BLS website, most of its index series — meaning a data set that tracks prices for a certain item over time — use an average index from the 36 months covering 1982, 1983, and 1984. The BLS assigns that time period an index of 100, and all later periods show changes compared to that baseline.
The BLS wrote:
An index of 110, for example, means there has been a 10-percent increase in price since the reference period; similarly, an index of 90 means there has been a 10-percent decrease.
Changes to the rate of inflation (what the CPI measures) are usually reported as a percentage. This is because a percentage most accurately reflects how much prices have fallen or risen between two points in time.
What the data actually says
The Facebook post above claimed that the graphic used index series from the CPI-U database, using "U.S. cities average" to define the area where the BLS collected the data.
We found index series for 12 out of the 13 items listed in the Facebook graphic. The BLS doesn't publish an index series for "Natural gas" within its CPI-U database, meaning the figures the Facebook graphic used could not have come from that source.
The graphic didn't say whether it used data that was "seasonally adjusted." The BLS said on its website that such an adjustment attempts to remove "the influences of predictable seasonal patterns from time series data."
We used seasonally adjusted data in our attempt to recreate the Facebook graphic (except for "baby food and formula," which did not have seasonally adjusted data available). As the Facebook graphic said, we pulled data for "U.S. city average" from the database.
The data from the actual BLS CPI-U database showed that, for 12 goods or utilities, prices rose slower during Trump's second term than during Biden's first. However, that was to be expected given Biden's term covered a time period more than twice as long as the initial 20 months of Trump's second term.
The actual BLS CPI-U data also differed from the Facebook graphic that the Denton County Republicans posted for every good or service listed. In fact, the Denton County Republicans post short-changed Trump in some places, as the actual data showed inflation had fallen for four of the products listed — not just one, as the graphic claimed.
We used the Denton County Republicans post for comparison because the page posted an early version of the graphic.
A 'fair' comparison
For good measure, here is what a "fair" comparison of the rate of inflation for 12 products during the first 20 months of Biden's presidency and the first 20 months of Trump's second presidency would look like:
According to the CPI-U's data for January 2021 to August 2022 and January 2025 to August 2026, the rate of inflation was lower for 10 of the 12 products during the first 20 months of Trump's second term.
It's worth noting here that the start of Biden's presidency coincided with the COVID-19 pandemic and the highest period of inflation recorded in the U.S. for at least 20 years. Experts disagree about the reason for the high rates of post-COVID inflation.
The Brookings Institution, a think tank based in Washington, D.C, wrote in June 2023 that:
Most of the rise in inflation in 2021 and 2022 was driven by developments that directly raised prices rather than wages, including sharp increases in global commodity prices and sectoral price spikes driven by a combination of pandemic-induced kinks in supply chains and a huge shift in demand during the pandemic to goods from services.
It assigned a smaller role to fiscal policy.
Meanwhile, researchers from the MIT Sloan School of Management found in July 2024 that 42% of the inflation seen in 2022 "could be attributed to government spending." Federal spending to bolster the economy during the COVID pandemic helped it bounce back but also caused a "surge" in inflation, according to the school's experts.
In sum, the Facebook post that circulated online claiming lower rates of inflation for 13 products during Trump's second term than Biden's first appeared to use fabricated data and also presented an unfair comparison. It's unclear whether various creators used AI to source, conjure and/or present the data.
For further reading, Snopes has previously investigated other claims about inflation.

'It's like a dog set loose on us' - fear over Kenya's crackdown on foreign traders
- Published
For Ndaikech Ali, who has been traversing the streets of the Kenyan capital eking out a living as a tuk-tuk driver for the past nine years, Nairobi's traffic - not xenophobia - has been his biggest concern.
During his time in the East African nation, the Burundian says he has always found Kenyans to be friendly and welcoming - that is until last week, when the president ordered a crackdown on foreigners working as traders or operating small-scale businesses.
"Now they have turned against us," he told the BBC at the Burundian embassy in Nairobi where many have been queuing this week for documents to allow them to travel back home.
"The threats are many… even from children," he said, adding: "It's a like a dog has been set loose upon us. We have been bitten."
President William Ruto made his remarks last week when addressing Kenyan traders gathered at state house - in reference to legislation before parliament that seeks to exclude foreign nationals from petty trade and to mandate the local sourcing of certain materials.
During his speech, he said that all foreign nationals operating small businesses had until 7 September to pack up shop, saying such low-level jobs should be reserved for Kenyans.
Ali, like others, panicked, saying it seemed the president's announcement had been interpreted by some Kenyans as a signal that foreign nationals were no longer welcome in the country.
"We face harassment and can't work," he says. "If our work is stopped, we lose the income that enables us to pay rent and buy food. When those jobs are taken away, the only option left is to return home."
Now he's gone, who will help me pay school fees"
Other Burundians and some other foreign nationals have rushed to border crossing points to leave the country, with reports suggesting that a number have ended up stranded there.
Some couples fear they will be forced to separate - and some families have already been divided.
"I have been here from 2019," said a Burundian man, who identified himself only as Prosper and who has a child with a Kenyan woman.
"When I heard the announcement, it was very painful because when I go, I'm forced to leave my family... and I love my family," he told the BBC.
In Nairobi's low-income neighbourhood of Majengo, Kenyan Grace Wamaitha said her Burundian husband had already gone - leaving the day after the president's 3 September directive.
She is distraught as she has been left trying to feed their five children - and has taken on extra work washing clothes.
"Now he's gone, who will help me pay school fees? I don't know what to do. Let them come back," she told the BBC.
In Nairobi and other major towns, migrants from the region can be found working in barber shops and salons, construction, operating motorbike taxis and street vending, as well as selling clothes, food and household goods.
Some have fled conflicts or economic hardship at home, while others have moved to Kenya in search of better opportunities. Within the East African Community (EAC), a regional bloc made up of eight countries, including Burundi and Kenya, the relative free movement of people is allowed - but employment and long-term residence do require permits.
Kenyan law also recognises the right of refugees to work and operate businesses, although they are also required to obtain the appropriate documentation.
Filmon Eyob, a co-ordinator within Nairobi's Eritrean community, agrees with concerns that the crackdown order will be used as pretext to harass foreigners.
He told the BBC that while many Kenyans had been supportive and welcoming, some Eritreans and Ethiopians had closed their businesses and stayed at home over the last week as a precaution.
The president's remarks also sparked a diplomatic row, with the Burundian foreign affairs minister warning that "hate speech against Burundi" could have repercussions for Kenyans abroad.
The authorities in Kenya have struggled to contain the fallout - and as the matter came to a head, Kenyan foreign affairs official Korir Sing'Oei visited and apologised to Burundians at the embassy this week, assuring them of protection from violence.
Critics argue that Ruto's remarks were a populist move that risked stoking xenophobia, although the government has denied this.
Since then, a series of official statements have sought to clarify the directive.
The government has now given a 90-day window for undocumented foreign nationals running small business to register and comply with local laws. During the process, those undergoing registration will be presumed to be living legally in Kenya.
Yet observers and those affected argue that it did not have to be this way.
Academic Hesbon Owilla told the BBC the president's comments were bound to be misinterpreted, especially by people who did not have the right documentation.
He says that while the proposed policy is good for Kenya and in line with global migration protocols, the communication about it ought to have been more diplomatic.
For those not in the audience, Owilla says people interpreted the president words as saying: "We are kicking these guys out."
The president did not stop at small-scale traders. A day later, he ordered India's Tata Chemicals to leave the country, saying the company had not provided sufficient benefits to the local Maasai community in Kajiado county.
Tata has been mining soda ash for years in Lake Magadi, a vast area often covered by a whitish salt crust. The lake's extreme briny environment sustains algae blooms that attract flamboyances of pink flamingos that thrive in the area.
Mining operations began at the lake in 1911 under a British colonial arrangement that is said to have remained largely intact, despite long-running land and resource disputes pitting the company and its predecessors against community and the government.
Economist Odhiambo Ramogi argues that the move to restrict foreign nationals from businesses is too broad - and could do with finessing.
He points out that Kenya hosts hundreds of thousands of refugees as well as other migrants, mostly from the EAC region, as well as other international investors.
Ramogi says that Ruto's intention seemed to go beyond "just protecting jobs for Kenyans".
The president's remarks have prompted a wave of support for foreign nationals, including by civil society groups and ordinary Kenyans who have criticised his approach.
In the wake of the criticism, Ruto, who is up for re-election next year, has sought to counter the backlash.
"Kenya will remain an open, secure and welcoming country, protecting opportunities for its citizens, safeguarding the rights of all persons lawfully within its borders," a statement by his spokesman said.
"Kenya's commitment to the East African Community of the African continent remains firm."
Ramogi says that in the end, it is Kenya that stands to lose when citizens of neighbouring countries are targeted.
He points out that Kenya earned $56m (£41m) in exports to Burundi last year, adding that the country would still benefit by allowing competition, as "locking out aliens simply means you don't want a competitive economy that gets to grow a lot faster".
"Now, if you got $56m out of a country, why are you worried about a hawker who's just trying to make, say, $200 in a month?
"It absolutely makes no sense what the president has done."
For Nairobi resident Lima Kabura, whose husband is Tanzanian, the president's remarks were just too hasty. She says he should have first established those who were in the country illegally.
"When they are forced out, I'm left with no work, no business and no husband," she said.

Allaying apprehensions over the surge in dengue cases in Tamil Nadu, the Directorate of Public Health (DPH) and Preventive Medicine on Wednesday (September 17, 2026) said the spread of dengue this year was neither unusual nor alarming, and urged the public not to panic.
The Directorate issued a statement to allay apprehensions among the public that dengue fever cases have increased significantly in the State during the current year.
It said that this year, the spread of dengue was neither unusual nor occurring at an alarming level. Every year, seasonal variations in dengue cases occur naturally during the monsoon due to changes in climatic conditions.
It said that a comparison of official data from January to September over the past three years provided a clear picture of the current situation. In 2024, a total of 34,339 persons were affected by dengue and 13 deaths were reported. In 2025, 15,688 persons were affected and 13 deaths were reported. In the current year, as of September 16, 16,334 persons were affected and nine deaths were reported, the release said.
However, as per the official data put out by the National Centre for Vector Borne Diseases Control, there were a total of 27,378 dengue cases in the State in 2024.
The DPH noted that usually, breeding of Aedes mosquitoes that transmit dengue increased during the monsoon. In particular, conditions conducive for increased mosquito breeding may occur from October to December, and hence, dengue cases were being continuously monitored, while preventive and control measures were intensified.
Control measures
Officers were deployed across the State to coordinate dengue prevention and control measures. Fever wards were established to monitor patients with fever and to provide timely treatment. Triaging was undertaken to assess the health condition of patients and provide appropriate treatment on a priority basis based on the severity of the illness.
The directorate said that mosquito control measures, including larval control and source reduction, were being taken up across the State.
DPH urges public to cooperate
Making an appeal to the public, the DPH stressed the need for the public to work along with the government in dengue prevention and control measures. It requested the public to ensure that water does not stagnate in and around their houses and to ensure that there is no water accumulation in unused plastic items, coconut shells, old tyres, flower pots, and other containers. They should identify and immediately remove mosquito breeding sources in and around their houses and extend full cooperation to the mosquito control and dengue prevention measures taken up by the government and local bodies.
If symptoms such as fever occur, they should approach the nearest primary health centre or government hospital to seek medical advice and appropriate treatment without delay. It said that dengue transmission can be controlled more effectively if the public extends cooperation for the preventive measures undertaken by the government.

U.S. President Donald Trump is seeking to bring a major part of national funding for health research under the control of his political appointees, Politico reported on Saturday (September 20, 2026).
Mr. Trump has directed his budget director, Russ Vought, to draft an executive order to create a board that would decide which grants would be funded by the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the news outlet said, citing two administration officials familiar with the meeting.
The board would include NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya and Mr. Vought, the director of the White House Office of Management and Budget, and would be required to reach unanimous decisions on grant awards, the report said.
The proposed arrangement would give Mr. Vought a direct role in determining how the health research agency distributes its congressionally-appropriated money, the report added.
The Office of Management and Budget, the White House and the Health and Human Services Department that oversees the NIH did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment outside regular business hours.
The reported move comes amid mounting criticism of the U.S. government’s research funding cuts, undertaken last year to target federal spending at major universities, resulting in the freezing or cancellation ofgrants at numerous institutions.
The Trump administration says these cuts are necessary to ensure the government funds only solid science and to reverse years of misguided priorities.

A patient enters an operating theatre for a procedure on the right knee. The limb is marked, the scans are available and the surgical team has checked the records. Just before the operation begins, the team stops. A nurse reads out the patient’s identity, the procedure planned, the side of the body to be operated on and the type of anaesthesia. The surgeon, anaesthetist and other members of the team confirm the details. This brief pause, known as ‘timeout’, may take only a few minutes. But it is one of several layers of checks designed to prevent a potentially devastating mistake.
This exercise is an example of what Syed Mohammed Ghouse, consultant robotic and transplant surgeon, Asian Institute of Nephrology and Urology, described as the ‘Swiss cheese mechanism’, in which several layers of checks are put in place so that if one safety barrier fails, another can detect the error before it reaches the patient.
The need for such multiple safeguards is at the heart of World Patient Safety Day, observed on September 17. The World Health Organisation’s theme for 2026 is ‘Safe care for noncommunicable diseases’.
Doctors say patient safety has to be viewed much more broadly than preventing an obvious surgical or medication error. Ranga Reddy Burri, president, Infection Control Academy of India, said the understanding of patient safety has now expanded considerably: the responsibility cannot rest only with doctors and nurses. Policymakers, accreditation agencies, patients, caregivers, families, communities and even housekeeping staff have roles to play. “A hospital just having an accreditation doesn’t actually guarantee the kind of safety that is required,” Dr. Burri said, stressing the need to train all stakeholders involved in a patient’s journey.
Where it begins
Patient safety begins even before treatment starts, notes Dr. Burri. The availability of sophisticated diagnostic equipment has not necessarily solved the problem of ensuring an accurate diagnosis. “The diagnosis quality has actually gone down over a period of time,” he said. He attributed part of the problem to doctors moving away from basic clinical examination, including auscultation, percussion, palpation and physical examination. He described the emerging situation as ‘no touch’ healthcare, where doctors can sometimes begin looking at a computer even before adequately engaging with the patient.
Neurologist Sudhir Kumar of Apollo Hospitals, Hyderabad, also pointed to the importance of ensuring quality of medical education as the number of medical colleges and seats increases. “If we don’t ensure quality services, then it will worsen the patient’s safety because diagnosis may be missed; treatment may not be perfect,” he said.
Medication problems
Medication safety remains another major area of concern. Dr. Kumar said spurious and fake medicines continue to pose a patient-safety risk despite the existence of drug inspectors and regulatory checks.
Dr. Ghouse pointed to another problem of look-alike and sound-alike medicines. With a large number of pharmaceutical companies and medicines available, drugs with similar names can create opportunities for errors, particularly when medicines are handled by someone who is distracted or not sufficiently alert. He said hospitals use measures such as separate labelling and storing look-alike and sound-alike medicines away from each other, along with other quality-control measures.
Technology has reduced some types of prescription errors, but doctors say it has not eliminated them. Dr. Ghouse said typed and printed prescriptions are still not universal, especially at small clinics. Dr. Kumar said prescription errors can also occur when different doctors prescribe medicines under different brand names or when medicines from the same group are inadvertently duplicated. “For example, a patient may end up taking the same medicine twice because different brand names make it difficult to recognise that the drugs are essentially the same.”
Within hospitals
Some patient-safety risks are less dramatic but can still have serious consequences, particularly among older patients. Dr. Burri said falls in hospitals, including falls while patients are going to the bathroom or getting out of bed, can result in major injuries. “Hospitals need to ensure that their physical environments are designed to prevent slipping and other hazards.
Patient safety also extends beyond just their wards or rooms. Dr. Kumar pointed to hospital fires, electrical problems and other infrastructure-related hazards as areas that require greater attention. He said while the number of hospitals was increasing, some facilities are decades old, raising questions about who regularly audits their wiring and electrical connections.
For Dr. Burri, infection prevention and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) remain central to the patient-safety conversation. Unnecessary antibiotic administration, delayed diagnosis, unhygienic environments and non-adherence to infection-prevention and control guidelines can all contribute to the problem, he said.
These risks can become particularly important for patients with chronic diseases, who may require repeated interactions with healthcare facilities. Dr. Burri said patients with conditions such as chronic kidney disease, lung diseases and cancer may have vulnerabilities that make infection prevention an important component of safe care. “Healthcare workers and administrators therefore have a central role in ensuring that infection-control practices are followed,” he added.
Data and AI
As healthcare becomes increasingly digital, patient safety is also becoming connected to data privacy. Dr. Kumar said medical information is private, but increasing digitisation has created new risks around cybersecurity and access to medical records. He pointed to instances of hospital data breaches and leaks and said multiple categories of hospital staff may have access to digital systems for operational reasons.
Artificial intelligence is increasingly entering healthcare, but Dr. Kumar said it should remain a tool rather than become a substitute for clinical reasoning. He said there was a risk that medical students and young doctors could begin relying on AI tools too early instead of developing their own ability to analyse symptoms and arrive at differential diagnoses.
Centering the patient
For all the technology, protocols and checklists being introduced into hospitals, the doctors point to one element that cannot be removed from the equation, the patient. Dr. Burri said patients, families, caregivers and communities must understand their own role in ensuring safety.

Meta announced a slate of new wearables during its annual Meta Connect showcase on Wednesday. The star of the event was the new Meta VR Glasses, which pack virtual reality tech into a lightweight smart glasses-style frame with a tethered puck. Meta also announced new pairs of screen-free smart glasses, along with some new AI features and style and frame options.
Meta Connect 2026: The 7 biggest announcements
This year’s Meta Connect featured a new lightweight VR wearable and camera-free Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses.
You can catch up on all the highlights from this year’s Meta Connect below.
Meta’s latest wearable offers full virtual reality in a smart glasses-style form factor. Unlike a typical VR headset, the VR Glasses don’t have any straps, and Meta says they’re “five times lighter than Meta Quest 3” at just 100g. Similar to Google’s Project Aura, the glasses are tethered to a pocket-sized puck with the compute hardware, battery, and storage, including a Qualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite, 128GB of storage, and 12GB of RAM. The 5K micro OLED “Infinite Display” has 2412 x 2288 pixels per eye, with a refresh rate of up to 120Hz.
The Meta VR Glasses are launching in spring 2027 for $1,299, pricier than the Meta Ray-Ban Display but less expensive than the Apple Vision Pro, while offering similar features. Users can connect the glasses to a Mac or Windows laptop for use as a virtual external display, with an option for a virtual surface keyboard and touchpad.
The VR Glasses also have access to the full Meta Quest catalog of apps and games and support for Xbox Cloud Gaming. Meta says the glasses are “the first IMAX Enhanced certified VR device ever,” and users will be able to watch “immersive live sports” with them as well as 3D movies. They even have a “hologram” feature that creates a “photorealistic digital version of your face” for using in calls while wearing the glasses, reminiscent of the “personas” on the Apple Vision Pro.
Meta is launching camera-free smart glasses
The highlight of the Ray-Ban Meta Audio is the feature they don’t have: built-in cameras. You can use them for things like listening to music, taking calls, or chatting with an AI assistant, but they can’t take pictures or record video — features that have sparked privacy and harassment concerns around Meta’s other glasses.
Meta says the new audio-only glasses are also its “lightest, slimmest AI glasses yet,” weighing just 43g. They offer up to 12 hours of battery life per charge, or 48 hours with the charging case. The Ray-Ban Meta Audio will launch on October 13th starting at $349 with 23 different color and lens combinations.
Refreshed Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 arrive with battery and design upgrades
Meta launched an updated version of its main Ray-Ban Meta glasses, starting at $449. The Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 offer up to nine hours of battery life, one hour more than the Gen 2. They also have “a new customizable action button for instant access to Meta AI” and a new six-mic array that Meta says “cuts more than 90% of background noise.”
The Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 has a slimmer design than the Gen 2 as well, with 27 color and lens combinations, including new Zena and Aviator frame styles. Notably, one thing that hasn’t changed is the built-in LED light that indicates when the glasses are recording, which Meta rolled out a privacy fix for last month.
Budget glasses launch along with new glasses styles
Alongside its pricier Ray-Ban glasses, Meta also announced some updates to its in-house line of glasses. It’s launching a new lower-cost version of the Meta Adventurer, which will start at $249 for a basic design with black frames and gray lenses, launching October 23rd.
Meta is also introducing a new “Mix & Match” program for customizing its glasses with different frames, lenses, and case colors. Plus, its EssilorLuxottica collection is getting two new styles, Capri and Nova, and the Kylie Jenner Starfire frames are getting a new ivory colorway. Meta’s also launching a new collaboration collection with Lisa of Blackpink.
Meta Glasses are expanding to more countries starting today, too, including Singapore, South Korea, Mexico, and the United Arab Emirates, with availability in Brazil “coming soon.”
Meta Ray-Ban Display is coming to more regions with some new features
A year after they originally launched, the Meta Ray-Ban Display are coming to more regions. The glasses are on sale in the UK and Canada starting today, and they’ll be available in France, Italy, and Germany starting on October 13th. Meta’s also introducing online ordering for customers in those regions and the US.
Meta’s launching a new Explore app for Display glasses where users will be able to “browse and use a growing selection of experiences built for your glasses.” The Meta Ray-Ban Display is also getting photo editing, an improved calendar, and mirrored phone notifications. Plus, Meta says the “hologram” feature launching on its VR Glasses is rolling out on the Meta Ray-Ban Display “in Early Access on WhatsApp to Meta Ray-Ban Display users in the US later this fall.”
After launching its new Muse assistant earlier this month, Meta says it’s “working on” bringing the AI to its smart glasses. When it arrives on the glasses, Muse will be able to do things like guide your workouts, log meals, book appointments, and “help buy products you see.”
Meta also announced some new features for Muse, including video calls with a customizable live avatar of the AI. Plus, Muse agents are getting their own email addresses for completing tasks and communicating with users.
Meta is making an AI ‘charm’
Mark Zuckerberg teased one last device, Muse Charm, a small AI gadget that houses the Muse agent and looks a little bit like a supersized Tamagotchi. More details will be shared “soon,” he said, but the product is supposed to ship in time for the holiday season.

MP Materials mines and processes rare earth minerals in California, including neodymium-praseodymium oxide used in high-performance magnets.
Credit:
David McNew/Getty Images
MP Materials mines and processes rare earth minerals in California, including neodymium-praseodymium oxide used in high-performance magnets.
Credit:
David McNew/Getty Images
All of these devices function because of 17 metals collectively known as rare earth elements. The scientists who gave the group that name in 1794 created a misnomer. Cerium alone is about as common in the Earth’s crust as copper.
However, separating rare earth minerals from one another and from raw ore is intensely difficult. As a result, countries that control the processing of rare earth minerals have a lot of political leverage.
China processes most of the rare earth minerals used around the world, and it isn’t just consumer electronics that depend on Chinese exports. The US military’s F-35 fighter jets and Virginia-class submarines need rare earths too.
I spent years adjudicating war games for the US Navy. War games force players to identify the hidden constraints that render a beautiful plan untenable. Rare earth processing is exactly such a constraint.
China showcased the power of its rare earths leverage with a series of export controls issued in 2025 that it agreed to suspend—at least until Nov. 10, 2026. Controlling the supply enables a government to slow a rival’s growth, or halt it. China’s ability to extend the suspension of its export controls or let them go into effect gives it leverage on the geopolitical stage. In the parlance of Theodore Roosevelt, it’s a very big stick.
The US has rare earth minerals, but few mines. For years, it shipped much of what it does mine overseas for processing. MP Materials’ Mountain Pass mine and processing facility restarted in California in 2017.
The US has rare earth minerals, but few mines. For years, it shipped much of what it does mine overseas for processing. MP Materials’ Mountain Pass mine and processing facility restarted in California in 2017.
Credit:
Tmy350/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA
China, which mined about 60 percent of the world’s rare earth elements used in magnets in 2024, handled about 91 percent of separation and refining.
Buyers using processing in China got material below the cost of making it themselves, and none of the cleanup bills or the bad press. But they ceded leverage to the processor in exchange. The trade was understood. It just didn’t look as threatening at first from a China that was still rising.
Why rebuilding is slow
The US Government Accountability Office cited estimates in 2010 that rebuilding a domestic supply chain including mining, separation, and magnet manufacturing would take as long as 15 years. Actually rebuilding that supply chain has been slow for several reasons.
China runs its plants with thousands of experienced engineers; the US has far fewer experts. Today’s industrial-scale cutting-edge technologies were developed in China, and the government there has no reason to share. Beijing also banned exports of the separation technology itself in December 2023.
The US has rare earth deposits, but little mining. The pink areas in this US Geological Survey map are believed to have potential for rare earth deposits.
Credit:
USGS
The US has rare earth deposits, but little mining. The pink areas in this US Geological Survey map are believed to have potential for rare earth deposits.
Credit:
USGS
The US government has committed more than $7 billion since April 2025 to try to rebuild US rare earth production capacity. The Pentagon bought $400 million of preferred stock in rare earth producer MP Materials in 2025, giving it 15 percent ownership of the company. MP Materials expects its next magnet plant to begin testing the equipment in 2028.
The Commerce Department also signed a letter of intent in 2026 to give a magnet maker, USA Rare Earth, $277 million in direct funding and a $1.3 billion loan, both aimed at developing facilities in Texas and Oklahoma.
But export roadblocks put up by China are making rebuilding that supply chain more difficult.
What happens on November 10
On Oct. 9, 2025, China’s Ministry of Commerce announced six wide-ranging export control measures. One, Announcement No. 61, affects what even factories abroad can export. A factory in Germany or Japan would need a Chinese license to export a product if Chinese-origin rare earths made up 0.1 percent or more of its value, or if it used Chinese rare earth technology.
Both controls snap back into place automatically unless both governments extend their pauses.
What stays in place
Some of the export rules were never suspended, including licensing imposed by China in April 2025 on exports of seven of the heavier rare earths.
Automaker Ford saw how the export controls can affect a company when it had to idle its Chicago assembly plant for a week in May 2025 for want of magnets—critical to speakers and electrical motors—because of the export rules. Ford CEO Jim Farley described his supply as “day to day” because he had no alternate source. Ford was able to resume production only with Beijing’s approval.
On June 22, 2026, China’s Ministry of Commerce put 10 US companies on its export control list. Neither Chinese nor foreign firms can sell those companies any goods that have both civilian and military uses. Most of them build drones, radar, aerospace systems, and military vehicles. Two of them—MP Materials and USA Rare Earth—are the federally backed American companies furthest along in building a mine-to-magnet chain.
Beijing said its move was a response to a similar move by the Pentagon. My interpretation is that China picked MP Materials and USA Rare Earth because they are best placed to reduce America’s need for Chinese processing.
An extension of the pause on Nov. 10 would honor the truce, but the heavy rare earth licenses and the June 22 ban on the targeted firms would still apply. The truce means both parties get to play nice. It doesn’t mean they are being nice.
Rebuilding a US rare earths supply chain would remove most US dependence on China for rare earths and the political leverage it implies. But it would take longer, startup costs run to the billions of dollars, and separation produces acidic, and sometimes radioactive, residues.
Building a supply chain with allies such as Australia or Japan, both of which have started to build capacity, would lower the risk of the US being cut off unilaterally. Japan has run this play with some success, but the suspended Chinese rules affect any use of their technology abroad.
President Xi’s Sept. 24, 2026, meeting with Trump may help determine the status of the Nov. 10 restrictions, but the larger conflict over leverage will continue.

Rogers has directly received campaign donations from people who appeared in the Epstein files.
Contrary to the claim's implication, Rogers received much of these funds during his 2024 Senate campaign, not his 2026 campaign. Furthermore, these donors sent most of the funds to independent PACs supporting Rogers, not directly to Rogers' campaign.
Being named in the Epstein files is not necessarily evidence of wrongdoing. It's unclear whether any of these donors knew of or were complicit in Epstein's crimes, and there's no evidence they were.
In September 2026, a claim spread online that Mike Rogers, the Republican candidate for a U.S. Senate seat to represent Michigan, had received nearly $4.7 million from donors who appeared in files related to the federal investigation of the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
The rumor spread on X, Threads and Facebook (screenshot). Some posts also claimed at least seven of Rogers' donors had ties to Epstein. Rogers' Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, also shared the rumor.
This claim is mostly true at face value, but it needs significant context.
It originated with a report in the Detroit Metro Times, a progressive news outlet, titled, accurately, "Donors named in Epstein files gave nearly $4.7 million to Mike Rogers and groups backing him."
The story explains that Stephen Schwarzman, co-founder and CEO of investment management company Blackstone, donated $4.5 million in 2024 to a super PAC that supported Rogers. By law, super PACs, which are allowed to raise unlimited money, can't coordinate their spending with the actual campaign. Schwarzman also donated a much-smaller amount directly to Rogers' Senate campaigns from 2023 to 2025.
Snopes independently verified the amount Schwarzman donated and that he appears in the Epstein files. However, as the Metro Times story states, there's no evidence Schwarzman and Epstein directly interacted. No one, including federal prosecutors, has publicly accused Schwarzman of wrongdoing connected to Epstein.
The other six donors who donated the remaining money had varying degrees of closeness to Epstein — but there's no evidence any of them knew of or assisted in his criminal activities.
As for El-Sayed, we found no evidence any people named in the Epstein files donated directly to his campaign. Two people with passing mentions in the Epstein files sent money to a super PAC supporting El-Sayed.
Rogers' campaign spokeswoman, Alyssa Brouillet, pointed to Rogers' time in the FBI "busting human traffickers" and said in an emailed statement that "any attempt at associating him with criminals is insulting and patently false."
Federal Election Commission data indicates Schwarzman sent "GLCF, INC" three donations totaling $4.5 million: $2 million in June 2024, $1 million in August 2024 and $1.5 million in September 2024.
GLCF stands for Great Lakes Conservatives Fund — a super PAC that solely supports Rogers, according to OpenSecrets, a nonprofit group that tracks campaign finances.
A Federal Election Commission search for donations from Stephen Schwarzman sent to Rogers' campaign committees shows the billionaire businessman also sent at least $13,600 to "Rogers for Senate," the committee name for Rogers' actual campaign, and $7,000 in 2025 to "Team Rogers," a joint-fundraising operation for Rogers. Schwarzman also sent $5,000 to "MR PAC," which stands for Michigan's Resurgence PAC — which Rogers used to raise money to support other politicians.
(Federal Election Commission)
Schwarzman in the Epstein files
Schwarzman's last name appears frequently in the Epstein files. For example, one document shows Epstein was emailed an invitation to a 2015 cocktail party to celebrate the release of the film "The Imitation Game" on behalf of Schwarzman and others. In another email, Epstein appears to call Schwarzman "terrific" after suggesting to someone that "attaching to Blackstone might be a good idea."
However, none of these emails indicates Schwarzman and Epstein ever met in person. There also aren't any publicly available pictures of Schwarzman with Epstein, although there is an authentic picture of the Blackstone CEO in conversation with Epstein's associate Ghislaine Maxwell at a New York gala.
In an emailed statement, a spokesperson for Schwarzman told Snopes it would be "categorically false and grossly irresponsible to claim or imply that Steve had any relationship with this despicable individual."
The spokesperson said Epstein did not attend the 2015 cocktail party, and the invitation was extended through a PR firm that worked with the film's distributors, not Schwarzman.
The same PR firm, the spokesperson said, invited Epstein to another 
Other donors' connections to Epstein files
Here's a list of other people in the Epstein files who donated to Rogers from 2023 to 2025, per Metro Times reporting and Snopes' independent verification using FEC data:
- Marc Rowan, Apollo Global Management CEO: $25,000 to GLCF, $14,000 to Rogers' campaigns and $7,000 to Team Rogers
- Ronald Lauder, Estée Lauder heir: $3,300 to Rogers' 2024 Senate campaign
- John Catsimatidis, grocery chain billionaire businessman: $13,600 to Rogers for Senate
- Joseph Baratta, Blackstone executive: $10,300 to Rogers for Senate
- Howard Lorber, real estate executive: $5,693 to Rogers for Senate
- John W. Childs, private equity investor: $8,530 to Rogers for Senate, $60,000 to GLCF and $12,000 to Team Rogers
Of the list above, Rowan and Lauder have the most documented interaction with Epstein.
Rowan planned a breakfast at Epstein's house and kept regular correspondence with him from 2013 to 2016. The files show Lauder and Epstein planned meetups in 2017, including luncheons and a museum tour. Lauder's signature also appears in the files on joint purchase agreements for artwork, which Epstein appeared to help with.
In an email, Apollo Global Management spokesperson Giovanna Falbo directed us to a Feb. 18, 2026, news release where the company referred to its investigation into Apollo's ties to Epstein and denied that Rowan had "either a business or personal relationship with Jeffrey Epstein."
Business Insider reported that Catsimatidis was in one of Epstein's 1997 address books. Catsimatidis told Business Insider he met Epstein once in the 1990s through a friend and never saw him again, although Epstein called the billionaire "once or twice, I don't know about what."
Epstein said in a 2016 email that 
Most mentions of a "Joseph Baratta" in the DOJ's Epstein files appear to actually reference an attorney — Joseph P. Baratta — not the Blackstone executive, Joseph A. Baratta. There are a couple of mentions of the executive, but nothing that suggests an actual relationship.
"Joe has absolutely no relationship with him, and it would be outrageous and patently false to suggest otherwise," said a spokesperson for Baratta, who also represents Schwarzman.
Lorber is referenced in relation to some real estate deals Epstein contemplated, as well as a suggested "war council" to help Trump respond to the aftermath of the Russia collusion investigation. There's no evidence such a "war council" ever materialized.
Similarly, the DOJ files include financial transactions connected to Childs, but there's no documented correspondence between Childs and Epstein.
In February 2019, Childs was charged with soliciting prostitution in a human trafficking sting. He denied the allegations. The charges were reportedly dropped in 2020 and his record expunged after the courts determined prosecutors brought the case in violation of his Fourth Amendment privacy rights.
We attempted to reach Lauder and Lorber to clarify the extent of their relationships to Epstein and await responses. We were unable to reach Childs.
The bottom line
Rogers and PACs supporting him did, in fact, receive millions from donors who appear in the Epstein files, largely from Blackstone co-founder Stephen Schwarzman. However, simply being named in the files doesn't mean a person knew of or assisted in Epstein's criminal activities. For example, the Epstein files release contained dubious allegations, newsletters Epstein subscribed to and what appear to be mundane business transactions, like for facility maintenance.
For further reading, Snopes has covered several claims about El-Sayed, Rogers' Democratic opponent.

The order of several pivotal scenes in Ali Hazelwood’s The Love Hypothesis was switched up for the film adaptation of the best-selling romance novel, directed by Claire Scanlon and starring Tom Bateman and Lili Reinhart.
The film centers around a fake dating ploy that benefits both parties — Olive (Reinhart) convinces her best friend Ahn (Rachel Marsh) that Ahn should shoot her shot with their mutual crush Jeremy and Adam (Bateman) makes his higher ups aware that he’s in a serious relationship and in no way planning to leave Stanford University, which has funded much of his research but pulled the plug based on rumors that he might depart. What starts out as a simple business arrangement develops into real romance, which faces its obstacles when a certain Dr. Tom Benton (Arty Froushan) comes to town.
Watch on Deadline
The very important Chapter 16 sex scene between Olive and Adam was moved up in the film, and Scanlon already felt the “pressure” to get that one right alone. Luckily an audience of 40% book readers and fans gave the green light.
“When we started, there was just a quick paragraph of the sex scene, and then I read the book, and [said to] Sarah Rothschild, who wrote a great adaptation, ‘I think we need to build out that sex scene.’ Then I went on TikTok and I saw everyone [saying] ‘chapter 16, chapter 16.” I was like, ‘Oh my goodness, this has to be more,’ Scanlon told Deadline. “Translating the book, which is over a chapter, to the screen — you can’t do that long with a sex scene. That would be not right. But just making sure that you got it tonally is always going to be tricky because everyone’s got their own internal dialog and their own imagination of what it all looks like. We were ready for all the criticism, and then there wasn’t any.”
To back up, a chaotic kiss with Dr. Carlsen initiated by Olive sets the fake-dating scheme of The Love Hypothesis into motion. Olive panics and smooches the first man she sees — who happens to be the notorious Dr. Evil — to throw Ahn off the scent late one Saturday night in the lab. This snowballs into a whiplash of planned PDA and falling in love between the scientists.
“We shot the first kiss on the first week. I wanted to make sure we got that dynamic established. And when we got that scene, I was like, ‘We have a movie’ because you just get all of it, watching it, trying to recreate the book cover in the actual scene. Paying homage to the book cover, and just in general, trying to get the tone of that scene, all the elements that were going into it. Ahn’s coming up the stairs, [Olive]’s running this way. He’s like, “What?” Scanlon said. “Then he’s pissed because when you think about it from his point of view, he hasn’t been touched for years by anyone. Everyone’s so scared of him. That fact that someone smacked a kiss on him and then immediately rejects him, like that’s gotta suck, you know?”
Dr. Carlsen quips about filing a Title IX complaint because Olive technically doesn’t wait for him to give consent before she kisses him. Another key moment that brings Title IX truly into question was shuffled to occur after the Chapter 16 scene, compared to book order. Carlsen’s colleague and seemingly close friend Dr. Tom Benton, whose research aligns with Olive’s pancreatic cancer work, offers her a position on his lab bench at Harvard University to continue conducting her experiments, but rather than base it off of Olive’s merit alone, he lays down the ultimatum that Olive must sleep with him in order to use his lab and equipment.

“Visually, it made more sense to have this lovely night, be on a high, and then the rug pulled out from beneath [Olive]. In so many ways, you have to truncate scenes and support the chronological order of things, and so it was something that we needed to manage and address. And then, because we changed that order, he couldn’t come at her and right after the conference, it had to be something different,” Scanlon said. “We liked the idea of him being able to say, “I had coffee. I had a coffee in my hand the whole time. I never didn’t have a coffee,” so he would have plausible deniability.”
What seems like an innocent move to bring coffee up to Adam’s hotel room at the Society for Biological Development Conference quickly turns sinister with the knowledge that Adam has already flown back to California. His implication that their working relationship be “equally beneficial” to that between Olive and Adam quickly sours his offer and her exciting opportunity, not to mention complicating matters between Olive and Adam as well as Adam and Tom by extension.
“She can’t get out. He’s blocking her from the door. There was a lot of talk about things that, technically, in a legal case, he’s probably done this so many times. He knows exactly how to do it, like so many people do,” Scanlon added. “[He] could have plausible deniability, but technically, we know how she looks, and we are experiencing what she’s experiencing, and you know darn well what he’s doing. We thought a lot about it.”
In the below interview, Scanlon further unpacks the denouement of the film, full circle moments, working in the romantic comedy space and whether an Ali Hazelwood cameo was discussed. She also teases upcoming project The Probability of Miracles, a TV show currently in production with Prime Video.
DEADLINE: Ahn is the one to tell Adam about Tom Benton, and they’re looking at each other in the mirrors. Can you talk about filming that scene?
SCANLON: We shot in that same space twice, the opening of the movie, which was very obfuscated, so you never see what Adam looks like because of [Olive’s] contact lenses. And then, obviously, what’s so interesting about shooting into the mirror? It’s a small space, but also, Ahn is feeling him out. Is [Adam] duplicitous? Is he on board? Does he know that Tom has this proclivity to sexually harass women that he works with? Is he complicit? So I think there’s this duality and reflection, “Are you a good person or not?”
You’re looking in the mirror and it’s kind of like, “Who are you? Who is this person in the mirror?” And then when she says, “Did you know?” And he’s like, “Know what? And she’s like, “He’s a piece of shit.” And he’s like, “Wait, what? And she’s like, “Okay, I gave you the benefit of the doubt. Rightfully so. Here’s what happened. “And he’s like, “You’re a good friend Ahn. And she’s like, “Yeah, duh.” And then he storms off to the tune of our version of Darth Vader’s theme.
DEADLINE: I was going to ask about that music sounding like Darth Vader.
SCANLON: And it’s when he comes in the coffee shop. In the rough cut, we actually just used John Williams, and it always elicited a laugh. And then our wonderful composer Laura Karpman, I was like, “Laura, you’ve got to pay your best John Williams homage at this moment,” and she had so much fun with it.
DEADLINE: Did you ever talk to Ali [Hazelwood] about a cameo? Was that ever thought of in the film?
SCANLON: Yes, and the answer was no. She came to set. I feel like she gave us her blessing, first with the script, but then she also came to set when we were shooting at Cal Tech. We did a day in LA. We shot mostly in Montreal.
We did a day in LA for exteriors with Lili, and it looks really good when she’s storming through the campus to go confront [Adam] after she finds out that Malcolm’s been fired from his team. Anytime you see a palm tree, odds are that, either, we were carrying two palm trees in Montreal, and we just would stick them in the background. Or when there’s a myriad of palm trees, that’s Caltech.
But she came that day, and she was so sweet. She is very quiet and unassuming. As [producer] Elizabeth [Cantillon] would say, she’s like a sprightly little elf putting pixie dust over everything in a wonderful way. You really see how she holds up other authors. She’s always advocating for others. She saw this and she said all these nice things about the film. She’s just really a wonderful advocate who uses her space in media to uphold others, and she’s done so with this film as well.
DEADLINE: The scene where they’re making the Rube Goldberg machine looked really fun and chaotic. Plus it’s not in the book.
SCANLON: We realized there were some scenes where she’s in his world, and we just wanted a scene where he’s in her world. So that’s where that came out about. First we were gonna do an ABC (Anything But Clothes) party. So you make balloons instead, or use a keg, or you make stuff out of like boxes, and it’s silly, but they’re fun.
But comfortability-wise, we were like, “That’s not gonna work.” It’s fun on the page, but we started talking to the costume designer, and they’re like, “Yeah, no, this is really hard for all those background actors to have anything but clothes on.” It would just have been a nightmare. And then the Rube Goldberg of it all, I remember Elizabeth being like, “We have to storyboard this.” And both the DP and I were like, “Oh no, no, no, no!” We know exactly how to approach this. It’s got to be chaos. It’s handheld. Nothing really is handheld in the film other than the sex scene and the Rube Goldberg machine. But just him being in her world and actually being able to hang and getting people to like him. He’s coming in and nobody likes him, and then being fun and helping and being game basically shows you, “Oh they really could get on. They might actually be each other’s people.”
DEADLINE: The epilogue two years later when the students are talking about rumors around Olive felt really full circle from when she walks into the Bass Building at the beginning of the film. Why did you want to bring it to an end that way?
SCANLON: Oh, for sure, it’s the two of them. There’s two girls coming in, and it was Ahn and Olive coming in the first go-around when they were nervous and starting. And Ahn’s like, “Let’s go up front. You can’t sit in the back. Can’t learn anything from the back.” And you’re watching two other girls, proxies for our two main stars. It is funny that Doctor Evil had a nickname and now it’s Doctor Smythe and her whole thing was trying to not make him Doctor Evil, but I think no matter what you do, the game of telephone is going to happen with scared young people starting school and they’re going to give you a nickname whether you like it or not, and it’s up to you to show, “Hey, yeah, I’m tough,” but like she said, someone got dehydrated from a party the night before. It wasn’t that she was a tough teacher, but it’s like a little bit of fear. Let’s let that ride. A little fear is good.
DEADLINE: Did you feel any similarities to Set It Up when you were filming The Love Hypothesis? Or maybe anything that informed you from shooting Set It Up? Rom coms are doing so well right now. I’m curious your thoughts there.
SCANLON: I would say my favorite films, my touchstone films that I always encourage people to watch when we’re working together on something like this — I did it on Set It Up — are His Girl Friday, It Happened One Night, The Philadelphia Story, Bringing Up Baby, and those were called screwball comedies. I don’t quite know what change happened to call them romantic comedies because aren’t they the same essentially? I love those. Those are my favorite movies, and I like how witty the women are. They are equals, and this is the 30s and 40s, and I would say nothing’s changed. They still hold true. All those films still feel fun and fresh, and women are definitely the drivers of those films, and I love that. That’s probably why I was drawn to them in the first place. I think, for a while, the genre got a little lazy. I don’t think I’m unique in thinking this. Relying on the tropes rather than having fun with them, thwarting them. I think Set It Up definitely gave wink winks to them. Another touchstone would be When Harry Met Sally, three of the four people in that movie are just normal looking people, and they’re just in funny situations and they create funny situations and they miscommunicate and those are all things that happen in daily life. So I think the you can be in a silly situation, but it’s grounded.
This is at Stanford. It’s in labs. They really look like Stanford students. We had this wonderful consultant, Sonia Cruiz, who was so great and told us everything we were doing wrong and helped us set up the beakers and the test tubes and everything. So were some of the grad students that were in background. They were real grad students, so they knew too, at Concordia University in Montreal. They were totally having fun with it as well, feeling good that their field of study was being honored in a major motion picture. In general, I really try and strive to have lots of comedy in romantic comedies, not short shrift the comedy. That is my background too, and then also not take anyone for granted, have flawed characters but grounded and real, fully, three-dimensional.
I want to mention Malcolm in that regard. Malcolm could just appear like so many characters I’ve seen in these tropes of “gay black friend.” “Gay Black best friend” and check, we did that. We did all the things we’re supposed to do per 2026 PC rules. That’s not what he is at all. He is a three-dimensional flawed character who’s not pulling his own weight. He’s not doing a good job. He’s blaming his friend. He is not doing a great job moving through the world. He’s supportive of his friend to a point, but then he’s also slacking. He’s fully realized, and when he is an asshole, he’s an asshole through and through. He yells at her, and it’s not her fault. And he has done damage, and he has to do the repair. That is a great character to me. It’s not just like, “Hey, he’s got the witty comment because he’s funny and he’s gay and he’s Black.” He is just a real person.
And we need people just like him who fuck up, and then they have to apologize, or they’re not your friend anymore. There’s only one or two ways that was gonna go. I love the character of Malcolm for that reason. And I think Jaboukie [Young-White] was truly the only person to be able to bring him to life. He’s so good. And Jabouki was in Set It Up. He got a SAG card on Set It Up. His character got the key” “I know this key says do not duplicate, but you must duplicate, or my boss is going to kill me.” I was so happy for that full circle moment.
DEADLINE: What’s next for you?
SCANLON: The Probability of Miracles is something that’s shooting right now. That’s another book to to television adaptation. That one’s for Amazon.
It’s a really unusual show. It’s not the YA trope that you’re used to because it’s about a teen with cancer so it’s really different. I was like, “why do they want a comedy director?” But they did. I did get some surreal stuff to shoot. I’m very excited. I haven’t seen my editor’s cut yet. They’re still putting them together, so I’m excited for that. But I will tell you that television show was the first time I’ve ever had the pleasure of working with a female DP, Lindsay George, and she was phenomenal.

She was out of this world, and I can’t wait to see how it all looks cut together because it was some beautiful cinematography, story aside, which is very impactful and powerful. And Ginny Goodwin is amazing in it. Ginnifer Goodwin, she plays the mum. It is gorgeous. I would watch it just for the visuals alone, and I think that it’s so high quality. Comedies can be very lazy, and TV can sometimes be lazy in terms of cinematography. I mean, not all of it. Obviously, like Widow’s Bay is incredible. I don’t mean to be reductive, but sometimes it is short-shrifted, especially in that space, and that is not the case with this at all. It is gorgeous.
I’m really excited, and it’s surreal. It’s definitely got a lot of magical surrealism because that’s what the story’s about.

Will FDA advisers recommend a multi-cancer blood test for approval? They'll vote
A key advisory committee that reviews medical devices for the Food and Drug Administration will meet today to vote on whether the agency should approve the first multi-cancer blood test. Grail, the company that makes the Galleri blood test under review, says it can detect up to 50 forms of cancer, many of which are not routinely screened for today.
The panel of independent experts will hear from Grail, FDA officials and the public before voting on a recommendation. The FDA often follows the advice from its panels, but does not have to. Ultimate approval by the agency could mean insurance reimbursement for the test, which costs $949.
There are hundreds of companies chasing the promise of blood tests to detect cancer, which is done with a simple blood draw and could help detect disease earlier by looking for genetic material or other cancer markers shed in blood or saliva. Grail says its Galleri test should be additive to standardized cancer screenings, like colonoscopies and mammograms, and not be used as a replacement.
While blood tests for cancer already exist in the market, none that screen for multiple cancers has undergone safety and accuracy reviews to win FDA approval so far. Many doctors and patients hope such technology will ultimately help detect disease earlier, when more treatment options could be possible.
The financial incentives to win FDA approval also became far more powerful after Congress approved Medicare to cover multi-cancer detection tests that are greenlighted by the agency. Based on its promise, the FDA expedited its review of Galleri, which is the furthest along in that approval process.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
As such, Galleri is seen as a kind of bellwether for the whole industry — and for the potential use of a blood test to screen for cancers in general.
"It's a new era for early cancer detection, and if the FDA approves it, it validates the overall concept," says Cristian Tomasetti, director of City of Hope cancer center's early detection and monitoring division. In 2018, Tomasetti was part of a team that developed a competing blood test technology that is the basis of a test made by Exact Sciences (since purchased by Abbott), which is also pursuing FDA approval. (Tomasetti is no longer involved with that company.)
The questions to answer
The FDA laid out key questions for the committee to answer about Galleri, centered on whether the clinical data show the test detects cancers reliably and early enough to justify use of such terms in its marketing. The agency also wants to consider harm from false results, and potentially require the company to include caveats in its marketing, such as warnings that a false negative does not rule out the presence of cancer, nor a positive detection signifying cancer.
The advisory committee will review two major clinical studies conducted by Grail, including one involving more than 140,000 patients in the U.K.'s National Health System, and another of over 35,000 North American patients, all over the age of 50. The interpretation of those studies has been somewhat controversial. On the one hand, the Galleri tests did not meet their primary end point of reducing mortality overall, nor did it reduce the combined number of Stage III and IV cancers. But in subsequent updates to its NHS study, Grail clarified that Stage IV cancer diagnoses (not combined with Stage III) decreased over its three-year study period, suggesting tests may have shifted cancer diagnosis to earlier stages.
While the trials have not fully proven the test's benefit, the key underlying question to the inquiry — not just for the FDA, but also for patients and doctors — is whether the Galleri test is accurate enough and can reliably catch cancers early enough to reduce deaths from cancer.
Tomasetti acknowledges that Galleri's tests did not meet their end points in their clinical studies. But he says that's in large part because the study specified very ambitious goals, such as showing reductions in mortality within a short period of three years. Mortality reductions are typically measured over the long term. Tomasetti says there are other problems that arise from the short duration of the studies; namely, in the initial years of testing, one would expect to detect more late-stage cancers that already existed in the population.
"This is kind of a technicality," that the study didn't meet its initial endpoint, Tomasetti says. "To me, it doesn't mean that the study — in terms of substance — failed to show evidence of what [multi-cancer detection tests] can actually do." He says longer-term studies are needed to confirm that using the tests regularly will help shift diagnoses from Stage IV to earlier stage diagnoses. Based on the totality of data, Tomasetti says he thinks the FDA appears poised to approve Galleri's test.
Oncologist Tom Beer agrees. Beer is chief medical officer for Abbott Cancer Diagnostics, working on a multi-cancer test called CancerGuard, which is also seeking FDA approval. Beer also sees patients in his clinical practice in Oregon, and says 70% of cancer diagnoses and deaths are from diseases like pancreatic cancer, for which no screening exists.
"I'm keenly aware every week when I'm in the clinic, of how many patients are diagnosed with cancers that we don't screen for," he says.

US State Secretary Marco Rubio says global system ‘broken’: ‘Can’t address potential conflicts like India-Pakistan’
Marco Rubio also pointed to US President Donald Trump's remarks stating the United Nations was “not living up to its potential”.
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday said the international system which exists is “broken”, and therefore could fail to address potential conflicts, citing India and Pakistan in this context.
He pointed to US President Donald Trump's remarks of the United Nations “not living up to its potential”, while adding that it “would be great” if there was a “functional international system” to deal with conflicts, news agency PTI reported.
“It would be great if we had a functional international system, for example, that could deal with a war between Thailand and Cambodia that occurred, or a potential conflict between India and Pakistan...Right now, we don't seem to have a functional international system that can address it,” the top US diplomat said.
Rubio's remarks come a day after Trump repeated his claim that he stopped India and Pakistan from going into a full-fledged war in May 2025, something which has consistently been rejected by New Delhi.
‘International system failing because it has grown beyond its mandate’: Rubio
Rubio spoke about the “utility” of the international system at present, saying it was visible to all. “We're here...I think the President has said that the United Nations, for example, has tremendous potential, but it's not living up to it…” Rubio told reporters in New York.
“I think multiple leaders...pointed to the fact that the international system is failing, and it's failing because it has grown beyond its mandate,” the US Secretary of State said, according to PTI. Rubio further said the system had “grown beyond its intent.”
“It's involved in all kinds of things that shouldn't be involved in, and it's unable to solve virtually any major conflict in the world,” Rubio added. He said there was consensus at the UN General Assembly on the point of view that the international system was “broken.” “But it's broken because it broke itself. It needs to be brought back to its proper focus and its proper role,” Rubio stated.
Rubio also said that the US would eventually “always act in the national interest of our country, not in the interest of the international order.”
What did Trump say at the UNGA?
Trump on Tuesday reiterated his claim that he stopped the conflict between India and Pakistan last year. He made the remarks at the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, where he defended the war with Iran and repeated his claim that he ended eight wars in his second term as US President.
“The Prime Minister of Pakistan, a terrific man, said that Donald Trump was responsible for saving 30 million lives, and probably many more than that,” Trump said at UNGA. The US President further claimed that leaders of the countries, where he intervened to end conflicts, wrote him a letter to express gratitude.

The military escalation between India and Pakistan came after the Pahalgam terror attack in April, 2025, in which 26 civilians were killed. Following this, India had launched strikes against terror bases in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir under ‘Operation Sindoor.’
Trump has, several times in the past, claimed that he brokered the ceasefire between India and Pakistan after the military escalation in May 2025.
