Why is Monaco staging a sprint race? F1 Q&A
- Published
Formula 1 has a rare Saturday race this weekend for the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.
Kimi Antonelli goes into round 15 of the season with an imposing 81-point lead in the drivers' championship over Mercedes team-mate George Russell.
BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions before the event in Baku.
What are your thoughts on having a sprint race next year at Monaco? I was very surprised to see that on the calendar, given that the race has so little chance of overtaking - Graham
- F1 to have 10 sprint races in 2027, including Monaco 
  - Published6 days ago
Formula 1 announced the 2027 calendar last week, with the number of sprint events increased from six to 10, and one of them Monaco.
This has proved controversial with some fans.
Why pick the worst track on the calendar for overtaking to have two races in one weekend, some have wondered. What's the point of having two boring races; isn't one enough?
The thinking behind it, though, is less about the races than about qualifying, and how making Monaco a sprint could mix up the weekend.
Monaco qualifying is renowned as one of the highlights of the season. In that case, surely two great qualifying sessions is better than one?
It was also pointed out by F1 that it gives the chance of two different grid orders and therefore more variability.
There is another factor to consider, too.
Monaco is one of the most demanding tracks on the calendar, and it is renowned as somewhere drivers have to build up to the limit progressively so they can become confident with knowing how the car will behave when they get there.
Get that wrong, push too hard too soon, and the chances of an accident are considerably higher.
So asking the drivers to go straight into a qualifying after a single practice session is a really difficult challenge.
It is likely to mean more mistakes, more action, more drama, and therefore more entertainment.
The same goes for grand prix qualifying.
Yes, by then the drivers will have done a sprint race. But there are always changes made to the cars for qualifying, so again the drivers will be going in blind to some degree.
Yes, the sprint is likely to be a procession. How could it be anything else? But it adds an extra degree of jeopardy to the whole weekend.
Do you think F1 might consider the F2 approach for the virtual safety car, where drivers cannot pit under a VSC but can pit under a full safety car? As a regular viewer of both series, I think this works well in F2 and is another way to solve the jeopardy a short VSC period brings to a race. - Caroline
The VSC was discussed at the so-called FIA sporting advisory committee last week, but sources say no consensus emerged there as to potential changes.
It was also on the agenda for the F1 Commission meeting on Monday but there were no significant developments.
Lando Norris, who lost victory in Madrid by the VSC timing, said after the race that the drivers had previously discussed with the FIA the idea that the VSC should be out for a minimum of a lap so this sort of thing could not happen.
But every potential 'solution' comes with consequences. In that case, F1 might end up with a full lap of VSC just to recover a bit of debris.
The VSC was introduced so that relatively small-scale incidents could be dealt with without the lengthy disruption of a full safety car.
It's accepted that the safety car affords possibilities to gain and lose out, so why should the VSC not do the same? The argument is that, generally, these even out over the season, although the Norris case in Madrid had particularly dramatic consequences.
Antonelli benefited from this one, for example, but has lost out in other scenarios this year. For example, when the VSC gifted Lewis Hamilton the lead in Barcelona, even if that was rendered moot by Antonelli's subsequent retirement.
Why did Mercedes put George Russell on a two-stop strategy in the Spanish Grand Prix when the race has the longest pit lane of the season? George was the only driver out of the top 15 finishers on a two-stop and did this decision cost him a podium finish? - Richard
Mercedes were a bit stuck when the virtual safety car was deployed on lap 14 in Madrid.
The team had split the drivers' tyre strategies - Kimi Antonelli took the conventional strategy and started on the mediums, Russell had gone for the hards.
With overtaking so difficult in Madrid, it was always likely that one option would turn out to be sub-optimal. The timing of the VSC was very unfortunate for those who started on hard tyres because it coincided with the pit-stop window for those on mediums.
Mercedes had two choices - stay out, or pit and change tyre compound, as drivers are obligated to use two compounds during a dry grand prix.
Charles Leclerc, who also started on hards and was running immediately ahead of Russell, stayed out. Mercedes pitted in the hope of trying to beat Leclerc.
Whichever tyre Russell chose was unlikely to make it to the end, so Mercedes knew at that point they would almost certainly have to stop again.
The hard tyre was comfortably the best race tyre in Madrid, and on his mediums Russell did not have the pace to narrow the gap to Leclerc to less than it takes to do a pit stop. So there was nothing to lose by pitting again.
Team boss Toto Wolff said: "He said the tyres were not in a great shape, the mediums. We didn't think they would go to the end. (We thought) the better opportunity was not to hang out and wait for a red, but to change the tyres and get on with it."
Russell said: "Maybe I could have stayed out with Leclerc but I would have still finished behind him. Maybe I could have not pitted on to the hard again but everything I would have done would have brought us to the same position."

During the Madrid race, Max Verstappen was told to hand the place back to Lewis Hamilton. Which he did. However, what would happen if Lewis had fallen maybe two or three cars further back. Does Max still have to hand back the place (and lose places to other cars) or would he just have to take a penalty? - Wayne
The scenario you paint actually happened in Madrid. Verstappen also got ahead of Antonelli on the first lap, so when Red Bull told him to let Hamilton by, he also had to let the Mercedes past.
Shortly after that happened, the message "no further action" was displayed on the timing screens and television coverage over the incident.
That was because Verstappen had given the place back by then. Otherwise, he would have been penalised.
So, yes, if a driver is adjudged to have committed an offence that requires giving the place back, they must do so regardless of whether there are at that point other cars between them.
There are two examples of this from Fernando Alonso's career.
In the 2005 Japanese Grand Prix, he passed Christian Klien's Red Bull by cutting the chicane, let him by again on the straight and then passed him into Turn One.
But race director Charlie Whiting did not notice that Alonso had let Klien back past, and after some discussions with the Renault team, he demanded Alonso cede the position.
That was two laps later, by which time Alonso was seven seconds up the road.
At Silverstone in 2010, Alonso, now at Ferrari, was forced off the track by Robert Kubica when trying an overtaking move at Vale, and ended up passing the Renault driver off the track.
Because he had been forced off, Ferrari decided not to give up the position. But Whiting told them they had to, after discussions with the team.
Problem was, at exactly that point, Kubica pulled into the pits to retire, so Alonso could not give the place back - and he was given a drive-through penalty.
Before he could serve it, there was then a safety-car period which closed up the field. Penalties could not be served under a safety car, so the two situations combined dropped Alonso right to the back of the field. He ended up finishing 14th, which was a costly blow to his title hopes.

The annual Made on YouTube event has just wrapped up, offering an early look at the features you can expect to come to Google’s dominant online streaming platform in the coming months. Former U of Manitoba law dean arrested in France, faces extradition to Canada: police
Jonathan Black-Branch facing Canada-wide arrest warrant for fraud
Jonathan Black-Branch, the disbarred former dean at the University of Manitoba's law school, has been arrested in Europe and is facing extradition back to Canada, where he's wanted on a fraud charge.
Winnipeg police spokesperson Const. Stephen Spencer confirmed Wednesday the arrest happened in France and the matter is currently before the French court system.
Police can't say more while the matter is before the courts, he said in an email, but "further information will be provided should the extradition application be successful" and Black-Branch is returned to Winnipeg.
He could not confirm when Black-Branch was arrested.
Black-Branch — who was under a Canada-wide arrest warrant issued March 30, 2026, on a charge of fraud over $5,000 — was hired as U of M's law dean in 2016, but left his post suddenly in 2020 with no formal explanation given.
Around the same time, an internal investigation by the university, based on a whistleblower complaint, found a senior university employee misspent university funds.
In 2023, a months-long law hearing by the Law Society of Manitoba found Black-Branch had committed professional misconduct and misspent more than $600,000.
He spent U of M endowment funds on expensive meals at the members-only Manitoba Club, personal education at Ivy League schools, accommodation, travel and other expenses while he was dean of the U of M's law school, according to the society's decision.
The U of M then asked Winnipeg police to investigate for possible criminal charges.
The Manitoba law society disbarred Black-Branch in 2024, removed his name from its rolls of barristers and solicitors, and fined him $36,000.
The same year, the U of M sued Black-Branch. A default judgment in May 2025 ordered him to pay the university nearly $680,000 and more than $3,000 in costs, plus three per cent annual interest.
A brief filed by the school in December 2024 said it had been unable to serve Black-Branch with its statement of claim, "despite all reasonable efforts."
At the time the lawsuit was filed, Black-Branch's last known address was in England. However, a process server there was unable to find him at that address or another that he might have owned, court documents said.

The 20-year-old Italian, who is running away with the world championship in only his second season in F1, is reflecting on his breakthrough year in the sport in an exclusive interview with BBC Sport.
A difficult debut season last year had left external expectations of Antonelli low at the start of 2026. But on a typically damp and cold January day at Silverstone, he already sensed that something special might be on the cards.
"It was just a few laps in the wet," Antonelli says, "but I just felt better in the car, much better than I felt last year. Also the car felt well, but I just felt better mentally in the car. Less tense, more relaxed and more mature."
Last year, he says, was "not great". "I was driving very tense most of the time, I wasn't able to extract the potential out of me," he says.
"This year, it's a lot different. The mindset has been the biggest change."
Fast forward eight months and the effects of that new headspace are plain to see.
After 14 grands prix, and with either eight or nine remaining depending on the war in the Middle East, Antonelli is a massive 81 points clear of team-mate George Russell.
Not only that, but he looks so in control. Always fast, always composed, a factor in every grand prix. Everyone knows the championship is basically over, barring some kind of dramatic misfortune.
Even then, Antonelli says he is "still finding my way" in F1.
The journey Antonelli has been on in the past two years is remarkable, and he says even he is "surprised" by the extent of his progress this year.
He was comprehensively outperformed by Russell in 2025. So when it was obvious that Mercedes would start the new regulatory era with an advantage, it was the Briton who started the season as championship favourite.
Russell duly won the opening race in Australia, but Antonelli was less than three seconds behind him at the flag. This, he says, was the second moment of realisation of what might be possible.
"I had a big, big crash in FP3," Antonelli recalls. "But then thanks to the mechanics - who all throughout the season have done an incredible job, but on that specific occasion, it is a miracle - I was able to go back in the car and push again in the high speed and getting close to the limit.
"The crash, definitely it compromised a little bit qualifying and the race because we couldn't set up properly the car. I mean, the car was still very quick. But it was not easy.
"Still being able to stay close despite that, I was like, 'OK, you know, it's not going to be a walk in the park. It's going to be very tough', but I knew already that it was a different story compared to last year.
"If it would have happened last year, I wouldn't have been able to overcome that."
Monza 2024 memory made Antonelli 'afraid to do a mistake'
Antonelli's first season in F1 was haunted by an incident that happened the first time he drove on a grand prix weekend.
At the 2024 Italian Grand Prix, the day before they formally announced Antonelli was the replacement for Ferrari-bound Lewis Hamilton, Mercedes gave him an outing in first practice at Monza.
He was blindingly fast on his first flying lap - but then crashed heavily on his second.
Team principal Toto Wolff played it down at the time, saying he was well aware there would be mistakes from Antonelli as he found his feet in F1. But behind the scenes the incident had had a big impact on the young man.
"Monza stayed in my head for a very long time," Antonelli says. "I think all throughout last season, at least. Definitely that was a big thing that was kind of slowing me down.
"This memory of being afraid to do a mistake, also because going through the difficult period (in the middle of 2025), this memory was even stronger in my head, if you know what I mean.
"Because it was already a difficult period and I was like, 'If I even do a mistake or I crash, it's even worse.'
"So yeah, it's been a thing that has been bothering me a lot last year. This year I was able to just put it behind."
Doing so has involved a lot of work behind the scenes, analysing what happened in 2025, understanding what had gone well, what had not, and why, and what he could do to improve.
"The mindset going into this season, it was mainly trying to be able to extract more out of my potential," Antonelli says. "Trying to, first of all, do a better job than previous year. But as well trying to put things more together.
"The preparation that I did in pre-season was very, very intense. But it helped me a lot to arrive ready for this season.
"Plus, I did a lot of work with my mental coach. Trying to get my head right, my thoughts right on understanding the goal, and understanding that the most important thing is to be ready and to stay present in the moment.
"Not trying to think about final results or what would happen if I wouldn't achieve that. But just trying to be present and trying to do the best with what you can do in the moment."
'First win, first pole, took a lot of weight off my shoulder'
Still, though, he admits to be "definitely surprised" at how much progress he has made.
"I knew that I was going to be better than my first year," he says. "Obviously, because I think last year, towards the end of the season, I started to put things more together, starting to extract more performance. But still, it was still not great.
"Whereas this year, it's a lot different. Also as well, with the first win, the first pole, it took a lot of weight off my shoulder."
Antonelli has blossomed. Everything seems to be coming so easily to him. If he drops back in a race, he recovers seamlessly and quickly. Overtaking moves are done quickly and decisively. There's not been a circuit on which he has lacked pace.
Russell, by contrast, has admitted to struggling and - while not trying to take anything away from Antonelli, who he is always quick to praise - has expressed his opinion that his his driving style does not suit this year's new cars.
All of which raises a key question - how much of what is happening this year is Antonelli stepping it up, and how much Russell falling back?
"That's a very difficult question," Antonelli says. "I've definitely stepped up.
"This year definitely everything is new. So it requires also a little bit of a different approach. And trying to adapt to a different car, which hasn't been easy."
His consistency this year, he says, has come from the fact he has found "a nice rhythm in the season".
"I always try to follow my routines," Antonelli says, "the way I approach the weekend. I try to approach it all the time the same.
"I'm still finding my way, but I've found a way that helps me to be consistent and also helps me to be consistently ready when I go in the car."
There are still moments when he misjudges things, though. He cites the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix, just days after his outstanding win in Monaco, one of the most dominant at that storied track for years.
"Monaco was a very high moment for me in the season, and then I went to Barcelona and I was probably a bit too excited, especially over a single lap," he says.
"So I was overdriving, I was chasing the lap time and the result didn't come in qualifying. I was actually a bit far back and didn't do a good lap.
"But that's because I was trying to do a bit too much after a very high moment in my career. And then I understood that that is not the way."
The lesson was applied after his spellbinding win from 19th on the grid at Monza, his home race, a result that Wolff said "closed a cycle" from his 2024 crash.
Antonelli says: "After Monza, I reminded myself, 'Don't make the same mistake as you did after Monaco.'"
He won the Spanish Grand Prix seven days later, an eighth victory from 14 races so far this season.
Success has inevitably led to fame, and with it attention.
"Life has changed a lot," Antonelli says. "I'm not going to lie. It's been a big change, but it's nice to see so much support. Definitely, one side is very nice, but on the other side, you have to be careful. You've got to protect yourself a bit more because obviously you're more exposed."
All year, Antonelli has talked about focusing on process, about doing the best he can on every single day, not thinking about the big picture.
Now, though, for the first time, he acknowledges the title - an achievement that would make him the youngest world champion in F1 history - is on his mind.
"Yes, I thought about it," he says. "But again, thinking about it, I came always to the same conclusion that the earlier I finish all this, the better it is.
"So I've got to just keep pushing. I keep doing the best I can every race. Because, yeah, that's the way. Just not finish. And until it's done, it's not over."

Germany says India can leverage Russia ties to help end Ukraine war
Germany believes India can use its long-standing ties with Russia to help end the Ukraine war, German envoy Jasper Wieck said.
Germany believes India can use its long-standing ties with Russia to help end the war in Ukraine, which is affecting countries through rising grain and fertiliser prices, German envoy Jasper Wieck said on Wednesday.
Wieck said Germany and India have a “common interest” in ending Russia’s war against Ukraine as soon as possible because of its economic and security costs. However, he told a media briefing that Germany does not believe Russia is willing to end the war for the time being despite Ukraine’s readiness for a ceasefire.
“We would love to see India involved in bringing that war to an end,” Wieck said. “First of all, you are a very powerful country so your voice is heard by everyone…I am sure that the leadership of India can use its very good contacts with Russia to push that file.”
Deep Dive
The envoy noted Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s recent message to Russian President Vladimir Putin that the war should end, but added that it is difficult to judge who can be the best mediator to ensure a political process for stopping the fighting.

“There are several candidates [as mediator] but I think it is better to have too many than too little. I would say that India, since it has these very established and long-term contacts and partnership with Russia on the one hand and at the same time is an interlocutor of Ukraine, you have all the possibilities to mediate and to bring in your diplomatic skills in bringing this war to an end,” he said.
India, which has refrained from publicly criticising Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, has also stayed away from any direct mediation. It has passed messages between the two sides and Modi has engaged both Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to call for an end to the hostilities through dialogue and diplomacy.
As Moscow appears unwilling to end the war, the European Union (EU) will continue pressuring Russia by providing military, economic and humanitarian support to Ukraine and imposing sanctions on Russia to increase the costs of the conflict, Wieck said.
Besides claiming the lives of thousands of soldiers and civilians, the conflict has directly impacted the interests of countries such as India and Germany because of increasing prices of grains and fertilisers. “But it also impacts us geopolitically and it touches on our interests, particularly Indian interests, because Russia is gradually drawn more and more into the arms of China, because it depends on the support of China more and more,” he said.
While arguing that more countries should stop buying Russian oil to cut off funding for the war, Wieck acknowledged India’s need to secure energy supplies for its 1.4 billion people.
“We believe that the world energy market is huge enough to have alternative sources of import, [but] I also know that the situation has become more complicated [because of the West Asia conflict,” he said. “In the mid and longer term, Germany is a very loyal and strong supporter of India in transitioning to renewable energy, which would make India independent from all of these conflicts around the world and sanctions by whoever.”
Wieck also drew a distinction between EU sanctions, which are linked to European jurisdiction, and measures such as the Russia sanctions bill passed recently by the US Congress, which can impact countries and are extraterritorial in nature.

SC: Constitution bench should deal with case to prevent delay
NEW DELHI: On a day when Election Commission found itself under the scanner, a two-judge bench of Supreme Court gave a split verdict on whether the issue of validity of the law on appointment of CEC/ECs be referred to a constitution bench, but later agreed to refer the case to a larger bench for the sake of early adjudication of the contentious issue.Validity of several provisions of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023 has been challenged on the ground that the law gives the executive "overwhelming" power to appoint its nominee as election commissioner, as the selection panel composed of the PM, a Cabinet minister and the leader of the opposition is designed to give govt a 2:1 majority. The petitioners contended that EC's independence would be compromised in this process.The 2023 law was framed to replace an SC verdict which had directed that selection be done by a committee of the PM, CJI and leader of the opposition until Parliament determined the composition by passing a law. "Speaking in one voice would have better served institutional cohesion. Unfortunately, the court is divided in its opinion," a bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and S C Sharma said.
The hearing in the case went on for five days and at the fag end of proceedings, the Centre had sought referral of the case to a constitution bench.
SC: Constitution bench should deal with case to prevent delay
Noting that appointment of CEC/ECs was being litigated for last 11 years in SC after a petition was filed in 2015, the bench decided that the case should not be referred to a three-judge bench, which is the normal procedure, but to a constitution bench to settle the issue once and for all. It reasoned that a decision by a three-judge bench would be of little worth and only delay adjudication of the significant issue(s) that these writ petitions raise."Thus, we direct that the papers be placed before the CJI for considering the desirability of constituting a constitution bench of such number of judges to decide the question of vires of Sec 7 and the other provisions of Act," the bench said.The bench expressed hope that the case would be given priority as the issues raised were of "foundational importance to the democratic fabric of the country and its citizenry"."Petitioners seem to be justified in expressing their anxiety that references to five-judge benches remain unresolved for years. If statistics are any guide, none can say with any reasonable degree of certainty when long-pending references will get resolved. Undisputedly, this is an area of grave concern and the inordinate delay in resolution of the references is itself a source of institutional embarrassment which all stakeholders ought to strive to avoid. Self-introspection, indeed, is required," it said."We, thus, take this opportunity of requesting the Chief Justice to also explore the necessity of constituting a permanent five-judge bench to decide pure constitutional issues. This is not something novel that we are saying. It has been opined time and again by responsible citizens and we simply endorse their opinion. Given that resolving constitutional issues is the primary task of judges of this court, that must remain its core priority.
Pendency of references for far too long, any period between five and 20 years or more, does not reflect well on the institution. It is time that the institution addresses the issue with the urgency and promptitude it deserves," the bench said.

Microsoft is launching a second generation of its Surface Mouse next month that includes haptic feedback support. The Surface Mouse also has a customizable action button for the first time, which is primarily designed for quick access to Copilot (of course), but can be configured to work with other shortcuts from the Surface app.
Microsoft’s new Surface Mouse has haptic feedback and a customizable action button
The $79.99 Surface Mouse will start shipping on October 13th.
“Its haptic feedback adds a small, purposeful physical response to the moment you usually only see on a screen: a click registering, a window snapping into place or an object aligning just right,” says Brett Ostrum, corporate vice president of Surface Devices. “It is subtle by design, but noticeable within seconds — and hard to give up once you have it.”
The haptic feedback works with things like clicks, drags, and alignment throughout Windows 11, but the tactile feedback also triggers in apps like PowerPoint, Affinity, Concepts, and Filmora. Microsoft added support for haptic feedback in Windows 11 earlier this year, and so far it’s mainly Microsoft and Logitech that are supporting it with dedicated hardware. Logitech’s MX Master 4 has haptic feedback, and its Pro X2 Superstrike (and today’s new X3) includes a haptic-based clicks system that doesn’t support the Windows 11 haptic feedback. The upcoming Surface Laptop Ultra also has a haptic trackpad.
After originally launching the Surface Mouse in 2016 and not updating it since, Microsoft has now redesigned it to be more comfortable for all-day use, with a soft-touch material at the top. Thanks to Bluetooth 6.0 support, you can now also pair it with up to three devices.
The new Surface Mouse will be available on October 13th, the same day Microsoft launches its refreshed Surface Pro 12-inch and Surface Laptop 13-inch devices. It will be priced at $79.99, and available in black and platinum color options.

A study by Chennai-based diabetologists has attempted to find out how India has managed to reduce the prices of new and expensive diabetes drugs and what lessons this could possibly hold for other low- and middle-income countries (LMIC). The study, ‘Making Modern Diabetes Medications Affordable and Accessible: Lessons from India for Other Countries’, was led by V. Mohan, chairman, Dr. Mohan’s Diabetes Specialities Centre, Chennai, and was published in the journal Diabetes Care.
What did the study find?
Of the 589 million adults in the world with diabetes, 80% live in LMICs, the study noted. Modern diabetes therapies such as GLP-1 receptor agonists as well as SGLT2i (sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors) improve cardiovascular and renal outcomes, while analogue insulins help reduce the risk of hypoglycaemia. However, affordability remains a barrier: diabetes requires lifelong care and management of complications.
India’s ability to maintain low medication prices is closely linked to its role as a major pharmaceutical exporter, the paper stated, noting the strategic legislative history of maintaining critical safeguards to prevent ‘patent evergreening’ and allowing for generic manufacture of drugs. It also found that the country has increasingly focused on strengthening domestic manufacturing capacity. There are concerns over global trade policies affecting prices and the availability of raw materials. A government incentive scheme has been introduced to promote domestic manufacturing of raw materials, and as of 2025, production has commenced for 26 molecules that were previously imported.
The paper notes that metformin and sulfonylureas continue to form the foundation of type 2 diabetes management in India - both are included in the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM). While DPP-4 (dipeptidyl peptidase 4) inhibitors, SGLT2i and GLP-1 RA have all been introduced, they are not currently in the NLEM. Initial uptake of these drugs was constrained by pricing. Following the competitive entry by multiple domestic manufacturers, the price of semaglutide, for instance in India, has dropped considerably now, and there has been a huge increase in sales; however, absolute monthly costs remain high relative to the household income in India, and, crucially, these are not covered by insurance, as they are, to a great extent, in the U.S.
Quick availability of generic and biosimilar drugs, deliberate regulatory and distribution strategies such as the government’s Jan Aushadi Kendras, and market competition have allowed for affordable drugs in India, the paper highlighted.
What does it propose for other LMICs?
Building local manufacturing capacity as a strategic public health investment, balancing patent governance that encourages easier access to newer molecules, predictable and structured price regulation, good distribution networks at reasonable retail prices and aligning pharmaceutical policy with health financing and ongoing monitoring of medicine quality, prices, prescription patterns and patient access can all help with improving access to affordable medicines, the paper noted. These core principles could also apply to high-income countries facing drug prices, the paper said.
Challenges ahead
Challenges that remain include urban-rural disparities in distribution and availability of medicines; tight regulations potentially affecting chances of drug innovation; differences in quality between generics and difficulties in maintaining strict pharmacovigilance; as well as limited formal evaluation of government schemes to look at their long-term impact on clinical outcomes.

JAKARTA – The official death toll from a passenger ship that capsized and sank in Indonesia’s Java Sea rose to 26 on Wednesday, up from the previous 20, with rescuers expecting to find more bodies as the ongoing underwater search widens, officials said.
The Virgo Transport 8 ferry was carrying 243 people, including 30 crew members, as well as an unknown number of vehicles, when it capsized in bad weather early on Sept. 13 during a voyage from Surabaya in East Java to Banjarmasin in South Kalimantan.
Coast guard and Navy personnel recovered 14 bodies from inside the ship over the past three days, and also found two bodies that had been washed ashore in Central Kalimantan province around 253 kilometers from the location of the accident, head of National Rescue Agency Mohammad Syafii said.
As of Wednesday, the total death toll stood at 26, with 109 people still missing and 108 survivors, he said.
Rescuers found five bodies on Monday, four on Tuesday and seven on Wednesday, Syafii added.
Wednesday’s search would focus on looking for more bodies in the ship’s cabins, said I Putu Sudayana, head of the Banjarmasin rescue agency.
Divers managed to break the windows of the cabins on Tuesday but could not enter due to murky water and strong currents, making it impossible to retrieve bodies that had already been spotted.
“Our underwater search is focused on the ship’s hull. That is where we are concentrating because we have found many passengers trapped inside the cabins,” he said.
After that, if possible, rescuers will shift the search to the vehicles on the ferry, but it could prove challenging, with many appearing to be piled on top of each other.
“This poses risks to the diving team,” Putu said. “If it is feasible and safe, we will carry out the search.”
Search and rescue operations have been extended until Sunday next week. Authorities said efforts to right the ship were underway, but it remained capsized on Wednesday.

No one wants to worry about a break-in. But no one wants to end up paying fees every month just to check their video doorbell feed or find out their window was broken, and most smart security systems (even the original ones that weren't touted as smart!) rely on your fear to have you paying month after month for the promise of catching burglars and stopping intruders for you.
These systems do work, and they can give you a lot of peace of mind. This comes with a hefty price tag, though, and plenty of people would be more than happy with a system they build themselves sans monthly fees. If you're not interested in a system that will call the police or fire department if you don't respond fast enough to something that turns out to be minor, or don't want to have strangers looking through your security cameras at your property, I'm here to help with that.
This guide collects a handful of our favorite smart home security accessories that won't paywall you left and right, and will give you local storage options for video so you aren't locked into the cloud. This way you can build the system that works for you. Here's everything I recommend if you want smart home security without the subscriptions.
What Exactly Is a Smart Home Security System?
Smart security systems can look like whatever you want, in my opinion, but there are a lot of starter kits you've probably seen. Smart-home brands like Abode and SimpliSafe have starter packs you've likely seen before with motion sensors, door sensors, and security hubs that sound an alarm when one of those sensors is triggered.
But smart home security can go way beyond that. Most systems let you add on cameras and even video doorbells to monitor movement around your home and catch people at your door who shouldn't be there. (This is also a handy way to know when it’s a package delivery or another random salesperson.) These systems are usually modular and customizable, whether you DIY or go with a brand. Overall, the goal is to protect and monitor your home through motion sensors and video feeds.
Home security brands usually have various subscription options and some kind of self-monitored, subscription-free tier, but you usually lose out on a variety of features to encourage you to subscribe.
What Do Smart Home Security Systems and a Subscription Get You?
I remember running into the issue of paywalled features for the first time a few years ago when I was testing Abode's smart lock. I liked the lock, but I woke up to unclear notifications that happened in the dead of night. Had the lock been hacked? Had it sensed itself being manually opened when we were asleep? There was no way to tell because Abode’s base level would only tell me the lock was interacted with without explaining how. I signed up for the Abode membership that day to be able to review the events, and luckily it was just a loss of Wi-Fi connection and reestablishment that happened within a minute of each other. Crisis averted.
The main thing that subscription services paywall is video storage, which allows you to review past events at your home. Sometimes it can also be notifications, whether that's the type of notification or the ability to review notification history. What is or is not paywalled largely depends on the brand and its offerings. Professional live monitoring, however, is almost always paywalled, whether that's an agent calling police when an alarm has been triggered or an agent reviewing flagged footage (e.g., motion alerts) to either notify you of a situation or call emergency services on your behalf. That’s one thing you can't DIY—if you’re on vacation or otherwise not able to call police if there's an issue, you're out of luck.
Base stations from home security companies like ADT, SimpliSafe, and Vivint will act as a smart-home hub to connect and control sensors and other devices, and be able to sound an alarm. It might have a keypad that you can use to arm and disarm the system too.
A lot of subscription services also have a higher tier that gives you an on-staff specialist who will review live footage if a camera is triggered, or even use the microphone to speak to an intruder. It's a useful feature if it's something you're worried about, but those subscriptions can cost as much as a casual grocery trip each month.
Do You Need a Smart Home Security System Starter Kit?
You don't need a formal, branded home security kit to protect your home, but if you're interested in window and motion sensors that will trigger and sound an alarm, you might want one. You can buy a kit and even have a brand representative come and install the devices for you. (But as someone who's seen the bill for those, I'd recommend installing everything yourself, since it has to be connected to your phone and personal accounts anyway.)
If you're just looking to know who's at your door, get alerted when a window is opened, or prove you have trespassers with video footage, DIY-ing your own system with a handful of devices that fit the needs you're looking for is a fine solution. Personally, I worry most about my front door, while someone else might worry about trespassers in their backyard. Buying accessories à la carte allows you to get exactly what you want without paying extra.
Best Subscription-Free Security Devices to Build Your Own System
Smart locks are my most-used smart-home item by far. Having a smart lock makes it so easy for my entire family to access our home, including my 4-year-old, who has memorized the code. Smart locks make it easy to confirm your door is locked when it should be, and you can see the access history to know who's opening it and when. These are two of my favorite options that don't require any sort of subscription to get event history in an app, but you will need to buy a separate Wi-Fi hub or bridge for both if you want remote access. However, that's a one-time purchase instead of a forever one.
Most video doorbells have a no-subscription option, but you'll usually lose out on video storage, so you can't scroll back and see what happened when an alert went off. You'll also miss out on some notification types and features like package detection. I think doorbells and video cameras are impacted the most by the loss of features without a subscription, since so many then lose the ability to show you what happened that day or who rang the bell. These video doorbells below get around that with local storage options, so your footage is saved to a microSD card rather than the cloud. However, if you don't properly secure the camera, you could lose the footage and camera both, since all data is stored in the device.
Similar to video doorbells, you'll often run into subscription fees for security cameras in order to store footage in the cloud and review it. Instead, choose one of these cameras for the inside or outside of your home that allows local storage, so you can live subscription-free. We've got a whole guide to subscription-free security cameras if you want more options. Again, make sure the camera is secured so you don't lose the camera and footage in one go.
Motion sensors are a primary feature of most smart home security kits, but they usually don't need a subscription fee to work—when a sensor is triggered, the base station will sound an alarm. The subscription really just allows for an agent to call your local authorities if the alarm sounds; otherwise, you'll just get a notification on your phone to find out if someone's where they shouldn't be.
If you're looking for motion sensors that will activate smart-home features like turning on a switch when you walk by, these aren't it. These are designed to set off an immediate alarm when any motion is detected. Check out our guide to the Best Motion Sensors for more ideas there.
This is another popular feature of smart home security kits. It's great for getting an alert on a door that doesn't have a smart lock, or wouldn't be regularly locked. Even better for windows or sliding doors that have no other way to alert you if they're opened.
I haven't tested these yet, but I've tested other products from these brands and have liked the experience, and share more about both below. They're next on my testing list for this story.

Madhya Pradesh to resume state govt bus services after 20 years on September 25
The Madhya Pradesh transport department is resuming bus services in the state after 20 years, with both intercity and intracity services planned.
Madhya Pradesh chief minister Mohan Yadav and Union road transport minister Nitin Gadkari will inaugurate the Sugam Parivahan Seva, a new public passenger bus service, at a state-level programme at BHEL Dussehra Maidan on September 25.
The transport department is resuming bus services in the state after 20 years, with both intercity and intracity services planned.
Drivers are being trained in modern technology, operations and safety standards for electric and CNG buses to ensure smooth functioning.
A transport department official said the buses will be equipped with GPS and panic buttons. “GPS will allow live tracking, while panic buttons will enhance passenger safety during emergencies. Intercity buses will connect two or more cities, while intracity buses will strengthen public transport within urban areas, offering reliable and convenient travel options,” said Rao Uday Pratap Singh, minister, transport department.
The state government has set a target of expanding the fleet to 15,000 buses over the next five years, with 2,500 to 3,000 new buses added annually. This expansion is expected to provide passengers across Madhya Pradesh with more travel choices.
Driver training is a key focus of the initiative. Institutes of Driving Training and Research have already been established in Indore and Chhindwara, while five regional centres are coming up in Bhopal, Betul, Chhatarpur, Ujjain and Gwalior. In addition, 22 district-level centres will soon be set up. These facilities will train drivers in modern technology, safety protocols and the operation of electric and CNG buses.

AI superpower ambitions take centre stage as Trump and Xi meet
- Published
"Whoever wins AI, WINS!"
US President Donald Trump has been blunt about his AI ambitions, as well as about who he considers the US's main rival to be: China.
His Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, has not said anything so forthright - but it seems he holds a similar view.
"China very much sees it as a race, they very much think China should be the leading force in AI - they see AI as a power maximiser," says Rebecca Arcesati, from the Mercator Institute for China Studies.
You can look beyond the rhetoric for evidence of this: AI has been a cornerstone of China's technological ambitions for more than a decade, whether Xi emphasises it publicly or not.
For Trump, beating China to AI supremacy outweighs any risks of the technology to humans - something he has described as "a hoax".
China's foreign ministry warned that "narratives of threat" and confrontation hinder global AI governance, calling for cooperation to ensure it benefits all.
It means when the two presidents sit down on Thursday there will be few more important topics than their AI ambitions - and what they say and decide will matter to the whole world.
Is the US in the lead?
There's no doubt the US and China are global leaders in AI but who is ahead depends on how success is measured.
American companies lead on so-called frontier models, with the highest-performing systems on most benchmarks coming from firms such as Anthropic, Google and OpenAI.
In February 2025, an AI model by China's DeepSeek "briefly matched the top US model" and as of March 2026, Anthropic's top model led the pack "by just 2.7%", according to researchers at Stanford University, external.
Part of the US advantage stems from the vast sums being invested in leading AI companies as the frontier labs burn through mountains of cash to build the infrastructure to train new models.
The stock market is booming and a large part of the US economy's expansion relies on the enormous growth - and projected profitability - of AI companies.
So that might partly explain why President Trump sees AI as key to US success.
Another factor limiting China's ability is the sweeping government restrictions placed on US companies that prevent them from selling advanced microchips to Chinese firms - these are crucial for developing cutting-edge models.
China's advantage
Despite the chip restrictions, new AI models are coming out almost monthly in both countries and it's unclear what "winning" the AI race would actually mean, or whether there is a finish line at all.
Many companies are racing to develop artificial general intelligence (AGI), a theoretical form of AI capable of learning, reasoning and performing a wide range of tasks at or above the level of humans.
The Chinese AI industry has so far focused not on creating frontier models but releasing what is known as open weight models - downloadable and tweakable in a similar way to open source software.
This contrasts with the approach taken by many US firms, which largely focus on proprietary models accessed through paid subscriptions or company platforms.
Chinese open weight models are being released at a rapid pace, with benchmarks showing the country's top models trailing US rivals by only a few months.
Models such as Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 have become popular in China and overseas because they perform close to the frontier models while remaining freely downloadable and adaptable.
Beijing's focus is more about deploying the technology across its economy, China analyst Lizzi Lee from the Asia Society Policy Institute said.
"AI isn't the moon landing," she said. "The US may lead at the frontier, while China could still gain enormous economic and geopolitical leverage by making capable AI cheap, open and ubiquitous."
AI is also very energy hungry, and China is very well placed there, Rebecca Arcesati told Tech Life on the BBC World Service.
"Chinese AI companies are able to access the electricity they need for a much lower cost and that really is an advantage," she said.
In robotics - a field of AI that some believe will be world-changing - China has become the world's biggest manufacturer of robots, with more than two million working in the country's factories, the International Federation of Robotics estimated.
The nation is also the world's biggest maker of humanoid robots, accounting for more than nine-tenths of global shipments in the first half of the year, according to independent policy institute Chatham House.
Chinese AI developers have showed "remarkable resilience and innovation" in spite of the shortage of advanced American chips, analyst Lian Jye Su from tech research firm Omdia said.
But US officials and AI firms have also alleged that Chinese developers closed the gap by using distillation - a technique that enables models to learn from more advanced platforms.
China's foreign ministry said in response that AI development was "fuelled" by the country's "vision of extensive consultation and joint contribution for shared benefit".
Safety concerns?
China and the US may be in fierce competition, but their governments' approaches to safety concerns are markedly different.
While some in the industry have recently warned that AI could pose an existential risk to humanity, Chinese researchers seem less concerned about that and are more worried about potential misuse of the technology and cyber war.
Responding to concerns over AI, Trump has said the US already has sufficient rules in place and that the only guardrails AI needs are a "high IQ" president.
"We're leading now over China by a lot, and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way," Trump said this week, adding that the US was not going to "stifle the growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution".
Washington has prioritised innovation and sought to reduce regulation in an effort to "keep American labs ahead", said information security officer Jayant Dave from cybersecurity firm Check Point Software Technologies.
Beijing has taken a different strategy to the US hands-off approach.
Xi urged the country's leaders to keep a close eye on AI's risks and ensure the technology was always "under human control".
"China has taken a relatively cautious and centrally-coordinated approach," introducing guides on data usage and algorithms before many other countries, helping to address many underlying concerns, Dave said.
The use of guidelines, though not legally binding, sets expectations while giving developers room to innovate, said National University of Singapore AI ethics lecturer Jonathan Sim.
Will they cooperate?
Despite calls for international cooperation, it remains unclear how the AI superpowers plan to address the technology's potential dangers - if at all.
The two countries have previously cooperated on existential threats such as nuclear weapons, but that was based on a shared understanding of the threat, which is not currently the case with AI, Dave said.
"Washington worries about capability escaping control. Beijing worries about capability threatening domestic stability," he added.
Trump has dismissed proposals for an industry-wide slowdown, arguing that it could allow Chinese developers to close the gap.
Ahead of the Trump-Xi summit, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng discussed establishing a notification mechanism for serious AI incidents.
While the messaging from Trump on China in recent weeks has been "more antagonistic", the fact that AI is expected to be on the agenda was a "good start", said policy analyst Leia Wang from the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
What we don't want, he added, was for an "unhealthy version of the race narrative to perpetuate", potentially escalating an already fierce rivalry in AI.

When I hauled a heavy suitcase into the overhead on my Amtrak train car, I thought I had everything I'd need for my trip.
Three jackets, two pairs of boots, and a scarf to match every sweater — I was ready for anything. However, I quickly realized I wasn't nearly as prepared for the five-hour ride itself.
My trip from New Jersey to Boston on the Northeast Regional line gave me just enough time to settle in, stretch out, and enjoy a little downtime. Soon, I learned that what I had — and didn't — made all the difference in how much I enjoyed my trip.
Here are five items I'm glad I brought, and three I wish I'd packed.
My ticket didn't include complimentary snacks, so I was glad I'd brought my own.
Due to the length of my ride, I knew I'd be hungry at some point.
My basic ticket didn't come with complimentary snacks from Amtrak, but I didn't mind much since I had brought plenty of food from home.
I stopped at a bagel shop before boarding, packed a homemade latte, and had more than enough snacks to keep me satisfied throughout the ride.
There was a café car about halfway through the train that I could've bought a few bites at, but I was happy to save the money anyway.
Headphones came in handy for listening to music and streaming TV.
Though the lull of the train can be soothing in itself, I was happy to have packed my headphones so I could listen to music during the ride.
These also came in handy when I wanted to catch up on TV shows without bothering anyone around me.
The only packing mistake I made was bringing wired headphones instead of wireless ones, because I couldn't charge my device and listen at the same time.
My hot spot came in handy when the train's WiFi didn't work super well.
Though Amtrak offers complimentary WiFi on routes like this one, I didn't find it reliable for everything.
It worked fine for sending texts or scrolling through social media, but it wasn't as reliable when I wanted to stream TV on my laptop. To stream better, I switched to my phone's hot spot.
I brought my tripod for capturing content, but it was useful for creating extra space at my seat.
I had originally packed my tripod to capture travel content, and it was helpful as I snapped photos and filmed videos.
I also found it surprisingly useful for creating extra space at my seat.
My tray table wasn't very big, so setting up my tripod on the floor with my phone to stream a show gave me room to keep my laptop on the table instead.
It's worth noting that I didn't have anyone sitting next to me, so I had plenty of floor space to work with. Overall, it made for a nice setup.
My Kindle comes with me almost everywhere I go.
Luckily, I didn't struggle to keep myself entertained since I had packed my Kindle. I'm a book lover, so five hours of uninterrupted reading time was right up my alley.
I prefer using an e-reader over a physical book when traveling because it's lightweight and doesn't take up much space in my bag.
Plus, for early morning or late-night rides with my Kindle, I don't have to rely on the train's reading light, which might disturb other passengers.
However, I found myself wishing I had packed motion-sickness medication.
I thought I packed pretty well for the trip, but toward the end of the ride, I started feeling nauseous. I've never had motion sickness on a train before, but I've also never been on one for this long.
So, when I started feeling dizzy in the last hour, I was caught off guard. I couldn't look at my phone screen anymore, so I leaned back and closed my eyes.
It really made me wish I had brought some motion-sickness medication along for the ride.
Having a travel pillow or blanket would've made my trip more comfortable.
My seat ended up being comfier than I thought, with a decent recline and footrests.
Looking back, though, I really wish I had packed some comfortable travel items, such as a neck pillow or blanket. This ride was early in the morning, and my return trip was late at night, so they would've come in handy.
Next time, I'll definitely bring a few more things to make the ride cozier and allow me to close my eyes for a bit.
Similarly, slippers would've been helpful for walking throughout the train car.
Another comfort item I didn't think about until I was on the train was slippers.
I like taking my shoes off during long trips, especially on airplanes, but for some reason, I felt hesitant to do so on the train.
I wish I had brought a pair of light slippers to wear during the ride and for those trips back and forth to the bathroom. It would've been another way to add to the overall comfort of a long Amtrak ride.

India had the highest number of children with no sanitation service in schools, with 50 million out of the world total of 244 million as of 2025, according to a new global report. Only Nigeria (34 million), Ethiopia (26 million), the Democratic Republic of the Congo (11 million) or Indonesia (8 million) had a comparatively large number of schoolchildren who had no access to sanitation service.
The data from ‘Progress on drinking water, sanitation and hygiene in schools 2015-2025’ shows the progress as well as the challenges India is facing in meeting the water, sanitation and hygiene goals that are part of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) set for 2030.
14% reduction in schools with no sanitation service
The report can also be seen as a decadal report card on the Swachh Bharat Mission, which was launched in India on October 2, 2014. The report cites the achievement of India which saw a 14% reduction in schools with no sanitation service.
Lack of hygiene service
The WHO/UNICEF report that is part of the Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) for Water Supply, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) shows that globally, 362 million children still had no hygiene service at their school in 2025. Of these, 20 million were from India.
It is not just lack of access that the WHO report flags about India but also gaps in data. “There is now sufficient data to estimate trends in basic hygiene coverage between 2015 and 2025 for all SDG regions except Central and Southern Asia where there were insufficient recent data to generate estimates for India, and therefore the region, beyond 2024.”
Drinking water
On the brighter side, India is among the 28 out of 62 countries that are on track to achieve universal coverage of basic drinking water in schools by 2030.
As of 2025, there were 258 million children who still had no drinking water service at their school. The number of children from Indian schools made up 12 million of this number or about 1 out 20 children in the world. The report shows that India has made a big progress in basic drinking water services in 2025 and average rates of change between 2015 and 2025. India, Panama, Syrian Arab Republic, Togo and Tuvalu increased coverage by over 4% per year, “demonstrating that rapid progress is possible”.
However, the report found that while gaps in basic water coverage persists between school levels and between rural and urban areas, this did not apply to India, Cambodia and Fiji.

Trump is bracing to lose his latest fight with the press
Trump’s lawyers said he barred three news outlets from the White House on security grounds. A judge seemed skeptical.
A hearing on President Donald Trump’s White House press ban ended without a ruling this afternoon — an admittedly anticlimactic outcome, but one that will likely change very soon.
The Trump-appointed judge in the case, Timothy Kelly, appeared skeptical of the administration’s arguments for banning CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House grounds last week. Kelly said he would rule “as soon as possible.” Until then, the ban remains in place.
By all accounts, Trump’s case is a feeble one. While the Justice Department attempted to argue on Wednesday that the three outlets’ reporting jeopardized national security, Trump himself kind of gave the game away last week when he said he had singled these organizations out over what he characterized as negative and inaccurate stories.
The move sat poorly even with people and institutions you’d expect to be sympathetic to Trump: Fox News was one of several outlets that boycotted White House events this week to protest the ban, for instance.
And ahead of today’s hearing, Trump himself seemed primed to lose. In a Truth Social post on Monday, he promised he would “almost without question” appeal any decision against him.
Go a little deeper
This is all emblematic of how Trump has escalated his attacks on the news media in his second term: not just by insulting and demeaning the press, but also by weaponizing otherwise neutral-seeming rules.
Every administration has policies that regulate who can access the White House grounds and under what conditions, for instance. But in early 2025, the White House took control of the press pool — the rotating group of reporters that frequently travels with the president — and soon sought to exclude disfavored organizations.
More insidiously, Trump has mobilized regulatory agencies like the Federal Communications Commission against his perceived critics, in some cases even threatening to revoke the licenses of local TV stations that air coverage and commentary he disagrees with.
While no licenses have actually been suspended, the FCC has mysteriously pulled some up for unscheduled review. And just the prospect of government retaliation has been enough to force some content off the air: Just two weeks ago, the late-night comedy host Jimmy Kimmel said his show wouldn’t air a scheduled interview with Texas Senate candidate James Talarico because of the FCC’s new scrutiny of political content.
This playbook isn’t a Trump original, as my colleague Zack Beauchamp has explained. In fact, weaponizing broadcast regulations was also a favored technique of former Hungarian Prime Minister (and infamous strongman) Viktor Orbán, who successfully used licensing rules and other bureaucratic technicalities to force independent media outlets into submission.
Likewise, revoking the press credentials of critical reporters has long been a favorite tactic of Russian President Vladimir Putin, Nico Perrino, the executive vice president of the nonprofit civil liberties group Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, said in a briefing on Wednesday: “These are things that are done by regimes that we do not want to emulate.”
Lest these comparisons get you down, however, recall that neither Hungary nor Russia has all the defenses that the US does. Defenses like, for example, an independent court system.
