Listed EV maker Ola Electric’s board has approved a fresh fundraise of up to ₹1,500 Cr, three months after the company raised ₹780 Cr through a QIP. In an exchange filing, the Bhavish Aggarwal-led company said it plans to raise the capital by issuing equity shares and/or securities convertible into or exchangeable for equity shares. The fundraise may be undertaken through one or more routes, including a further public offer, rights issue, QIP, private placement, or the issuance of instruments such as convertible debentures, warrants, American Depository Receipts, and Global Depository Receipts. The proposal is subject to approval from shareholders and other regulatory or statutory authorities. The filing did not disclose the proposed use of the proceeds. The latest proposal follows Ola Electric’s ₹780.24 Cr QIP in June. The QIP formed part of an earlier approval to raise up to ₹1,500 Cr, which Ola Electric’s board cleared in October 2025 and shareholders approved the following month. Of the net QIP proceeds of ₹744.87 Cr, the company earmarked ₹225 Cr for repaying or prepaying borrowings and ₹335 Cr for organic growth initiatives. Another ₹184.87 Cr was set aside for general corporate purposes. According to its QIP placement document, Ola Electric and its subsidiaries had outstanding borrowings of ₹1,637.61 Cr as of May 20, 2026. The fresh fundraise proposal comes as Ola Electric invests in its EV, battery cell manufacturing, and battery energy storage system businesses, while trying to revive sales and narrow its losses. Last month, the company launched the S1Z escooter range, powered by its locally developed 46-series LFP Bharat Cell. It also expanded its energy storage portfolio with the second-generation residential Ola Shakti, the industry-focused Shakti Rack, and the utility-scale Mahashakti. Ola Electric is also overhauling the sales model it has followed since launching its first escooter five years ago. The company opened its first dealer-operated stores across seven states yesterday and plans to build a network of more than 500 dealerships over the next two quarters. The changes come as the company looks to regain ground in India’s electric two-wheeler market. Ola Electric’s registrations declined 7.7% MoM to 13,132 units in August from 14,226 units in July, according to Vahan data. However, its market share improved to 7.6% from 6.8% during the period as overall electric two-wheeler registrations fell more sharply. On the financial front, Ola Electric’s consolidated net loss narrowed 22% YoY to ₹336 Cr in Q1 FY27 from ₹428 Cr. However, its operating revenue plunged 45% to ₹455 Cr from ₹828 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Sequentially, revenue rose 72% from ₹265 Cr, while loss narrowed from ₹500 Cr. The company’s board also approved an increase in its authorised share capital to ₹8,721.87 Cr from ₹8,318.50 Cr today, subject to shareholders’ approval. Meanwhile, in another senior management change, Ola Electric’s COO Hyun Shik Park resigned due to personal reasons, effective from the close of business today. The company’s board also approved the reappointment of Manoj Kumar Kohli and YourStory founder Shradha Sharma as independent directors for a second five-year term beginning December 6, subject to shareholders’ approval.

Update | September 23, 13:10 IST Electric two-wheeler startup Ultraviolette Automotive has raised $85 Mn (about ₹813 Cr) in a Series E round co-led by Yali Capital and TDK Ventures. Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan and other investors also participated in the round. Cofounder and CEO Narayan Subramaniam told Inc42 that the startup would use the capital to expand its manufacturing capacity and product portfolio, as well as strengthen its distribution network in India and overseas. “We are looking to enter new markets, including the US, Latin America, and Southeast Asia. The idea behind the fundraise is to cover all these different areas. To begin with, it is going into facility expansion, where Tesseract will now see a rapid ramp-up as well,” he said. Subramaniam said Ultraviolette expects to begin production of its Tesseract electric scooter and Shockwave electric motorcycle over the next few months. Both products have missed their original delivery schedule. When Ultraviolette unveiled them in March 2025, it said deliveries would begin in Q1 FY26. Neither has entered customer deliveries yet. Ultraviolette’s website now says the Tesseract’s final variants and configurations will be unveiled in Q1 2027, with deliveries commencing shortly thereafter. The startup has not disclosed a revised delivery timeline for the Shockwave. While India’s E2W market is dominated by relatively affordable scooters, Ultraviolette is positioning the Tesseract as a performance-focused offering. The startup claims that the Tesseract is India’s first scooter built on a 100-volt architecture, compared with the 48-volt systems commonly used in the segment. According to the startup, the architecture offers greater power and efficiency, as well as faster charging. Meanwhile, cofounder and CTO Niraj Rajmohan said Ultraviolette’s revenue grew around fourfold to about ₹130 Cr in FY26 from approximately ₹30 Cr in FY25. The startup is yet to file its audited FY26 financial statements. In FY25, its operating revenue jumped 114% YoY to ₹32.3 Cr, while its net loss widened 89% to ₹116.3 Cr. Original | September 11, 14:16 IST Electric two-wheeler (E2W) maker Ultraviolette Automotive is set to raise an additional ₹373.04 Cr as part of its ongoing Series E funding round from investors Yali Capital, TDK Ventures, among others. As per an MCA filings accessed by Inc42, Ultraviolette’s shareholders consented to allot on preferential basis through private placement 8.15 Lakh Series E3 compulsorily convertible preference shares (CCPS) worth ₹2,435 each, aggregating to ₹197.5 Cr. The startup also allotted 7.24 Lakh Series E4 CCPS, netting ₹175.5 Cr. “The investments are part of a currently ongoing fundraise; we have nothing further to add at the moment,” the startup said in response to Inc42’s questions pertaining to the round. Of this, Ultraviolette has raised ₹249.2 Cr from Yali Capital’s Yali Deeptech Fund I as well as TDK Ventures. TDK Ventures first backed the startup in August 2025 when it led its $21 Mn funding round while Yali Capital will be new to Ultraviolette’s cap table. There are a host of angel investors participating in this round including, Adi Hirji Jehangir, Anshumi Desai, Janak Desai, Mahak Khabia, Zafar Ahmadullah, among others. The investment comes almost a year after the startup raised $45 Mn as part of the Series E round from Zoho and Lingotto. Overall, the startup has raised more than $135 Mn till date from other investors like TVS Motors, Qualcomm Ventures, Breathe Capital and Mudhal Partners. The new investment comes as the E2W manufacturer is building its manufacturing facility, the BIGGA factory. Ultraviolette To Invest ₹1,000 Cr In Manufacturing The E2W maker is investing more than ₹1,000 Cr over the next five years to expand its manufacturing footprint, with its upcoming BIGGA Factory set to take its annual production capacity to as much as 2.5 Lakh vehicles in the initial phase. The startup intends to invest approximately ₹800 Cr in the new facility, while another ₹200 Cr is being deployed to expand its existing Bengaluru plant. The new facility will initially have an annual capacity of 2.5 Lakh vehicles, which can eventually be scaled to 5 Lakh vehicles, cofounders Narayan Subramaniam and Niraj Rajmohan told Inc42. The capacity expansion comes as Ultraviolette looks to move beyond its initial premium, performance-led positioning and target larger segments of the E2W market with new products such as the Shockwave and Tesseract. However, the startup said the strategy itself has not changed. “Ultraviolette was conceived from the outset as an electric-vehicle platform company,” the founders said, highlighting that the F77 was the first expression of this approach, followed by the X-47 crossover. The upcoming products, they said, will allow the company to address “significantly larger customer segments” while retaining its focus on technology, safety, performance and range. The cofounders claim that demand across its existing portfolio already exceeds 10,000 units a month, while it has received tens of thousands of bookings for upcoming products. It plans to commission capacity progressively in line with demand. Ultraviolette currently has an installed capacity of around 30,000 vehicles annually at its Bengaluru facility, which is being expanded to 50,000-60,000 units. The plant will continue to serve as a manufacturing, engineering and technology hub after the BIGGA Factory comes online. It is also targeting international markets, with exports expected to account for around 25% of revenue over the next five years. “BIGGA Factory converts that technology foundation into industrial scale,” the founders said, positioning the facility as a key step towards building a global electric-mobility business. To note, the startup launched its F77 motorcycles in the United Kingdom, in November last year, and claimed to be present in 12 countries across Europe, as of its last fundraise. For the month of August, overall E2W registrations fell by 16.2% to 1.72 Lakh units from 2.05 Lakh units in July, based on Vahan data. Ultraviolette sold 583 E2Ws, down 17% from 702 vehicles in July. It holds 0.3% market share in the domestic market.

Russian disinformation campaigns are varied in their falsehoods and strategies.
The narratives range from a deepfake Tom Cruise criticising the Paris Olympics to portraying a recent Russian attack on a train near the Ukraine-Poland border as a false-flag operation.
Some efforts are blatant deepfakes, such as stamping the BBC logo on a video wrongly blaming Ukraine for a deadly missile salvo on its own citizens in Kramatorsk four years ago.
The tactics evolve too, from disseminating deceitful narratives through the Telegram messaging platform to “poisoning” AI systems by littering the internet with false stories in the hope they will be regurgitated by chatbots.
It is systematic and Andy Burnham has seen enough, announcing a new anti-disinformation agency, the National Centre for Information Defence.
“We’re talking about an insidious campaign that reaches into people’s homes and twists what they feel about their own country and community – creating a narrative of decline, stoking division and sowing despair,” he said.
Experts say picking off individual examples is the wrong approach and Burnham is right to tackle what he describes as a “poisonous tide”.
Going after isolated examples of disinformation is a “losers’ game”, says Ned Mendez, head of research at Alliance4Europe, a nonprofit that analyses these destabilising threats.
“You can spend all your time looking for a TikTok or a post on X but it’s not an effective use of your day. It’s the infrastructure that is the problem, so this is a step in the right direction, going after the networks,” he says.
Sophie Williams-Dunning, a cyber analyst at the Royal United Services Institute (Rusi) thinktank, says there is now a “sophisticated ecosystem which exists to exacerbate provokable users for one reason or another”.
Although Burnham is targeting “hostile state information attacks”, this ecosystem does not just include Russia, which likes to amplify “divisive content”, says Williams-Dunning.
It also includes far-right influencers who immediately jump on social flashpoints like the Southport and Belfast riots and individuals simply looking to make money by producing highly engaging content riffing on disruption.
The Burnham announcement is “welcome, if overdue”, says Williams-Dunning, who adds that there will be an accompanying debate about free speech and the right level of government intervention. Inevitably, malign networks will amplify those free-speech concerns, she says.
It is not just Russia deploying information attacks. China and Iran have both used deepfake newscasters to advance their goals.
One recent study, conducted mostly in February by the Social Market Foundation, a British thinktank, found that more than a quarter of posts on X that relate to news were misinformation, a third of which were anti-immigration or Islamophobic.
The UK government defines misinformation as the inadvertent spread of false information, while disinformation is the deliberate creation and spread of falsehoods to create harm or disruption. The two can intertwine to highly disruptive effect.
Labour has become increasingly concerned about Russian disinformation affecting the UK. The Starmer government in May cited information warfare from Moscow when it warned Britain was “confronting an industrial-scale attack on the UK’s and our allies’ information environment, aimed at undermining our security and democratic systems”.
Earlier this year MPs on the foreign affairs select committee called for the creation of a national counter-disinformation centre, in a similar vein to Sweden’s Psychological Defence Agency and France’s Vigilance and Protection against Foreign Digital Interference service.
Experts said Burnham’s announcement at least shows the UK government catching up, although Keir Starmer’s administration showed an awareness of social media’s contribution to unrest by launching the National Internet Intelligence Investigations unit after the Southport disturbances in 2024. Operated by the police, it monitors social media to help local forces “manage public safety threats and risks”.
The UK government has been taking action prior to Burnham’s announcement, however. In May it sanctioned employees of the Social Design Agency and ANO Dialog, Russian entities which it said the Kremlin uses for large-scale interference campaigns.
One example is the Doppelgänger network, so-called due to its technique of imitating the appearance of established media organisations including Le Monde, the Guardian, Der Spiegel and Fox News.
Other examples include the 2023 surge in reports of bedbug infestations in France, falsely blaming Ukrainian refugees. The disinformation leaked into the British press and the French government concluded the stories were being artificially amplified by Russian-linked social media accounts
One of the most longstanding misinformation campaigns has centred on the idea that London is “dangerous” and “lawless”. Analysis of Reddit accounts by King’s College London found the number of such posts rose from 874 in 2008 to 258,444 in 2024.
Robert Topinka, reader in digital media and rhetoric at Birkbeck, University of London, said Russia did not necessarily start such storylines, but enthusiastically amplified them.
He cautioned that counter-disinformation efforts should not assume “people are just being fooled by some sort of outside actor”. Rather, he said, Russia tends to find a point of tension and then create more content around it.
“What really is happening is people are feeling like Britain is run-down – that’s the real source of it,” said Topinka.
AI is adding a new dimension. Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta says AI-generated content is now a “near-standard” part of disinformation campaigns.
The UK thinktank Demos recently highlighted a chatbot “poisoning” campaign where falsehoods published online by a discredited Russian organisation, including the bodies of deceased Ukrainian soldiers being processed into meat products, were repeated by chatbot models.
The National Centre for Information Defence will have a lot of work to do.

At 8.37am local time last Wednesday, a huge mass of rock and ice sheared free from a mountain, sliding 1,200 metres to the valley floor in Nepal’s Langtang national park, about 60km north of the country’s capital, Kathmandu.
Horrifying images and videos soon emerged of a torrent of mud, water and debris that swept down the Lhende Khola valley at speeds approaching 150km/h. Flowing down the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers that run between Tibet and Nepal, the flood water swept away homes, roads, bridges and power plants. Along the Trishuli, water levels rose by as much as nine metres in half an hour. As of the time of writing, the death toll of the disaster approached 1,000 people, with more than 4,400 on both sides of the border missing.
As the rescue effort continued – hampered by bad weather, poor access and the threat of further flooding due to two lakes that have formed after the landslide – Nepali prime minister Balendra Shah said the catastrophe was “not an ordinary” event.
Shah said on social media that “the risks we face in the Himalayan region are increasing alongside climate change … It is now time for us to strongly raise with the international community the issue of the disasters we are experiencing as a result of climate change.”
More on the scale of this disaster and what it tells us about our climate crisis, after this week’s headlines.
In focus
What caused last week’s catastrophe was not immediately clear: initial reports suggested the floods could have been caused by an earthquake in the area that triggered a landslide, while early satellite imagery suggested that a glacial collapse was to blame. Subsequent satellite analysis showed that bedrock underneath a glacier collapsed, with the landslide registering as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.
“It seems that a massive rock face with the glacier on top of it has essentially gone,” says Adrian McCallum, a senior lecturer in geotechnical engineering at the University of the Sunshine Coast in Australia. One seismologist called the landslide “one of the largest in the last decade or two in the world”.
As Nepal’s Shah said in his statement, our environmental crisis cannot be separated from this disaster. The Himalayas – spanning Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan – are warming twice as fast as the global average, putting the region at increased risk of avalanches, landslides and floods. The UN said in 2023 that Nepal’s mountains had lost close to one-third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global heating.
While scientists haven’t definitively linked the Lhende Khola landslide to the climate crisis, they have pointed out that rising temperatures mean permanently frozen mountain slopes are at risk of melting and destabilising.
“Increased temperatures result in increased melt, which results in increased water,” McCallum says. “Movement of water into voids within either soil or rock … destabilises what once may have been a more solid rock mass or soil environment.”
With global heating, mountainous areas are also at risk of permafrost degradation, “glacial lake outburst floods” (GLOFs), and increasingly erratic rainfall, raising flood and landslide risk.
Glacial lakes form behind natural dams as a result of glacier melt, and can cause catastrophic outburst floods if their natural dam walls are breached. More than 12,000 deaths have been attributed to such floods globally.
Given the risks to downstream communities in the Himalayas, scientists have pointed to the need for early warning systems, which would require coordinated international monitoring efforts.
“Wherever the glaciers are receding … you have the potential for a GLOF to occur,” McCallum says, such as in the European Alps and the South American Andes. In North America, an outburst flood causes periodic problems in Juneau, the capital of Alaska.
To be clear, there was no GLOF involved in last week’s landslide. But Nepal has more than 2,000 glacial lakes, and 21 of those, according to the UN, are considered potentially dangerous.
As climate academic Bill McGuire wrote for the Guardian this week, global heating will “leave no part of the planet untouched. As the world processes the horror of the events in Nepal and Tibet, it is a lesson that we ignore at our peril.”

A Latur farmer broke down in the presence of Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis during his visit to Latur district in the Marathwada region to assess the drought-like situation. Elsewhere, Deputy Chief Minister Eknath Shinde visited Akola district on Wednesday.
The tour of CM and DCM comes after Mr. Fadnavis on Tuesday (September 22), announced the formation of a subcommittee to handle the drought issue under the chairmanship of Revenue Minister Chandrashekhar Bawankule, while issuing a drought GR by Saturday (September 26) announcing the financial assistance for the farmers, who faced crop loss due to long dry spell.
Nilanga, a taluka-based farmer, sobbingly said, “Pani nahi, nuksan jhala ahe (No water, suffering heavy losses.”
Giving assurance to the farmer, Mr. Fadnavis said, “In the next two days, the drought government resolution will be issued, providing relief to farmers. The focus will be to provide assistance to farmers for rabi crops and make availability of drinking water, fodder for cattle, and food grains.”
Mr. Fadnavis on Wednesday (September 23) visited Nilanga taluka in Latur and Dharashiv districts, which received around 50% rainfall. “Latur is the worst hit by drought this year and received less rainfall compared to last year, when the rainfall was at least 65% to 70%. This has caused crop loss,” Mr. Fadnavis added.
Eknath Shinde visits Akola
Deputy Chief Minister Eknath Shinde visited Akola district and said, “There is no alternative but to announce a drought after witnessing the situation. Last year also farmers suffered due to heavy downpour, and I stood with them; this year also I will stand behind them. Will do whatever is required to do as farmers also have the right to the State government treasury.
According to State government data, the State is at present witnessing a 17% rainfall deficit, as it has recorded 787.2 mm of rainfall against a normal rainfall of 953.2 mm. Several regions in the Marathwada region, including Latur, have received less than 50% rainfall. The deficient rainfall in the State is being attributed to El Niño.
The opposition leader NCP-SP Rohit Pawar, who has been leading a protest to declare a drought in the State, responded to the plight of the farmer, saying, “It is heart-wrenching to see a farmer breaking down before the Chief Minister”. Highlighting the demand of ₹50,000 per hectare to farmers and Rs 25,000 per family to agricultural labourers, he added, “I have been witnessing all this from last eight to ten days in Vidarbha and Marathwada.”
While NCP-SP MP Supriya Sule credited NCP (SP) Supremo and her father Sharad Pawar for writing to Mr. Fadnavis and said, “The action have been taken only after Sharad Pawar raised the issue with the government through his letter.

The iSpring WRO4000 is an all-in-one whole-house RO system with 7-layer filtration, smart monitoring, automatic flushing, leak detection, and up to 4,000 GPD output. It delivers purified water across the home while maintaining an efficient 2:1 pure-to-drain ratio.
iSpring Water Systems, a trusted US-based provider of water filtration solutions, announced the launch of the WRO4000, an intelligent all-in-one whole-house reverse osmosis system designed to deliver high-quality purified water to every tap while making daily life simpler and more convenient. The launch of the WRO4000 highlights iSpring’s continued dedication to helping families enjoy cleaner, safer water through pioneering, reliable water systems.
Table of Contents
Pure Water Meets Smarter Living: The Innovation Behind the WRO4000
As modern families place great value on quality of life, their expectations for water treatment solutions have evolved beyond basic purification to include smarter operation, greater efficiency, and hassle-free maintenance. Engineered to meet these evolving needs, the iSpring WRO4000 whole house reverse osmosis system introduces a range of innovations, including:
Powerful 7-Layer Filtration
The iSpring WRO4000 delivers outstanding purification performance through its advanced 7-layer filtration, which combines a descaler, spin-down sediment filter integrated with KDF media, ultrafiltration membrane, RO membrane, UV filter, and CTO carbon block filter. Working together, they effectively reduce TDS and remove over 1,000 contaminants, including heavy metals, PFAS, fluoride, and sediment, to provide households with a continuous supply of ultra-clean water.
Intelligent Monitoring and Control
Designed for effortless system management, the iSpring WRO4000 combines real-time monitoring with intelligent connectivity. Its built-in LED display keeps key operating data, including inlet and outlet flow rates, TDS levels, and water tank levels—clearly visible at all times. Through smart IoT connectivity, users can also access water usage insights, monitor filter status, and reach customer support anytime, anywhere by simply scanning a QR code.
Set and Forget Operation
The iSpring WRO4000 features automatic flushing with customizable frequency settings. Once configured, the system performs flushing based on a preset schedule, reducing the time and effort required for routine maintenance. It also integrates leak detection that continuously monitors system status and sends alerts when a leak is detected, further enhancing overall system reliability.
Portable and Easy to Deploy
The iSpring WRO4000 is equipped with lockable wheels at its base, an innovative feature offering enhanced convenience and flexibility. With 360° swivel wheels, the system can be effortlessly moved and positioned, making setup and relocation easier than ever. After the system is in place, the wheels can be securely locked, which ensures the system remains stable during ongoing operation.
Enhanced Water Output and Efficiency
High flow and low waste are two impressive features of the WRO4000. Delivering up to 4,000 gallons of filtered water per day, the system easily meets the daily water needs of a large family, from drinking and cooking to showering and laundry, with virtually no waiting time. Furthermore, this whole house RO system boasts an efficient 2:1 pure-to-drain ratio, maximizing water efficiency without compromising purification performance. By cutting down on wastewater, the system actively supports an eco-friendly and sustainable lifestyle.
Abundant Purified Water for Every Corner of the House

'I have never felt heat like that' - a survivor on watching 33 cellmates die in Nigeria
- Published
Usman Muhammad pauses by the entrance to a tiny Nigerian prison cell and leans his forehead against the wall unable to speak.
The day before he had been trapped inside the stifling room, measuring roughly 6m (19.7ft) by 3m (9.8ft), with more than 50 other prisoners.
Thirty-three of his cellmates died in the cramped conditions in the prison in Minna, the capital of Nigeria's Niger state - and four died later in hospital.
The mass deaths caused an outcry and sparked protests, including attacks on public buildings, as relatives and locals demanded answers.
Federal officials had initially blamed the deaths on a diphtheria outbreak but exactly what happened is now the subject of an investigation.
"I have never felt heat like that in my life. When we touched each other's bodies, it felt like fire burning," Muhammad tells the BBC once he is able to gather his thoughts.
When he was locked inside, there was standing room only amid humidity levels of more than 90%, which in some circumstances can be dangerous to human health as it prevents the natural cooling mechanism of sweat drying on the skin.
The temperature outside was above 25C and the only ventilation came from a small, high-up window.
"One of us fainted and we started knocking at the [cell] door. When [a guard] came we asked him for water. He looked at the guy that fainted and closed the door. That's how they started dying one after the other," Muhammad says.
Like the others who had been detained, the young man, in his 20s, is an artisanal miner, eking out a living searching for precious metals at mine sites.
The federal government has tried to crack down on this alleged illegal activity as it says it costs the country revenue, damages the environment and can be linked to wider criminal activity.
Officers from the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) had arrested a large group of miners near Minna last Tuesday and Wednesday.
The prisoners were held at its detention centre in the city, but the NSCDC has not shared either the names or the number of those it was holding.
As the hours inside the cell wore on, the heat and dehydration became unbearable and Muhammad says some of the detainees began drinking their own urine and collecting sweat from their bodies to try to stay alive.
He describes seeing people in distress and struggling to breathe.
"People were calling for help, some were already very weak."
But no-one came to help, he and others allege.
"While in the cell, we were shouting and telling them that people were dying," another survivor Adamu Isah told the Reuters news agency.
"We tried to break down the door when they refused to open it… At one point, a security officer came to the door.
"We were shouting and telling him that people were dying, but he said it wasn't his problem if people died."
Finally, on Thursday, the cell door was opened and the guards saw the dead bodies.
The NSCDC has not directly responded to the accusations of neglect and maltreatment but has said that 24 of its personnel are now in custody in connection with the deaths, including its suspended Niger state commandant Suberu Aniviye.
"The people who were killed are not flies. How can this go unlooked? We will get to the bottom of this," Niger state Governor Umaru Bago told the BBC.
As the organisation involved is a federal body rather than a force under his jurisdiction, such as the police, the governor is unable to exert direct influence but he welcomes the investigation that has been ordered by the government in capital, Abuja.
A 10-member committee has now been set-up to determine exactly what happened.
It has two weeks to establish the causes of the deaths and identify who was responsible and can recommend legal action against anyone found culpable.
No officer, regardless of rank, would be protected and any attempt to obstruct the investigation would be taken seriously, Interior Minister Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo said.
As he leaves the cell after talking to the BBC, Muhammad says he hopes that by speaking out he can help find justice and bring some closure to this traumatic event.

The United States’ withdrawal from key aid programs has put has put healthcare in Africa and the Global South “under growing strain” a new report warns.
The report says the Trump administration’s cuts to programs such as US Agency for International Development (USAID), as well as the Covid-19 pandemic and rising costs of living globally have brought “new urgency” for the need to reform healthcare in the region.
The report, titled A Sovereign Future For Health, was created by the Accra Reset, a global health initiative led by John Dramani Mahama, Ghana’s president, that believes countries in Africa and the wider global south should have greater control over their health development rather than being dependent on aid from western countries and international institutions.
A key statistic cited by Mahama and Accra Reset is that Africa produces less than 1% of its vaccines while carrying about 25% of the global disease burden.
The report cites how abrupt changes to global health financing, such as the US withdrawal from several global health initiatives, forced countries within the global south to urgently restructure their finances. The report points to the Trump administration’s decision to dissolve USAID, which pushed Nigeria to absorb the 28,000 health workers who were previously employed by the agency at a cost of $200m.
External financing for health in Africa contracted by close to 70% between 2021 and 2025, the report notes, meaning that African countries historically dependent on aid were forced to adapt quickly.
The withdrawal of the US Emergency Plan for Aids Relief (Pepfar) funding for South Africa, which provided over $400m a year annually and is credited with saving 26m lives globally since 2003, led to HIV clinics closing across the country. That left 1.4 million people living with HIV to face uncertainty about their treatment.
Such funding cuts caused “severe and devastating” disruption globally, according to research presented at the 26th International Aids Conference in Brazil earlier this year.
At the World Health Assembly in May, Mahama said Ghana lost $78m following the closure of USAID programs which affected maternal healthcare, the treatment of malaria, nutrition and HIV/Aids interventions.
The initiative’s latest report, published on Monday, comes amid these major cuts to international aid and growing pressure on countries to take greater ownership of their health systems. Mahama refers to these aid cuts as a clear example that donor dependency is not sustainable.
“The Accra Reset is not an argument for traditional donors to do less on global health. It is an argument for doing it differently and doing it better. As countries take greater ownership of their health futures, donor countries should step up to support that transition – following the lead of countries that set their own priorities, and work alongside them to determine where outside support is most valuable,” said Naveen Rao, senior vice-president of the health initiative at the Rockefeller Foundation. “The Accra Reset shows how we can evolve to back country-led solutions while advancing our shared health and economic interests.”
Mahama notes in the report that the “past few years have shaken global health cooperation to its foundations”.
“The Covid-19 pandemic exposed the risks created by concentrated production and unequal access to essential health products; rising debt and fiscal pressures have constrained national health budgets; and declining development assistance is placing programs and services under growing strain,” he continued, adding: “These shocks have brought new urgency to reform debates that have continued for years with limited progress. It was in this context that we launched the Accra Reset and its Sovereign Health Agenda – to give renewed political force to the reform agenda and place the agency of countries of the Global South at its centre.”
The report comes alongside a recent survey revealing the progressive attitudes many US citizens have towards foreign aid. Some 75% of Americans – including more than one in two (52%) who primarily support Donald Trump – agree that the US should restore disease prevention aid to contain the Ebola virus, according to polling of over 2,000 US adults commissioned by the Rockefeller Foundation.
The polling also revealed that 65% of US adults support international cooperation even if it means compromising some national interests; 64% also believe Americans have a shared responsibility to others, including people in other countries whom they do not know.
The Guardian has contacted the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) for comment.

Bablu Das was fishing in the Teesta River on Monday morning (September 21, 2026) when his phone rang. It was the sluice gate operator from the Gajoldoba Teesta Barrage upstream. “An elephant calf is going downstream. Save it,” the man screamed from the other side.
A few minutes earlier, the alert gate operator, Tapan Das, had spotted the four-day-old calf floating down a swirling Teesta and lifted the gate further to prevent it from smashing into the structure.
The calf was crossing the river near the barrage when the strong currents swept it away from the herd. Its mother crossed the river and started a frenetic search for the calf.
Some 5 km away, Bablu Das and his friends — Ajay, Mithu, Biswanath and Gopal — had rowed their dinghy, manoeuvring it with bamboo staves to stay on course, and located the calf, which had popped its trunk out of the raging river, like a periscope, to breathe.
In a video shot by one of the boatmen, a voice could be heard: “Ekdom baccha re! Dhor, dhor, dhor [It’s a small calf. Save it].” The dinghy chased the calf, and a minute later, Amit and Biswajit yanked it onto the boat before running a check. It was still breathing.
“The calf looked nervous. Its body was very cold. We tried to calm it and steered the boat to the riverbank,” Mr. Das told The Hindu.
The reunion
In the meantime, forest officials from different ranges of the Baikunthapur Forest Division had driven along the river bank with a veterinarian to prepare for what Samiran Raj, the Range Officer of Belacoba Range, termed “the most important part of the mission — the reunion with its mother”.
The calf was taken to the upstream of the barrage, the very place where it was separated from the herd, where the team found the elephants waiting for the calf.
Mr. Raj, who had accompanied the team, said the team could not identify the mother. The “intention was simple” – release the calf on a dry stretch of the riverbed and wait. “The calf would call its mother, allowing her to identify her baby and come back to take it,” he said.
But there was a problem. Hundreds had gathered to make reels, and the commotion kept the herd away, which hid behind the swathe of tall wild grass growing along the riverbank. The calf kept coming back to its rescuers as it felt safe, said Mr. Raj. Moments later, it began calling for its mother from a distance. The mother responded and emerged, sauntering towards the calf and letting out a loud rumble before enveloping it in her trunk.
Mudit Kumar, the DFO of Baikunthapur Division, termed the two-hour operation a “beautiful story of rescue and reunion” and lauded the local fishermen and the forest team.
Local heroes
Back in their village, the five fishermen were being hailed as heroes. The videos had gone viral, and local NGOs had been prompt to felicitate them. Surrounded by villagers at a daily evening adda, where the day’s topic was the brief social media fame of the five rescuers, Mr. Das told The Hindu that this was not their first rescue effort.
“We have been coordinating with the forest department and have rescued elephant calves and deer. We live next to the Teesta and spend our entire day there, fishing,” said Mr. Das, who is also the secretary of the Uttarbanga Matsyajibi Forum.
While the Forest Department praised the five fishermen's “courage, local knowledge, boating skills, and timely assistance,” Mr. Das said they had limitations. “We operate a small dinghy and don’t have life jackets. While we will go to any extent to save a life, we urge the government to help us,” he said.

While the hindbrain may form a distinct fate first, most of the volume of the mature brain (pink) comes from the forebrain.
Credit:
KATERYNA KON/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY
While the hindbrain may form a distinct fate first, most of the volume of the mature brain (pink) comes from the forebrain.
Credit:
KATERYNA KON/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY
Late last week, we started seeing headlines about how new research was suggesting we might have two brains instead of the one that seems to show up on MRI scans. As is so often the case, these rumors can be traced back to a single press release put out by one of the universities where the work was done.
You do not have two brains. It’s a silly way to look at the results of the new paper.
But there are far better ways to look at the results, ways that can help us understand how the brain gets put together and illustrate some of the general ideas behind developmental biology. So let’s take a look at what the research actually shows and place it in the context of brain development.
Where are you?
You may think body segments are something that show up in things like crustaceans and insects. But our nervous system also develops in segments. Vertebrates have four major ones: the forebrain, midbrain, hindbrain, and spinal cord. (Some of these later develop segments within them, but we’ll skip over those.) The new paper is largely focused on providing part of the answer to an obvious question: how do those segments get there?
That sort of question is the bread and butter of developmental biology, a field that focuses on how organisms start off as a single cell and, through a series of carefully timed and choreographed processes, produce all the tissues found in adults.
To think about the question, we need a bit of context. By the time the first cells that are committed to develop into neurons show up, the vertebrate embryo already knows its head from its tail, and its back from its belly. (We won’t go into how the embryo learns that, but we know a lot about that, too.) The embryo consists of three tissues at the time: the endoderm, which will line our guts, the mesoderm, which will form muscles and bone, and the ectoderm, which will go on to form the skin.
Neural cells form as a thickening of the ectoderm that runs down the center of the embryo from head to tail. The center of these thickly packed cells drops down, while the sides fold up, eventually forming an oval-shaped tube that pinches off from the rest of the ectoderm. All the signals that run up your spine, every sound and shape you process, every thought you will ever have—all of these and more depend on the descendants of these cells.
A section across a vertebrate embryo as development proceeds. At first, there’s nothing on top but ectoderm. At the center of the left-right axis of the embryo, the ectoderm thickens and adopts a neural fate (upper right). The neural precursors then start shifting in a way that causes them to adopt a deep V shape (lower right). This process eventually brings the two ends of the developing neural tissue together, and they merge, forming a tube (lower left).
Credit:
JOHN TIMMER
A section across a vertebrate embryo as development proceeds. At first, there’s nothing on top but ectoderm. At the center of the left-right axis of the embryo, the ectoderm thickens and adopts a neural fate (upper right). The neural precursors then start shifting in a way that causes them to adopt a deep V shape (lower right). This process eventually brings the two ends of the developing neural tissue together, and they merge, forming a tube (lower left).
Credit:
JOHN TIMMER
(While this is being presented as a sort of “how vertebrates develop,” there are key differences among them. In mice, the formation of neural tissue happens nearly simultaneously along the entire head-to-tail dimension. In chickens, the process starts in the head and moves slowly to the tail, such that there are already brain structures forming at a time when some of what will be the spinal cord doesn’t even know it will be a nerve cell yet. And tadpoles form a fairly simple spinal cord that gets expanded and reorganized as they change into frogs. So, while the general process is similar in all vertebrates, many species have adapted it to different styles of development.)
By all appearances, all these newly formed neural cells look more or less the same. So we end up back at the original question: how do the segments of the nervous system form?
Remember that, by the time these cells start forming, the embryo already knows its head from its tail. That raises two very simple possibilities. One is that the ectoderm cells that the nerve cells form from already know where they are, and so the nerve cells inherit positional information from them. The alternative is that after the neural cells form, their non-neural neighbors can send signals to them to tell them where they are. So if cells in the head make a different collection of signaling molecules from those in the tail, this can transfer positional information to the developing nervous system, telling it where to form the brain and where to form the spinal cord.
Dividing up the brain
The new work builds on decades of studies that have identified many key regulators of early processes. One of those earlier findings was that the ectoderm of the early embryo activates two genes, one in the front half of the embryo, one in the back. So nerve cells can inherit at least some crude positional information from the ectoderm they form from.
The key to this work is that the researchers modified a copy of these genes so that it activated fluorescent proteins wherever the gene was translated into a protein. So, they engineered mice where half of the early ectoderm glowed red, and the other half glowed cyan. These colors were maintained as the embryo formed nerve cells and the cells started to develop into the brain.
They found that while the hindbrain glowed red, the rest of the brain glowed blue. The inherited positional information set up one of the key boundaries in the brain. In other words, as soon as cells know they’re going to eventually develop into neurons, they know whether they can potentially form part of the hindbrain and not the mid- or forebrain. (This is, roughly, where the idea of “two brains” in the press release comes from.)
Other experiments expanded on this. Similar genetic tools let them activate a fluorescent protein in individual cells in the early ectoderm. They found that, in 96 percent of the cases, the descendants of these single cells were all in the hindbrain, or all in the midbrain and forebrain. They also worked with human stem cells and showed similar things were happening there: Exposure to the right signals would tell the stem cells where they were, and the nerve cells inherited that information as they formed. If you wanted to form neurons that are only found in the hindbrain, you have to first send the stem cells down the hindbrain path.
Early cell labeling shows that the hindbrain and spinal cord (red) remain a separate fate from the midbrain and forebrain (cyan).
Credit:
Jokhai et. al.
Early cell labeling shows that the hindbrain and spinal cord (red) remain a separate fate from the midbrain and forebrain (cyan).
Credit:
Jokhai et. al.
There obviously may still be some flexibility here—the 96 percent exclusive behavior they saw is not 100 percent. It’s not clear whether that’s a limitation of their experimental system or just a product of the fact that cells at the border between the front and back of the ectoderm can change fates if they wander a bit in the right direction. Things happen very quickly in early development, and it’s also not clear how the timing of what we can see compares to the timing of what’s going on with the genes that were used to mark different cells.
It’s also less certain what’s going on at the other key borders. Differences between the mid- and forebrain seem to arise later, and largely due to the action of signaling molecules that diffuse through the developing brain and provide positional information. In contrast, very little is known about how the hindbrain and spinal cord adopt different fates; the new paper cites only one reference on the topic. That reference suggests they are also separate fates very early in development, but it seems that more work needs to be done there.
Why does any of this matter?
Obviously, the different areas of our brain and the spinal cord go on to form very different structures, which later perform very different functions. So forming these segments is important. But it’s also important that the different identities get established early—in fact, it’s essential to their ability to develop so differently.
There are two key reasons for this. The first is that having a different identity allows cells to respond to the same signal in different ways. For example, early on when it’s a relatively simple tube, pretty much the entire nervous system is exposed to the same two signals: a molecule called sonic hedgehog diffuses from the bottom of the tube, and a group of molecules called BMPs from the top.
You might expect that, since all the cells of the tube are neural precursors, they’d respond to the same signals in the same ways. But they don’t. Instead, their segment identity directs these signals into overlapping sets of responses that differ in the different areas of the brain. In other words, when midbrain cells see BMPs, they respond in different ways than the cells of the spinal cord do. By dividing the nervous system up early, cells inherit a developmental history that allows a limited number of signals to trigger a great deal of complexity.
(The way that developmental history changes how things are interpreted also enables the signals to be recycled. BMPs initially tell cells whether to develop as neurons or not. Later, they tell developing neurons what identity to adopt once the neuron matures. Later still, BMPs help direct the migration of mature neurons in the developing spine. We don’t have to evolve entirely new signaling systems in order to do different things.)
The other thing is that the junction between segments can be a distinct environment, one where cells are exposed to influences from both of the neighboring identities. At the midbrain-hindbrain boundary, for example, cells activate a distinct set of genes that include signaling molecules that go on to influence the development of the neighboring tissues on both sides of the boundary. As you’d expect from the above, these signals made at the border trigger different responses in the midbrain and hindbrain, since those two segments have different developmental histories.
While the new work says nothing about how many brains you actually have (it’s one with several distinct regions within it), it provides another piece for the puzzle of how the incredible complexity of our brains gets generated from a flat sheet of cells that, just a few hours before, would have happily developed into our skin instead. And it provides a great window into how organismal development works in general and the sorts of experiments we can do to help however many brains we have understand these processes.

Amid protests, the Arunachal Pradesh State Cabinet on Wednesday (September 23, 2026) adopted a resolution approving the constitution of an Empowered High-Level Committee “to guide and coordinate” the pre-feasibility report survey and associated activities for the proposed Siang Upper Multipurpose Project or SUMP.
Villagers along the Siang River belt are resisting the pre-feasibility report for the project, which will generate an estimated 11,000 megawatts (MW) or more of hydroelectricity. Two of the project’s three designated sites are in Siang district, and one is in Upper Siang district.
The State Cabinet, headed by Chief Minister Pema Khandu, noted that the Union government had declared SUMP to be a national project in 2008, underlining its strategic significance for the country. It also noted that the project could strengthen water and energy security, help mitigate floods in the Siang-Brahmaputra basin, generate employment, and support long-term socio-economic development of the Siang region.
“The resolution reflects the State government’s continuing commitment to ensuring that the survey is carried out in a transparent, peaceful, and people-centric manner,” a statement from the Chief Minister’s Office said.
The Cabinet underlined concerns raised by some sections of the people in Siang and Upper Siang districts “regarding misinformation and disinformation” being spread by certain vested interests. It resolved that conducting the pre-feasibility report peacefully depended on sustained, meaningful engagement with the residents of these two districts.
“The voices, welfare, and aspirations of the likely project-affected families and local communities have always been, and will always remain, central to the process,” the State Cabinet said.
Meanwhile, local authorities organised a series of interactive school exhibitions on the SUMP, involving 640 students across four schools in Siang district. “The exhibitions formed part of a targeted educational outreach initiative to foster awareness about river management, sustainable hydropower, and the SUMP among students in Rumgong, Kaying and Pessing villages that may be affected by the project,” an official statement said.
The Centre and State governments have defended the SUMP, insisting it was needed to counter the 60,000 MW project China is constructing on the Yarlung Tsangpo in Tibet.
The Yarlung Tsangpo flows into Arunachal Pradesh as the Siang, which meets two other rivers — Dibang and Lohit — to form the Brahmaputra in Assam.

Greetings from Edinburgh, where a cheeky tour guide makes art history hilarious
Growing up, I had a knack for getting distracted on school field trips to museums and art galleries.
Could I be blamed?
Teachers marched us through halls of what felt like the same Baroque painting over and over. Endless soft bodies painted against pale blue skies, their stories offered up with little explanation.
It didn't feel like any of it was meant to be fun.
Then I discovered Coco, the self-described "time-traveling tart."
The brainchild and alter ego of comedian Max Norman, Coco — 6 foot 7 without heels — leads interactive and (mostly) factual tours through galleries in London and beyond.
During the Edinburgh Fringe Festival last month, she made her way to the National Galleries of Scotland for what was billed as a "cheeky romp" uncovering the "gossip, glamour and glorious absurdity hiding behind the art."
Gloriously absurd it was.
Coco had us curtsy before paintings of kings and queens of Great Britain's past, then treated us to lessons about the indulgences and insecurities that made them feel all too human.
We played dead on the floor in a lesson about the fall of the Jacobites in 18th century Scotland (let's just say swords are no match for guns).
Then we all eagerly galloped like horses from one gallery room to the next. I do not remember why — which may have been the point.
Norman created Coco as "revenge" on his artist mother, who used to drag him through art galleries across London.
For anyone who spent their own childhood staring blankly at an Old Master while waiting for someone (anyone!) to make it interesting, Coco feels less like revenge — and more like justice.

DoorDash will pay $131.5 million to settle a New York City probe into its pay practices for delivery workers. The company said the agreement will result in payments to more than 260,000 Dashers. The company also acknowledged that between April 2022 and June 2026, some employees were underpaid or paid late.
More than $115 million of the settlement will go directly to workers, while the remainder will cover civil penalties and other costs. The settlement also resolves a dispute over how DoorDash calculated pay for time workers spent logged into the app between deliveries. The company has apologised and said it has fixed the technical issues that led to the payment errors.
DoorDash admits payment mistakes
DoorDash acknowledged the problems in a statement announcing the settlement and said the errors were not intentional but still unacceptable.
In a blog post, the company wrote, "Simply put, we screwed up. Our mistakes meant some Dashers were underpaid or paid late. While these mistakes weren't intentional, that doesn't make them okay. We pride ourselves on operational excellence at DoorDash - and this was not excellent, nor was it acceptable. 
Dashers should be paid in full, on time, every time. We are sorry to the Dashers we let down."
According to DoorDash, around 264,000 Dashers will receive payments, including about 209,000 for missing or late payments. The company said around $6.6 million in payments never reached workers, while another $5.7 million arrived days or, in some cases, weeks late.
The average missing payment was $7.70, while 65% of affected Dashers were underpaid by $1 or less. The company said the median settlement payment will be around $48.
$83 million of settlement covers pay calculation dispute
Not all of the $131.5 million settlement relates to missing or late payments. DoorDash said $12.3 million will cover Dashers who were underpaid or paid late, while more than $83 million resolves a disagreement with New York City over how to calculate pay for online or on-call time.
This refers to periods when a Dasher is logged into the app and available for work but is not actively completing a delivery. DoorDash said it used a different method to calculate this time and maintained that its approach was fair, practical and legal. Rather than continue the dispute, the company agreed to use the city's calculation method going forward.
The remaining $16.7 million will go to the city's Department of Consumer and Worker Protection as fines and other costs.
DoorDash blames technical and complex delivery issues
DoorDash said some of the payment errors were caused by technical bugs and complicated delivery situations. These included trips crossing city boundaries, deliveries involving multiple pickup or drop-off locations and orders that were partially completed or cancelled.
The company also said some payment problems stemmed from incomplete or inaccurate banking information provided by Dashers. DoorDash said less than 1% of all payments to its New York City Dashers were affected.
"We’ve addressed the issues that caused these errors and made changes to prevent them from happening again,” DoorDash highlighted.
The company said it has strengthened its compliance programme and improved validation of banking information to identify potential payment problems before they result in missed payments.
Workers to receive payments without filing claims
The settlement covers workers identified through the city's analysis of DoorDash records, so eligible Dashers do not need to file a claim or submit evidence to receive their payments. Workers will be contacted directly with payment details. DoorDash said affected workers will receive at least $10, even when the amount they were originally underpaid was lower.
New York City officials said more than $115 million will be distributed directly to workers. The city has also established a monitoring programme under which DoorDash will provide detailed monthly data for three years to help officials check compliance with payment rules.
The settlement follows New York City's introduction of a minimum pay rate for app-based delivery workers. The current rate is $22.13 per hour, excluding tips. DoorDash added its Dashers in New York City have earned more than $1 billion since the city's pay standard took effect in 2023, with average pay before tips at roughly $30 per active hour.

Deepina Pal, 26, has been living with chronic kidney disease since she was 16 and has been on dialysis for nine years. She takes about 10–12 different kinds of medicines every day for multiple autoimmune and other chronic conditions, including medicines for blood pressure, cholesterol, thyroid and heart conditions, as well as migraine and other problems. Some need to be taken three times a day.
She sets alarms and records her medicines on her phone. When she was first prescribed medication for blood pressure, she became extremely drowsy and slept for long periods. Her family later understood that her blood pressure was falling. For people on dialysis, regular blood tests can lead to changes in medication.
Deepina’s experience reveals an important factor when it comes to taking many medications: the number of medicines does not, by itself, mean that treatment is inappropriate. The safety concern is whether every medicine remains necessary, effective and suitable as a person’s health changes.
Multiple conditions, several medicines
Polypharmacy is generally described as the regular use of five or more medicines; the use of 10 or more is often termed hyperpolypharmacy. It is particularly common among older people living with multiple chronic conditions, although complex treatment regimens can occur at any age.
A review of 27 studies involving 11,649 older adults in India found pooled rates of polypharmacy and hyperpolypharmacy of 49% and 31%, respectively.
“Not every case of polypharmacy is inappropriate,” says S. Manicka Saravanan, consultant, geriatric medicine, Apollo Hospitals, Greams Road, Chennai. A person living with diabetes, hypertension and heart disease, for example may need several medicines. The concern only arises when medicines no longer have a clear benefit, duplicate one another, interact adversely or create a treatment burden that outweighs their benefit.
The World Health Organization identifies medication safety in polypharmacy as one of its priority areas under its Medication Without Harm initiative.
The risks
Smitha Jain, consultant, internal medicine, SIMS Hospital, Chennai, says problems can arise when medicines prescribed by different specialists are considered separately rather than as one treatment plan.
A patient may inadvertently receive duplicate medicines, particularly when several doctors prescribe for different conditions. Drug combinations can also cause harm. Some medicines used in heart failure or for blood pressure can affect potassium and kidney function; antifungal drugs can interact with anti-epileptic medicines, while some combinations can increase blood-thinner levels and the risk of bleeding.
Taking an extra dose can also be dangerous. An additional diabetes medicine may cause hypoglycaemia, while missing certain medicines, such as anti-epileptic drugs, can trigger seizures.
Older adults are particularly vulnerable because age-related changes, kidney or liver impairment, frailty, cognitive problems and multiple illnesses can alter how medicines are handled by the body. Side effects such as low blood pressure, low sodium, dizziness and confusion can increase the risk of falls.
Review and safety checks
A medication review should ask why each medicine was started, whether it is still needed, whether the dose remains appropriate, and whether there are side effects or interactions, says Dr. Saravanan. Kidney and liver function, nutrition, cognition, mobility, falls risk, cost and difficulties with swallowing or complex timings should also be considered.
Doctors recommend that patients bring all their medicines to appointments, a “brown bag” review can uncover duplicate prescriptions as well as over-the-counter, herbal or alternative products that doctors may not know about.
An updated medication list should be shared between specialists, particularly after hospitalisation or a change in treatment. Pharmacists can also help identify interactions and dosing problems. Pill organisers and alarms may reduce missed or repeated doses.
Some medicines may eventually be reduced or stopped when their benefits no longer outweigh their risks. This process, known as deprescribing, should be done carefully and not by stopping medicines abruptly. Electronic prescribing systems can flag some interactions and duplicate medicines, but clinical judgement remains the most important.
The aim is not simply to reduce the number of medicines, but to ensure that each one has a clear purpose and that the overall treatment remains safe as the patient’s circumstances change.

The story so far: The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) summoned Meta officials for a hearing on Wednesday (September 9, 2026) as a part of an inquiry on child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM) on Instagram. An investigation by British public broadcaster BBC threw up many ads that linked out to CSEAM on other platforms. The IT Ministry has also summoned the company on the issue.
What did the BBC investigation show?
In July, BBC reported that the organisation saw dozens of ads promoting CSEAM on Instagram with a test account. CSEAM is banned around the world, and attracts strict criminal penalties. Meta said in a statement, “Before these cases were brought to our attention, our enforcement systems had already identified and disabled several of the violating ads and the accounts behind them.”
Also Read: Google to report child abuse content directly to Indian authorities
The company said that it automatically removes millions of CSAM posting accounts each year, but that “no system is perfect and that determined criminals will continue to try to exploit our platform”. This month, the Tech Transparency Project reported that it found hundreds of CSAM ads on Facebook and Instagram, including some that were served to India.
Why are CSEAM ads appearing on Instagram?
While social media platforms prohibit CSEAM, automatic moderation systems, that use some AI to detect unlawful media, are not able to catch all violative submissions. The Tech Transparency Project, a US-based nonprofit, said that what Meta was doing was not enough even within the scope of what it could. The nonprofit said that even in cases where Meta was taking down CSEAM, it was tagging the ads as adult sexual content, and so “may be undercounting instances of child sexual abuse”.
While the firm revised this information for ads reported by TTP, “did not fix the flow of child exploitation content in its advertising system,” and continued to show CSEAM ads to certain audiences, the nonprofit said. One of the ads appeared to feature an unidentified “underaged European royal,” TTP said.
Amusing or addictive? The algorithms powering our social feeds
Many such ads were placed by “resellers” for ad spots on Meta’s platforms based in China, who account for billions of dollars of ad revenue. TTP pointed to a Reuters report that indicated that ads going through this channel were subject to a more relaxed enforcement regime, where the platform earned $18 billion in 2024. This channel is intended for Chinese firms who want to advertise to overseas customers.
Even with a human reporting CSEAM posts, action was not guaranteed, TTP found. “With 57% (73) of the CSAM ads reported to Meta, the company sent back a message that said, “We’ve taken a look and found that this ad doesn’t go against our Advertising Standards”,”, TTP said.
What was NCPCR’s reaction to the report?
NCPCR issued a notice on July 3, the same day the BBC report came out, demanding an explanation from the company. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) also sought an explanation from the company.
Shortly after Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s July 23 video message to Indian youth was briefly removed from Facebook due to an “error,” MeitY summoned Meta’s global public affairs director Joel Kaplan to demand an explanation on that removal. In that meeting, the BBC reporting was also discussed. The summoning came as the government sent a massive volume of takedown notices for Instagram posts on the Jantar Mantar protests, and footage from the protests and the ensuing police crackdown went viral.
Meta provided written responses to both MeitY and NCPCR. The latter declined a Right to Information request by The Hindu for a copy of the company’s response, arguing that providing this information would impede its investigation.
After the written response, Meta officials were summoned by NCPCR this month. Neither side provided a description of the meeting.
What powers does NCPCR have to conduct an inquiry like this?
Like the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), the NCPCR’s founding law, the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005, gives the body the powers of a civil court under the Criminal Procedure Code (replaced recently by the Bhartiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita Bill, 2023).
As such, it has the statutory power to demand explanations on issues of child safety from private organisations and can demand reports from law enforcement.
NCPCR’s remit includes “matters relating to children in need of special care and protection including children in distress,marginalized and disadvantaged children, children in conflict with law, juveniles, children without family and children of prisoners and recommend appropriate remedial measures,” and to “[i]nquire into complaints [relating to] non implementation of laws providing for protection and development of children,” the commission said.
NCPCR has in the past issued notices to firms like Netflix in response to the show Bombay Begums, and to Bourn Vita maker Mondelez over sugar content in their malt powder.
