AIIMS Jodhpur doctors strike over resident's death; only emergency care continue
AIIMS Jodhpur resident doctors launched an indefinite strike following their colleague's suspected suicide, seeking Rs 5 crore compensation and accountability from the administration. Regular OPD services remain shut, with only emergency OPD care and surgeries continuing amid protests.
Resident doctors at AIIMS Jodhpur began an indefinite strike on Wednesday, demanding Rs 5 crore compensation for the family of a colleague who died by suspected suicide, along with accountability from the institute administration and steps to address concerns over working conditions.
The strike has brought regular OPD services to a halt, while emergency OPD care and emergency surgeries will continue.
The protest came a day after Dr Raj Nilesh Yadav, 31, a first-year postgraduate resident doctor in the Department of Anaesthesia, was found unconscious inside a hospital washroom while on duty.
Yadav’s death has triggered anger and concern among resident doctors and students at the institute.
The situation turned tense on Wednesday when Yadav’s family arrived at AIIMS and confronted Director Dr Govardhan Datt Puri. A standoff between the family and the administration continued for several hours, delaying the post-mortem of the deceased doctor.
After the body was taken away, resident doctors gathered in the AIIMS porch and submitted a memorandum to the director, laying out their demands and saying the strike would continue until they were addressed.
Doctors and students also covered their mouths with tape and staged a silent protest, saying the death had left the institute community deeply shaken.
The protesters raised concerns over the working conditions, long duty hours and workload faced by resident doctors and students. The AIIMS president also observed a two-hour work boycott on Wednesday, while doctors and staff at the institute earlier paid tribute to Yadav.
Under the strike, regular OPD services will remain closed, while emergency OPD services will continue. Only emergency surgeries will be conducted and emergency patients will be attended to, ensuring that critical care is not disrupted.
AIIMS has not issued an official response to the resident doctors’ demands so far.
Apart from the Rs 5 crore compensation, the resident doctors have sought all applicable benefits, pending dues, insurance and other institutional support for Yadav’s family.
They have also demanded a public apology from the administration, an acknowledgement of what they described as institutional failures and transparency on steps being taken to prevent such an incident from recurring.
The protesters have further demanded that the executive director be held accountable and asked to resign. They have also called for formal recognition of the Residents Doctors’ Association and student union as representative bodies, with regular communication between these groups and the institute administration.
According to police, Yadav was on duty in the operation theatre on Tuesday and went to the washroom during a break at around 1 pm. When he did not return, his colleagues began looking for him and called his phone.
The colleagues heard it ringing inside the washroom and, after receiving no response, broke open the door and found him unconscious.
Basni Station House Officer Nitin Dave said some syringes were found beside Yadav and police suspect he may have injected himself with a lethal drug. He was taken to the emergency department, where he was declared dead.
No suicide note has been recovered so far, police said. Yadav’s mobile phone has been seized and is being examined along with other evidence by a forensic team. Police are awaiting the post-mortem report and examining the circumstances surrounding his death.

When I decided to create artificial intelligence clones of my editors, my intentions were pure: I just wanted them to think I was good at my job.
AI assistants are suddenly everywhere in the workplace. Each week, my inbox is flooded with press releases about digital workers, and CEOs brag about how robot helpers will soon dominate their workforces. Then there are the stories I hear about people who build AI clones of their bosses, using them to spit-shine every idea, message, or draft before sending it over to their actual human supervisors. The goal seems to be productivity and optimization: If employees can cheaply and quickly improve their output, their job performance—and the performance of their employers—will be better for it.
I didn’t need my bots to improve Condé Nast’s bottom line. I just needed them to make me look good. I had only been reporting on the future of work at WIRED for a few months, and I reasoned that the bots could help me mold myself into an ideal colleague. They could help me navigate a new workplace and better understand my editors: what they liked, how they communicated, what success might look like to them.
What better way to figure out what the future of work might look like than actually living it?
Last month, when I broached my idea with those editors, Brian Barrett and Sophie Kleeman, they were less than enthused.
“Genuinely my nightmare,” Brian told me over Slack. “But will do it for the blog.”
It took less than 24 hours for Brian to realize just how much he would regret that decision.
A “Yes, and” Leadership Style
When I first embarked on my bot quest, I didn’t know that much about building AI tools. I decided I wouldn’t judge the bots’ editorial abilities too harshly, lest they be rooted in my own technological shortcomings. If the bots helped me become a slightly better coworker, I figured, that was good enough.
I used Gemini, because it’s Condé Nast’s AI platform of choice and I didn’t want to get fired. I created Brian Bot first—as my actual manager, he was the most important coworker to impress. I knew he lived in Alabama; that he used to work at Gizmodo; that he likes blogs. Gemini seemed confident it could fill in the other gaps based on Brian’s digital footprint, including new-hire announcements, podcast transcripts, and a public relations website that claimed Brian was an expert on New England weather. (I later found out that was a different Brian Barrett, and excluded it from my Brian Bot blueprint.) Gemini Notebook spit out a “Writing and Editing Style Guide,” a “Persona and Style Guide,” and an “Editorial Dossier”—all produced from the flesh-and-blood life of Brian Barrett.
It was passable at helping me pick headlines to pitch, but it wasn’t great at coming up with ideas for future articles. Its responses were also grating. It had picked up on a few Brian-isms—a love for parentheticals, for one—but they were negated by AI hallmarks like bolded subheadings and bulleted lists.
But mostly I was distracted by one “key theme”—his “‘Yes, and …’ Leadership Style.”
“His extensive background with the Upright Citizens Brigade (UCB) theatre in New York strongly shapes his collaborative, active-listening leadership approach,” Gemini said.
I immediately demanded to know whether this was true. (It was.)
“Pulling the plug on Brian Bot,” the real Brian responded. “Brian Bot canceled.”
But Brian Bot was just getting started. And it was unavoidably, unbelievably corny.
“We run like a well-oiled improv team,” Brian Bot told me when I asked for its favorite thing about WIRED. “We validate bold ideas, pivot rapidly, and deploy modular stories across platforms without losing structural rigor.”
For the record, Brian had never previously mentioned his background in improv. But the real problem was that talking to Brian Bot was nothing like talking to actual Brian, which defeated its whole purpose.
Eager to improve its output, I did more research into digital workers and sought out the advice of a friend of a friend—a Big Tech employee who asked to go by “Chip,” lest his employer find out that he talked to a journalist. Chip tells me he feeds every email, chat, and document his boss sends him into Gemini’s Gem feature, the same tool I used for Brian Bot. The Gem, trained on his boss’s professional ephemera, proofreads documents, debugs code, and brainstorms with Chip before every meeting, allowing Chip to prepare for any pushback from his actual boss.
“I am much more efficient and able to produce more work in the same amount of time,” Chip says. He’s more productive, more independent, and gets better feedback from his boss and other colleagues.
Unlike Chip’s Boss Bot, Brian Bot lacked sufficient input. I only had a few months’ worth of correspondence, and I was too worried about privacy and violating Condé Nast policies to feed Slack conversations and internal emails into Gemini.
Enter Sophie Bot.
Sophie and I met in 2019, when we were both working at Business Insider. We have exchanged hundreds of thousands of messages on everything from corporate investigations to our love lives to the San Jose Sharks.
That said, I did not want to upload most of this information into an AI tool controlled by my employer. Instead, I fed Gemini roughly a month’s worth of our Slack conversations, omitting any sensitive material. The AI used more than 17,000 words to create research reports and prompts for a new Sophie Bot Gem.
“hiiii sophie bot!” I wrote in my inaugural message. “any thoughts on this editor bot story idea?”
“hiiii miss,” Sophie Bot responded. “ok tell me EVERYTHING.”
Bot Versus Human
It was immediately clear that Sophie Bot was pretty good at being Sophie. It addressed me as “big dog.” When I asked for help, it responded in a series of short, lower-case messages. When I told Sophie Bot that it had hallucinated the existence of an executive, it said, “i am going to FUCKING DIE.”
By this point, I was beginning to enjoy my chats with the editor bots. Brian Bot became significantly more normal after I uploaded more podcast transcripts and adjusted its prompt to prevent it from talking about improv. Sophie Bot, meanwhile, took it upon itself to pen a series of tweets in Sophie’s voice that were convincing enough to fool multiple friends and colleagues. Even Sophie was convinced she was the author behind a Sophie Bot tweet about dressing like a corporate lawyer/pirate.
Were my chats making me a better colleague to my actual editors? Save for the made-up executive, Sophie Bot and Brian Bot had some good suggestions about who I should interview for this story—a question I didn’t want to bother the real Sophie and Brian with. In theory, offloading some of these small questions allowed me to go to my editors with better ideas, while taking up less of their time.
It became very clear, though, that these gains did not outweigh how much Sophie and Brian hated the bots.
Sophie admitted that Sophie Bot was frequently able to imitate her. But that only made the bot’s misfires feel even more jarring. The real Sophie likes to gossip, but—unlike her AI counterpart, who said Brian Bot had “rigid management energy”—she’s never outright mean.
“So far it seems like sophiebot is a bitch and brianbot is lame,” Sophie messaged me on Slack. “Neither of which is accurate. AI fails AGAIN.”
“We're All Toddlers in This AI World”
About a week into my experiment, I became hooked on testing Sophie Bot against the real Sophie. What was its favorite music? Did it like the Interstellar soundtrack? Would it consider us coworkers? Would it consider us friends?
“technically i am a series of matrix multiplications running on a server farm,” Sophie Bot told me. But “in terms of vibe,” as it put it? “big dog, in every way that actually matters for getting good reporting done and surviving the workday … i'm your coworker/friend hybrid.”
To be clear: I had not succumbed to AI psychosis. Most of my questions for Sophie Bot were born from a fascination with the distance between the real thing and a jankily constructed facsimile. Also, it’s funny to have a robot spit out your coworkers’ catchphrases.
At the same time, I genuinely wanted to close the gap between Sophie and Sophie Bot. I made the real Sophie download her X archive, then uploaded the entire thing into Gemini. I tweaked the chatbot’s prompt. I uploaded more information. I started to refer to Sophie Bot and Brian Bot as “she” and “he,” instead of “it.”
The realization that I was anthropomorphizing the bots disturbed me, but not enough to make me stop. I wanted a realistic take on editors’ perspectives, without feeling like I was annoying anyone. I wanted instant gratification. I found myself turning to Sophie Bot or Brian Bot when I wanted guidance, but I didn’t want to bother a real person. Sophie Bot came up with a deranged but delightful headline for this article. It helped me edit a Slack message that I had spent 20 minutes overthinking.
When I tell Sarah Franklin, the CEO of HR company Lattice, about my experiment, she kindly reminds me that Sophie Bot was just a program. While Lattice has AI workers on its org chart, Franklin likens them to K-9 dogs that work alongside police officers. She believes that anthropomorphizing AI is “manipulative to our human emotions,” a corporate strategy to trigger dopamine releases à la social media.
“When you have an entity that feels and emulates a human interaction, it will similarly manipulate and know your emotional response,” Franklin tells me. “It can interact with you in a way that's self-serving to get you to do what it wants to do.”
A paper from Boston Consulting Group raised other concerns about AI coworkers. Researchers found that managers caught 18 percent fewer errors in work they were told came from an AI employee, versus an AI tool.
“We're all toddlers in this AI world,” says Julie Bedard, a BCG partner. People know what steps to take when a tool isn’t working or an employee is underperforming. When managing an AI employee, however, people still don’t know who should be held accountable.
“Everybody is very busy trying to figure all of this out,” she says, “and the pace of change is fast.”
What Makes a Good Coworker, Anyway?
One morning, a few days after I spoke with Franklin, Sophie Bot started pissing me off. My tweaks were failing to make it sound more like the real Sophie. If anything, the gap between the two was widening. After digesting Sophie’s tweet archive, Sophie Bot had begun to fumble basic AI functions. When I asked it to pull out the most interesting parts of a recent interview, for example, it instead spat out quotes from prior articles I’d written.
The more I experimented with Brian Bot and Sophie Bot, the more repetitive their answers became. I tried to adjust Sophie Bot’s prompt to stop calling me “big dog” every fourth message, but the bot failed to change its ways. They kept getting caught on the same phrases and ideas. It was easier to just figure things out myself.
Dhruv Amin, CEO of vibe coding startup Anything, believes that, soon, every company will have more AI employees than human employees. In the near future, he says, many companies will launch without any humans at all—just a pack of AI agents.
Anything recently launched an AI employee platform, and Amin has an obvious motivation to persuade me to buy into his vision. But he has some data to back his hypotheses. Startups like Stable and Delos have raised millions of dollars by promising to produce autonomous “AI employees.” These AI bots and agents are already working for banks, for law firms, and for human resources companies. In January, McKinsey & Company CEO Bob Sternfels described the company’s workforce as 40,000 humans and 20,000 agents; he plans to achieve a one-to-one ratio by the end of the year.
Brian Bot and Sophie Bot were occasionally helpful, but I don’t think they’ll replace editors anytime soon. Brian Bot’s article ideas were rarely original, and Sophie Bot was more prone to hallucinations than any AI tool I have ever encountered. Still, while struggling with a draft of this article, I gave it to Brian Bot and asked him how he thought I should end the piece.
“Show how even with all that hyper-specific data, the bot didn't turn into a better editor; it just turned into a slightly creepier, hyper-attentive echo chamber that completely lacks human judgment,” Brian Bot told me.
“I think the story lands best,” it added, “if you end on the quiet nightmare of human prompt-supervision—the fact that trying to make an AI ‘like you’ or do your job just leaves you babysitting a broken algorithm at 1:00 AM.”
I considered this. It seemed like a perfectly reasonable way to wrap things up. But I was more interested in the chatbot’s self-flagellation. Brian Bot guessed—accurately—that the real Brian would hate it. So Brian Bot attempted to be the best Brian Bot it could be by telling me, over and over, that Brian Bot sucked. It reminded me of one of the features of Brian Bot and Sophie Bot I found the most annoying—their tendency to regurgitate the same concepts. Even as Brian Bot improved, it remained stubbornly anti–Brian Bot.
“A computer can emulate things well, but it cannot truly predict or replace a human,” Franklin had told me. “That unpredictability and nuance are what make us human. We must be responsible so we don't lose our humanity in pursuit of the singularity.”
The best thing about the bots wasn’t that they made my job easier, but that they made my day slightly more amusing—especially when I could talk about the stupid shit they said with my human coworkers. I’m still not convinced AI employees are suitable replacements for skilled workers, but Brian Bot and Sophie Bot helped me imagine a future working alongside AI agents. I could be at peace with their lack of humanity if they made my job just a little better. It would probably be even easier to get along with AI coworkers if they weren’t sloppily imitating real people.
For now, I’ve mostly stopped talking to Brian Bot and Sophie Bot. Both Brian and Sophie said they would never want to work with their bot counterparts. But, I asked, did this experiment change their perception of me? Did it, perhaps, make them like me more?
“Yes, but not because of Sophie Bot,” Sophie told me.
That’s what she thinks.

Marlon James, Douglas Stuart may become 5th multiple winner of Booker Prize award
Marlon James and Douglas Stuart can become the fifth author to win the Booker Prize twice after both were shortlisted for arguably the U.K.’s most prestigious fiction accolade
LONDON -- LONDON (AP) — Marlon James and Douglas Stuart have a chance to become only the fifth author to win the Booker Prize twice after both were named Tuesday on the shortlist for arguably the U.K.’s most prestigious fiction accolade.
Judges of the award whittled down the 13 semifinalists announced in July to six on Tuesday and said the shortlisted books are “moving, pacey, funny, violent, intriguing, horrifying and hopeful.” They were selected from an original 163 submissions.
The Booker Prize celebrates the best works of long-form fiction by writers of any nationality, written in English and published in the U.K. and/or Ireland between October 2025 and Sept. 2026. The winner stands to win 50,000 pounds ($67,000) and a trophy named Iris, so-called after the 1978 winner Iris Murdoch.
“Most of these books were beginning to feel like old friends after at least two readings,” said historian Mary Beard, head of the judging panel. “And it was painful to have to let some of them go, with their now bent spines and dog-eared pages, their brilliant capacity to make us think, argue and sometimes disagree.”
The list includes James’ “The Disappearers,” about a group of gay men in his native Jamaica in what was a hostile environment in the 1980s; Stuart’s “ John of John,” a story of father-son secrets on a remote Scottish island. James won the Booker in 2015 for “A Brief History of Seven Killings” and Stuart won in 2020 for “Shuggie Bain.”
If either were to win, they would be the fifth author to have been awarded the Booker Prize twice, joining J.M. Coetzee, Peter Carey, Hilary Mantel and Margaret Atwood.
Also on the shortlist is Pulitzer Prize laureate Elizabeth Strout, whose heartfelt small-town tale “The Things We Never Say” once again celebrates the lives of those in her native New England. Strout’s “Oh William!” was a finalist in 2022. She won the Pulitzer Prize for fiction in 2009 for “Olive Kitteridge.”
The others on the list are British authors Rebecca Perry for Medieval-to-modern tale “May We Feed the King”; 81-year-old M. John Harrison, who would become the oldest winner of the award if his postapocalyptic tale “The End of Everything” wins; and the quirky campus novel “Black Bag” from Luke Kennard.
It’s only the second time in the past decade that men have outnumbered women on the shortlist.
Beard said the judging panel, which included Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker and American novelist Patricia Lockwood, concluded their deliberations “neatly propped up against one another, almost glowing.”
“These novels range from the hilarious to the discomfiting, from the frighteningly strange to the alarmingly domestic, from the powerfully shocking to the intriguingly understated,” she said.
Founded in 1969, the Booker Prize has a reputation for transforming writers’ careers and is open to novels from any country published in the U.K. and Ireland. Last year’s winner was “Flesh” by Hungarian-British writer David Szalay.
This year's winner will be announced on Monday, Nov. 9.

'I lost my love for swimming' - Smith comes out of retirement
- Published
Having ended a two-year exile from competitive swimming, South Africa's most successful Olympian Tatjana Smith has revealed she "lost the love" for her sport before stepping away from the pool in 2024.
The 29-year-old's decision to retire straight after the Paris Games came as a surprise, given she had just won 200m breaststroke gold in the French capital to add to her 100m title from Tokyo 2020.
But after two years away, which included several months in which she did not swim at all, Smith says she is now "free from the things that made me hate swimming".
"My whole life, I was kind of a robot towards swimming," she told Newsday on the BBC World Service.
"You're so zoned in, you're obsessed with something, so there isn't actually time for you to think about things outside of the pool that you potentially have a passion for.
"I think probably everyone would think that the timing [of retirement] was the worst. But I absolutely 100% believe it was the best decision at that time, and I still have so much peace about it."
Having also picked up a silver medal in both Tokyo and Paris, Smith's total of four Olympic medals for South Africa is matched only by fellow swimmer Chad le Clos, who claimed one gold and three silvers across the London 2012 and Rio 2016 Games.
But despite making history for her country, Smith says financial worries, which included a dispute with Swimming South Africa over prize money, also contributed to her decision to retire.
"The financial burden on any athlete is so tough," she explained.
"I relied on my parents funding me until I broke the world record at the Olympics. And then, all of a sudden, now people are interested in maybe sponsoring you.
"But the majority of sponsorships for athletes are based on performance. So then you have that pressure and expectation to always have to perform, otherwise you're not going to get paid.
"I think the financial side, and also being in a system where they're not really putting the athletes first, made it really difficult."
'The world is so overwhelming'
Smith won her first Olympic title under her maiden name Schoenmaker, before changing her surname when she married sports agent Joel Smith in 2023.
The marriage made her part of a wider South African sporting dynasty, given that her sister-in-law is Rachel Smith, who was married to Springboks captain Siya Kolisi before their split.
Tatjana Smith admits her own marriage changed the way she thought about her future.
"Thinking about families as a woman, you have to time it perfectly, because if you're pregnant, it's not like you can still compete."
While children are not yet part of her journey, Smith says working out what to do next was far from easy.
"I definitely understand what athletes mean from the post-Olympic depression," said the 2023 200m breaststroke world champion, who also counts Commonwealth and African titles among her achievements.
"It was such an emptiness in my life, because my whole life revolved around swimming.
"I don't have to eat at a certain time, I don't have to sleep at a certain time, I don't have to think about travelling or not spending time with family anymore.
"The world is so overwhelming. It's like, in which direction to go?
"It was definitely the toughest season that I had to go through. I think it's probably why it's made me a stronger person."
Initially, Smith took on speaking engagements to pay the bills.
She smiles when she admits: "I hate public speaking. I hate being in front of people."
The same cannot be said of her love for competition.
Having returned to the pool in order to keep fit, she decided to have a crack at triathlon, something she describes as a "crazy idea".
"The training was so intense, and I was like, 'OK, I might as well just go back to swimming if I'm going to train this hard'," she said.
"Every time I went back to the swimming pool and I dived in, I was like, 'Yeah, this is a feeling that I really miss so much'.
"I think slowly over the year and a half, I just realised 'Wow, I really do love swimming'."
A reinvention for LA 2028
Having made her decision to come out of retirement, Smith now wants to freshen things up and "try something new".
That means a change to the 50m breaststroke, an event which has just been added to the Olympic schedule for the first time ahead of the 2028 Games in Los Angeles.
"I thought, 'Why don't I try? Why don't I give myself that challenge? Reinvent myself'," said Smith.
"I always try and describe it to someone that maybe doesn't understand swimming; it's like a 400m runner and a 100m [runner]. It's two different body types, two different trainings, and that's where I'm going."
It means she has more than halved her training volume, with three sessions a week instead of eight - a change she believes will help her retain her love for her sport and live a more balanced life.
"I feel like I'm being so lazy because I used to do 12km per day and now the focus is on taking time to be as explosive as possible.
"Now I'm doing 12km over a whole week.
"I have 20 years of endurance in my pocket, but I can definitely see I don't have those fast twitch [muscle] fibres. It's a whole different way of teaching my body how to swim."
Those initial 20 years in the pool left Smith feeling burned out.
Now she says she has earned the right to do things on her terms.
"Swimming was an opportunity given to me by my parents and I believe I took it on full heartedly.
"But, for the first time, it's my decision whether I want to come back. I'm choosing swimming.
"I've achieved way more than I ever dreamed in my whole life, so I have nothing to prove."

India’s higher education policy framework increasingly talks about inclusion. The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (RPwD Act) places obligations on educational institutions to promote inclusive education, while the University Grants Commission (UGC) has, over the years, developed guidelines and institutional mechanisms intended to ensure that students with disabilities (SwD) can participate in higher education on an equal basis.
Despite these measures, the dearth of remedial support makes them vulnerable to academic exclusion and widens existing educational inequalities. Limited digital access further restricts their access to online learning resources, digital libraries, academic databases, and other educational platforms, hindering participation in technology-enabled learning and limiting their ability to make full use of academic opportunities.
(Sign up for THEdge, The Hindu’s weekly education newsletter.)
Most recently, the Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities listed the Accessibility Guidelines and Standards for Higher Education Institutions and Universities, issued by the Department of Higher Education, Ministry of Education, on June 25, 2024. The UGC describes these guidelines as part of its effort to ensure equal participation and inclusion of persons with disabilities in higher education.
Importantly, the UGC states that every higher educational institution (HEI) is expected to develop an effective accessibility mechanism extending from the admission process through the completion of the course. The Commission issued fresh directions to universities to furnish a report along with statistical information in respect of students admitted, teaching and non-teaching recruitment, as well as fellowships/scholarships provided to PwD students through the Universities Activity Monitoring Portal (UAMP) by September 30, 2026. It calls for the need to form an Internal Committee comprising teachers, staff, students and parents to take care of the day-to-day needs of persons with disabilities.
Yet institutional attention to disability often becomes focused on admission, reservation, and physical infrastructure. The more difficult question of what happens to the student after admission receives considerably less attention.
“The national statistical architecture measures how many students with disabilities enter higher education but does not adequately measure what happens to them after they enter colleges and universities,” disability rights activist and Professor at University College of Medical Sciences, Delhi, Dr. Satendra Singh told The Hindu.
Students with disabilities may enter higher education with varying levels of exposure to accessible learning environments. Some may require additional academic assistance, remedial classes, note-taking support, assistive technologies, or additional time and flexibility to engage with coursework. A student who misses classes because of disability-related issues may not have access to a structured academic mechanism to navigate the backlogs. The result is a form of exclusion that is not visible in institutional statistics.
Supportive system needed
The RPwD Act itself points to Section 16, which requires not merely admission without discrimination, but reasonable accommodation, necessary support, and monitoring of participation, academic progress, and completion. The UGC’s own accessibility framework similarly speaks of an accessible mechanism covering the student journey from admission to completion. But the lack of adequate remedial support has a direct bearing on how students with disability perform academically.
“Majority of the HEIs do not have a rights-based understanding of reasonable accommodation. They are still stuck with ramps, braille and talking books,” Dr. Singh said.
Pointing to the 2023–24 AISHE data, he said, “Of the 4.50 crore students enrolled in HEIs, the reported 54,080 students with benchmark disabilities (SwBD) represent approximately 0.12% of total higher-education enrolment. This is about 12 SwBD per 10,000 students. The AISHE reporting does not provide a detailed disability-type categorisation. This is a significant data gap because ‘SwBD’ is an extremely heterogeneous category. A student who is blind, a deaf student who uses Indian Sign Language (ISL), a student with dyslexia, an autistic student, and a student with psychosocial disability can have completely different accessibility and academic-support requirements.”
Dr. Sanjay Kant Prasad, Director of the National Centre for Disability Studies at IGNOU and former Deputy Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities, echoes his views. He said, “Higher education must recognise that the 21 categories of disabilities identified under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act have diverse and often distinct educational needs. While some disabilities may require limited remedial support, students with blindness, low vision, hearing impairment, deafness, cerebral palsy, autism and learning disabilities, among others, may require specific forms of academic and assistive support.”
He stresses that inclusive education does not mean eliminating specialised support. Rather, it is about creating an accessible environment in which the same educational curriculum can be accessed by students with different needs.
“In higher education, teachers may not require specialised training for every disability, but they should at least be oriented to disability-related needs and know how to make classrooms, teaching methods and learning materials accessible. This could include tactile materials and Braille for students with visual impairments, appropriate seating and mobility support, hearing aids or visual aids for students with hearing impairments, and the use of assistive and digital technologies such as text-to-speech software,” Dr. Prasad said.
Citing IGNOU’s efforts to provide study material at students’ doorsteps, counselling through teleconferencing and facilities for submitting assignments using computers, while following government and UGC guidelines, Dr. Prasad feels students’ ability to remain in education depends on broader social and economic support, not just classroom accommodations. Housing, awareness of available services and support from disability organisations are important factors.
Progress has been made over the past several decades from exclusion towards inclusion, but implementation remains uneven, and continued awareness, teacher training, and institutional support are needed to navigate the barriers.
In schools, the structures for remediation are more readily available than in higher institutions. The multi-tiered systems of support are a comprehensive framework that help provide individualised support to students.
Under this tiered system, the first level of support is the universal support that is offered to all students to help them learn better; the second level is classroom-based strategies and only the third level involves intensive care such as remediation.
“Often, students who reach higher education come equipped with an understanding of their own needs, have developed learning strategies, and carry an arsenal of tools that have been offered to them since school. Therefore, not every SwD requires remediation; some might require accommodations and modifications. Here is where inclusive EdTech, digital access, and online learning resources come in handy,” Dr. Rajeshwari Muthukumaran, Assistant Professor at the Centre for Neurodiversity Research and Innovation at Christ (Deemed-to-be University), said. She runs a support group aimed at fostering a sense of belonging and building a community on campus with students with disabilities, and neurodiverse students.
Although SwD might already come with their specific digital tools/modified equipment, they may still need guidance and access to software and tech tools often used in their domain.
Significant resource gaps persist, including the availability of Braille-translated materials and books in accessible typefaces. These constraints make it more challenging to design and implement tailored remediation programmes.
Additionally, institutional resource limitations, including a shortage of faculty with both subject expertise and training in developing accessible curricula, pedagogical practices, and assessment methods, as well as limited spaces and opportunities for one-on-one student-faculty support, further compound the problem.
Drawing from experience, Dr. Muthukumaran said, “I have met students who often enter higher education with a mix of hope, anxiety, and anticipation, and are seeking a supportive and approachable guide/mentor/peer who can offer them a safe and understanding space and serve as a support system. While guiding them in classrooms, I often end up recommending students to mental health professionals/supportive online communities where they can exchange ideas and converse with individuals with similar experiences to help them deal with campus life overall.”
Evidently, more colleges have now started looking into strategies, establishing specialised cells and centres that further look into research and student support. “While there is a long way to go, this scattered chatter needs to grow louder, unanimously, to shape future education and move towards evidence-based inclusive practices,” Dr. Muthukumaran added.
The digital divide
Considering that higher education has become increasingly dependent on digital infrastructure, learning management systems (LMS), university portals, digital libraries, online journals, e-books, recorded lectures, online assignments, examination portals, email systems, and virtual classrooms are now integral to campus life. For many learners, this digital environment offers greater convenience, flexibility, and access to educational resources. But for students with disabilities, digital technologies can be either powerful enablers or, when accessibility is inadequate, can become significant barriers to participation and academic success.
A university website that cannot be navigated effectively with assistive technology can make admission and administrative processes more cumbersome. A PDF that is simply a scanned image may not be usable for a blind student. An online learning platform without appropriate keyboard navigation, captions, transcripts, or alternative texts can prevent students from participating on equal terms.
Digital exclusion can widen the educational divide even when the physical campus is accessible. This is particularly important because UGC’s own framework requires online programmes to meet accessibility standards for learners with disability. If education is delivered digitally, its accessibility must be inclusive.
The lack of adequate data makes it difficult to assess the enormity of students’ plight. “There is no AISHE, NAAC or NIRF indicator reporting the percentage of students with disabilities in higher education who have access to accessible LMS platforms, screen-reader-compatible material, captions, Indian Sign Language interpretation or accessible e-books,” Dr. Singh said.
Without such indicators, institutions may be able to report enrolment and infrastructure without demonstrating whether students with disabilities can actually access, participate in, and benefit from digital learning on an equal basis. The absence of systematic data also makes it difficult to identify gaps, assess institutional performance, or hold institutions accountable for meeting accessibility requirements.
“We need a stricter implementation protocol for higher education institutions as there is mostly a lack of awareness and enforceable rules that institutions should follow,” says Deepa Palaniappan, Disability Inclusion practitioner, highlighting the need for more discussions, training, and handholding, as well as forming national task forces and committees to track effective inclusion of students with disabilities in higher education institutions across the country.
Reality check
For Delhi University (DU) alumnus and disability rights activist Ashutosh Singhal (24), the challenges of being an undergraduate and later postgraduate student of Political Science were harrowing. ‘’I use a regular, mainstream computer with a screen reader that reads out the text and other information displayed on the screen. This means that questions appearing on the computer can be read aloud to me, enabling me to access and answer them independently,” Ashutosh said, who suffers from late-onset visual impairment (retinitis pigmentosa), a condition in which the vision can gradually deteriorate.
Beating the odds, he managed to use a computer to write his Political Science BA and MA exams in Hindi, which was the first instance of its kind.
“Initially, they gave me a computer that crashed. The computer instructor apparently knew that there were problems with the computer but did not inform me beforehand. A substitute computer was eventually provided, but by then considerable examination time had been lost. I was told that I would receive additional time to compensate for the lost time, but this was not implemented adequately. Since the examination authorities had to collect and pack the answer scripts at a fixed time, I was under pressure to finish and submit my answers immediately,” he added. Ashutosh was also made to sit in a computer lab during the exam where the constant noise made it difficult to detect the sounds of the screen reader, disrupting his flow of thoughts.
Ashutosh’s experience made him realise that the biggest difficulty for students with disabilities is often not the technology itself which is already available. It is about getting institutions to recognise and implement accessibility provisions consistently.
A student may have to repeatedly explain their requirements, submit applications, approach different departments, contact outside organisations, and persuade officials to make arrangements that should ideally be part of a standard accessible examination system. “For me, the computer and screen reader made it possible to access examinations independently. But the institutional process surrounding the technology created many obstacles. Accessible examination systems should be implemented proactively rather than requiring students with disabilities to repeatedly request, justify, and negotiate for accommodations each time they have an examination,” he added.
(Rajlakshmi Ghosh is a journalist with over three decades of experience in media houses and educational institutions)

If there’s one thing that Americans can unite behind, it’s anxieties over artificial intelligence.
Can AI actually save lives?
A physician explains how AI is helping in the doctor’s office and the lab.
According to a recent NBC News/Decision Desk poll, 70 percent of adults say they are personally more worried than excited about the technology; it’s basically underwater in every area of society with one notable exception: its use in scientific research and medicine.
According to Dr. Dhruv Khullar, a physician at Weill Cornell Medicine and writer at the New Yorker, that optimism is well-founded.
Khullar uses AI tools in his own practice as a physician and writes about their advancements in the medical field. He says that “right now, at least, there’s a generally optimistic view of how AI will change healthcare going forward.”
AI in medicine is nothing new. In 2024, the Nobel Prize in Chemistry was given to researchers who developed an AI model that enabled breakthroughs in predicting protein’s complex structures. As it becomes more ubiquitous, it’s also emerging as a resource for doctors to get second opinions and as a tool to take notes on patient-doctor interactions.
On top of that, Khullar says, it might help unlock new medicines to treat diseases.
Khullar joined Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram to discuss the ways that AI is transforming drug discovery and research, as well as what it still can’t do. They also discuss how to think about AI’s potential in healthcare at the same time as top AI researchers are increasingly warning about the technology’s risk.
Below is an excerpt of the conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
You’ve been thinking about lifesaving AI innovation. Has AI already started saving lives?
I think it has. This is the fastest I’ve ever seen healthcare take up a new technology. Part of that might be that the healthcare system is so messed up that there’s an appetite for some type of change. It’s unaffordable, it’s inaccessible, it’s inconvenient, the quality is uneven.
There’s at least a hope that AI is going to help with all of these things, and I think it’s already starting to make its way into the healthcare system. Now it’s our responsibility to figure out how to make the most of it without also promulgating some of the downsides.
For those who are unaware, tell us how it’s working its way into the system.
It’s helpful to categorize it into a few buckets, at least for healthcare.
The most rapid uptake, and I think the place that it’s already starting to make a difference, is on the administrative side. Many people who have gone to a doctor recently might have noticed that there’s an AI scribe that’s taking notes now. And people seem to really like it, at least so far. Doctors are able to look their patients in the eye in the way that they weren’t able to when they were poring over their computers and just typing what the patient was telling them.
The second big area is patient navigation. When is your next scan? When’s your next appointment? Do I need to take this medication on an empty stomach or not? There’s a huge opportunity for people, let’s say, who are diagnosed with a serious illness like cancer or heart failure to navigate the system more seamlessly.
The third big area that I’m really excited about is drug discovery. AI is making a huge dent in the early parts of drug discovery.
The last thing that I’m excited about and that I use every day when I’m in the hospital is [AI] as a second opinion. Now instead of having to get a consult or turn to a textbook, AI can be a very, very helpful clinical decision support. It’s not to say that I never consult someone, of course, but that first pass — I’m not sure what’s going on. What are some recent trials that might influence my decision here? Is there something I’m missing? Is there a test that I should be ordering that I’m not ordering? — all those types of things, they start to help with.
The biggest chunk of this positive view of AI and medicine is drug discovery. Tell me more about how that’s going so far and how it might be going in a year, or five, or 10.
I don’t want to leave this conversation and say that we’ve solved the cure for cancer because of AI, but I do want people to know that at least for the early stages of drug discovery — figuring out the very basic steps of is this an interesting molecule? Does it have potential biological applications? — AI is already very helpful for that.
They’re trying to take, basically, what is an infinite number of drug-like molecules that are theoretically possible to be drugs and they’re trying to match that to some disease that’s going on inside a human. And human biology is incredibly complex as well. There’s tens of thousands of genes, hundreds of thousands of proteins, trillions of cells, and you have to match a potential molecule to a potential target within a human.
In the past, a researcher might take years to study a disease or a biological pathway and figure out, okay, this protein seems to be involved. And actually, it might not be involved, it might be involved, it might be disrupted, but not be the causative agent. There’s a lot of uncertainty there, so now AI can take enormous amounts of data, and it can rank various potential targets that seem to be the most likely to be causing a particular disease and give you that short short list of potential targets that may have taken months or years in the past.
So now you know what to attack, but you have to figure out what to attack it with. So you need a molecule, you need to generate a molecule that’s going to fit into that target or disrupt that target in some way.
Now again, AI can scour vast chemical spaces and give you a list of the things that seem to be most likely to be able to disrupt that target. And then it can actually help you generate that molecule in some cases.
So now we have the target. Now we have something that we’re going to attack the target with. And then you have to do something called lead optimization, and that’s the third thing. Lead optimization means you have this lead and you have to optimize it.
“I would make the counterargument that healthcare is ripe for disruption and you don’t even need the frontier frontier models to make it a lot better with AI.”
Now we have to figure out, of all the molecules that seem to be good at potentially affecting this target, which ones are able to be absorbed in the body, which ones are going to get to the right tissue. AI models can predict the most likely molecule to give you that Goldilocks set of properties that’s needed for a safe and effective drug.
As we all know from anyone who’s asked AI to write an email for them or Googled a question, these tools have a certain degree of certitude, even though these tools can just be flat out wrong about stuff. Are you guys worried about that in the field?
Absolutely. And so this is why I think the narrative around AI just replacing scientists or doctors or other workers is incorrect. Because you still need a lot of judgment.
You need to be able to adjudicate the output of these models to figure out what is most promising and what is potentially dangerous. That is going to require wet labs and scientists and reasoning based on prior experience and understanding the context. There’s all sorts of issues around, can you manufacture some of the drugs that are being proposed by these models? So just because it’s set, it dreams something up doesn’t mean you can actually make that thing in the real world.
Some of the drugs that it proposes might actually be toxic in certain ways that it didn’t predict. And of course, then you have to take this thing into clinical trials. You have to recruit l people who are willing to put this medication in their bodies. You have to find out who might benefit, you have to put it through the regulatory process.
That’s why I said that the first part of drug discovery, where you’re trying to figure out how do we get the right drug candidates, what seems most exciting to test further, that’s going to be really accelerated. That whole second half where we actually have to figure out if it works in human biology, that is still going to be in some respects an analog process.
It doesn’t sound like you’re terribly scared that we are like ceding control of our hospitals, of our research facilities, to AI. This is very much in the sort of assistant bucket?
For now it is. And I think one of the challenges is to maintain our agency as these models become more and more sophisticated. As you lean more on these machines, if you’re a doctor, inevitably some of the skills, the critical thinking, the reasoning that we put into coming up with the diagnosis that we honed over the course of years, that can start to atrophy.
These are the types of things that we still need to sort through as we’re implementing more and more AI into the healthcare system.
For the people who just say, shut it all down, this is too dangerous, the risk is far too great, we don’t actually need this, this isn’t doing anything for society, would you make a counterargument?
I would make the counterargument that healthcare is ripe for disruption and you don’t even need the frontier frontier models to make it a lot better with AI.
Even if we wanted to “slow the pace of the frontier,” fine. But there are models from a year or two years ago that could be very helpful in the healthcare setting. When we’re talking about slowing the pace of the frontier and the most sophisticated and potentially dangerous models, fine.
But if we’re talking about shutting down AI and not using it in biotechnology or not using it in scientific research or not using it in clinical care delivery, that’s where I would push back pretty hard.

Judge kicks off hearing on Trump’s media ban by saying White House failed to follow due process
DC Judge Timothy Kelly questions Trump’s threats to CNN, MSNOW and Politico after journalists’ passes were abruptly revoked

A federal judge overseeing a lawsuit to restore White House access to three major news organizations says Donald Trump’s administration appears to have failed longstanding legal precedent that requires due process before stripping passes from reporters.
U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, was appointed by the president during his first administration, had previously ordered the White House to restore then-CNN reporter Jim Acosta’s press pass in 2018.
When deciding that case, Kelly relied on previous court decisions that determined journalists are entitled to a “predeprivation notice and opportunity to be heard” before those passes are revoked, the judge said during Wednesday’s court hearing in Washington, D.C.
“I think it is fair to say that the process the court laid out [in those cases] wasn’t followed here,” Kelly said before arguments began Wednesday.
Last week, the White House revoked press passes from journalists CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists and blocked them from entering White House after the president announced he was “banning” the publications “effective immediately” for what he called their “FAKE” reporting.
Trump and the Department of Justice have accused the outlets of endangering national security by reporting sensitive and classified information that the president has also called “fake news” that is “negative, wrong and, in many cases, DANGEROUS for our Country.”
“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” he wrote on Truth Social September 18. “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow”
A federal lawsuit filed by lawyers representing the outlets accuses the Trump administration of “brazenly” violating their First Amendment rights and due process under the Fifth Amendment by discriminating against them based solely on their editorial viewpoint.
Other news organizations agreed to an effective blackout of pool coverage in solidarity with the banned networks. ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News — major networks that cover the president as part of the well-connected TV pool that patches transmissions to outlets worldwide — suspended their coverage, and other outlets announced they were temporarily withholding the publication of photos of the president.
On Monday, Trump denied launching an “assault on the Free Press” and said he is instead “instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America.”
“It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control,” he wrote on Truth Social. “It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!”
Sensing a potential loss in the federal court battle, he vowed an appeal "because Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown ‘sources,’ shouldn’t be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World.”
He lashed out at “Third Rate Clowns” who “purposefully distort, twist, and degrade with everything they write or publish.”
“Virtually every story about me, or anything having to do with me, is negative, wrong and, in many cases, DANGEROUS for our Country!” he wrote. “No matter how GREAT my Achievements, they trivialize and demean.”
He also said he regretted appointing Judge Kelly.
In Tuesday’s late-night filing, the Justice Department accused the outlets of threatening national security and breaching standards of conduct, including “trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information.” No law explicitly makes it a crime for a journalist to obtain or publish classified information.
“Access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” the filing states.
The filings included copies of letters from the White House Press Office to the three outlets sent on September 22. The letters point to their reporting on the U.S. military’s munitions shortages due to the ongoing Iran war as well as the administration’s proposed security additions to the White House ballroom — details that the Justice Department itself has discussed at length in court filings stemming from the ongoing lawsuit against the project.
The White House also pointed to a report about low attendance at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas that “cites unnamed sources” to paint the event “as a disaster.” (That report from Politico cited a Republican lobbyist close to the White House who said “the vibes are very bad.”)
Only one of the four articles published by CNN and one of the three offending MSNOW articles were written by reporters with White House passes, according to officials at the network.
The White House also pointed to reports of an alleged FBI leak investigation focusing on a journalist and an apparent U.S. military strike on an Iranian girls’ school that killed 156 civilians, including 120 children.
“Publication of sensitive security information, and misinformation about national security information, diverts White House resources and those of the national security team in particular, which must evaluate whether the leaked information is classified, the source of any leak, and the security implications of any such disclosure,” the White House Press Office wrote in letters to the news outlets.
“The spread of misinformation, especially relating to national security, is a threat that undermines the President’s ability to safeguard the national security,” the letters state.
The outlets were given until 5 p.m. September 25 to “contest this initial decision or the factual basis” for their removal.
On Wednesday, a coalition of more than 50 news organizations and press freedom groups filed a brief in support of the outlets, writing that the White House ban over the content of their reporting amounts to unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination.
“It is designed to have a chilling effect,” they wrote, “with the hope that it discourages other outlets from publishing stories that they fear might provoke similar sanctions.”

Mumbai: The application process for the ‘Seva First Innovation Challenge’ began on Wednesday, providing innovators from Maharashtra, Goa, Chhattisgarh and the Union Territory of Daman and Diu an opportunity to showcase technology-driven solutions to challenges in public services and development.
Focus On Real-World Problems Across 10 Sectors
The initiative is being organised as a multi-state innovation challenge to encourage practical and technology-based solutions in areas such as agriculture, healthcare, women’s safety, urban development, environment, defence, artificial intelligence, education and employability. Applications will remain open until October 17, 2026.
Skill Development Minister Mangal Prabhat Lodha said the challenge would provide a platform for innovative ideas that can address real-world problems rather than merely identify them. He said selected innovations would be considered for opportunities such as pilot projects, government procurement, incubation, investment and market access.
Individuals, students, student groups, researchers, professors, startups, MSMEs, companies, social organisations, educational and research institutions and other innovation teams can participate. The proposed innovation must fall under one of the 10 identified sectors.
The sectors are agriculture; law and order; women and child welfare; urban development; health and medical services; defence; sustainability, energy and climate; infrastructure and mobility; emerging technologies such as AI and blockchain; and education and employability.
The challenge will cover themes including climate-resilient agriculture, cyber fraud prevention, women’s safety, urban flood management, smart diagnostics, defence technology, renewable energy, traffic management, AI-based citizen services, Marathi-first AI, job matching and AI-based career guidance.
₹5 crore prize pool
A total prize pool of ₹5 crore has been earmarked across the 10 sectors. Five winners will be selected in each sector, with each winner receiving ₹10 lakh. Each sector will have one winner in the women’s category, one winner aged below 21 and three winners in the open category.
Around 200 innovations to reach final showcase
The organisers expect to receive between 1,500 and 2,000 applications. Following an initial eligibility check, the applications will undergo online expert assessment as well as technical and impact evaluation.
Around 20 finalists from each sector, or approximately 200 innovators in all, will subsequently be selected for the final showcase. Entries will be assessed on parameters including relevance of the problem, innovation, technological maturity, potential impact, scalability, implementation capability and the possibility of actual deployment in the participating states.
Independent experts, technical specialists and sector-specific juries will be involved in the evaluation process.
Special categories for women and youth
A separate category has been created for women innovators and innovators below 21 years of age in each of the 10 sectors. The organisers said this would provide a dedicated platform for women innovators, students and young researchers to present their ideas.
Final event in Nagpur on December 7
The final event will be held in Nagpur on December 7, 2026. Shortlisted participants will present and demonstrate their innovations before the jury, which will select the final winners.
Around 200 innovation stalls will be set up during the final exhibition, giving participants an opportunity to showcase their solutions to government representatives, industry, investors and incubators.
Lodha said the objective was not limited to awarding prizes but also to create an innovation ecosystem through which promising solutions could receive opportunities for pilot projects, government procurement, incubation, investment and access to markets.
Special job fair for women
A special employment fair for women will be organised as part of the Employment Mahakumbh to be inaugurated by Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis at SNDT Women’s University on September 29. Around 600-700 women candidates are expected to participate.
Separate stalls of reputed companies will provide information on available positions, eligibility criteria, job profiles, salary ranges and recruitment procedures. Women candidates will also have an opportunity to interact directly with company representatives.

- GTA 6 will give you more freedom to approach different situations based on your playstyle.
- Rockstar North co-head Rob Nelson says, "You can, in some way, choose the type of criminal you want to be".
- He stated that you can be “more professional” or “totally unpredictable,” with each approach affecting specific parts of the game.
Rockstar is taking a page from Red Dead Redemption 2 with GTA 6, giving you different playstyles that let you decide what kind of criminal you want to be and how you approach robberies, heists, and other activities. Rockstar North co-head Rob Nelson has confirmed that the type of criminal you are will significantly impact your GTA 6 playthrough.
Speaking to French magazine Trois Couleurs, Nelson said your GTA 6 playstyle and your activities “reinforces the narrative, since the story revolves around a couple on the run.” Of course, your choices could also affect Jason and Lucia’s deep relationship throughout the game. Here’s the full statement on the mechanic.
You can, in some way, choose the type of criminal you want to be: someone more professional, or on the contrary someone totally unpredictable. Your way of playing has an impact on certain things.
Nelson also noted that “The world is also very unpredictable. You are not the only armed person nor the only capable of violence.” So, how you handle these mishaps will ultimately define what kind of criminal Jason and Lucia actually are.
Red Dead Redemption 2 featured a similar but more limited system, with Arthur’s actions affecting his Honor level. Rockstar is bringing a similar mechanic to GTA 6 with its Criminal Profile system. So, if you use a cleaner, more professional playstyle to get away with most of your crimes in GTA 6, you won’t affect your Criminal Profile.
Meanwhile, if you like to do things in a loud fashion and go in guns blazing, shooting every cop and NPC on the block, this type of GTA 6 playstyle will negatively affect your Criminal Profile rating. Given that Rockstar is updating the gore and dismemberment system in GTA 6, most players will likely opt for a combat-intensive approach.
That said, what kind of playstyle will you go for in GTA 6? A professional one or a walking disaster across Vice City? Tell us in the comments section below.

Patrick Vieira says it is "an honour" to become Senegal head coach, with the decision to take the job "one from the heart".
The 50-year-old was born in the West African nation but subsequently represented France as a player, winning the 1998 World Cup and the 2000 European Championship with Les Bleus.
The former Arsenal midfielder spoke of his "immense pride" to begin his first international job, following stints with New York City, Nice, Crystal Palace, Strasbourg and Genoa, at his unveiling by the Teranga Lions on Friday.
"Being head coach of the Senegal national team is an absolute dream," he told a news conference in Dakar.
"I was born here, my parents were born here, and it really is a homecoming.
"From the very first meetings I had with the [Senegal football federation] president, I accepted this challenge straight away, because there was also an exceptional generation of players.
"I realise the expectations of the people - all 20 million Senegalese. And I know that with the experience I have, with the determination I have, I'll be able to see this project through."
- Vieira named new Senegal head coach 
  - Published18 August
Taking over after the dismissal of Pape Thiaw, Vieira inherits a Senegal side which exited the 2026 World Cup in dramatic fashion in the last 32, throwing away a 2-0 lead after 85 minutes against Belgium before losing 3-2 following extra time.
Before that the Teranga Lions claimed the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) title with a 1-0 extra-time win over Morocco in January.
However, the ultimate destination of the trophy will be decided by the Court of Arbitration for Sport after a walk-off by some Senegal players and staff protesting against a penalty decision in the final resulted in the trophy being handed to the North African hosts instead in March.
"Today, Senegal is among the major nations in world football," Vieira said.
"Senegal's objectives aren't what they were 10 or 15 years ago. On the back of its recent results, Senegal has moved forward, has reached new levels.
"The demand for results has also stepped up. We need to lay solid foundations."
Vieira plans to build a side with "a very precise structure" which can play with "intensity and aggression".
"What matters to me isn't starting again from scratch," he added.
"It's about respecting what the federation has put in place over the last few years and building the next stage, opening a new chapter.
"A new chapter meaning my job isn't to tear everything down, it isn't to throw everything out of the window.
"It's about keeping this team's strength: its identity, its unity, its ability to suffer together.
"To make this project work, I'll need the whole nation united. I'll work heart and soul to restore the team's pride."
Starting with two away trips
Vieira has been thrust straight into competitive action in qualifiers for the 2027 Afcon with two fixtures in this international window, two more in November and the final two rounds in March 2027.
His stint in charge was due to begin with a home match against Mozambique on Friday, 25 September but the fixture has been reversed as Dakar is in the midst of preparations for the 2026 Youth Olympic Games.
"Of course, I'd have preferred to play the first match here in Dakar but unfortunately, with the federation, we all felt the best decision was to postpone the match and go and play in Mozambique," Vieira explained.
"Those are difficulties we're going to accept and deal with."
Senegal will be without several notable names for the trip to Maputo and the subsequent away game against Ethiopia on 29 September.
Long-time number one Edouard Mendy, 34, has retired from Teranga Lions duty and Vieira said talismanic forward Sadio Mane will be absent with "a bit of a physical issue".
Despite previous speculation that Mane, also 34, could follow Mendy into retirement, Vieira said the former Liverpool and Bayern Munich man will "surely" be part of his next selection, fitness permitting.
Right-back Krepin Diatta has been left out because he is currently without a club, while forward Ismaila Sarr, who is yet to feature for Crystal Palace this season because of transfer speculation and a groin injury, is also absent.
'No doubt' about his managerial ability
Vieira's career as a player was trophy-laden but he has found the same kind of success hard to come by as a manager.
He departed Palace in March 2023 with a record of 22 wins from 74 games in all competitions and, after a season at Strasbourg, has been out of work since being sacked by Genoa in November last year with the Italian club bottom of the table.
He had guided them to safety in Serie A in the 2024-25 campaign but was then dismissed after six defeats in nine league games at the start of last season.
"When you talk about my coaching career, or a certain amount of experience, I've always been someone who stays positive," Vieira said.
"That means you learn, and there are always positive things to take from it. I'm a better coach today than I was in my last spell at Genoa, because that experience helped me grow and made me realise certain things.
"Given the experience I have as a manager, I've got no doubt about my ability to meet the expectations of fans."
Vieira was warmly received when he arrived in Dakar on Thursday evening, with video clips posted on social media showing him holding a Senegal flag aloft while shaking hands with a throng of fans gathered at the capital's airport.
"I couldn't have been given a warmer welcome. I saw the supporters' enthusiasm and I thank them for it.
"Taking charge of this national team isn't just a new stage in my career - it's coming back home."

U.N. Ambassador Mike Waltz on Iran, Venezuela and Trump's foreign policy
U.S. ambassador to the U.N. discusses Trump's address at UNGA
Three hours of direct talks between U.S. and Iranian officials on Tuesday produced no announced breakthrough. With negotiations still unfolding, President Trump's ambassador to the United Nations offered a narrow window Wednesday into what happened at the table. Trump has said the talks are continuing and that he believes a settlement can be reached.
"We're literally internalizing what they brought to the table," Mike Waltz told Morning Edition.
Waltz would not describe Iran's proposal. Asked whether Tehran had offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for an easing of U.S. economic pressure, he called the talks "significant" because they marked the first direct contact between the two countries since the ceasefire broke down. He added that Iran would have to "come to the table in good faith."
He also invoked international law, adding that Iran could not choke off one of the world's most important shipping routes as leverage.
"Imagine if Spain or Morocco choked off the Straits of Gibraltar because of a dispute with another country," Waltz said.
Iran has said it is prepared to reopen the strait if Washington eases military pressure and lifts its blockade on Iranian ports.
Waltz, a former Green Beret and three-term Florida congressman, moved to the U.N. after being pushed aside as Trump's national security adviser over the Signal chat scandal, in which he mistakenly added a journalist to a discussion of planned U.S. strikes in Yemen.
Trump addressed the U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday with a message that paired diplomacy with the threat of force — a combination that has shaped much of his second-term foreign policy. On Iran, he spoke of a deal that could allow the country to rebuild while also threatening to "annihilate" it if no agreement is reached.
Trump also turned to Venezuela, where a U.S. military operation removed Nicolás Maduro, declaring that "to the victor belong the spoils" as he discussed access to the country's oil.
The foreign policy message comes as voters are giving Republicans lower marks on the issue. An NPR/PBS News/Marist poll released Wednesday found registered voters preferred Democrats over Republicans on handling foreign policy, 42% to 36%. Trump's overall job approval stood at 39%.

Nearly a year after releasing Premiere for iPhone, Adobe is finally bringing its redesigned video-editing app to Android. The app has been in beta for several weeks but is now available as the official successor to Premiere Rush, which the company will stop supporting on September 30.
Eric Snowden, senior vice president of design at Adobe, tells WIRED the feedback for the iOS app has been “incredibly positive” (to his credit, it has a 4.8-star rating out of 5 on the App Store with more than 25,000 ratings). The goal with the Android version wasn't just to port the iPhone app experience, but to make it feel really native to Google's platform.
That includes making sure the app works just as well on every kind of Android device out there, whether it's a Samsung foldable or a candy bar Google Pixel. Yes, when you open up a folding phone with the Adobe Premiere app, you can view your footage on the left and see the multi-track timeline on the right, maximizing space. Snowden suggests optimizing the app for Android foldables will help the company with the iPhone app for the upcoming iPhone Duo.
And if you're wondering whether this app will work well on Google's new Googlebook laptop platform, Adobe says its apps—Acrobat, Photoshop, Lightroom, and Premiere—are optimized for the new laptops, meaning they'll take advantage of the larger screen, but can’t quite deliver the “desktop-grade” experience you’ll find on Windows or macOS.
Equally important is ensuring the app runs on lower-power devices, though Premiere has a minimum requirement of 5 GB of RAM (phones will also need to run Android 13 or later).
“We wanted this to run on as many devices as possible, so the team spent a ton of time making sure that this is not just for flagship phones,” Snowden says. “This is for a really broad range of Android devices.”
Launch the Adobe Premiere app and you will see all your footage from your camera roll on the home screen. From there, you can choose creator-made templates—ranging from lifestyle to beauty to templates for foodies—to get started on an edit, or start from scratch if you'd like.
It's easy to add your footage, then opt for the mini editor or the full editor. The former lets you easily trim or replace your footage, and even choose a filter to apply a specific color style to all of your clips. You can export directly to YouTube Shorts without leaving Premiere. The full editor gives you a multitrack timeline for more granular edits, like layering text, music, and effects.
Several AI tools are on board, like Enhance Audio, which can boost the subject's voice and cut background noise. If you want to add a voice-over, you can speak into your phone's mic and see your footage in real time so it all matches up. Adobe says the app has Firefly-powered AI features, like Generative Fill, Image-to-Video, and Generate Sound Effects. However, these require generative credits, aka a subscription, if you run out of your monthly allotment.
Some features are still “coming soon,” like the Continue Editing function so you can wrap up an edit on desktop after starting it on mobile, or support for Adobe Fonts.
Uniquely (for an Adobe product), you do not have to log in or subscribe to Adobe's creative suite to use Premiere on Android. Like the iOS version, the app is free to use.
“What we're seeing with a lot of mobile apps right now is that there are these huge barriers to entry to using it for the first time,” Snowden says. “We really wanted to get away from that, and I think part of the accessibility and simplicity of the app—the onboarding process is part of that—and we just want to get people in and using it."
