Control Resonant gives Dylan several supernatural tools, and Combat abilities are one of them. These can change how you experience each enemy encounter. Each ability serves a different role, giving you several ways to approach dangerous enemies.
However, since you are always in a situation of this or that, it is important to know which ones to choose. In our guide below, find all Control Resonant Combat abilities and learn how to unlock them.
List of Control Resonant Combat Abilities and How to Get Them
Combat abilities come from Resonant encounters scattered across several areas of Control Resonant. Each Resonant presents specific choices, so your selection determines which power becomes available. Combine these abilities with solid Artifacts in Control Resonant, and clearing enemy waves becomes a cakewalk.
With that being said, here is the complete list of Combat abilities in Control Resonant, along with what they do and how to get them:
| Combat Ability | What it does | How to Unlock | 
|---|---|---|
| Barrage | Fires projectiles toward a target for ranged damage. | Defeat the Artist Resonant during the Orientation prologue. | 
| Volatile Anomaly | Summons an ally that you can throw and detonate for explosive damage. | Defeat the Artist Resonant during the Orientation prologue. | 
| Shield | Absorbs damage and enables a powerful Shield Bash against enemies. | Defeat the Artist Resonant during the Orientation prologue. | 
| Push | Sends enemies backward and can knock them into hazards or off ledges. | Defeat the Dancer Resonant in the West Incursion Zone. | 
| Ground Slam | Slams enemies from above, with stronger area damage from greater heights. | Defeat the Dancer Resonant in the West Incursion Zone. | 
| Ignite | Adds Fire damage and Burn to melee attacks and several abilities. | Defeat the Deserter Resonant in the Patterned Factory. | 
| Inferno | Creates increasingly intense Fire waves that apply Burn over time. | Defeat the Deserter Resonant in the Patterned Factory. | 
| Spore Burst | Rapidly fires Mold projectiles while building the Infected status effect. | Defeat the Collective Resonant beneath the Park. | 
| Growth | Summons a Mold ally that fires spores and builds Infected over time. | Defeat the Collective Resonant beneath the Park. | 
| Spike | Summons an Astral Spike that attacks enemies and builds Astralized. | Defeat the Physicist Resonant at the Underpass Spire. | 
| Astral Rebuke | Launches enemies upward with a homing spike while building Astralized. | Defeat the Physicist Resonant at the Underpass Spire. | 
| Command | Takes control of an enemy and turns them into an ally during combat. | Defeat the Co Director Resonant in the Unknown Field Office. | 
What Is Combat Ability in Control Resonant?
Combat abilities are supernatural powers Dylan uses to damage, control, or weaken enemies during fights. You unlock them primarily by defeating Resonants, which act as optional boss encounters throughout the game.
After defeating a Resonant, you usually choose one ability from a limited group of options. Choosing one option can prevent you from using the alternatives during that playthrough. So, if you are playing to get the achievements and trophies in Control Resonant, check if you need a specific one to unlock them.
You can also reset the Combat ability. Reset Items let you revisit those choices through the Gap when you want another loadout. These powers interact with status effects, Falter, Power, and weapon attacks, shaping your overall combat approach.
Which Combat Abilities to Pick in Control Resonant?
If you want to maximize your damage output and trigger finishers in Control Resonant faster, picking up the right Combat abilities can be crucial. Your best choices depend on how aggressively you want to fight and which effects you prefer. Despite that, there are some Combat abilities we recommend using that combine for the best damage output:
- Barrage: Barrage provides reliable ranged damage while helping you eliminate weaker enemies safely.
- Push: Push creates space quickly and can instantly kill enemies near environmental hazards.
- Ignite: Ignite adds Burn to attacks while increasing damage and Falter across your offensive abilities.
- Spore Burst: Spore Burst rapidly builds Infected, making it useful against tougher enemies later.
- Astral Rebuke: Astral Rebuke launches grounded enemies upward, creating opportunities for follow-up attacks.
- Command: Command turns stronger enemies into temporary allies, adding useful support during difficult encounters.
That is everything you need to know about Combat abilities in Control Resonant. Which ones are you using to complete your build? Let us know in the comments.
How do you unlock Combat abilities in Control Resonant?
Defeat Resonants throughout the game, then choose from their available Combat ability options.
Can you change Combat abilities in Control Resonant?
Yes, you can use Reset Items through the Gap to revisit your previous Combat ability choices.

It always creates apprehension because the sight is somewhat gory, but a nosebleed, in general, isn’t a cause for major concern. Occurring mostly in the under 10s and the over 45s, nosebleeds are very common: about 60% of the population is estimated to experience one in their lifetime. They can occur in one or both nostrils, but usually affect one. The medical term for a nosebleed is epistaxis.
How do they occur?
Our noses are lined with a moist, delicate tissue, the nasal mucosa. This lining cleans the air that we breathe in, and also warms and moistens the air. The mucosa is made of many tiny blood vessels, lying to close to the surface. These blood vessels can easily be irritated, injured and broken. When they break, they cause a nosebleed.
There are two types of nosebleeds: anterior and posterior. An anterior nosebleed, which is the most common type, starts at the front of the nose. These types of nosebleeds can mostly be treated at home. A posterior nosebleed takes place place deep at the back the nose, may cause heavier bleeding and could result in blood going down the back of the throat. This type of nosebleed requires medical attention.
Why do they occur?
Common causes include the inside of the nose becoming dry, usually due to a change in temperature, picking the nose, or blowing the nose too hard.
When the air is very dry, it causes the nasal mucosa, which is meant to be moist, to dry out, making it prone to crusting and bleeding. Dry air can occur in hot places with low humidity, areas of high altitude and in air-conditioned or heated spaces. People with upper respiratory infections, sinus infections, allergies or other ailments such as rhinitis may also sneeze, cough or blow their nose frequently, making them more prone to bleeds. The frequent use of medications such as antihistamines, nasal sprays or blood thinners, could also make people vulnerable to nosebleeds, as could breathing in strong fumes.
Nosebleeds can also occur due to injuries to the nose, the insertion of objects into the nose, a deviated septum, recreational drug use as well as less common causes such as having blood disorders, alcohol use, nasal polyps or tumours.
Being pregnant may also increase the chances of nosebleeds.
When to see a doctor
In general, nosebleeds aren’t serious and can be treated at home. In some circumstances, however, it is best to consult a medical professional. You should see a doctor if: the nosebleed has followed an injury or accident; if there is heavy bleeding or the bleeding lasts longer than 30 minutes; blood has been swallowed; if there is a feeling of weakness, dizziness, lightheadedness or if you have breathing difficulties, chest pain or a rapid heart rate. A doctor should also be consulted if the person with the nosebleed has other health issues such as a bleeding disorder, or high blood pressure, or if the person is a child under two years old.
How to stop a nosebleed
To stop a nosebleed, there are some first-aid measures that can be taken:
- Sit upright so the head is above the level of the heart, lean forward slightly
- Breathe through the mouth and gently blow the nose to clear it
- Use the thumb and index finger to pinch the both nostrils shut. Do this for 10 minutes.
- Use an icepack on the bridge of the nose at the same time as the pinching
- Check in 10 minutes, and if the bleeding has not stopped, repeat the pinching for another 10 minutes
- Once the bleeding has stopped, lean forward and clean the nose with lukewarm water
- See a doctor immediately if the bleeding does not stop in 30 minutes
Preventing nosebleeds
Using a humidifier in the house especially in dry air conditions, trimming children’s fingernails, managing allergies, using a nasal saline spray or petroleum jelly to keep the inner lining of the nose moist and avoiding smoke exposure can all help prevent nosebleeds.

The 2026 Urban Local Body elections were held recently in Rajasthan for 309 urban local bodies and 10,244 wards, with polling held on 09 and 11 September and counting on 14 September. The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) won 4,182 wards, followed by the Congress with 3,619, while Independents secured 2,273 wards. The results also saw the BJP secure majorities in several municipal corporations, while Congress and Independent candidates won in some others (here, here).
In this context, a video is circulating on social media (here, here, and here), claiming it shows a BJP candidate crying after receiving just one vote in the Rajasthan civic elections. The post also alleges that even his own family members did not vote for him. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows a BJP candidate crying after receiving just one vote in the 2026 Rajasthan civic elections.
Fact: It is true that a BJP candidate named Kailash Chandra received one vote in the 2026 Rajasthan civic elections. However, the viral video is unrelated to this incident. The man seen in the video is Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) leader Shivchandra Ram, who was seen crying during a press conference in June 2026 after being denied an MLC ticket in Bihar. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to several media reports (here, here, here, and here) published in June 2026 featuring the same video. According to these reports, the person seen crying during a press conference is RJD leader and former Bihar minister Shivchandra Ram, who broke down in tears after being denied an MLC ticket. RJD’s Sunil Singh had filed the nomination for the Grand Alliance for one of the 10 seats in the Bihar Legislative Council, which reportedly angered Ram. He alleged that the party had promised to make him an MLC but had betrayed him, following which he announced his resignation from all RJD posts, while clarifying that he had not left the party. This confirms that the viral video is unrelated to the 2026 Rajasthan civic elections.
To investigate the claim that a BJP candidate received only one vote in the 2026 Rajasthan civic elections, we conducted a Google keyword search and found multiple reports (here, here). According to these reports, BJP candidate Kailash Chandra received only one vote in Ward No. 13 of the Parbatsar Municipality in Rajasthan’s Deedwana-Kuchaman district. Congress candidate Hina Khanam received 376 votes, while Independent candidate Rasheed Khan received 195 votes. The reports also state that Kailash Chandra was a voter in Ward No. 12 but was fielded by the BJP from Ward No. 13, meaning he could not vote for himself.
We then checked the election results available on the official website of the Rajasthan State Election Commission. The results for the Parbatsar Municipality show that Kailash Chandra, the BJP candidate from Ward No. 13, received one vote.
To sum up, an unrelated video of a Bihar RJD leader crying is falsely linked to the BJP candidate who received one vote in the 2026 Rajasthan civic polls.

Five baby orangutans have been found in a forest in India, prompting authorities to investigate if they were trafficked into the country from south-east Asia.
The orangutans, native only to the islands of Borneo and Sumatra and known for their shaggy red fur, were found in Balasore district of Odisha state, thousands of kilometres away from their natural habitat.
Odisha’s environment minister, Ram Singh Khuntia, said wildlife investigators were trying to establish how the rare apes reached India.
“We suspect that an international racket might be involved in this,” Singh said.
International commercial trade in orangutans is prohibited under Cites – a global agreement governing trade in endangered wildlife.
The five babies were found by forest department officials who were patrolling in the Jaleswar range in Balasore district.
Officials believed the orangutans had been in the area for just a few days, and they have now been placed in quarantine at a zoological park in Odisha.
According to the World Wildlife Fund, about 104,000 orangutans remain in Borneo and Sumatra, down from more than 230,000 a century ago.
The Tapanuli orangutan (Pongo tapanuliensis), a third species, is classified as critically endangered, with fewer than 800 believed to survive in the wild.
In November, conservationists found the Tapanuli population had been reduced by 7% after severe flooding in Indonesia.
Between 33 and 54 Tapanuli orangutans were estimated to have been killed in widespread floods and landslides in North Sumatra province.
Previous research has suggested annual losses of 1% of the Tapanuli orangutan population would be sufficient to lead to eventual extinction.
The entire Tapanuli population dwells solely in the West Block of the Batang Toru, a forest threatened by mining, palm oil plantations and a large hydropower project.

Three infants died after a fire broke out at the Special Newborn Care Unit (SNCU) ward of Rajiv Gandhi Institute of Medical Sciences (RIMS) in Telangana’s Adilabad district late on Monday (September 21) night. The incident occurred around 11.40 p.m. As many as 25 other infants being treated in the ward were safely rescued and evacuated in time.
According to Adilabad District Medical and Health Officer (DMHO) Sadhana, the fire was caused after an air-conditioner in the reception area of the SNCU burst into flames.
“The SNCU has two flanks, one with 11 beds, and another with 13 beds, while the Kangaroo Mother Care area located opposite the SNCU has four beds. The sections are enclosed and have glass windows. When the fire broke out, smoke accumulated inside the unit. As soon as the fire was noticed, the attendants of patients broke the glass windows and evacuated the babies from the affected areas,” the DMHO said.
The rescued infants were subsequently shifted to nearby private hospitals for further treatment. The two infants who died, aged five and four days respectively, were preterm babies. One of them died immediately after the incident, while the other succumbed four hours later. The third infant, a two-day-old girl who was born prematurely at 28 weeks and weighed 1.1 kg, was in a critical condition and died while being shifted to a nearby hospital, confirmed Director of Medical Education (DME) N. Vani.
Upon receiving information about the fire, a fire tender was rushed to the hospital and the blaze was brought under control. The exact cause of the fire was is yet to be ascertained. The police have registered a case and launched an investigation into the incident.
Adilabad Superintendent of Police (SP) Akhil Mahajan said the incident occurred at around 11.40 p.m., and police teams reached the hospital within three minutes, by 11.43 p.m. “Although Ganesh immersion processions were under way and a large number of police personnel were deployed, our teams were able to reach the spot within three minutes and assist in evacuating the children,” he said.
CM conveys condolences
Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy expressed grief over the incident and conveyed his condolences to the families of the infants. He stated that the death of infants was extremely tragic. The Chief Minister directed officials to ensure better medical treatment for the children undergoing treatment at the hospital and to continuously monitor their health condition.
Mr. Reddy ordered an inquiry into the incident and directed officials to submit a report on the causes of the fire. He further instructed authorities to strengthen fire and other safety measures in hospitals across the State to prevent similar incidents in the future.
Govt. support
Health Minister C. Damodar Raja Narasimha, who inspected the fire incident site, expressed grief over the deaths and conveyed his condolences to the bereaved families.
The Minister also reviewed the rescue and relief measures undertaken following the incident and the arrangements made to safely shift the infants undergoing treatment in the SNCU to other wards. He also sought updates from doctors on the condition of the infants and other children receiving treatment and directed them to provide the best possible medical care while closely monitoring their health. The Minister later met the families of the affected children and assured them of the government’s support.
“The condition of other children who were in the ward at the time of the incident was stable and none have developed any complications,” said a note from the Minister’s office.
He was accompanied by Adilabad MLA Payal Shanker and Principal Secretary, Health, Medical and Family Welfare, Dr. Christina Z. Chongthu.
A preliminary inquiry indicated that an electrical short circuit in an air-conditioning unit may have triggered the fire, causing plastic components to burn and filling the SNCU with thick smoke, the Minister said. A detailed enquiry by an expert committee would ascertain the exact cause and identify any lapses in safety standards, he added.
The Minister said RIMS staff, district officials, Fire and Police personnel acted swiftly to disconnect the power supply, evacuate the infants and provide emergency medical care.
He said a 150-bed Mother and Child Health (M&CH) Building would be established at RIMS, taking its bed strength from 800 to 950. Plans were also under way to develop the institute into a super-speciality hospital, besides setting up Hematology and Emergency Trauma Care wings.
The Minister said steps were being taken to increase postgraduate medical seats in Paediatrics, Gynaecology, Radiology and other departments and strengthen the out-patient and in-patient services at RIMS.

Today's Talking Points:
'Risk free' 5 per cent
The yield on every US Treasury note or bond, with the exception of the two-year note, traded above 5 per cent on Wednesday, with the five-year yield crossing that threshold for the first time since 2007. The two-year yield is only 5 basis points away, so it's conceivable that the whole US Treasury yield curve could be above 5 per cent later this week. That would also be a first since 2007.
It's only a number, but it could have psychological significance. It could tempt all kinds of investors to diversify away from expensive stocks and lock in attractive returns on 'risk-free' assets (the real yield on 10-year TIPS is 2.78 per cent, the highest since 2008).
On the other hand, today's 5-year auction was awful. These yields are a reminder that we are in a brave new world, where the cost of capital is high and seemingly heading higher. Debt servicing — for consumers, businesses and the Treasury — is getting more expensive. Buckle up.
Here Xi comes
Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington for his summit on Thursday with US President Donald Trump. The visit will be marked with pomp, pageantry and platitudes, but will it yield much else? Investors' expectations are low, but Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent indicated on Wednesday that there may be some progress on trade.
Bessent said the US is open to extending the trade truce that expires on November 10 or considering a possibly larger trade deal, without giving details, other than it was the Chinese delegation's proposal. If Trump and Xi reach agreement on trade, there's unlikely to be much cooperation on AI. Mutual trust is low, and neither side wants to slow down development.
Diesel down
US diesel futures slid 2 per cent on Wednesday to a two-week low, reacting to comments from Trump the day before that he backs a ban on US diesel exports as a way to cool record high prices at the pump. Politico also reported that the administration was preparing a 90-day ban, which a White House official denied.
Confused? Trump will no doubt be desperate to get diesel prices down, especially ahead of the US midterm elections in November. But while an export ban might play well politically, it may not have the desired effect, as it could push US refineries to cut the amount of crude they process, which would reduce the amount of gasoline and other products produced, which could raise prices.

When an oil and gas company buys logo space on an AFL jersey, it isn’t trying to convince fans to buy its products.
Fremantle Dockers supporters cannot, for example, go to their local service station to buy a barrel of Woodside Energy oil or a canister of its liquefied natural gas.
This differs from the way most companies’ sponsorship deals are designed to convince consumers to buy their hamburgers, drink their beer and bet on their platform.
When Fremantle’s number one ticket holder, Tame Impala frontman Kevin Parker, wore the team jersey with the Woodside logo covered on tour during his team’s finals push, it reignited demands to drop the oil and gas sponsor over its contribution to rising temperatures.
This all raises an obvious question: if a fossil fuel producer doesn’t sell to the public, why spend millions putting its name on a footy jumper in the first place, and subject itself to public criticism?
‘Good feeling’
Companies like Woodside tend to sponsor sporting teams and community organisations to stockpile social capital, a reservoir of goodwill they can draw on to absorb the shock of inevitable public backlashes.
Fossil fuel companies, in particular, want to retain strong public support as they rely on state and federal policymakers – and sometimes local councils – to expand and operate. Community-led opposition movements can frustrate their projects.
This helps explain why extractive industries seek out highly visible sponsorship deals with the sporting teams closest to their operations.
The Australian business arm of Indian conglomerate Adani, known as Bravus, sponsors the North Queensland Cowboys, positioning its brand alongside a regional club near its coalmine.
Prof Emma Sherry, dean of school of management at RMIT University, says companies that have “complex relationships” with local communities often direct money to sports because they hope to build on fans’ emotional loyalty to their favourite teams.
“We often see that money go to the arts, and of course, we often see it in sport,” says Sherry, who specialises in sport management.
“What the companies are trying to do is use people’s love for their team to create a similar good feeling towards the company.”
None of this is in itself nefarious, as there’s an unwritten social contract that companies give back to the communities they work nearby.
But the issue is complicated when the high-profile sponsor is at the forefront of the carbon-emitting business, and is trying to use sport and other community activities to change views.
When Woodside and Fremantle renewed their long-term sponsorship deal at the end of 2024, the oil and gas company included an awkwardly worded claim that the two WA-based organisations both had a “focus on sustainability”.
That position recently became harder to defend after Woodside scrapped its long-term emissions and clean energy targets.
In response to the “Woodside, get off my chest” campaign calling for the sponsor’s removal, a company spokesperson said Woodside was committed to its partnership with the Dockers and was “looking forward to continuing our work together”.
An investigation by climate communication charity, Comms Declare, found that major coal, oil and gas companies are reaching children through schools, museums, science centres, sporting clubs, and other youth programs.
Many of the institutions that accept the companies’ funding are “operating under genuine financial pressure and are providing valuable services to children and families”, it found.
With sponsorship of 47 programs – including having its name emblazoned on the surf singlets worn by kids in the beach “nippers” program run by Surf Life Saving Western Australia – Woodside features heavily in the report.
‘We’ll have to stop playing’
The link between fossil fuel companies and sport is not new; oil and gas company Santos is a major commercial partner of the Wallabies and energy company Alinta Energy previously served as one of Cricket Australia’s main sponsors.
Yet fan unease is growing into a familiar backlash, much like the rising community resistance to promotional efforts by sports betting platforms.
Just as big tobacco once felt indispensable to rugby league, large commercial deals can make fossil fuel companies seem untouchable, right up until the culture shifts and alternative sponsors step in.
While the AFL grand final is forecast to be played in cool conditions on Saturday, large parts of Australia, including Victoria, have just emerged from their hottest winter on record.
Sherry says that growing climate awareness, particularly among younger fans, is showing sporting codes how a changing climate threatens their future.
“Sport relies on the natural environment to be successful. For example, we have heat policies, and if the temperatures keep going up, we’ll have to stop playing,” says Sherry.
“It is one of those things that’s becoming increasingly visible, not just from a sponsorship perspective, but also people realising that, if I’m in a snow sport and the snow melts, then my sport doesn’t exist.
“Or if I rely on grassy fields to play, and there’s a drought, I won’t be able to play.”
- 
  Jonathan Barrett is Guardian Australia’s business editor

A payments business that operates across Africa and is ultimately controlled by an Indian billionaire has announced its intention to float on the struggling London Stock Exchange.
Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, is planning one of the biggest UK listings in years, in a boost for the shrinking London market that has faced a string of recent departures.
The company is understood to be hoping to raise about $800m (£601m) from the initial public offering (IPO) and is targeting a valuation of $8bn to $9bn, which would make it one of London’s largest listings in recent years.
Airtel Money has 53 million monthly active users across 13 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, including Uganda, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo.
It operates through a network of branches and kiosks, which enable customers to load money on to their phones, withdraw cash and access other money services, and the company generated revenues of just under $1.4bn in the last financial year.
Airtel Money’s parent company is Airtel Africa, a telecoms provider that is part of the Indian conglomerate Bharti Enterprises, which is ultimately controlled by the billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal. Airtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but said it wanted Airtel Money to be listed separately.
“From a company perspective, [the listing] gives us flexibility for the future,” said Airtel Money’s chief executive, Ian Ferrao.
“We evaluated multiple [stock] exchanges, including the Middle East because we’ve got a headquarters in Dubai, along with European and North American exchanges. Ultimately, shareholders felt that London was the right choice. We still believe there is deep capital available … all the global institutional investors are here.”
Ferrao added: “Most importantly there’s a deep understanding of emerging markets in the London market and Africa specifically.”
Airtel Money said it would announce more details about the float in early October, including the indicative price range and number of shares to be offered, with final pricing to follow later in the month.
Airtel Africa had originally targeted a listing in the first six months of 2026 but delayed it to the second half of the year, blaming unfavourable market conditions as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Several other companies also pushed back planned IPOs amid the market volatility caused by the conflict.
Airtel Africa owns just under 78% of Airtel Money and will remain a long-term investor after the IPO. Minority stakes are held by TPG, Mastercard, the Qatar Investment Authority and Chimetech Holding.
Revenue in Airtel Money’s most recent quarter to 30 June climbed 38% to £399m, according to Airtel Africa.
The decision to float Airtel Money in the UK could mark a turning point for the City, which has struggled to attract listings in recent times and has also been hit by departures, partly as a result of overseas takeovers of UK companies.
Airtel Money’s planned listing could be one of the biggest debuts since the international payments company Wise floated in 2021 with a valuation of £8.75bn. Wise has since moved its main listing from London to New York.

Xi-Trump summit: China’s state car has already proved a match for the US ‘Beast’
The custom-built Hongqi N701 caught the eye of then-president Biden when he met the Chinese leader in San Francisco in 2023
US President Donald Trump has made no secret of how little he agrees with his predecessor, Joe Biden, on many things.
So, as Chinese President Xi Jinping is about to arrive in Washington on Wednesday, local time, there is one object that may offer a small moment of entertaining comparison between the two American leaders: Xi’s car.
Xi is expected to bring his own ride – a custom-built Hongqi N701, the Chinese state limousine that has accompanied him on overseas trips since 2022.
In a brief exchange captured on camera during Xi’s visit to San Francisco in November 2023, then-president Biden and his guest stopped beside the Chinese limousine. “It’s a beautiful vehicle,” the American leader said.
“It’s our Hongqi. Domestically made,” Xi responded with a smile, telling his staff to open the door so that Biden could take a look at the highly secure rear cabin.

When Japan shut its borders during the COVID-19 pandemic, expats and longtime friends Hillary Hewins and Blake Piper started spending their weekends in Atami, a small seaside city just a 40-minute bullet train ride from their adopted home of Tokyo.
Known during the 17th and 18th centuries for its soothing hot springs, Atami steadily surged in popularity during the four decades after World War II as a destination for Japanese holidaymakers. Sprawling concrete resorts opened, and the city center filled with lively bars, cabaret shows and other nightlife venues, all lit up by flashy neon signs.
When Japan’s bubble burst in the early 1990s, Atami’s prosperity collapsed as well. In five short years, hotel revenue dropped by around 25% and dozens of properties were abandoned. By 2011, visitation numbers had plummeted by 55% from their peak. The local population shrunk accordingly, from 50,000 residents to about 30,000 today.

Playing loud music on the bus? That will cost you hundreds of dollars in Singapore
- Published
Bus passengers in Singapore can now be fined up to $500 Singapore dollars ($391; £293) for placing their feet on seats or playing loud audio, as well as eating, drinking or littering onboard.
A fine of up to $5,000 will be imposed for more serious offences, such as causing obstruction or danger to fellow commuters within bus terminals or "the soiling of any part of a public bus, bus interchange, or terminal".
"These will foster a safer, more considerate and pleasant public transport environment for all," the Land Transport Authority (LTA) said in a news release.
The new regulations, announced on Monday, align with existing rules on Singapore's railway, or Mass Rapid Transit (MRT), network.
But while there have long been punishments for MRT passengers caught eating onboard, for example, rules on buses were typically company policies enforced by drivers, who could ask commuters to alight.
Now these nuisance behaviours have become official legal offences carrying immediate fines.
Authorised bus staff – such as ticket inspectors and bus interchange staff – can issue official notices to passengers who are suspected of committing an offence, according to LTA.
Bus drivers - or "captains", as they are called in Singapore - will not be given the same authority, leaving them to prioritise their duty of safely operating the bus. They can, however, tell commuters to stop disruptive behaviour, and those who refuse to cooperate may be asked to alight the bus or, in severe cases, face police intervention.
Singapore is not alone in trying to make public transport more peaceful. As transit networks grow, cities around the world are actively cracking down on bad behaviour to ensure a peaceful commute for all passengers.
Earlier this year, the Polish city of Kraków introduced similar rules targeting public transit nuisances, with commuters now facing a fine of up to 200 złoty ($52; £39) for disruptive behaviour.
These behaviours include playing music, watching videos without headphones, or taking particularly loud loudspeaker calls on buses and trams.
In the United Kingdom, existing laws ban using "sound-producing equipment" without permission if it annoys others, carrying potential fines of up to £1,000.
Some politicians have pushed to specifically fine "headphone dodgers" across all public transport, including buses.
These rules in Singapore, Kraków, and the United Kingdom show a growing trend of transport authorities stepping in to protect passengers.
As Singapore's Land Transport Authority (LTA) puts it: "Public transport is a shared space, and every commuter has a part to play in ensuring a gracious and pleasant commuting environment."

Jeff Garlin revealed in a recent interview on The Daily Beast’s “Obsessed” podcast (via Entertainment Weekly) that he had undiagnosed bipolar disorder during the making of ABC’s “The Goldbergs,” which he notably exited from after an HR investigation into multiple claims of inappropriate conduct against him. The 1980s-set family sitcom, which ran for 10 seasons and 229 episodes from 2013 to 2023, starred Garlin opposite Wendi McLendon-Covey. Garlin exited in 2021.
“At the time, I was undiagnosed bipolar,” Garlin said on the podcast, noting he got his diagnosis after exiting the series. “I was miserable on the show, and I was miserable with my performance. And [Wendi] was always trying to tell me, ‘Hey, you’re really great on the show.’ I didn’t believe her. I just got to the point where I had to quit, and she was very resentful.”
Popular on Variety
Garlin added, “Being bipolar, I was either one of three things: dark, dark, dark, dark, didn’t talk and look at anyone; happy to the point of mania, never turning off my thing; or mean — really, really mean.”
McLendon-Covey reacted to Garlin’s comments on Instagram by disputing his comments: “Huh. Let’s just say I remember things very differently, as does the crew, the other actors, the writers, and our executives.”
When Garlin exited “The Goldbergs” in 2021, two sources close to the production confirmed to Variety that it was a mutual decision between the actor and the network. Shortly before, Garlin addressed allegations against him in an interview with Vanity Fair, acknowledging that an HR investigation into his on-set behavior had been ongoing for the past three years and dismissing a rumor that he had been fired from the series.
“We have a difference of opinion, Sony and myself. Okay. My opinion is, I have my process about how I’m funny, in terms of the scene and what I have to do. They feel that it makes for a quote ‘unsafe’ workspace,” Garlin said at the time. “Now, mind you, my silliness making an unsafe workspace — I don’t understand how that is… I am always a kind and thoughtful person. I make mistakes, sure. But my comedy is about easing people’s pain. Why would I ever want to cause pain in anybody for a laugh? That’s bullying. That’s just uncalled for.”
The allegations against Garlin ranged from unwanted hugging and touching people on set to telling jokes that made others uncomfortable. McLendon-Covey later said during an interview with Andy Cohen for SiriusXM that Garlin’s exit was “a long time coming.”
“That it finally happened, it was like, ‘Ok, finally someone is listening to us.’ But that was kind of hard though because we had lost George Segal in real life,” she added. “To have to go through another loss on a sitcom…you can’t keep asking your audience to mourn people. That’s not why they tune in… I’m exhausted by that topic and the PTSD of it all. I just feel like the less people know about that, the better. No one benefits from knowing anything.”
“The Goldbergs” was in the middle of filming its ninth season when Garlin was fired. As Variety exclusively reported at the time, producers decided to keep Garlin’s character on the show for the rest of the season by using off-camera dialogue and unused takes pulled from earlier episodes, as well as previously shot images of Garlin. The actor’s stand-in was also used in group scenes, but he was shot from the back. The final result was visually awkward and earned so many complaints on social media that McLendon-Covey even weighed in at the time.
“This season threw us for a loop because it’s hard to incorporate someone who doesn’t want to be there and wants to leave mid-scene, and we weren’t about to rewrite the second half of the season,” the comedian wrote on Twitter at the time. “We’re doing our best.”
When “The Goldbergs” kicked off its 10th and final season last fall, the show killed off Garlin’s character.

Jamaica celebrates that its reparations case against Britain referred to final appeals court
Jamaica says its reparations case against Britain has been referred to the United Kingdom’s highest court of appeal for the Caribbean island
KINGSTON, Jamaica -- Jamaica’s government announced Wednesday that its reparations case against Britain has been referred to the United Kingdom’s highest court of appeal for the Caribbean island.
The unprecedented legal maneuver marks a watershed moment in the fraught historical relationship between Britain and its Caribbean realms, moving a centuries-old grievance from the realm of political rhetoric into one of the highest echelons of the British legal system: the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.
“It is really a very big deal, and the world is watching us,” said Olivia Grange, Jamaica’s minister of culture, gender, entertainment and sport. “What we are doing is historic, unprecedented and a major development in the reparatory justice movement. Talk of reparations has for a very long time been just that: talk. But Jamaica is known for action. The tide is changing, we are getting things done.”
The king’s decision to advance the petition rather than dismiss it is highly significant. While the British government has consistently rejected calls for financial reparations, the Crown’s referral effectively delegates the legal parsing of these historical grievances to the Privy Council in London.
Addressing the House of Representatives earlier, Grange emphasized the magnitude of the king’s cooperation: “Now, the king could have ignored us. The king could have delayed responding to us. The king could have made a decision not to refer the questions to the Privy Council.”
While the petition was formally addressed to the king, Charles has no personal say on whether it would be referred to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council; he would act on the advice of government officials.
Jamaica’s government said the king’s decision was made known via its lawyers in Britain.
The move comes more than two weeks after Jamaica petitioned the king to refer a series of questions about slavery, and the U.K.’s responsibility to pay damages, to the Privy Council.
The petition filed on Sept. 7 navigates a unique constitutional corridor. Because Charles remains Jamaica’s head of state, the island nation was able to directly petition him using an ancient legal mechanism that former colonies that have already transitioned to republics cannot access.
Grange acknowledged this constitutional irony, noting that Jamaica’s delayed transition to a republic — a longtime goal of the ruling Jamaica Labor Party — has actually proven to be a “blessing in disguise.” Because the island retains the king as its sovereign, it possesses the constitutional standing to force a legal review of the Crown’s historical obligations.
The move has not been without its domestic critics, some of whom questioned the diplomatic optics of the filing.
“There were no missteps in the filing process. There were no diplomatic blunders as some would want to give that impression,” Grange stated on Wednesday. “We were engaging, not with a foreign state, but with our head of state. It is a legal petition. It is not an interstate negotiation, or a demand for payment. It asked legal questions that must be determined by our highest court.”
Grange also disclosed that Jamaica has formally offered to help other Commonwealth realms that still share the monarch to file similar slavery reparation petitions.
Members of a Caribbean regional trade bloc known as Caricom met last week in Barbados to talk about reparations as they pushed for a unified strategy. The British government has acknowledged that slavery was “abhorrent,” but it has rejected demands for reparations or an apology.

Ukraine’s Zelensky warns of painful winter for Russia if energy truce talks fail
The leader described Russia’s Putin as the ‘patient zero’ from whom the idea of war keeps spreading further
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned Moscow at the United Nations on Wednesday that his nation would strike back and make the coming winter deeply painful for Russia, if the two sides cannot agree a truce on energy attacks before the cold sets in.
Ukraine and its allies are racing to secure limited agreements on energy infrastructure and Black Sea shipping before winter, fearing renewed Russian strikes on power and heating facilities, while Moscow continues to show little interest in wider negotiations to end the war.

When Greg Kiser gave the mayor and county judge a heads up about a change underway at his hospital, they responded with sighs of relief. One of the town’s biggest employers wasn’t closing.
“They said, ‘Greg, we can’t make it without this hospital in our little town,’” said Kiser, who’s been CEO of Three Rivers Medical Center in Louisa, Kentucky — population less than 3,000 — for 32 years.
It wasn’t an unreasonable fear. The hospital is part of Quorum Health, a private equity-owned chain of mostly rural hospitals that filed for bankruptcy in 2020 after years of funneling hefty payments to its investors. Now, it’s back on the brink of insolvency.
Kiser’s news was good news, as he saw it. Quorum is in the process of converting to a nonprofit organization, bringing all 11 of its hospitals along with it. Individual private equity-owned hospitals have transitioned to nonprofit status before, but it’s unheard of for an entire chain to do so. The change promises tax advantages, discounted drugs through the 340B program, and the ability to apply for grants. Most importantly, cash generated would go to patient care instead of private equity investors.

New Delhi, Sep 23: Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had flagged multiple issues, including deletion of names, in various states during the voter roll cleanup but the poll body was unanimous in its decisions related to the pan-India Special Intensive Revision of voters' list, officials said on Wednesday.
The officials made the remarks in the wake of a media report that the two Election Commissioners had objected to the Election Commission's steps 14 times in 10 months amid the SIR.
Responding to queries, the officials said the two commissioners had flagged decisions related to deletion of names in various states during the poll roll cleanup and handling of voter database.
EC sources maintained that all decisions of the Election Commission of India, including SIR, have been unanimous and with the approval of both the Election Commissioners and the Chief Election Commissioner.
Officials said the law governing the functioning of the Election Commission and a Supreme Court judgment underline that as much as possible, decisions should be taken unanimously and if need be, majority view should prevail.
The Indian Express reported that questions were raised on issues related to the SIR of electoral rolls within the three-member Election Commission (EC) itself, time and again by two of the three Election Commissioners, Sandhu and Joshi.
The national rollout of the SIR has been under the supervision of all three Commissioners. But Sandhu and Joshi have formally objected, on record, at least 14 times over the last 10 months -- four times on a single day -- to decisions taken and orders issued, they say, without their knowledge, the report in the English daily said.
Opposition parties have slammed the EC over the SIR, claiming it was meant to target electors not aligned to the BJP and its allies.

An Islamic State group member was sentenced on Wednesday to 20 years in prison for aiding the terrorist organization that took credit for a suicide bombing that killed 13 US service members and about 160 Afghans at the Kabul airport five years ago during the US military’s chaotic withdrawal from the country.
A federal jury in Virginia had convicted Mohammad Sharifullah in April of providing material support to the IS affiliate known as Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP). But jurors could not agree whether he bore some responsibility for the airport bombing on 26 August 2021.
US troops were conducting an evacuation operation at the airport when a suicide bomber detonated an improvised explosive device near an entry point known as Abbey Gate. Sharifullah’s role in the attack was scouting a route to Hamid Karzai international airport, prosecutors said.
Sharifullah, 28, received the maximum sentence for his one-count conviction in an international terrorism case that Donald Trump heralded last year during a speech to a joint session of Congress.
Sharifullah did not testify at his trial and declined to address the court before the US district judge Anthony Trenga imposed the sentence. The judge said the defendant was a “dedicated terrorist” who expressed no remorse for the “unfathomable” grief and suffering that he had caused.
Trenga heard victim impact statements from several parents of US service members. From a podium only a few feet from where Sharifullah sat, they took turns paying tribute to their children’s sacrifices and describing how the attack has shattered their families.
Mark Schmitz of Missouri asked Sharifullah to turn and look at him as he spoke about the life and death of his 20-year-old son, Marine Corps L/Cpl Jared Schmitz.
“They may have taken his life, but they’ll never take his legacy,” Mark Schmitz said. “A bomb killed my son. It did not kill what he stood for.”
Paula Knauss-Selph, whose son, army SSgt Ryan Knauss, was killed in the Abbey Gate bombing, said the family was “forever changed” by the attack.
“No justice will ever be enough to mend my broken heart,” she said.
Sharifullah requested a 17-year prison sentence, while prosecutors sought 20 years. His lawyers said he was never an ISKP leader and had not been convicted of any conduct related to the airport suicide bombing.
“He was brought here because the government believed he participated in the Abbey Gate attack, a theory which it was unable to prove at trial,” defense attorneys wrote.
Prosecutors said in their sentencing memo that “from his teenage years, when he pledged an oath of allegiance to [ISKP], Sharifullah’s carnage was driven by hate. Hate towards Americans.”
Jurors convicted Sharifullah of providing material support to ISKP. They deadlocked on whether any deaths at the airport “resulted from” that conspiracy. Sharifullah could have faced a possible life sentence if the jury had unanimously decided that question.
According to prosecutors, Sharifullah told a journalist that he wanted to “catch and kill the crusaders” from the United States for invading his country after the attacks of September 11. They said Sharifullah was involved in dozens of other attacks, including a March 2024 assault on a Moscow concert hall that killed roughly 140 people.
Defense lawyers argued that prosecutors failed to present any evidence tying Sharifullah to the Kabul bombing besides his own words during hours of FBI questioning. His team said Sharifullah told FBI agents what he thought they wanted to hear, possibly because he was afraid of being tortured in Pakistani custody before he was brought to the US.
A review by US Central Command found that the Abbey Gate bomber was Abdul Rahman al-Logari, an IS member who had been released from an Afghan prison by the Taliban. According to an FBI affidavit, Sharifullah recognized the alleged bomber as an operative he had known while incarcerated.

Ronaldo spurred on by 1,000 goals and Portugal glory
- Published
Cristiano Ronaldo considered retiring after the World Cup but says he opted to extend his glittering career as he believes he can help Portugal to further success - and reach a personal milestone of 1,000 career goals.
The 41-year-old confirmed in the summer that the 2026 World Cup would be his last, although his long-term future remained uncertain.
However, he has been included in Jorge Jesus' 25-man squad for Portugal's Nations League campaign, which begins against Wales in Lisbon on Thursday night.
In the lead-up to the contest with Craig Bellamy's side, the Al-Nassr forward also targeted the 21 goals needed to reach that magical 1,000 mark.
Asked if he thought about retiring from international duty after the World Cup, Ronaldo responded: "Yes, I did.
"Of course, I'm always thinking on my decisions, my future, the present also. I'm a thinker, you have to think."
The former Sporting, Manchester United, Real Madrid and Juventus player said: "I had a conversation with our president, with our coach. I still believe that I'm able to help the national team to reach what they want.

In May, Apple agreed to pay out $250 million as part of a class action lawsuit over claims the company overhyped its Apple Intelligence tools, specifically the long-delayed Siri AI overhaul.
Although the revamped Siri AI voice assistant is now available for owners of newer iPhones via iOS 27, you may still be eligible to claim cash back for past purchases. This settlement covers customers in the US who made their purchases from June 10, 2024, to March 29, 2025, and bought certain iPhone 15 or iPhone 16 models from Apple. If you qualify, you might receive up to $95 for each phone.
This settlement revolves around Apple’s promotion of Siri features to sell iPhones. “I expected to receive a Siri Apple Intelligence feature and did not receive it,” reads part of the statement you have to sign when filling out the claim form. As part of the settlement, Apple denies any wrongdoing.
“We resolved this matter to stay focused on doing what we do best, delivering the most innovative products and services to our users,” read part of Apple’s statement from May about the settlement.
To file a claim, visit the dedicated website: smartphoneaisettlement.com. Click the blue button in the top-right corner of the page labeled File A Claim. First, you’ll be asked whether you have a Claim ID and PIN to enter. It’s not required for you to already have this info on hand. On the final page, you’ll need either your iPhone’s serial number or Apple Account ID on hand to file the claim.
Not sure where your serial number is located? Open the Settings app, tap General, then choose About. Your serial number will be a string of letters and numbers near the top of the screen.
You can choose to receive the settlement money through PayPal, Venmo, an electronic bank transfer, or a paper check. If you have multiple devices and want to make claims for all of them, then you’ll need to fill out the form again for every eligible device. iPhone owners have until December 21 to make their claims.

We write a lot at STAT about artificial intelligence and medicine. But I hadn’t seen a paper quite like this one before. “Although the brain is often construed as a single organ, the brain may itself derive from two parallel progenitors that emerge early in development and that, respectively, form the forebrain/midbrain versus the hindbrain,” the researchers write. “Analogously, the heart derives from two parallel progenitors, the first and second heart fields, which converge to form a single organ.”

73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it
- Published
As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.
Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.
When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.
"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.
I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.
Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.
From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.
Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.
The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.
As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.
And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.
"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.
"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."
Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.
Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.
Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.
Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.
After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.
Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.
1 of 4
Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.
"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?
"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."
There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.
Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.
"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.
"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.
"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."
Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 - in a front two.
"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."
Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.
"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.
"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."
Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.
"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."
It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.
"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."
1 of 3
The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.
Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder - something he recognises and exploits.
Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.
"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.
"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.
"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.
"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.
"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back."
1 of 3
With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.
Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.
He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.
In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

Is it unprofessional to bring iced coffee to a job interview? Gen Z is being dragged for it
Some say it projects an unserious attitude. But others defend their right to caffeine
The list of acceptable items to bring to a job interview might include, but isn't limited to: your CV, your portfolio, your winning personality, your best foot forward.
But what about your iced latte? That's the debate currently raging online after a job recruiter recently called out Gen Z for showing up to corporate interviews "with iced coffee, iced latte, in hand" in a now-viral TikTok video.
In the video, which has been viewed more than 420,000 times since it was posted last week, U.S. recruiter Caitlin Wehniainen says she believes showing up with an iced beverage comes across as too casual, "like it's just a stop in your list of errands for the day."
"It looks like you went to Target, then you went to Starbucks and now you’re stopping by your interview before moving on to the next thing," Wehniainen said.
"Don't just waltz into your interview all casual with an iced coffee. It just looks like you didn't have time to finish your coffee beforehand."
The video has divided generations and the internet, with some agreeing that bringing a beverage to a job interview is unprofessional and others defending their right to remain caffeinated.
"It's not about the f--king coffee,"someone posted on Threads. "It's about reading the room, being able to be part of a community and society, compromise, and tolerate discomfort," they added.
It's about basic etiquette, someone else commented on Reddit.
"Arriving at an interview with a beverage for only yourself would be just as impolite as if the interviewer were drinking coffee but didn’t offer you a beverage," they added.
Conversely, how a company reacts to a beverage is a litmus test, others argued.
"In 2026 being YOU is a competitive advantage, and any environment that tries to micromanage something as small as whether or not you brought coffee to an interview is NOT a place you will thrive," marketing professional Zoë Hartsfield wrote on LinkedIn Tuesday.
"No wonder 58 per cent of Gen Z has a side hustle or runs their own company."
Generational divide?
The iced coffee debacle isn't the first time Gen Z has been dragged over etiquette and other so-called soft skills. Last year, the term "Gen Z stare" entered the lexicon, which describes the "blank, expressionless" look that the younger generation gives to older generations, particularly in customer service settings, according to Know Your Meme.
And like the "Gen Z stare," some argue the iced coffee debate touches on deeper issues, like how young adults and teens are coping with the lingering effects of COVID-19 lockdowns while facing the worst youth unemployment rate in decades and having to navigate AI's impact on entry-level jobs and recruitment processes.
- The 'Gen Z stare' mocks youth for staring into the void, but is anyone laughing?
- As more teens turn to AI for emotional support, experts say it's no substitute for human connection
Gen Z largely came of age during the isolation of the pandemic, tend to prefer digital communication and report higher rates of anxiety than previous generations. Recent surveys have shown that some managers are hesitant to hire younger workers, citing a lack of soft skills like communication and collaboration.
But is the younger generation really bringing iced coffees into job interviews?
Allison Venditti, a Toronto-based human resources expert, says she can count on one hand the number of times it has happened to her, and that's no different to how often it happened 15 years ago.
"We just have TikTok to hear about it now," Venditti, founder of Moms at Work, an advocacy group for working mothers, told CBC News.
"Most folks, Gen Z or otherwise, take the recruitment process seriously and come well prepared and do a great job."
Is there a middle ground?
That said, Venditti says she does have some iced coffee horror stories, like the time someone brought one in to an interview and accidentally dumped it all over themselves and their papers.
"We spent about 15 to 30 minutes cleaning it up. We also had to find a new room to do interviews as it was sticky. It was awful for all involved," she said.
But maybe there's a middle ground, others argued.
If you do bring an iced beverage into a job interview, don't swirl it around, slurp, put it on the interviewer's desk or hold it in your right hand, since that will make it wet when you shake hands, says Benjamin Chipman, a branding and marketing specialist based in New York City.
"You maybe have one sip that you get to take throughout the entire interview, because that is your opportunity to think a little bit when they are asking you a question," he said in a video posted to LinkedIn.
Which is better than responding with a Gen Z stare, some might argue.
Regardless, the short answer to whether bringing an iced coffee into an interview is unprofessional, is "yes," Venditti says.
"Would you bring a sandwich? No? Then don't bring that, either."

The story so far: The Union Health Ministry has said that stem cell therapy for Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) cannot be offered as routine or commercial treatment and can be used only as part of a duly approved clinical trial. The advisory, issued on September 16 to States and Union Territories that have adopted the Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010, follows a landmark Supreme Court judgment in January that examined the use of stem cells for autism.
What exactly has the government said?
The Health Ministry has reiterated that stem cell therapy can be offered as standard clinical care only for disease conditions or indications included in the Ministry’s approved list. Autism is not among those indications.
For ASD specifically, the Ministry has said that therapeutic use of any type of stem cell must remain restricted to duly approved clinical trials, following the National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research, 2017, and other applicable regulatory requirements. It should not be offered as a routine, standard or commercial clinical service.
The advisory is an attempt to ensure enforcement of an existing regulatory framework, particularly after the Supreme Court ruling.
Why is this significant for autism?
Autism is a neurodevelopmental condition. There is currently no established stem cell treatment that has been shown to cure autism or to provide sufficient evidence of benefit to make it a standard treatment.
The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), in its evidence review on stem cell therapy for ASD, examined the available scientific evidence and concluded that it did not support using stem cells in addition to behavioural and supportive therapies. It recommended that stem cell therapy for autism should not be offered as standard or routine therapy and that its therapeutic use should be restricted to approved clinical trials.
This distinction is important — a treatment being investigated in a clinical trial does not mean that it has been established as an effective treatment. A clinical trial is the mechanism through which safety and efficacy are tested.
What did the Supreme Court say?
The issue came before the Supreme Court in Yash Charitable Trust & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors., decided on January 30, 2026.
The petition raised concerns about the commercial promotion and administration of stem cell “therapy” for autism. The court examined the scientific and regulatory position and held that, given the evidence available at present, stem cell therapy for ASD could not be offered by medical practitioners as a clinical service outside an approved and monitored clinical trial or research setting.
The court also said that, until further research establishes stem cell therapy as a sound and relevant medical practice for ASD, offering it as routine clinical treatment would not meet the reasonable standard of care expected of medical practitioners.
The court recognised the difficult situation faced by families of people with autism who may look for experimental treatments when conventional interventions do not produce the hoped-for results.
It therefore also addressed patients who were already undergoing such treatment before the judgment. Rather than abruptly discontinuing treatment, the court directed the Health Ministry to work out a mechanism, in consultation with AIIMS and the National Medical Commission, to provide the best possible solution and facilitate their continuation until they could be redirected to institutions conducting clinical trials.
So is all stem cell therapy prohibited in India?
No, that is not what this latest advisory states. The latest advisory does not say that stem cells can never be used clinically. It draws a distinction between approved standard care and experimental use.
The Ministry’s current approved list covers 18 adult and 14 paediatric indications. These include several blood cancers and blood disorders, as well as conditions such as multiple sclerosis and systemic sclerosis. For these indications, the relevant treatment is haematopoietic stem cell transplantation performed appropriately; the Ministry’s list specifically states that mesenchymal stem-cell transplantation is not recommended for any disease condition.
Autism is not on this list.
The 2017 National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research also make a fundamental distinction between established haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation and experimental applications. They state that, apart from approved indications, stem-cell use in humans must be within an approved and monitored clinical trial.
What is the way forward for use of stem cells in children with autism?
The advisory states that this therapy cannot be simply prescribe or administer as a routine therapy/treatment.
If stem cells are being investigated for ASD, the treatment has to be part of a properly designed and approved clinical trial. Such research requires the appropriate regulatory and ethical approvals. Depending on the nature and manipulation of the stem cells, different regulatory requirements apply.
This is the key difference between research and treatment being that a clinic cannot describe an experimental intervention as an established therapy and charge patients for it as ordinary clinical care.
What about clinics already offering it?
The Health Ministry has asked State and District regulatory authorities to ensure compliance and to disseminate the Supreme Court’s directions to government and private clinical establishments involved in stem cell research, treatment, promotion or administration.
The National Medical Commission (NMC), in an advisory dated September 5, has separately reiterated that stem cell therapy can be offered as standard clinical care only for approved indications. It has said that unauthorised administration, prescription, promotion or advertisement beyond those indications would constitute professional misconduct. State Medical Councils have been asked to examine complaints and take disciplinary action where professional misconduct is established following due process.
There can also be consequences for clinical establishments. The Health Ministry has referred to Sections 32 and 40 of the Clinical Establishments Act, which provide for cancellation of registration and penalties in applicable jurisdictions.
What should parents understand from this?
The advisory does not mean that research into stem cells and autism has stopped. It means that such research has to remain research until there is convincing evidence that establishes safety and efficacy.
For parents, perhaps the most important distinction is between a clinic saying that stem cells are being studied for autism and saying that stem cells are an established treatment for autism.
The first is a legitimate area of scientific investigation, subject to approvals. The second is not supported by the present evidence or India’s regulatory framework. ICMR’s assessment remains that stem-cell therapy should not be offered as routine treatment for ASD.
The September advisory puts renewed emphasis on enforcing the distinction between an experimental intervention being tested under scientific oversight and a commercial treatment being sold to families as established care.

The Tokyo International Film Festival has named Australian director Rolf de Heer president of the international competition jury for the festival’s 39th edition.
De Heer has spent more than 40 years in Tasmania, Australia, directing, writing and producing films across a broad range of genres and subjects. His 1993 feature “Bad Boy Bubby” won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice International Film Festival, along with the festival’s Fipresci Prize. Four of his films have made the official selection at Cannes, among them “Ten Canoes” (2006), winner of the Special Jury Prize in the Un Certain Regard section.
This year’s World Focus lineup at TIFF will include Australia Spotlight, a dedicated showcase of Australian cinema mounted with the Australian Embassy in Japan. The series will screen de Heer’s “The Survival of Kindness” (2022), a competition entry at the 73rd Berlin Film Festival that went on to win the Fipresci Prize there.
Popular on Variety
“For any of us attending the Tokyo International Film Festival, it is a privilege,” de Heer said. “For me, as a filmmaker, it is even more so. The more films I manage to make, the fewer films I manage to see, especially on the big screen. But as a part of this jury, I have the duty, the obligation, to see at least 15 films and talk about them with other filmmakers.”
Hisamatsu Takeo, festival director of TIFF, said he was delighted to welcome de Heer as jury president. “With his distinctive perspective and unwavering commitment to filmmaking, de Heer has spent decades opening up new possibilities in cinema,” Hisamatsu said. “We look forward to the fresh dialogue and discoveries that his wealth of experience and deep insight will bring to this year’s Competition and its diverse selection of films.”
De Heer trained at the Australian Film, Television and Radio School and has since written or co-written 14 screenplays that reached the screen as feature films. His director’s credits run to 15 and a half features spanning a range of budgets and genres, and he has produced or co-produced 16 fiction films and five documentaries.
Career highlights include “Dingo” (1991), starring Colin Friels and jazz musician Miles Davis; “The Tracker” (2002), which began de Heer’s collaborations with Australian Aboriginal actor David Gulpilil; and “Charlie’s Country” (2013), for which Gulpilil won the best actor award at Cannes. “Alexandra’s Project” (2003) earned Helen Buday a best actress award at the San Sebastian Film Festival after the film screened in competition at the Berlin Film Festival.
The 39th TIFF will run Oct. 26-Nov. 4. TIFFCOM, the festival’s industry market, will take place Oct. 28-30.
