A video showing a large crowd gathered on a road and a flyover is being widely shared on social media, claiming that it shows the crowd at Congress leader Rahul Gandhi’s ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ event in Indore on 19 September 2026 (here, here, here). Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video shows people gathered for Rahul Gandhi’s ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ event held on 19 September 2026 in Indore, Madhya Pradesh.
Fact: The viral video is old and unrelated to Rahul Gandhi’s event. It shows a rally organised in Indore on 9 August 2026 to mark World Tribal Day. Hence, the claim made in the post is MISLEADING.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to a Facebook post by Vinoddj Vlog posted on 10 August 2026. The account confirmed in the comments that the video was recorded during the Adivasi Diwas (World Tribal Day) celebrations in Indore. Further, we found a YouTube video uploaded on 9 August 2026 by @DineshSolanki_indori, which features the same truck and location seen in the viral video. This video also identified the visuals as being from the World Tribal Day celebrations in Indore. This confirms that the video predates Rahul Gandhi’s ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ event, which was held in Indore on 19 September 2026.
Further, we also found similar visuals shared by Lokesh Mujalda, president of Jai Adivasi Yuva Shakti (JAYS), on Instagram on 9 August 2026. The post stated that a large number of people had gathered in Indore for World Tribal Day celebrations.
We identified the location seen in the viral video as Bhanwarkuan Square in Indore, which was one of the locations along the route of the World Tribal Day procession. A comparison between both can be seen below.
Media also reported that thousands of people participated in the World tribal day procession that took place in Indore (here, here). Actual visuals showing the ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ event can be seen here and here.
To sum up, an old video of the World Tribal Day rally is being shared as visuals of crowd at Rahul
Gandhi’s Indore event.

Karoline Leavitt was the youngest-ever White House press secretary before announcing her departure in August.
In a podcast episode of "Hang Out with Sean Hannity" released Tuesday, she spoke about her decision to step back from her role in the Trump administration to focus on her family.
"Being a working mom was the hardest thing I've ever had to do in my life," she said.
Leavitt, 28, shares two children with her husband, 60-year-old real-estate developer Nicholas Riccio. She told Hannity that her struggle to balance work and motherhood began shortly after her first child was born in July 2024.
Leavitt watched on live TV as Trump survived an assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania, the same day she brought her son, Niko, home from the hospital. She returned to work as the Trump campaign's national press secretary just days after giving birth.
"As a three-day postpartum woman, that was very traumatic, and I had a choice to make," Leavitt said. "I had producers calling, 'Can you come on TV and talk about this?' And I felt as though I owed it to the president to do that."
Her appointment as White House press secretary didn't make her work-life balance any easier, Leavitt said.
'I don't know if I can do this anymore'
Leavitt told Hannity that the long hours her job required took a toll on her 2-year-old son.
"I would leave for the White House very early in the morning, and he would cling to my leg as I would walk out the door, and we would have to hide him sometimes so that I wouldn't have to break his heart again," she said. "And sometimes I would drive to the White House in silence, like, 'I don't know if I can do this anymore.'"
After giving birth to her daughter, Viviana, in May, Leavitt said she realized it was time to make a change.
"The president deserves someone in that job who can give it their all 24/7," she said. "And after having two kids, I just realized I couldn't."
Trump "couldn't have been kinder" about her decision to leave the White House, Leavitt said.
"It was the hardest decision I've ever had to make because I loved my job and I love the president and our team and I believe so much in what he's doing," Leavitt said. "But, as he jokes, I do love my kids more, and you know, I realize they need me home right now, especially during these young years."

TOI correspondent from Washington: In a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly on Wednesday with US secretary of state Marco Rubio, India’s external affairs minister S Jaishankar raised New Delhi’s “interests and concerns” over Washington’s newly enacted Russia sanctions legislation, exposing a widening rift between the two sides even as the US publicly sought to portray the relationship as firmly on track.
The difference in their post-meeting social media messaging was striking. Jaishankar's account was unusually specific: the sanctions legislation was the first issue he mentioned, alongside the Gulf and Ukraine. Rubio's post on X made no reference to the sanctions issue. Instead, he wrote: “Great to meet with Indian External Affairs Minister @DrSJaishankar in New York today,” saying the two were “building on the US-India strategic partnership” and coordinating on regional priorities and upcoming multilateral efforts.
The diplomatic gloss barely concealed the widening gap after New Delhi bluntly warned Washington last week that using the new sanctions authority against India could affect bilateral relations. The Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act (SRIA), which President Donald Trump signed last week, gives him authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian oil and gas. India, which is one, has said it remains committed to securing affordable energy for its 1.4 billion people and will take measures to protect its economic interests.
There is also an increasingly awkward optics problem for Washington. Analysts have pointed to the US exemption allowing continued Russian uranium imports for itself even as Washington threatens punitive measures against other countries buying Russian energy. The US imported or used substantial Russian-origin enrichment services in 2025, while Washington has been scrambling to build alternative domestic capacity.
Former US official and South Asia analyst Evan Feigenbaum has similarly highlighted what he sees as a double standard in Washington's pressure on India, particularly after Trump announced that the US was exploring a deal to buy potash from Belarus, a close Russian ally. Trump has defended the proposal as a way to obtain cheaper fertilizer for American farmers.
Meanwhile, in further signs that Trump’s actions -- regarded as whimsical by critics -- are hurting Americans as much as the rest of the world, US diesel prices have crossed $6.50 a gallon nationally (approx Rs 165 per liter), adding costs for farmers, truckers and virtually every part of the agricultural supply chain. The administration is now scrambling to restrict diesel exports amid tanking poll numbers for Trump.
Indian officials likewise have repeatedly emphasised that energy decisions will be based on national interests and economic considerations, ignoring abrasive rhetoric from some US lawmakers. Senator Richard Blumenthal, a principal architect of the sanctions legislation, warned India and China during the congressional debate to “clean up your act” and buy their oil and gas elsewhere.
The emerging tension is particularly notable against the backdrop of Washington's elaborate courtship of Beijing. Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in the US on Wednesday for a three-day state visit, with Trump personally scheduled to greet him at Joint Base Andrews -- a rare gesture -- and a full state arrival ceremony and White House state dinner planned for Thursday.
The spectacle underscores the asymmetry in the relationships: Washington is literally pawing the ground and playing doggo before Beijing even as it is willing to risk friction with New Delhi. The Jaishankar-Rubio meeting meanwhile offered a revealing snapshot of an increasingly complicated US-India partnership -- one in which the language of strategic cooperation is becoming harder to reconcile with the increasingly contentious economic component of the relationship.

The BJP on Wednesday celebrated the birth anniversary of Dogra Maharaja Hari Singh and praised his move to accede to India in 1947. Meanwhile, Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah highlighted the role of party founder Sheikh Muhammad Abdullah, who was dropped from the official holiday list of J&K by the Lieutenant Governor’s (LG) administration.
The BJP held a series of functions in Srinagar and Jammu on the occasion. Speaking on the birth anniversary of the Dogra Maharaja, BJP leader and J&K Waqf Board chairperson Darakshan Andrabi said, “Maharaja Hari Singh took the wise decision in 1947 by acceding to India. How much have we benefited from the decision. Today we are with India, our country,” said Ms. Andrabi.
Ms. Andrabi described Mr. Singh’s rule as inclusive. “In his court, there were Hindus, Muslims, Sikhs, Christians. Everyone had to get equal rights,” said Ms. Andrabi.
J&K Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha also paid homage to the Maharaja in a message on X. “Maharaja Hari Singh was an enlightened statesman and progressive thinker who introduced several significant reforms focused on the welfare and empowerment of the people. His principles of public service, equality and inclusive development continue to hold significance and inspire people,” said Mr. Sinha.
There was an official holiday in J&K on the birth anniversary of the Maharaja on September 23. It was included in the holiday list by the Lieutenant Governor’s administration in 2022. However, the birth and death anniversaries of National Conference (NC) founder Sheikh Abdullah as holidays were dropped from the list, which has sparked strong reaction from the NC.
NC legislator Tanvir Sadiq questioned the move to drop Mr. Abdullah’s anniversaries as holidays. “It doesn’t take a rocket scientist to see the irony. A leader associated with land reforms that empowered the tiller and transferred land ownership to the poor has his holiday removed, while a holiday commemorating the ruler under whose reign Kashmiris endured repression is celebrated. No hatred. No prejudice. Just history. Facts are facts,” said Mr. Sadiq.
J&K CM Abdullah said Sheikh Abdullah’s role in J&K’s history was well known. “The sacrifices made by the NC could not be forgotten. No one can forget the role of Sher-e-Kashmir here. The BJP was attempting to present history differently whenever it disagreed with a particular narrative,” said Mr. Abdullah.
He said to those people who didn’t take part in the fight for freedom, what lesson will they teach us? “RSS and the ancestral party of BJP, everyone knows their role in the fight for freedom. Everyone knows who apologised and what they did,” he added.

The Imperial Japanese Army secretly considered imposing martial law in Tokyo in January 1945, during the final stages of World War II, amid concerns that large-scale U.S. air raids would severely disrupt public order, according to a newly reviewed historical document.
The study, however, significantly underestimated the likely scale of destruction from such air raids. Martial law, which would have allowed the military to assume administrative authority and other powers, was ultimately never imposed.
According to the document, the army estimated that more than 13,700 people would be killed in two air raids. In the Great Tokyo Air Raid of March 10, 1945, however, around 100,000 people, mainly in downtown areas, were killed — far exceeding the estimate.

If you want to save, make sure to click one of the promo codes at the top of this page to secure your discount.
What Is the Best Google Workspace Plan?
Google offers four different Workspace plans, though only three are relevant for most people. There’s Starter, Standard, and Plus, as well as Enterprise, which is only available if you contact Google’s sales team. There isn’t a minimum number of users on any of the plans, but the bottom three options (Starter, Standard, and Plus) support up to 300 users. If you need more than that, you’ll need an Enterprise plan.
Although you have access to all the apps regardless of the plan you choose, there are some important differences, particularly between the Starter and Standard plans. Both include secure storage through Google Drive, but Starter comes with 30GB per user while Standard comes with a massive 2TB per user. Plus bumps that up to 5TB per user. Across all plans, storage is in a shared pool, so each additional user adds to the total pool of storage your organization can use.
Gemini is also a big difference between Starter and Standard. Although both have access to the Gemini app, Starter only has Gemini in Gmail and Vids. Standard (and Plus) includes Gemini across the full suite, including in Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive, Meet, and Chat.
Starter is a great option for anyone just getting started, regardless of whether you’re a freelancer or a small business with a handful of employees. In addition to 30GB per user and limited access to Gemini, Starter comes with a few other limitations. It doesn’t support e-signatures in Docs, nor advanced features of Meet, such as noise cancellation. The bread and butter of Workspace is all here, though. You get a custom domain in Gmail, up to 100 participants in Meet, and the full Google suite of productivity apps.
Standard, as the name suggests, is Workspace proper, and it’s built for teams that need room to grow. That shows up most clearly in storage space, jumping from 30GB to 2TB per user. Standard basically cuts all the red tape on Starter. There aren’t any limitations on Gemini (it’s available across the full suite), Meet features like noise cancellation are available, and you can host up to 150 participants in a Meet call. Standard even comes with expanded access to NotebookLM, Google’s AI-driven note and research tool, with different chat modes and up to 20 generative audio overviews per day.
At the top of the range is Plus, which is focused on larger businesses. You don’t get any extra apps with this plan, but you do get 5TB of storage per user, along with up to 500 participants in Meet calls. The real reason to upgrade to Plus is security and admin controls, however. It includes Vault for data retention, along with LDAP access—basically a server for centralized account management, if you aren’t familiar.
Most people should use the Standard plan, not only for the large amount of storage space over Starter, but also due to the extra Gemini functionality. If you need to upgrade to Plus down the line, you can. And, more than likely, you’ll have a member of your IT team begging you to do so.
Why Teams Love Using Google Workspace Flows with Google Workspace
Google has updated Workspace a lot over the past several months, building in new functionalities via Gemini throughout the suite. But earlier this year, Google announced that it’s bringing all of those functionalities together through Workspace Flows. It’s a no-code automation tool that lets you build automatic workflows; i.e., update a Sheet when there’s a new email in Gmail from a particular address. The interesting thing about Flows, however, is that Gemini is built into it.
You can set up basic automations, which is great given how interconnected Google’s Workspace apps already are, but Flows become powerful when you throw Gems into the mix. Gems are AI agents built with Gemini, and you can create them with specific parameters.
Let me give you an example. Say you need a marketing plan, and an employee sends you a draft. You can have a workflow set up with a Gem that’s been trained on the budget, requirements, and tone of the campaign to quickly know if it can be approved or not. Or, you can create a Gem to scan your email, trained on your organization chart and role responsibilities, to notify you whenever you receive an email that has action items for you.
Flows give you a way to add a bit of context and reasoning to the often rigid constraints of simple automation systems, and they can save you a lot of time in the process. You may be able to gather customer feedback and put it into Sheets easily, for example, but Gemini can automatically sort, summarize, and categorize that feedback so you know what you should tackle first. Flows are centralized in Workspace, as well; you don’t need to install add-ons or configure anything outside of setting up your Workspace account.
Google Workspace Flows is a new tool integrated with Google Workspace. It is powered by Google’s Gemini AI and helps you get tasks done with Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Calendar and Chat. It can fix up emails, make plans, correct sheets, or write a follow-up message. No apps or links are needed.
Does Google Workspace Offer a Free Trial?
Even with a discount, Google offers a free trial for all new Workspace subscribers. Your first 14 days are free, regardless of which plan you choose, and even with the promotional pricing, you can sign up using our links at the top of this article. Just make sure to cancel if you don’t want to continue. After 14 days, you’ll be billed, and that will be the start of your new billing cycle.

DRI, BSF seize 12 kg foreign-origin gold worth Rs 17 crore via Bangladesh route
The DRI and BSF seized multiple consignments of foreign-origin gold in West Bengal and Patna. The operations were aimed at disrupting smuggling networks using the Bangladesh route.
The Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI), in coordination with the Border Security Force (BSF), has seized around 12 kg of foreign-origin gold worth nearly Rs 17 crore in a series of operations targeting cross-border smuggling through the India-Bangladesh border.
The seizures were made in West Bengal and Bihar, with the gold recovered from locations near the border as well as from a train passenger. The operations uncovered multiple consignments allegedly smuggled into India through the Bangladesh route.
In West Bengal, BSF personnel of the 161 Battalion recovered 27 pieces of unclaimed foreign-origin gold weighing around 3.15 kg near the India-Bangladesh Border Road in the area under BOP Gongra on September 20-21. The DRI subsequently took over the proceedings and seized the gold under the Customs Act, 1962.
In another operation on September 21, BSF personnel at BOP Mahakhola recovered 10 pieces of 24K foreign-origin gold weighing around 1.16 kg. The gold was found concealed near a handpump in Hathkhola village, ahead of the India-Bangladesh border fence. The DRI subsequently took over the recovered gold and seized it under Section 110 of the Customs Act, 1962.
Earlier, on September 10-11, BSF personnel had recovered 48 foreign-origin gold bars weighing around 5.9 kg near the India-Bangladesh border fence in the BOP Pathergata area. The consignment was subsequently taken over and seized by the DRI.
In Patna, DRI officers recovered and seized 15 gold bars and four small cut pieces of foreign origin, weighing around 1.71 kg, from a train passenger.
The gold was allegedly concealed in a cloth knee cap wrapped around both his legs. The investigation indicated that the gold had been smuggled from Bangladesh. The passenger has been arrested.
The DRI said the operations were part of its continued efforts, in coordination with the BSF, to disrupt networks involved in the smuggling, transportation and distribution of foreign-origin gold through the Bangladesh route.

The Bihar cabinet on Wednesday (September 23, 2026) gave its nod for setting up two universities, including Bihar’s first women’s university at Patna, which has been named after Maa Sita.
It also gave its administrative approval for the salaries and other related expenses of its officers and employees, Cabinet Secretariat Department’s Additional Chief Secretary Arvind Kumar Chaudhary told reporters in a post-cabinet briefing.
The other university, which has been named after Rashtrakavi Ramdhari Singh ‘Dinkar’ , will be set up at Begusarai, he said, adding that the decision was taken on the occasion of Rashtrakavi Dinkar’s birth anniversary. This is an important initiative towards carrying forward Dinkar Ji’s literary legacy and spirit of national consciousness to the new generation, he added.
A sum of ₹15 crore each has been approved for the two universities for payment of salaries and other related expenses of the officers and employees.
The Women’s University, Patna, will have jurisdiction over all the constituent and affiliated women’s colleges located at Patna except women’s colleges that come under Patna University, whereas all the constituent and affiliated colleges located in Begusarai and Khagaria will come under the jurisdiction of Rashtrakavi Ramdhari Singh ‘Dinkar’ University at Begusarai.
The constituent and affiliated colleges of Kameshwar Singh Darbhanga Sanskrit University, Darbhanga will not come under the jurisdiction of the newly created Dinkar University. Both Mata Sita Women’s University, Patna and Rashtrakavi Ramdhari Singh ‘Dinkar’ University at Begusarai have been created under the provisions of Bihar Special University Act 2026, Mr. Chaudhary said.
A total of 24 decisions were taken at today’s cabinet meeting chaired by Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary.
Sugar mill in Nawada
It also gave its nod to set up a new sugar mill at Warsaliganj in Nawada district. Revenue and Land Reforms Department transferred 99.39 acres of land at Mauja Makanpur, Warsaliganj Circle of the district to the Sugarcane Industries Department for the purpose.
Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary, in his post on social media ‘X ’, said that the decision will bring an investment of more than ₹500 crore and directly benefit thousands of farmers from Nawada, Nalanda, Sheikhpura, and Jamui.
Dairy and fisheries
In a decision that will bring relief to cattle rearers, the cabinet also approved Rs 160 crore under Mukhya Mantri Gaudhan Vikas Rinn Yojana (Chief Minister Bovine Development Loan Scheme) for a period of three years from 2026-27 to 2028-29, ACS said, adding that livestock farmers will receive a 100% subsidy on the interest charged on bank loans.
It is a government welfare initiative designed to financially empower cattle rearers, boost milk production, and generate rural employment.
Other important decision
The State Cabinet decided to appoint Ms. Kanak Kumari in the Bihar government on compassionate grounds. She is the dependent wife of the late Subedar Santosh Kumar, who was martyred in Leh (Jammu and Kashmir) on February 16, 2025, during a war or war-like situation.
It also decided to officially name the underground Sub-Way constructed under Patna Smart City Ltd near GPO roundabout, connecting the Multi Modal Hub with Patna junction, as “Acharya Kishore Kunal Sub-Way”.
Mr. Kunal was a former IPS officer and founder secretary of Mahavir Mandir Trust who died on December 29, 2024.
The cabinet also approved the law department’s proposal for the release of convicted prisoners by granting remission as a one-time measure on October 02, 2026, on the occasion of the birth anniversary of the Father of the Nation, Mahatma Gandhi.
The State government proposes to release convicted prisoners belonging to identified categories by granting them the benefit of special remission on the occasion.

College wrestler, 19, named as hiker who fell to his death near 400ft waterfall in Yosemite
Ryan George’s wrestling team at Santa Rosa Junior College mourned the athlete, writing on social media, ‘He had this way of lighting up a room’

A 19-year-old college wrestler from California has fallen to his death while hiking near a waterfall in Yosemite National Park, according to reports.
Ryan George’s wrestling team at Santa Rosa Junior College, about an hour’s drive northwest of San Francisco, announced the tragic news in a Facebook post Monday.
“This past weekend we received the tragic news that Ryan passed away at Yosemite National Park, following an accident,” the team wrote.
The Press Democrat, a local newspaper, reported that George was hiking with friends near Illilouette Falls on Sunday when he slipped and fell to his death. The waterfall is roughly 370 feet tall and flows all year long.
“If you knew Ryan, you know he was one of the most genuine, positive people you could ever meet,” his wrestling team said. “He had this way of lighting up a room, making you feel welcome, and bringing out the best in everyone around him. Always smiling, always encouraging, always full of life.”
Details surrounding George’s death, such as what led to the fall and the aftermath, are unknown. The Independent has reached out to the National Park Service and the Mariposa County Sheriff’s Office for comment.
George got into wrestling during his freshman year of high school. He was a football player at Montgomery High School in Santa Rosa and was too heavy to join the wrestling team. But that didn’t stop him.
“He worked really, really hard and he got his weight down,” Ian Hesz, who was George’s high school wrestling coach, told The Press Democrat.
George won an individual North Bay League title at Montgomery High, and then earned All-American honors last wrestling season as a freshman at Santa Rosa Junior College, according to the outlet. On Friday, just days before his death, George earned second place at the Dave Pacheco Invitational meet at Sacramento City College.
“It was good watching him find what he loved,” George’s older sister, Jaida, told The Press Democrat. “He was always playing and wrestling when he was a kid.”
The siblings’ father died when George was a baby and their mother died just weeks ago, according to the outlet.
In a GoFundMe page created on behalf of Jaida, a loved one wrote, “In July, we lost our Beloved Taji and now, just 2 months later, her daughter Jaida is facing another heartbreaking loss with the passing of her Little Brother Ryan Jr. this past Sunday.”
“She is grieving the loss of two people she loves deeply, while also facing all that comes with losing family members so unexpectedly, on top of it all being a New Mommy to her precious Son who is only 2 months old,” read the fundraising page, which generated more than $9,000 in donations by Wednesday.

Tesla's supervised self-driving system often misreads speed limits, Belgian safety group finds
Sept 24 : Tesla’s FSD automated-driving system frequently exceeded speed limits and attempted to overtake cyclists on streets where it's prohibited, a road-safety advocacy group said, citing tests it conducted in Belgium.
The Belgian group Johanna.be - which advocates for pedestrian and cyclist safety - tested Tesla’s system over three days in July, covering about 400 km (249 miles). It found that FSD often exceeded speed limits in 20 km/h and 30 km/h zones, and incorrectly displayed higher speed limits to drivers, potentially misleading them about how fast the vehicle should travel.
Tesla’s FSD driver-assistance feature can perform most driving tasks but requires drivers to pay strict attention. Dutch regulator RDW approved the system in April, with Belgium and a handful of other countries following suit. An EU-wide vote could happen on October 6.
Several EU countries, including Sweden, have expressed concerns about FSD exceeding speed limits, while countries that approved it say drivers remain responsible for complying with traffic laws.
Tesla and RDW did not respond to Reuters requests for comment.
Tesla released a study earlier this month saying that FSD-enabled Teslas do not speed excessively and drive at speeds matching surrounding traffic.
Xavier Lesenne, spokesperson for the Flemish government’s transportation ministry, which approved FSD in Belgium earlier this year, said it is "a learning system that continuously processes new and additional information" and adapts over time. Lesenne said the driver "remains 100 per cent responsible" and must be ready to intervene "should the system make an error or fail to correctly apply a traffic rule."
Lesenne said data from Tesla shows the technology "holds significant potential for accident prevention today."
Johanna.be found that FSD exceeded the limit in the majority of the tested 30 km/h road segments around Brussels, averaging 44 km/h.
Even though the vehicle's screen showed the system recognised 30 km/h speed-limit signs on the roadside, it often displayed an incorrect speed limit of 50 km/h.
"It is akin to a passenger constantly reassuring the driver that the speed limit is 50 km/h in nearly every 30-zone through which they pass," the report said.
Videos collected by the group show the FSD-enabled Tesla attempting to overtake cyclists on streets where doing so is not allowed.
The European Transport Safety Council has previously raised concerns about whether FSD can comply with differing road rules across Europe.
The Johanna.be report also noted positive aspects of the system, saying it "behaved cautiously and courteously around pedestrians and cyclists, often yielding proactively."
But those benefits "do not offset the documented failures to comply with speed limits and cycle-street regulations."
The NGO said it sent the report to the Flemish ministry and RDW, urging both to reassess the approvals.

It is sometimes called "momnesia," "mommy brain," "pregnancy brain" or "baby brain" — the forgetfulness, mental fogginess and cognitive changes that many women may experience during pregnancy. For instance, a woman might walk into the kitchen and forget why she did, or perhaps misplace her car keys in the bathroom.
Scientists know it is a real biological phenomenon, and now have found a possible explanation, identifying a specific brain circuit that becomes disrupted under the sustained high levels of oestrogen that accompany pregnancy.
They conducted experiments using laboratory mice designed to mimic the sustained elevated oestrogen experienced during pregnancy, finding that this led to temporary memory impairment in the animals without mood changes.
Underlying this in the mice, they found, was how the high oestrogen affected a neuronal pathway between two brain structures — the hypothalamus, which acts as a control center and integrative hub, and the hippocampus, which is central to memory formation.
High oestrogen increased the activity of hypothalamus neurons, which in turn suppressed activity in the hippocampus and impaired memory, they found.
"Momnesia" becomes most evident in late pregnancy and may continue into the postpartum period but usually dissipates after childbirth. Short-term and long-term memory can be affected, including spatial, social and verbal memory such as having difficulty remembering names or words, or struggling to recall familiar information.
"It is not serious or medically disabling, although it does affect daily functioning and confidence," said Zheng Sun, a professor of medicine at Baylor College of Medicine specialising in endocrinology and molecular biology and one of the leaders of the study published in the journal Science Bulletin.
"Typical examples include forgetting why one entered a room, misplacing an item, losing the thread of a conversation or needing reminders for appointments. It is widespread. About 80% of pregnant women notice those changes, but that figure largely reflects self-report and subjective experience rather than objective testing," Dr. Sun said.
The findings suggest that the phenomenon does not represent a general decline in cognitive ability.
"The important point is that pregnancy does not simply make someone 'less intelligent.' The effects appear to be more subtle and specific to certain cognitive tasks," said Yanlin He, director of the Brain Glycemic and Metabolism Control Laboratory at Louisiana State University's Pennington Biomedical Research Center and another of the study leaders.
Mouse experiments
The mouse experiments shed light on what is happening in the brain. Oestrogen is a hormone that governs a woman's pregnancy, menstrual cycle and puberty, spurring physical changes that help the body support the fetus, foster fetal development and prepare for childbirth. Its levels increase during pregnancy, peaking in the third trimester.
The researchers found that a protein called "oestrogen receptor alpha" transmits estrogen's signals into cells in the hypothalamus.
This region has abundant brain cells called GABAergic neurons that typically transmit calming signals to other parts of the brain. The study showed that high oestrogen levels over-activate the inhibitory signals by these neurons in the mice, and this directly affected the hippocampus.
The researchers performed memory tests including object and location recognition, finding impairment in mice given high oestrogen levels compared to those that were not.
When the researchers experimentally turned off the hypothalamus-to-hippocampus neuronal pathway, the mice no longer experienced oestrogen-induced memory problems. But experimentally activating the same pathway impaired memory in the mice, even without higher amounts of oestrogen present.
"When we genetically removed estrogen receptors from these hypothalamic neurons, estrogen-induced and pregnancy-induced memory problems in mice were also reversed. We suspect that a similar circuit may play a similar role in humans, although you cannot do this type of invasive study directly in humans," Dr. Sun said.
The researchers complemented the mouse experiments with a study assessing memory performance in 70 women, including some across different stages of pregnancy and some who were not pregnant, using tests of long-term, short-term and working memory. These tests revealed memory impairments that manifested during late pregnancy, correlating with high circulating oestrogen levels.
"Importantly, higher circulating estrogen levels were associated with poorer performance on several memory-related measures even after accounting for other potential contributing factors. This provides human evidence consistent with the mechanism we identified in mice," Dr. He said.
"However, we should emphasise that we did not directly manipulate or measure this specific neural circuit in pregnant women. Therefore, the human findings support the hypothesis but do not establish the same level of causality as the mouse experiments," Dr. He said.

Neutral venues and no 'away' fans - how Israel v Republic of Ireland became so contentious
- Published
An elite-level European football match will be played on Sunday at a neutral stadium, with no 'away' fans, and reduced television coverage.
That the match is even taking place had been in doubt - one side had to vote on a motion confirming whether or not they would participate amid significant opposition from fans, pundits and politicians.
But the vote confirmed the fixture would go ahead, and now the Republic of Ireland will travel to Debrecen, Hungary, for a Uefa Nations League 'away' match against Israel, played against a backdrop of ongoing and increasingly volatile disagreement between the two countries about Israel's military offensive in Gaza.
And on 4 October, the Republic will face the same opponents in a 'home' match in Backa Topola - a small town in Serbia.
No tickets have been sold to Irish fans for either fixture, and Irish public broadcaster RTE will air a stripped-back version of match coverage, with no commentators, pundits, or half-time analysis.
So how did a Uefa Nations League match become one of the most contentious fixtures in football?
Venue changes have not quietened protests
As soon as the Republic of Ireland were placed with Israel - plus Austria and Kosovo - at the Nations League draw in February, the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) faced calls from some to boycott the matches because of Israel's military action in Gaza.
The FAI eventually took a vote of its delegates in July, in which 75 members voted to play the matches and 32 voted to boycott.
Not playing the matches could have harmed Irish football in the long-run, the FAI said, amid the possibility of Uefa sanctions for refusing to fulfil the fixtures and the potential loss of millions of euros in income.
As well as curtailing its coverage, RTE will not take advertising or sponsorship income from the matches, saying it will only "meet its contractual obligations" to broadcast the fixtures.
No tickets are being sold to Irish fans for either the 'home' or 'away' matches, with a small allocation available for Israeli fans for the first fixture, which has been the case at multiple previous Israel home games held in Hungary.
Hungary has been deemed a suitable host nation for Israel matches because the two nations enjoy stronger diplomatic ties than those between Israel and many other European nations, and it has been willing to provide the necessary policing and security arrangements for matches to operate smoothly.
The FAI decided in the summer to play its 'home' fixture against Israel at a neutral stadium, citing "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil".
Reports have claimed the FAI was concerned protests could prevent the match from taking place in Dublin.
The FAI gave no official reason for the selection of Backa Topola, but choosing a venue in Serbia - in a town so remote - in theory renders security management easier and reduces the possibility of protest.
In 2025, Serbian foreign minister Marko Duric described Israel as one of Serbia's "closest friends and strategic partners". Serbia has also purchased military equipment, including drones and missiles, from Israel in recent years.
The decision to play in neutral stadiums has not curtailed opposition.
Fans of various Irish clubs have demonstrated against the matches during domestic fixtures in recent weeks, and on Monday more than 160 Irish athletes signed an open letter by the Irish Sport for Palestine group urging a boycott. The signatories include boxer Tyrone McKenna and former European champion athlete Ciara Mageean.
FAI CEO David Courrell said last week Uefa had rejected a request for the teams to be kept apart in future draws, director of football John Martin described the games as a "very uncomfortable situation for everyone". Manager Heimer Hallgrimsson, meanwhile, said playing the match did not constitute legitimisation of Israel's "genocide".
"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," Hallgrimmson said. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."
In response, the Israel Football Association accused Hallgrimsson of "ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity".
The Republic of Ireland faced Israel in Women's EuroBasket qualifiers last autumn and earlier this year after "extensive deliberations".
Irish support for Palestinians is long-standing
The Republic of Ireland has been among the European countries to most keenly show support for Palestinians since the start of Israel's military offensive in Gaza in October 2023.
More than 73,000 people have been killed in Israeli attacks, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations (UN).
In May 2024, alongside Spain and Norway, Ireland officially recognised a Palestinian state, and later that year joined South Africa's Gaza genocide case against Israel in the International Court of Justice.
The country has also boycotted Eurovision since 2025 because of Israel's ongoing participation in the song contest, was the first EU country to ban goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank, and has issued travel bans for Israeli government ministers.
On Monday, Irish foreign minister Helen McEntee said: "Ireland's view is clear - international law is being breached. We are seeing an attempt to erase a population."
Israel has criticised Ireland's standpoint and claims its actions in Gaza constitute self-defence, after the armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages.
Last summer a UN commission of inquiry found that Israel has committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, and this year a further investigation determined that the country has deliberately targeted children with military force, resulting in genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
Israel has repeatedly rejected allegations it has committed genocide.
The Republic of Ireland is not the only nation to have expressed reluctance to face Israel in international football.
In 2024, Belgium refused to host Israel on home soil, and the match was held instead in Debrecen.
The president of the Norwegian Football Association, Lise Klaveness, made a public statement last year saying Israel should be suspended from European competitions, and Turkey also called for Israel to be banned.
BBC Sport reported last autumn that Uefa executives were considering a vote on whether to ban Israel, under pressure from representatives from a number of nations.
But any plan to hold a vote was pulled when the first phase of a ceasefire was announced last October.

A planned executive order that would have greatly enhanced White House influence over grants at the National Institutes of Health is “looking dead,” according to one person familiar with the decision and Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine).
On Tuesday, Collins, the Appropriations Committee chair, sent a letter to Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought and NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya, decrying the White House plan to establish a commission of political appointees, including Vought, with veto power over grant awards. The tempering of the executive order was first reported by Semafor.
“I urge you not to move forward with this proposal, which would undermine … the Federal government’s objective of funding biomedical research projects based on scientific merit and value rather than political ideology,” Collins wrote in the letter.
Her concern was shared by several other lawmakers, who released their own statements earlier this week. By Wednesday, some of those same officials were celebrating the Trump administration’s seeming reversal.
“It shouldn’t take public outcry to prevent President Trump and Russ Vought from laying waste to the NIH and defunding lifesaving research because they think it’s ‘woke’ or want to extort a university,” Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.), vice chair of the Senate Appropriations committee, said in a statement.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
The idea for the executive order came out of a widely reported Oval Office meeting Friday, when Vought accused the NIH of funding projects that do not comport with the goals of the Trump administration, The Washington Post reported. President Trump seemed to support the idea of moving NIH grants more firmly under political control in part so that he could further target research funding for Harvard University, according to Politico.
It was just the latest attempt by OMB to bring science funding more tightly under agency control by taking a more hands-on approach. Many of those efforts have been challenged by Congress, however. Last year, Vought mandated that the NIH fund grants in their entirety up front, rather than dispersing funds on a yearly basis. This meant that the agency had less cash on hand for new grants. But that funding strategy, called “Multiyear funding,” was curbed in the 2026 appropriations bill, which also slightly increased the NIH budget after OMB proposed a massive cut. Congress is on track to do so again this year.
Earlier this year, OMB delayed signing off on NIH spending in its 2026 budget. The agency similarly last year instituted a brief pause on NIH being able to spend any money. And in May, OMB rocked the scientific community by proposing a rewrite to the bedrock guidance for all federal contracts that deemphasized peer review and empowered political appointees in driving decisions. The proposal received tens of thousands of comments in opposition, and its implementation was blocked by Congress’s stopgap spending bill.
Its most recent executive order also received immediate pushback from Congress members on both sides of the aisle, and in both chambers.

After years of accusations that the Hyderabad Cricket Association (HCA) has been ignoring cricket in rural areas, it is now pushing ahead with an ambitious plan to revamp the cricketing structure in the State. Mahabubnagar and Karimnagar are set to be the first to see these winds of change, with both set to get functioning academies by summer.
“Karimnagar and Mahabubnagar will get floodlights soon. Apart from that, we are also focusing on Khammam and Warangal. Once land is acquired everywhere, by December hopefully, and handed over to HCA, we will take up the works,” HCA secretary M. Jeevan Reddy said at a press conference here on Wednesday.
The association, however, will continue to rely on private grounds in Hyderabad owing to the expensive land costs in the city.
HCA is also looking to expand its administrative footprint to cover all districts of Telangana. Plans are being drawn to bring them all under its umbrella and then decentralise the operations across the State.
Former secretary T. Shesh Narayan, who now heads the District Infrastructure Development Committee, stated that tenders will soon be called for investing in the infrastructure of Karimnagar and Mahabubnagar. He said that the focus will not be solely on developing cricketers.

“We need to explore all talent in the districts, not just the players but also umpires, physios, trainers and more. Once they are identified, they can be trained in Hyderabad and then get full-time jobs,” Shesh Narayan, who also serves as the HCA spokesperson, explained.

Public health experts have called for tighter regulation of celebrity endorsements of harmful products following President Droupadi Murmu’s appeal to artistes to refrain from promoting substances detrimental to health, made against the backdrop of Maharashtra’s action over a Vimal Elaichi advertisement featuring Shah Rukh Khan, Ajay Devgn and Tiger Shroff.
The President, speaking at the 72nd National Film Awards in Gujarat on Tuesday (September 22, 2026), said popular artists, particularly those who influence children and young people, should promote disciplined lifestyles and refrain from endorsing substances harmful to health.
The remarks come as the Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) examines whether the Vimal Elaichi campaign amounts to surrogate advertising for Vimal Pan Masala. The FDA has issued show-cause notices to the three actors, alleging that the advertisement creates an association with a pan-masala product whose manufacture, storage, transportation, distribution and sale have been prohibited in Maharashtra.
The issue has also reached the courts. The Delhi High Court on September 14 declined to entertain a challenge to the FDA notices on territorial-jurisdiction grounds and directed the petitioner to approach the appropriate court in Maharashtra. The court did not adjudicate on whether the advertisements amounted to surrogate advertising.
Public health advocates have long raised concerns that celebrity endorsements can give socially acceptable imagery to products associated with tobacco, areca nut and other harmful substances, particularly among younger audiences. Cancer specialists have also warned about the health consequences associated with tobacco and areca-nut consumption.
Also read| Due diligence: On surrogate advertising
The Vimal campaign is not the first instance in which Bollywood celebrities have faced scrutiny over such endorsements. Amitabh Bachchan, Salman Khan, Saif Ali Khan and Akshay Kumar have, at different times, been associated with advertisements for pan masala or related products. Kumar withdrew from a Vimal campaign in 2022 following criticism.
The renewed debate raises a broader public health question over whether regulations governing advertising are keeping pace with the influence of celebrity endorsements, particularly where advertisements for apparently permissible products may create associations with products that are restricted or harmful.
Speaking to The Hindu, Arun Gupta, convener of Nutrition Advocacy in Public Interest (NAPi), said appeals to celebrities needed to be backed by a clear legal framework covering the endorsement and advertising of harmful products, including tobacco and ultra-processed foods.
“I wish appeals were taken seriously and work in India, especially when it comes to endorsement and advertising of harmful products which include ultra-processed food products and tobacco products,” he said.
Mr. Gupta said the government should act on the President’s appeal and enact a clearly worded law to prohibit the marketing of unhealthy products.
“This is the only way to curb the trend. Why I am saying this is because the current legal framework is more of self-regulation and is ineffective even though the government believes it to be working,” he said.
Sandeep Nayak, chairman — Oncology and executive director — Surgical Oncology and Robotic Surgery, KIMS Hospitals, Bengaluru, said the President’s remarks highlighted the public-health consequences of celebrity endorsements of tobacco-linked products.
“As oncologists, we witness daily the catastrophic impact of pan masala, alcohol and tobacco addiction in our clinics. When high-profile icons lend their names to these brands, they inadvertently glamorise carcinogenic products for millions of impressionable youth,” he said.
Dr. Nayak said products such as silver-coated cardamom and flavoured mouth fresheners marketed under tobacco-associated brand names could function as surrogate advertisements.
“Using identical brand titles, logos and colour palettes — whether for pan masala or alcohol extensions —” creates a strong association with the primary brand, he said, calling for tighter regulation of such brand extensions.
Giving an insight into the scale of tobacco use in India, the National Family Health Survey-5 (2019-21) found that 21.4% of Indians aged 15-49 used smokeless tobacco, with the prevalence higher among men (29.6%) than women (12.8%). The latest Global Adult Tobacco Survey (GATS), conducted in 2016-17, estimated that 28.6% of Indians aged 15 years and above — nearly 267 million people — used tobacco. The survey also found that smokeless tobacco was the most prevalent form of tobacco use in the country.
A World Health Organisation study estimated the economic cost of diseases and premature deaths attributable to tobacco at ₹1.77 lakh crore in 2017-18, more than 1% of GDP, while treatment of tobacco-related diseases accounted for 5.3% of total health expenditure. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) has estimated that smokeless tobacco and areca-nut use caused more than 120,000 oral-cancer cases globally in 2022, with 88% occurring in South-Central Asia.

India is investigating LG Electronics and Samsung for allegedly paying lower tariffs on imported display parts of high-end TVs, five sources told Reuters, putting under scrutiny the premium entertainment devices both South Korean giants have bet big on.
Lengthy import tariff and tax investigations have been a sore point for foreign investors in India and embroiled companies like Samsung and Volkswagen, though Indian officials say they are simply enforcing the law of the land.
The latest investigation concerns imports of display parts that go into making panels for OLEDs, or organic light-emitting diode technology, which offer superior picture quality and are made by LG Electronics and Samsung in India, a key growth market for them.
The market for pricey OLEDs is still niche globally; however, with just 6.5 million units sold last year, research firm Omdia says. Counterpoint Research data shows India’s TV market was worth $4.7 billion last year, with OLEDs having a near 4% share.
Indian officials have alleged the companies wrongly claimed a concessional 5% tariff on imported OLED glass screens called open cells, arguing the rate has for years been reserved for the older LCD and LEDs, which dominate mass-market sales, said the sources, who declined to be identified as the matter is confidential.
For OLED parts, India’s Directorate of Revenue Intelligence believes Samsung and LG should have paid a 15% duty, said two of the sources aware of the investigation.
The companies are privately opposing the position of Indian authorities as they believe OLED is nothing but an advanced form of LED technology and the same Indian tariffs should apply, the sources added.
The sources did not comment on the financial details of the amount of duty allegedly underpaid. Typically, following an investigation, authorities can issue tax demand notices and impose penalties of up to 100% of the duty evaded. Companies can legally challenge such demands in courts.
Samsung said in a statement to Reuters that it is “reviewing the matter and cooperating fully with the relevant authorities, adding it is firmly committed to complying with all laws.”
LG and the revenue directorate did not respond to queries.
SCRUTINY IN TV MARKET
Officers from the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence visited Samsung’s India headquarters in Gurugram near New Delhi to question officials in recent weeks, four sources said.
LG was instead sent written questions by Indian authorities on its OLED imports and has submitted its responses, along with a voluntary, unspecified monetary deposit to cover any extra duty that authorities may request, said one of the sources.
LG last year listed its India unit on Mumbai stock exchanges, where it currently has a market capitalisation of nearly $12 billion. It said in August its TV segment was witnessing “very high-quality growth”, with its India TV market share around 26% and OLED share almost 59% in value terms.
Samsung also sells many OLEDs in India, with one Made in India 65-inch TV priced at $2,415. The company is contesting another $520 million India tax demand since last year for allegedly misclassifying imports of networking gear.
LOBBYING PUSH
While Indian authorities investigate LG and Samsung, their industry groups in August launched a campaign to push India’s IT ministry to recommend OLED display parts should be covered under the low, concessional duty regime of 5%.
In nearly identical confidential letters, the Consumer Electronics and Appliances Manufacturers Association and industry body MAIT said the tariff law “restricts the benefit” only to LCD and LED display parts, creating an “anomalous situation”.
“Manufacturers of more advanced OLED TVs are denied the same benefit, resulting in higher input costs and reduced competitiveness,” said the letters, reviewed by Reuters.
Government data shows India’s imports of displays, including TV parts, rose 15% in a year to $5.6 billion by March 2026, highlighting the nation’s reliance on such overseas supplies.
The industry is also lobbying for more exemptions on OLED display manufacturing overall, saying only old LCD technology manufacturing machines enjoy duty exemptions.
“This absence of parity results in higher capital costs for setting up OLED manufacturing,” said the letters. “This also hampers growth of manufacture of higher technologies in India and is thus against ‘Make in India’.”
The industry groups and India’s IT ministry did not respond to Reuters queries.

Logitech just introduced several new gaming accessories in its Pro line of products. This includes a mouse, keyboard, mousepad and headset.

Indians are discovering the thrill of shopping without paying
- Published
You are hungry. Or you are not. It doesn't matter.
You open FoodNeverComes, pick from 22 cuisines and start scrolling. Butter chicken looks good. So does bibimbap. You add a few dishes, watch the total climb and hit checkout. A tracker says a rider is on the way.
Then you get a dummy AI-generated call from inside the site. He is outside your building, he says, but cannot find your street or door. Except there was never any food in the first place. The order exists only on the screen.
"Order the food. Skip the bill," says the site., external Its slogan is blunter: "The food never comes - but the dopamine does."
Built by two 26-year-old software developers - Purvansh Parmar and Anshul Sharma - from Udaipur in India's northern state of Rajasthan, FoodNeverComes says it has attracted more than 2.7m visitors since its launch in June.
It now offers 22 kitchens, 327 dishes and 319 real recipes, complete with fake prices, a simulated checkout and a fictional delivery experience.
FoodNeverComes belongs to a new internet genre: "dopamine sites", which recreate the rituals of consumption without the consumption. There are fake shopping sites, fake delivery services and even fake holidays.
The genre took off in South Korea, external and has since travelled well beyond, spawning a growing crop of sites - Dopamine Shop, external or Fakehaul, external, for example - that mimic everything from food delivery and shopping to travel.
What, exactly, are we enjoying when we enjoy buying something?
The idea began with the founders' own shopping habits. Parmar and Sharma met on a computer science diploma course and later started NeuroX AI, which builds software and AI products and makes Instagram content. They noticed it in their own lives: online baskets filling up with things they wanted, but never actually bought.
Sharma would browse electronics, fill an online basket and abandon it. Parmar's mother did much the same. "She would add things to the cart and say, 'I will order this later'," he recalls.
Parmar's own version ended at food delivery checkouts. During a two-month project in Mumbai, he says, he was spending 5,000-10,000 rupees a week on food, sometimes ordering treats he did not necessarily need: Belgian waffles, ice cream and, once, a large jar of sour cream he barely wanted and gave away to friends.
He believes "perhaps the real craving was not always for the food, but for the ritual of ordering it".
What begins as genuine hunger, the two argue, can become associated with the pleasure of ordering. Over time, boredom, anxiety or habit can trigger the urge even when the hunger has disappeared.
"Sometimes you're not hungry at all. You're bored or busy, and then you realise that ordering food makes you feel good. You start associating the act of ordering with that dopamine hit. Eventually, it's not just the food you want," says Parmar.
Ravi Dhar, director of the Yale Center for Customer Insights, calls this "anticipatory utility" - the pleasure of looking forward to consumption. It is especially strong with things that capture the imagination - a new pair of shoes, a holiday, a restaurant meal - because anticipation becomes part of the experience.
Sometimes, Dhar says, anticipation can be more pleasurable than ownership: "The thrill is in the chase." Once the object is acquired and the tension resolved, psychological arousal falls.
Neuroscience has a name for this gap between the chase and the catch, and it complicates a popular idea. Dopamine is not simply the brain's pleasure chemical, whatever the internet's talk of "dopamine hits" might suggest.
Kent Berridge, a University of Michigan neuroscientist who developed the theory of "wanting" and "liking", says they are separate processes. Wanting is the motivational pull towards something; liking is the pleasure of having it. They often travel together, but not always. Dopamine, in his account, drives the first, not the second.
Tempting food or products online are likely to activate this wanting system, which Berridge calls "incentive salience".
"Some situations can trigger 'wanting' by itself," he says. We can pursue something intensely even when the eventual pleasure is weak - or, in more everyday terms, want something more than we ultimately like it.
Dr Anna Lembke, a Stanford University addiction psychiatrist and author of Dopamine Nation, makes a similar distinction.
"To call dopamine a chemical of pleasure is an oversimplification," she told me. "Dopamine is the molecule that says 'get more of' or 'do more of', but it doesn't necessarily equate to pleasure."
What she adds is the role of ritual. Cues and habits attached to a reward can become reinforcing in their own right, she says: in addiction, the routines leading up to drug use can eventually matter as much as the drug itself. "Anticipation of reward can be as reinforcing as the reward itself," she says.
Can repeatedly ordering imaginary food satisfy a real craving? Berridge says the ritual could produce a "dopamine hit and strong 'wanting', and also evoke faint conditioned 'liking'".
But he would expect the "novelty to soon wear off", and would be "surprised" if many people returned to place more than about 10 imaginary orders.
Dhar is more open to the possibility that simulated consumption could serve as a kind of release valve.
"While we still need more empirical data to know if simulated shopping can satisfy a consumer urge, evidence from simulated consumption in gaming shows it can be highly effective," he says.
But there is an equally plausible danger: the ritual may simply rehearse the behaviour it is supposed to replace.
Lembke says the evidence is not in yet, and the effect may depend on the person. But her own bet is that, over time, the sites could "reinforce the same addictive neural networks they are trying to simulate".
"The one up side, though, is that people using these sites have on some level already admitted to themselves they have a problem, and that admission is often the first step in recovery," says Lembke.
Sharma ran an accidental experiment of his own. When his phone screen cracked, he spent a week on Amazon comparing six or seven replacements and adding them to his basket. Then he repaired the handset.
"I enjoyed the process of research and putting the phones in the cart," he says. "Eventually I didn't buy a phone."
He now catches himself doing the same on food delivery sites, particularly when anxious, filling baskets without checking out. "I realised that I suffer from this problem," he says.
The site's blog explores the "serious side" of the fake takeaway, from food-delivery addiction and why fake ordering feels good to cravings, guilt and the psychology of the shopping cart.
The founders have since taken the idea beyond food. A second site, TripNeverLeaves, lets users plan a holiday - destination, flight, seat, hotel and activities - then sends them on a virtual flight that never leaves the runway. They say it has attracted more than 100,000 visitors.
Who those visitors are is harder to establish. But Lembke says younger people may be especially vulnerable to reinforcing digital rewards because the "developing brain is a vulnerable brain".
"In childhood and early adolescence, the front lobe, which acts like the brakes on appetite, is not yet fully connected to the emotion centres of the brain. Hence, teens are more likely to take risks without appreciating the negative consequences, and more likely to get addicted to reinforcing substances and behaviours, once exposed," she says.
For now, the founders say the sites are not about making money. They plan to keep them free and eventually share the data with neuroscientists and psychologists.
What looks like a joke about ordering too much food has stumbled into a bigger question about modern consumption: if so much of the thrill comes before we get the thing, do we need the thing at all?

Latest CDC report on youth behavior has some good news — and MAHA vibes
CDC survey finds mental health and suicide risk among U.S. teens has improved
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Mental health symptoms and suicide risk among American high schoolers improved in 2025 compared to two years prior. That's according to the latest report from the national Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance Survey, conducted by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) every two years.
The new report, which primarily highlights students' diets, physical activity and sleep, found improvements in the number of students who ate fruits and vegetables compared to the previous survey. While there was not much improvement in levels of physical activity, more students reported playing on a sports team compared to in 2023.
"We see in this report that our children are eating healthier, engaging in team sports, and experiencing fewer feelings of sadness and hopelessness," said Dr. Jennifer Shuford, CDC's Deputy Director and Chief Medical Officer at a press conference held last week to announce the report's findings. "This is good news for kids, for us, and for our country. The focus here is clear: healthier youth today, healthier adults tomorrow."
The survey, commonly known as the YRBS, has been running for more than 35 years. This year's report differs from previous years' which emphasized the dangers teens face from drugs, alcohol and sex. While the 2025 survey collected a range of information, the report highlights topics important to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and his MAHA – Make America Healthy Again – movement. It talks about nutrition, exercise, sleep, screen time and mental health while leaving out things like teen smoking and vaping and exposure to violence.
It also leaves out discussion of health disparities among ethnic groups, which was a feature of past reports.
Improvements in youth mental health
In 2021, the American Academy of Pediatrics declared a national emergency in child and adolescent mental health.
"After the pandemic, we had our all time high of suicide attempts and ideation and visits to the ER with suicidality," says child and adolescent psychiatrist Dr. Vera Feuer, Chief Clinical Officer at the Child Mind Institute.
But the new report, which also presents trends over the past decade, shows a decline in suicidal thinking and behaviors, which initially showed up in the 2023 YRBS data. This year's report finds that levels of persistent feelings of sadness or hopelessness among high schoolers have fallen in recent years – from 42% in 2021, to 40% in 2023 and 33% in 2025.
Similarly, the number of students who seriously considered suicide fell from 22% in 2021 to 14% in 2025. The number who made a suicide plan (which ups the risk of attempting suicide) also fell from 18% in 2021 to 12% in 2025.
While these percentages still represent large numbers of teens, the latest findings are "encouraging," adds Feuer.
"What we're seeing is that since 2021, there's actually been a really nice improvement in many mental health indicators for young people," says pediatrician Dr. Scott Hadland, chief of adolescent medicine at Mass General Brigham for Children in Boston. "I think that's a cause for optimism."
New emphasis on health and wellness
However, the new report stands apart from past years' reports in what's highlighted as well as what's not, says Hadland, who is part of the team that administers the survey in Massachusetts. The survey questions haven't changed but what the report emphasizes or omits has.
"There is a real emphasis on health and wellness," says Hadland. "And look, that's very important."
The highlights in the new report "align with the Make America Healthy Again initiative led by President Trump and Secretary Kennedy – who are committed to preventing chronic disease across our country, especially in our nation's youth," Shuford said at last week's press conference.
Missing pieces
But other factors that are also important in the health and wellbeing of the country's youth are missing in the report, says Hadland.
"As somebody who looks at this report every year, it really stood out to me that we were missing rich data on what's going on with substance use with young people," he says. In past years, the survey captured both positive trends – decline in smoking – as well as more troubling ones – rise in vaping in recent years, he explains.
Similarly, the new report is also missing information on sexual behaviors among teens, as well as their exposure to firearms and other forms of violence, which featured prominently in past reports. Guns, for example, remain the leading cause of death among children and teens in this country.
Another piece of data that's missing in the new report, says Feuer, is how connected students feel in their school.
"School connectedness and kids feeling like they belong in schools and that adults and children in schools care about them is a really important protective factor for mental health," she says.
The report also omits any mention of LGBTQ+ youth and has fewer details based on race and ethnicity of students, note both Feuer and Hadland.
"The extent to which we could observe health inequities by race and ethnicity and then by membership in the LGBTQIA+ community were really much more absent in this report," says Hadland.
"There are significant disparities when we look at behaviors among different groups of students," acknowledged Mike Underwood, acting director of the CDC's Division of Adolescent and School Health, in response to a reporter's question about data on LGBTQ youth.
He said that data was collected and is available on the YRBS website for anyone to look up.
"We encourage states and communities to go and look through their data," he said.

OpenAI and Anthropic both recently released new models aimed at lowering costs. Anthropic announced Opus 5.5, the latest version of its main mass-market workhorse model, used for tasks like coding and other complex knowledge work.
And OpenAI announced GPT-6 Sol and Luna, the latest versions of its middle-of-the-road or smaller models focused on efficiency and speed.
These new releases are not about groundbreaking new capabilities. Rather, they’re about efficiency. As both OpenAI and Anthropic target enterprise customers, they’re racing to compete with open-weight models as organizations have explored changing their practices and using model routers to use these pricey, frontier models less in favor of cheaper alternatives.
Anthropic and OpenAI argue that these new releases push the envelope at the frontier (albeit mostly in modest ways), while bringing costs substantially down.
Opus 5.5: A more affordable, more competitive flagship
Opus 5.5 is at the higher end of the models announced today, but the wider context here is that Anthropic is playing a bit of catch-up in its race with OpenAI. OpenAI earlier this month released GPT-6 Astra, which has sometimes been modestly beating Opus 5 in benchmarks and user sentiment. (By price and capability, Astra is competing with both Opus and Fable.)
Benchmarks by Anthropic and its partners now show Opus 5.5 performing better at coding and knowledge work than GPT-6 Astra in some cases, albeit modestly.
The real story here is cost. From Anthropic’s announcement: “Input and output tokens are $4 and $20 per million, 20% less than Opus 5. Cache reads (which make up the majority of agentic and coding work costs) are $0.20 per million tokens, 60% less than Opus 5. Opus 5.5 also generates output more than 30% faster than Opus 5.”

Obama often criticized Fox News. He also did fewer interviews with Fox News and took fewer questions from its correspondents compared to other news networks. His administration also said it was willing to exclude Fox News from interviews. Some accused his administration of blocking the network's access in one instance, but a spokesperson claimed it was a communication error and the administration backtracked.
However, the Obama administration never outright blocked, banned or ejected Fox News reporters from press briefings.
In September 2026, U.S. President Donald Trump banned three major news outlets — CNN, MSNOW and Politico — from the White House. The outlets subsequently filed a lawsuit accusing the administration of violating the First Amendment.
Soon after, former President Barack Obama condemned Trump's ban and speculated about the consequences if he had banned Fox News during his administration. In response, some people online claimed Obama had retaliated against Fox News (archived) in a similar way during his first term. For example, television personality Piers Morgan wrote on X (archived), "Obama did ban Fox, and waged almost constant war against press freedom."
(X user @PiersMorgan)
As Snopes previously reported in 2018, while Obama criticized Fox News and snubbed the network's requests for interviews, he never banned the network outright from the White House. As such, we rate this claim as mostly false.
In October 2009, a New York Times report (archived) stated Obama's Treasury Department attempted to exclude Fox News from a roundtable interview with the executive-pay czar Kenneth R. Feinberg. Major news networks were sharing a "pool" camera crew for these interviews. According to the report, other networks protested Fox's exclusion.
However, a 2009 Talking Points Memo report referred to the situation as a "miscommunication." The report said:
TPMDC dug into it, and here's what happened. Feinberg did a pen and pad with reporters to brief them on cutting executive compensation. TV correspondents, as they do with everything, asked to get the comments on camera. Treasury officials agreed and made a list of the networks who asked (Fox was not among them).
But logistically, all of the cameras could not get set up in time or with ease for the Feinberg interview, so they opted for a round robin where the networks use one pool camera. Treasury called the White House pool crew and gave them the list of the networks who'd asked for the interview.
The network pool crew noticed Fox wasn't on the list, was told that they hadn't asked and the crew said they needed to be included. Treasury called the White House and asked top Obama adviser Anita Dunn. Dunn said yes and Fox's Major Garrett was among the correspondents to interview Feinberg last night.
A Treasury spokesperson told Talking Points Memo, "There was no plot to exclude Fox News, and they had the same interview that their competitors did. Much ado about absolutely nothing." Fox News did conduct the interview with Feinberg.
The Obama administration didn't hold back in its criticism of Fox News in the aftermath of the controversy. When questioned by NBC News about the administration's tone regarding Fox News, Obama said:
We're going to take the media as it comes. And if media is operating basically as a talk radio format, then that's one thing, and if it's operating as a news outlet, then that's another. But it's not something I'm losing a lot of sleep over.
Obama spokesperson Josh Earnest reportedly admitted that the White House had demonstrated its "willingness to exclude Fox News" from interviews, but that it had not done so, according to Talking Points Memo. Earnest added, "The president and other high ranking officials and people like Ken Feinberg have done interviews with Fox in the past and will do them in the future."
In a 2010 interview with Rolling Stone, Obama accused Fox News of focusing more on its point of view than objectivity. "It's a point of view," Obama said, "that I think is ultimately destructive for the long-term growth of a country that has a vibrant middle class and is competitive in the world."
As Snopes previously reported, former Fox News White House correspondent Major Garrett asserted that though there was "never an effort to shut me out of the briefing room," ongoing tensions between the Obama administration and Fox News hindered his ability to do his job. In a November 2018 interview with The Hill, he said:
The White House would always pull me aside and say "well, really, Major, we're not at war with you," and I said "stop talking to me like that because when you're at war with my network you by definition are questioning and assailing my journalistic credibility and the work I do here every day," he said. "So don't tell me it's not about me, it is about me."
"Now, they never tried to pull my pass, but they had this sort of arms-length relationship to Fox and tried to demonize it on a daily basis. So that's another part of American history and journalism in the White House press corps I think at least should be noted at this moment," he said.
As we previously reported, Fox News' White House correspondents were called on less during press briefings compared to other major television networks. In September 2009, when Obama made the talk show rounds to talk about healthcare reform, he snubbed "Fox News Sunday" and did not appear on the show until his last year in office in 2016.
In 2013, The Washington Post reported that Obama's Department of Justice surveilled a Fox News reporter and obtained a search warrant for his emails while conducting an investigation into national security leaks in 2009. The investigation also looked into other reporters but appeared to specifically target Fox News.
The Obama administration never banned Fox News outright, but no love was lost between the two groups. While Fox News accused the administration of cutting it out of one interview, the administration blamed it on miscommunication and gave the network access while not hiding its disdain for the network.
For further reading, Snopes previously covered the misrepresented claim that former U.S. President Joe Biden cut reporters from the press pool.
Snopes' archives contributed to this report.

Trump gets a Greenland deal
But the island is still a part of Denmark.
Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump’s campaign to take over Greenland has reached a peaceful end — for now.
What happened? Trump signed a new security agreement with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland while at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, outlining an expanded US military presence on the island.
The deal is the result of months-long negotiations between the two countries and Greenland, which is a semi-autonomous territory of the Kingdom of Denmark. Crucially, it reaffirms the “sovereignty and territorial integrity” of Denmark and Greenland, something Trump has spent the last year-and-a-half-plus threatening to sweep away.
What’s the context? Trump returned to office last year proclaiming that US “ownership and control of Greenland is an absolute necessity” for US national security, even though Denmark — and by extension Greenland — is a NATO ally.
That rhetoric quickly escalated, and by this January, Trump was suggesting that the US could even use force to take the island. “If we don’t do it the easy way,” he said — buying Greenland from Denmark, or perhaps bribing its residents to secede — “we’re going to do it the hard way.”
This, understandably, freaked Europe out, prompting multiple countries to deploy small numbers of troops to Greenland.
Does this mean Trump is done trying to take over? We can always hope. It’s possible Trump will claim this as a win and move on, even though Tuesday’s deal doesn’t fundamentally change the nature of the US-Greenland relationship. (Last week, he referred to it as “a dream come true” for the US.)
That being said, Trump’s desire to own Greenland always made more sense as an attempted legacy move than anything else, whatever his professed justifications. So while he might be happy to take the win for now, with the war in Iran still on and the midterms fast approaching, it shouldn’t be surprising if he’s clamoring for ownership again before his term is up.
And with that, it’s time to log off…
