The Best Samsung Phones
Featured in this article
There's the iPhone, and then there are Samsung Galaxy phones—the two most popular phone brands in the US. But whereas Apple is the sole company behind the iOS mobile operating system, even the best Samsung phones face stiff competition in the Android world. (And yes, Galaxy phones are Android phones, though Samsung calls its layer over Android “One UI.”)
Google's Pixel phones are our favorite Android devices, but Samsung's offerings are just as great and often have better hardware. Alongside Google, Samsung promises the longest software support for its cheap and high-end devices. That means you don't have to upgrade as often, since it will stay up-to-date, secure, and bug-free longer. But the Korean giant has many, many models at varying prices, so what's the best Samsung phone? We sort it out here in this guide. We also have tips and tricks to get the most out of your shiny new hardware.
Check out our mobile guides, including the Best Samsung Galaxy S26 Cases, Best Samsung Galaxy S25 Cases, Best Android Phones, Best Cheap Phones, Best Pixel Phones, and Best Folding Phones.
Updated September 2026: We’ve added the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8, Galaxy A37, and Galaxy Z Flip8; mentioned the Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra and Galaxy S26 FE; removed some older devices; updated the best time to buy section; and updated prices.
Why Buy Samsung?
The best part of the Android world is the choice of hardware. Want a phone with a headphone jack? Sure! Want a phone that fast-charges in around 30 minutes? It exists. So why stick with the stalwart Samsung?
In our experience and research, Samsung's smartphones have a track record of reliability, and because it's a major player, it has a wider network of authorized repair centers than competing Android manufacturers. Yes, there was the Galaxy Note 7 fiasco and even the issues with the first-gen Galaxy Fold, but Samsung now has a customer satisfaction score equal to Apple's, according to the American Customer Satisfaction Index. That said, we haven't read great things about the company's US customer support team.
With its flagship phones, you get top-of-the-line specs, exceptional build quality, and long software support. We primarily pick Pixel phones over Samsung because we prefer Google's software experience, but there are plenty of people who like Samsung's take on Android. As always, keep an open mind and consider all your options.
Is Now the Best Time to Buy?
Samsung announced its new foldable range in August, and it won't upgrade the S-series until next year. If you're after the best Samsung phone, now's a good time to buy. But keep the company's launch time frames in mind if you want the latest and greatest.
- The flagship Galaxy S series launches at the start of the year during Samsung's Galaxy Unpacked event. The Galaxy S26 series went on sale March 11.
- The budget Galaxy A series typically arrives in the spring. There are several A-series phones, so they usually dribble out during the first few months of the year. In 2026, the company launched the Galaxy A17 in January, and the Galaxy A37 and Galaxy A57 went on sale in April.
- The folding Galaxy Z series always lands in the summer, and 2026's event was in August, when the company unveiled the Galaxy Z Fold8, Z Fold8 Ultra, and Z Flip8.
- The midrange Galaxy FE series is the “Fan Edition,” but this is more or less a slightly cheaper variant of the Galaxy S-series. The Galaxy S26 FE was just released this month (September 2026).
Consider these dates as you shop, because you may want to hold off for the new model, or it can help inform you about when to expect the best discounts.
How Long Are Samsung Phones Supported?
Android phones used to have disastrously poor software support. Two years after you bought your $1,000 phone, it would no longer receive software updates. Thankfully, Google began promising longer software update cycles for its Pixel phones, which pushed Samsung to match it.
The following Samsung phones will receive seven years of software updates from their release date, which includes Android operating system updates and monthly security patches. The latter keeps your phone secure, and new OS versions can add new features.
- Galaxy S26 FE, S26, Galaxy S26+, Galaxy S26 Ultra
- Galaxy S25 FE, Galaxy S25, Galaxy S25+, Galaxy S25 Edge, and Galaxy S25 Ultra
- Galaxy S24 FE, Galaxy S24, Galaxy S24+, and Galaxy S24 Ultra
- Galaxy Z Fold8, Z Fold8 Ultra, and Z Flip8
- Galaxy Z Fold7, Z Flip7, Z Flip7 FE,
- Galaxy Z Fold6, and Z Flip6
Samsung's Galaxy A-series phones, from the A16 and up, will receive six years of updates. Most other older Samsung devices, like some in the Galaxy A-series or older flagships, will receive four years of OS updates and five years of security patches starting from the release date. This varies because Samsung has kept changing its policy year over year, but you can find more information here.
To find out if your Samsung phone has a pending update, go to Settings > Software update > Download and install. It should check for any updates and download them, then you'll see an option to install. Make sure you back up your phone before installing any update. We have a guide here.
Why We Recommend Buying Unlocked
Most people buy phones directly from their carrier, but if you're reading this guide, we suggest you buy an unlocked smartphone. When you buy a carrier phone, it's “locked” to that network. That means if you want to switch carriers, like moving from Verizon to T-Mobile, you'll have to ask your carrier to unlock the device, and this can be a huge headache. (Especially if you're traveling and want to use an international SIM card.) Carriers usually have a few requirements to unlock a phone, like making sure your device is paid off or waiting a set period of time. Unlocked phones, on the other hand, don't have this problem. You're free to use whatever carrier you want, whenever.
Carriers also mask the true cost of a smartphone. AT&T may entice you with a $ 36-per-month payment for a shiny new Samsung flagship, but in reality, that means you're paying $1,300 for a smartphone over 36 months. Did you really want to spend that much? Or will a cheaper phone suffice? Also, you're more likely to get software updates faster as they come directly from Samsung, and there's often far less preinstalled bloatware to deal with.
All in all, buy unlocked! You can buy unlocked Galaxy phones directly from Samsung and most third-party retailers like Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart.
The Settings to Change on Your New Samsung Phone
Samsung has an annoying habit of announcing a bunch of cool new features with its smartphones, then leaving them turned off by default. If you've never fiddled with your phone's settings, there's a good chance you're missing a lot of fun, helpful features.
This can include things like changing the navigation from onscreen buttons to gesture navigation, adding the battery percentage icon next to the battery bar, or keeping the display always on instead of requiring a tap on the screen. Good news for you! Since our reviewers routinely switch phones, we drummed up a list of the most important settings to change when you get a Samsung phone. Read it here. Pro tip: We can't stand Samsung's default keyboard, so we almost always switch to Google's Gboard instead.
Explaining “Qi2 Ready” Samsung Phones
Qi2 is the new wireless charging standard—it takes a page from Apple's MagSafe technology and embeds magnets directly into the smartphone, allowing it to connect to accessories and chargers magnetically, even the same ones available for iPhones. It could increase accessory compatibility across devices, which is a good thing. The magnets ensure precise charging, so you never worry about a misaligned phone that won't charge. It offers better efficiency and can potentially charge faster. We have more details in our Qi2 explainer here.
Confusingly, Samsung's 2025 and 2026 flagship phones are “Qi2 Ready” and technically not true Qi2 smartphones. This means they can support Qi2 when paired with a magnetic case, but on their own, the S25 and S26 series don't have built-in magnets (you can still charge wirelessly). It's disappointing and creates more confusion. We've already encountered some cases with varying degrees of magnetic strength, and some cases don't quite work with basic Qi wireless charging stands.

Qualcomm Snapdragon vs. Exynos Chipsets
A Samsung phone sold in the US may not be the same as a Samsung phone sold in the UK. That's because Samsung's Galaxy S-series flagship phones have long relied on two different processors. Devices sold in the US and select markets are powered by Qualcomm's Snapdragon processors, while other regions use Samsung's homegrown Exynos chipsets.
The performance gap between these processors isn't as wide anymore, but there have been issues in the past. Exynos chips tended to overheat a few years ago, though they sometimes offer slightly better battery life than their Qualcomm counterparts. This also greatly affected camera quality, since the chip handles image processing. Again, none of this is as big an issue as it used to be, but it's worth keeping in mind as you shop.
Other Samsung Phones to Consider
If you don't see a Samsung phone mentioned in this guide, it may be because it isn't sold in the US and is a little harder to source for testing. But here are a few other Samsung phones we've tested.
Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra for $2,100: An incremental upgrade over the Z Fold7, the Z Fold8 Ultra is for foldable phone fans who want the best and are willing to pay for it. The familiar book-style form factor offers a 6.5-inch cover screen, like a regular candy bar phone, and opens to give a tablet-sized 8-inch display with a fainter crease than before and a stronger hinge. Naturally, you get top-notch performance, all-day battery life, and Samsung’s best camera in a folding phone, with a 200-megapixel main shooter, 50-megapixel ultrawide, and 10-megapixel telephoto lens.
Samsung Galaxy S26 FE for $700: The Samsung Galaxy S26 FE is a perfectly decent phone with good battery life, a lovely big display, and a solid triple-camera system, but nothing about it justifies the extra $100 over last year’s almost identical S25 FE. The processor is slightly better, but that’s about it. In fact, Samsung downgraded the USB-C port to USB 2.0 in the S26 FE, so we think you’d be better off buying the S25 FE above while it’s still available.
Z Fold7 for $2,000 or Z Flip7 for $1,100: If you want a Samsung foldable without the eye-watering price tag, consider 2025’s Galaxy Z Fold7 or Galaxy Z Flip7 if you can find them discounted. The Fold7 is a little thicker with a more prominent crease in the screen. The battery life isn’t great, and the ultrawide camera is weaker, but there isn’t a huge difference between it and the Fold8 Ultra. It’s a similar story for the Flip7, with the Flip8 bringing minor hinge improvements, a refined, lighter design with a less noticeable crease, a faster processor, and more useful software features for the outer display.
Samsung Galaxy S25 Edge for $1,300: Have you ever wanted a really thin and lightweight phone? No? Well, Samsung has an option for you anyway. The Galaxy S25 Edge was a unique one-off last year (it's doubtful we'll see a successor) and matches several features of the Galaxy S25 Ultra, like a titanium frame, stronger front glass, and 4K 120 frames per second video recording. All the cameras even have autofocus. But it made several sacrifices to achieve its amazingly slim 5.8-mm frame (for context, the S25 Ultra is 8.2-mm thick). There's no stylus, no telephoto camera, and worst of all, the battery capacity has been slashed. We've seen this before—thin phones have always compromised on battery life, and this is no different. We constantly had to baby this phone's 3,900-mAh battery with mixed usage, and that's just not acceptable. (The iPhone Air did it better.) If you find yourself constantly near a power source and think you'll enjoy the slim and light design, then go for it.
Samsung Galaxy A17 5G for $249: On paper, the Galaxy A17 seems like a really great deal. It offers six years of software support, an AMOLED screen, expandable storage, and a decent camera. Unfortunately, it's held back by lackluster performance. The problem is the very limited 4 GB of RAM in the US model, which ruins the overall experience. If you had to use your smartphone in an emergency, I would not trust the A17 to be reliable. But if your needs are extremely minimal, it may suffice.
If you're looking to save some cash, it's fine to buy Samsung's Galaxy S24 range from 2024, as long as the prices are a good deal lower than the original MSRP. (They're hard to find at most major retailers.) These phones will still get support for a while, and they're pretty great. I don't think it's worth buying anything older.
Should You Invest in Samsung’s Ecosystem?
Samsung is one of the few smartphone manufacturers that can match Apple's hardware ecosystem. The company makes smartphones, but you can also expand your experience with a Galaxy Watch8 smartwatch, Galaxy Buds4 Pro earbuds, Galaxy Ring fitness ring, Galaxy Tab S11, and even a Windows-powered Galaxy laptop.
There are perks, like some features on the Galaxy Ring and Watch8 being available only when paired with a Samsung phone, and its earbuds automatically switching between Samsung devices based on what you're using. There aren't many exclusive features when using a Galaxy phone with a Galaxy laptop, but capabilities like Quick Share let you send photos and documents between your devices (even to iPhones via AirDrop!).
Again, it's not necessary, and these other devices might not be the right ones for you within their respective categories, but if you're chasing hardware parity, you have that option with Samsung.
What Is Galaxy AI?
With the Galaxy S24 series, Samsung launched “Galaxy AI," a selection of artificial intelligence features, many of which are powered by Google's Gemini large language models. These enable smart features that may be helpful in your day-to-day, like real-time translations during phone calls, real-time transcriptions in Samsung's Voice Recorder app, the ability to summarize long paragraphs of text in the Samsung Notes app, or changing a sentence's tone with the Samsung Keyboard.
In the Galaxy S25 series, Galaxy AI expanded to include Gemini as the default voice assistant and the ability for Gemini to work with multiple apps simultaneously. It also debuted Drawing Assist, which lets you sketch or enter a prompt and get an AI-generated image. Now you can also use video in real time with Gemini, even from the cover screen of the Galaxy Z Flip7.
And in the Galaxy S26 series, the AI features got even more helpful. The Document Scanner built into the camera app can now erase fingers and creases and minimize distortion before converting the photo into a PDF. Audio Eraser is now available in any media app to reduce distracting background sounds in videos, so you can hear the subject clearly. And there's now built-in call screening to better filter out robocalls. Samsung also debuted Google's Task Automations in the Gemini assistant, allowing you to ask Gemini to book you an Uber or order something from DoorDash, Uber Eats, or GrubHub, though it's pretty slow.
You can find many of these features in Settings > Galaxy AI to toggle them on or off. We also have an explainer on how to limit Galaxy AI to on-device processing.
What Is Samsung DeX?
Samsung's DeX (short for “desktop experience”) launched in 2017, and it lets you plug your Samsung phone into an external monitor and launch a desktop version of Android, all powered by the phone. You can find a list of compatible Samsung phones here—the Flip7 is the first Galaxy Flip to support DeX—and you'll need a monitor, mouse, and keyboard, plus a cable to connect the phone to the monitor. (You can also cast DeX to select screens wirelessly.)
In DeX mode, you can resize Android apps and open them all in separate windows. It's a proper computing platform, though you probably won't want to use this as a permanent laptop replacement or anything of the sort. It's great if you're visiting another office, or working out of a coffee shop or airplane (if you have a portable display). We have a whole guide to setting up and using DeX here.
What Happened to the Galaxy Z TriFold?
I have not tested Samsung's Galaxy Z TriFold, and it seems I never will. (I had some brief hands-on time with it at CES 2026, but Samsung did not provide WIRED with a test unit.) This folding phone, which had an MSRP of $2,800, officially went on sale in the US at the end of January, but three months later Samsung discontinued it because of high manufacturing costs.
Yes, unfolding it from a fairly compact phone to a massive 10-inch tablet was amazing and the stuff of dreams, but it didn't justify the high price; you can buy a killer phone and excellent tablet for way less than $3,000. The luxury of having them in one pocket is incredible, but more than a $1,000 incredible? I think the TriFold is the true “phablet” Samsung promised so long ago, and the folding mechanism is novel and a marvelous feat. Hopefully, when the smartphone market picks back up, Samsung will revisit this design. It's great for productivity junkies who frequently juggle multiple apps. Alas, it's just a dream now. You'll have to stick with the standard Z Fold. —Julian Chokkattu
How We Test Phones
WIRED has been covering Samsung smartphones since they entered the market. With each Samsung smartphone we test, our reviewers always put their personal SIM card inside and spend as long as they can (a few weeks) using the phone as their own. We do camera testing and compare the results with similarly priced devices; we benchmark performance and play graphically demanding games to see how they fare; we try out all the new features; and we even take calls to make sure they go through and that voice quality is fine.

How Premier League teams have really started - according to xG
- Published
How have Premier League teams really started?
At this stage last season Liverpool were top, with five wins out of five, and Tottenham were third. Given that they finished fifth and 17th respectively, it shows that the table shouldn't be taken too seriously this early on.
While any statistics should be taken with a pinch of salt - given such a small sample size of games and the fact that some teams have had more difficult starts than others - they do provide a more accurate picture of how the season could unfold.
Expected goals (xG) tells us how much teams have dominated games, based on the number and quality of shots they've taken and faced. Basically, how well they've performed in general before finishing, shot-stopping and plain old luck come into play.
And Premier League history shows us that the more a team dominates games, the more points they win in the long run.
It's best to exclude penalties as refereeing decisions and defensive clumsiness give a false impression of how good teams actually are at attacking and defending, especially at this early stage.
Champions Arsenal may have suffered their biggest defeat in three years last weekend at Brighton but they've still been the best team overall based on xG difference.
Leaders Manchester City are not too far behind them in terms of how much they've dominated their games, while there's nothing fortunate about unbeaten Brentford's impressive start to the season.
Manchester United constantly seem to flip between feast and famine, when often they've simply been fine. Despite their underwhelming start, only three teams have a higher xG difference so far.
The likes of Nottingham Forest and Bournemouth have also been better than their position in the early table suggests.
At the other end, Aston Villa, Crystal Palace and Newcastle have been the least impressive in terms of their overall performance, with the latter perhaps the most surprising given their position in the top half.
It's still early days, so there's no need to panic just yet, but it shows that those teams have a lot of room to improve - something Villa did to great effect after a slow start last season by finishing fourth.
Worryingly for the established sides though, the promoted teams seem like they won't be going down without a fight, with both Hull and Ipswich making genuinely solid starts to the campaign.
Pecked by the Seagulls
Looking at teams' numbers going forward, Brighton have the best attack so far based on the number and quality of chances they've had, followed by Manchester City, Brentford and Manchester United.
Although the Gunners are more admired for their defensive prowess, it's still surprising that eight teams have a higher xG than champions Arsenal, while Liverpool and Chelsea also rank in mid-table.
Brighton not only have the highest xG but have also been one of the most ruthless sides in front of goal, scoring 15 non-penalty goals from their 10.7 xG.
The only team to be more clinical than the Seagulls is their avian cousins the Magpies, who actually have the lowest xG in the league so far.
Newcastle have scored twice as many goals as a team historically would given the chances they've had - 9 goals from 4.5 xG - but head coach Matthias Jaissle will no doubt want his team to create more and not have to rely on such sharp finishing as the season goes on.
In contrast, Coventry, Sunderland, Nottingham Forest and Tottenham have all scored three goals fewer than they really should have given the opportunities they've had in their first five games.
It'll be interesting to see whether those teams genuinely have a problem with their finishing or if their luck in front of goal simply begins to change in the games to come.
Same old Arsenal... mostly
As mentioned earlier, champions Arsenal are renowned for their defence and they still have by far the best backline in the league - even taking their heavy defeat by Brighton into account.
While Forest head coach Oliver Glasner has work to do to get his side scoring goals, he's already instilled a solid foundation to build from at the back, as has Andoni Iraola at Liverpool.
There's a lot of construction work needed in the capital as Crystal Palace, Fulham and Chelsea have all been far too open at the back so far this season, although Xabi Alonso's side are not quite as terrible as the 12 goals they've conceded suggests.
Brighton's brilliance going forward has come at the cost of them not being particularly solid in defence, with Fabian Hurzeler's team perhaps a little fortunate not to have conceded more often.
Everton and Leeds have also conceded three goals fewer than expected given the chances they've faced, although both sides have been among the strongest defensively overall.
Just five games into the new campaign, it's too early to be making any concrete claims about how sides will perform but their underlying numbers have given us a glimpse of what might be in store this season.

Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington on Wednesday for a three-day state visit that began with an unusual gesture from US President Donald Trump, who personally went to Joint Base Andrews to welcome the Chinese leader and his wife, Peng Liyuan.
Trump and first lady Melania Trump were at the Maryland air base for the arrival ceremony, marking a rare occasion in which a US president personally greets a visiting foreign leader at the airport rather than waiting for the guest to arrive at the White House. The visit is Xi's first state visit to Washington in more than a decade.
The welcome comes as the US and China remain at odds over trade, artificial intelligence, Iran and Taiwan. The three-day programme is expected to combine high-level diplomatic discussions with extensive ceremonial events, including a formal state dinner at the White House on Thursday.
Trump, Melania personally welcome Xi at Joint Base Andrews
Trump and Melania arrived at Joint Base Andrews aboard Marine One ahead of Xi's arrival. The president then moved with his motorcade to the location of the arrival ceremony, where a military honour guard, band and other formations were assembled.
The airfield was prepared for a formal welcome, with black SUVs and limousines positioned near the tarmac and the Air Force band marching in formation. Members of different branches of the US military were also present as preparations continued for Xi's arrival.
Trump's decision to greet Xi at the air base instead of waiting for him at the White House is being viewed as an unusually personal welcome for a visiting foreign leader. The gesture is part of an elaborate programme intended to match the ceremonial reception Trump received during his visit to China earlier this year.
Melania said her husband decided to personally greet Xi because “they have a great relationship.”
“He’s coming on our soil, and we need to welcome them with the most respect,” she said during an interview with Fox News Channel's “Fox & Friends.”
Melania also said she had been closely involved in planning the itinerary for Xi and Peng.
“Every detail, I was involved,” she said, adding that the visit involved extensive protocol and planning.
Three-day visit comes amid tensions over trade, AI, Iran and Taiwan
Xi's visit comes at a time when relations between Washington and Beijing remain tense despite efforts to maintain what the Trump administration describes as “strategic stability”.
Trade, artificial intelligence, Trump's war with Iran and China's designs on Taiwan are among the major issues surrounding the visit. Expectations for a major breakthrough are low, even as the two leaders prepare for closed-door discussions.
The visit also follows Trump's trip to China in May. The elaborate reception in Washington is intended to reciprocate the ceremonial grandeur surrounding Trump's visit.
When Trump arrived in Beijing, Xi did not personally meet him at the airport. Chinese Vice President Han Zheng was there instead. Air Force One was met by a red carpet, a military honour guard, a military band and about 300 Chinese youths carrying Chinese and American flags and chanting, “Welcome, welcome! Warm welcome!”
The children wore white and light blue uniforms that mirrored the traditional colours associated with the presidential aircraft.
Wicker criticises 'lavish welcome'
The ceremonial reception has also drawn criticism from within the US.
Sen. Roger Wicker, the Republican chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, criticised the “lavish welcome” for Xi.
Wicker said during a speech in the Senate on Tuesday that Trump should not have invited the Chinese leader “based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party.”
Wicker suggested that Trump could use the state dinner to discuss issues including “the purposes of China’s massive military buildup, or about China’s clear support for Iran.”
He also said that “during every minute of dialogue” Trump should keep in mind that “his guest is a brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America.”
Rubio says US must engage China at highest levels
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the need for high-level engagement with Beijing, saying the United States and China are “the two largest economies in the world” and “probably the two most powerful militaries in the world.”
“The idea that we would not interact with them at the highest levels is irresponsible. It’s outrageous. We have to,” Rubio told reporters Wednesday while he was in New York.
The administration has presented the engagement as part of efforts to maintain strategic stability between the two countries despite their disagreements.
White House state dinner to follow on Thursday
The airport welcome is only the beginning of a packed three-day programme.
On Thursday, Xi and Peng are scheduled to return to the White House for a formal arrival ceremony. The programme will include a review of troops before Trump and Xi turn to discussions on the major issues facing the two countries.
The day will culminate in a black-tie state dinner at the White House.
The dinner is expected to include prominent technology industry figures, including Nvidia's Jensen Huang and SpaceX's Elon Musk. The broader guest list is expected to feature several major US technology executives.
Trump has repeatedly signalled that he wanted the visit to have an elaborate ceremonial character. In recent weeks, he spoke positively about his new helicopter landing pad being ready for Xi's visit while expressing regret that the White House's large ballroom would not be completed in time.
Melania and Peng to visit Asian art museum
Melania has also planned a separate programme with Peng Liyuan.
The two are expected to visit the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art, where they will explore cultural connections between the United States and China.
Melania said she had been involved in planning the major components of the visit, including the state dinner and the cultural programme for the two first ladies.
The visit reflects the broader effort to combine formal diplomacy with cultural events during Xi's stay in Washington.
Xi and Peng to visit National Archives
On Friday, Xi and Peng are scheduled to return to the White House for private tea with Trump and Melania.
The two couples will then travel to the National Archives in Washington, where they are expected to view historic documents connected to the relationship between the United States and China.
The White House has said the documents will underscore the historical relationship between the two countries. The National Archives visit will form the concluding part of Xi's three-day state visit.
Who is travelling with Xi?
Peng Liyuan is confirmed to be travelling with Xi and will return to China with him on Friday.
The exact composition of Xi's business delegation was not confirmed in the material provided. The visit comes after Trump travelled to China with several prominent US technology executives, including Apple's Tim Cook, Tesla's Elon Musk and Nvidia's Jensen Huang.
Xi's delegation is expected to include business representatives, but the names of the executives travelling with the Chinese president had not been confirmed.
Why Xi's Washington visit matters
The visit is Xi's first trip to Washington since 2015, when he was received by then-US President Barack Obama.
It comes as the two countries continue to manage disagreements over trade, technology and broader geopolitical issues. Artificial intelligence, Taiwan and Iran are among the sensitive subjects surrounding the talks, while trade remains a central part of the bilateral relationship.
A US-China trade agreement reached last year is also due to expire in November, adding another economic issue to the backdrop of the visit.
Against that setting, Xi's arrival has combined an unusually elaborate ceremonial welcome with closed-door diplomacy. Trump has sought to demonstrate warmth towards the Chinese leader, while critics in Washington have questioned the extent of the welcome and urged the administration to raise contentious security and geopolitical issues directly.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday lauded the rhino conservation efforts in the country and said the Project Rhino has been initiated for financial and technical support to the range states for protection, habitat management, and understanding population dynamics of the endangered species.
On the occasion of World Rhino Day, Modi said the country celebrates the magnificent greater one-horned rhinoceros and lauds all those at the forefront of its protection.
“Assam now holds nearly 80 per cent of the world’s rhino population and Kaziranga’s efforts to end rhino poaching have been extensively appreciated,” he said in a post on ‘X’.
The prime minister said on one hand, rhinos have either returned or are well protected in parts of Bihar and West Bengal, on the other hand, success of reintroduction of rhinos in Dudhwa (Uttar Pradesh) is creating history.
“This shows the sustained commitment of our people towards animal protection and active wildlife management in the range states,” he said.
Taking species conservation in the country forward, Modi said he was happy to share that Project Rhino has been initiated for financial and technical support to the range states for protection, habitat management, genetic improvement and understanding population dynamics.
World Rhino Day is a day of awareness for all five rhino species and the work being done to save them. Since 2011, World Rhino Day has been celebrated internationally on September 22 by rhino experts and advocates around the world.
The day is especially important to raise awareness of the plight of rhinos because they are regularly poached for their horns which are sold illegally and used in traditional medicine — despite no scientific proof that these remedies work.

Lieutenant-Governor (L-G) Taranjit Singh Sandhu on Wednesday directed civic authorities to conduct safety audits of public parks across the Capital. The L-G gave the order after reviewing safety arrangements at a meeting attended by the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) Commissioner, the Commissioner of Police, and the Vice-Chairman of the Delhi Development Authority (DDA), Lok Niwas stated in a release.
The move comes after a 17-year-old girl was gang-raped allegedly by three men who posed as police personnel at Astha Kunj Park near Kalkaji Mandir in south-east Delhi on Monday. All three accused were arrested on Tuesday. A city court remanded the accused in two-day judicial custody on Wednesday.
The Delhi police have not sought their custody so far. Further investigation is under way in the case.
According to the Lok Niwas statement, the safety audit will examine lighting, deployment of guards at all entry and exit points, patrolling inside parks – particularly after sunset – and cleanliness and sanitation facilities. Authorities have also been asked to look into whether some parks can be handed over to residents’ welfare associations or private entities for maintenance and upkeep.
‘Seek public feedback’
The L-G directed officials to engage with nearby schools, colleges, and other institutions to seek feedback on facilities at parks. Regular visits by beat constables and police personnel responsible for the respective areas have been ordered to strengthen security, the release stated.
In a separate statement, the DDA stated that its field staff and security personnel have been directed to maintain heightened vigilance, particularly during evening and night hours. Parks with multiple gates may restrict late-evening access to selected entrances. The authority has also initiated measures to identify dark spots and install additional lighting and CCTV cameras at vulnerable locations, it stated.
The DDA will also coordinate with the Delhi police to monitor suspicious or illegal activity around parks, it added.
Metro integration
Meanwhile, the L-G approved six multi-modal integration plans for metro stations and two road projects at the 70th governing body meeting of the Unified Traffic and Transportation Infrastructure (Planning & Engineering) Centre. The projects aim to improve last-mile connectivity and ease congestion.

OpenAI is pushing further into the hotly contested market for personal agents — this time with voice.
The company is adding its most advanced voice system to ChatGPT's website and mobile app on Wednesday. OpenAI's release allows users to speak to delegate single and recurring tasks that require multiple steps, a browser, and disparate apps. The company has been rolling out launches ahead of its big OpenAI DevDay event next week.
OpenAI's product lead for ChatGPT voice, Atty Eleti, gave a demo to Business Insider. Only speaking with the app, he had the tool analyze his DoorDash spending, pay $5 to book a pickleball court, and reorganize his calendar.
"In the future, we really imagine people using voice as the primary modality to interact with AI," Eleti said, "and that's kind of our North Star that we're working towards."
Personal AI assistants like Instinct and Meta's Muse are having a moment in Silicon Valley as the industry peddles apps tailored to handle cumbersome internet tasks. OpenAI has many of these capabilities in ChatGPT, though it hasn't yet released a narrower offshoot. This voice tool is a play for the AI-assistant buzz.
In the short term, the improvements make it easier for people to delegate work to ChatGPT by speaking while they're on the go. In the long run, they'll serve OpenAI's hardware ambitions: Bloomberg has reported that the company is building a smart speaker for release in 2027.
Wednesday's release connects OpenAI's voice model, GPT-Live, to AI models that can perform tasks on computers or in browsers, a focus the company maintained before the personal AI agent craze. GPT-Live, which can listen and respond simultaneously, was already turned on for ChatGPT's basic conversational mode and connected to agentic models on the desktop app.
Voice mode, as Eleti sees it, has three main benefits. Speaking is quick and natural — "you can blurt out your thoughts," he said. You can do it with your hands off a device. And it can help you with vocal tasks, like learning a language or practicing a speech. Eleti and his colleagues use it while commuting and on walks, he said.
Eleti said more than 150 million people already use ChatGPT's dictation and voice mode tools. Still, the team faces an uphill battle. Though smart speakers have shown some staying power, offices are still organized around desktop computers.
Plus, though it's quicker to speak than type, it's also quicker to read than to listen. Eleti said his team considered this dynamic when deciding how ChatGPT would respond to audio prompts.
"We don't think of this as just pure voice in and voice out," Eteli said. "It's about voice in and then the right output back. Sometimes it's text, sometimes it's voice, sometimes it's a mix."

Henry Pollock: Northampton chief expects more players to work with promoters like Eddie Hearn as he lifts lid on negotiations
Henry Pollock put pen to paper on a new multi-year deal with his boyhood club, Northampton Saints, on Tuesday, having signed with Eddie Hearn's Matchroom Talent Agency earlier this year.
Wednesday 23 September 2026 22:26, UK
Northampton Saints director of rugby Phil Dowson believes more players could follow Henry Pollock and work with promoters like Eddie Hearn to grow their profile.
On Tuesday, Pollock put pen to paper on a multi-year extension with his boyhood club, with the England international agreeing a deal worth £400,000 per year.
At just 21, Pollock already has 13 England caps and made five appearances for the British & Irish Lions during last year's tour of Australia.
Pollock's profile continues to grow, with the flanker becoming the first rugby union player to join Eddie Hearn's Matchroom Talent Agency at the start of the year. Dowson revealed that the boxing promoter "drove as hard a bargain as he possibly could" during negotiations.
Reflecting on Pollock's decision to join Hearn's agency, Dowson said: "I think we'll see more of it.
"I think headlines and social media engagement, and all that, is positive for the game. Fundamentally, I talked to the coaches about this. We want more people watching the game, more people talking about the game and, ideally, most importantly, more people playing the game at loads of different age groups.
"If Henry Pollock and Matchroom are getting some traction with the public, I think we should encourage that, but also take into account that we've got to continue to deliver that in the right way, and I think we have them."
Hearn told The Telegraph that he believes the 21-year-old is worth more than seven figures, predicting Pollock's value will "skyrocket" over the coming years while also arguing that the value of rugby will rise.
Dowson also lifted the lid on the boxing promoter's role in the negotiations, lauding him for helping him grow Pollock's profile, adding that part of the negotiations were handled by a "traditional rugby agent".
"Eddie's been excellent. He's raised the profile of the game," Dowson said.
"He's raised the profile of Henry and he's done what an agent's supposed to do. He's driven as hard a bargain as he possibly could.
"I've got a lot of respect for Eddie and how he goes about his work and some of the stuff he said in the media was really pertinent.
"I think there's elements of the contract which weren't done by Eddie, which were done by his traditional rugby agent.
"There are things from a marketing point of view and the extracurricular stuff that Eddie really looks after Pollock with, which we'll see more of.
"He wasn't necessarily doing every single negotiation from a rugby point of view."
Pollock has explained in the past that he had an open mind to the next steps of his career, but on Tuesday said he was "massively happy to re-sign with Saints".
Some fans had questioned why the negotiations had taken so long to complete, with the flanker's loyalty coming under scrutiny, but Dowson said the process was made easier by Pollock's desire to stay.
"It's still his job, it's still his career. He needs to make sure he's getting the right deal for his aspirations and all those other elements that come with it," Dowson said. "I don't just mean from a financial point of view, I mean from a full, holistic sort of point of view.
"Would there be loyalty in sport if he wasn't offered a contract? Would that be us not being loyal? I think we've got to be careful around that.
"He's playing really well. He's got lots of people talking about rugby. That's great. We wanted to keep him and he wanted to stay. That's a great position for us to start negotiations from, and that's the great thing about sport.
"People can have an opinion around it, but I don't think it was overly dragged out, to be honest, and I don't think it was ever done... there was no animosity in any way from my perspective."

It could have been a scene from Cape Fear: a quiet evening, an ordinary home, a sudden intrusion by a stranger convinced that the law has betrayed him.
In early July 2022, Democratic representative Pramila Jayapal of Washington and her husband were watching television at their Seattle home when men drove past their house screaming threats: vile, racialized, and unmistakably political. They called the police. The men left. Thirty minutes later, one returned, blasting music and approaching the porch. When officers arrived, they found him armed with a loaded handgun, a round already chambered. A neighbor heard him shout, “Go back to India. I am going to kill you.”
Jayapal later described the episode not as an aberration but as evidence of a broader transformation in American politics—a climate in which grievance increasingly functions as permission and intimidation is framed as justified political expression. The threats did not stop. Nor is Jayapal alone. For years, Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia lived under constant threat as one of Donald Trump’s most aggressive defenders in Congress. She reported hundreds of death threats, largely from ideological opponents.
But when Greene publicly broke with Trump—over the Epstein files, Gaza, and what “America first” had come to mean—the direction of the threats shifted. After Trump labeled her “Marjorie Traitor Greene,” messages arrived threatening her son by name. One threatened her assassination. Another claimed that a plane ticket had already been purchased. In November 2025, Greene announced her resignation from Congress, citing threats to her family. “I think that comes to a point,” she said, “where any American can look at that and say that’s a high bar and way too much to ask.”
What Jayapal and Greene have in common is not ideology, temperament, or policy; it is exposure. Both became targets in an era in which political violence is no longer confined to the fringe, no longer clearly condemned by leaders, no longer monopolized by either the right or the left—and increasingly treated as a legitimate instrument of political pressure.
What happened to Jayapal and Greene is no longer exceptional; it is revealing. Their experiences point to a deeper transformation: Political violence has moved closer to the center of American political life, touching elected officials across parties and becoming a recurring feature of contemporary conflict rather than a rare deviation.
Since 2016, Americans have argued fiercely not only about whether political violence is rising but about who is responsible. One dominant narrative attributes the problem primarily to the radical right: white nationalism, militias, election denial. A competing narrative insists that violence emanates just as strongly from the radical left, manifested in riots, assaults on police, and organized disruption in cities and on campuses. These claims are not merely rhetorical; they shape public trust, elite behavior, law enforcement priorities, and—most dangerously—the willingness of partisans to condemn violence committed by those they regard as allies. But what does the evidence actually show?
America’s political violence problem is neither one-sided nor symmetrical. Taken together, the evidence from federal threat assessments, terrorism databases, protest incident data, and congressional security records points toward the same conclusion. Political violence in the United States declined for nearly two decades after the 1990s and then rose sharply beginning around 2016. For decades prior to that year, politically motivated violence was concentrated overwhelmingly on the far right. Today, violence associated with the right and left is closer to balance, even as it takes very different forms. Right-wing violence has been substantially more frequent and far deadlier than left-wing violence since 2016—aimed at elections, federal institutions, and public officials—while left-wing violence has been more common in mass protest settings, from the 2020 George Floyd unrest to clashes over immigration enforcement, typically involving property destruction and confrontations with police.
Although uncertainty remains at the margins, the evidence strongly suggests that since roughly 2016, political violence on both the right and the left has reached levels unseen in the United States since the upheavals of the 1960s. These patterns reflect not a single ideology but the deeper forces of violent populism: hardened identities, perceived existential threats, collapsing institutional trust, and elite rhetoric that frames politics as a struggle between enemies rather than fellow citizens.
Much of the public disagreement about whether political violence is rising and who is responsible for it stems not from ideology alone but from competing definitions about what should be counted.
In scholarly literature, political violence is generally defined as the use or credible threat of physical force for political ends. Those ends may include coercion, intimidation, punishment, or symbolic signaling intended to influence public behavior, political outcomes, or institutional authority. Under this definition fall assassination attempts, armed assaults on public officials, bombings, arson attacks, violent intimidation, riots against buildings with explicit political aims, and organized plots to use force against political targets.
Just as important are the exclusions. Political violence does not include ordinary criminal activity lacking political motivation, interpersonal violence driven by private disputes, or lawful protest—even when protests are disruptive, angry, or unlawful. Nor does it include harsh rhetoric alone, however inflammatory, unless it is paired with a credible threat of force. These boundaries matter, because collapsing political violence into crime or protest obscures its distinct causes and consequences.
The hardest problem is determining intent. Political violence is defined not only by what happens but by why it happens—and intent is often ambiguous. When a crowd burns a police precinct, is the act political rebellion, criminal opportunism, or both? When a gunman attacks a synagogue, is the motive ideological antisemitism, personal grievance, or mental illness layered atop political belief? When an individual sends a death threat to a lawmaker, is it expressive rage, partisan trolling, or preparation for real-world violence?
Reasonable scholars answer these questions differently, often using dissimilar evidentiary thresholds. Some datasets require explicit ideological statements; others infer political intent from targets, symbols, or timing. Some classify riots as political violence only when their organizers articulate political goals; others focus on behavior rather than rhetoric. None of these choices is neutral, and each shapes the resulting picture.
These definitional choices explain why prominent datasets sometimes appear to disagree. Federal law enforcement datasets emphasize lethality, capability, and threats to national institutions. Protest-oriented datasets capture frequency and geographic spread. Terrorism databases prioritize ideological framing and tactical similarity to global movements. Each captures something real—and each misses something important.
For this reason, no single dataset can settle the debate. Accordingly, my work triangulates across several sources, combining federal threat assessments, incident-level databases, congressional security data, and survey research. The goal is not to produce a definitive body count but to identify patterns that recur across independent measures: who is targeted, how violence is carried out, how lethal it is, and how those patterns have changed since 2016.
This approach does not eliminate uncertainty. But it does attempt to move beyond partisan narratives and toward a more accurate understanding of how political violence in America has evolved—and why arguments over its meaning have become almost as intense as the violence itself.
The most authoritative window into political violence in the United States comes not from media tallies or advocacy groups but from the federal agencies charged with tracking national security threats—above all, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Yet even here, readers encounter a fundamental problem: There is no single, formal US government definition of “political violence.” Instead, federal agencies operate with overlapping categories—domestic terrorism, domestic violent extremism, hate crimes, threats against officials, and antigovernment violence—each shaped by legal constraints, investigative mandates, and statutory language rather than a unified conceptual framework.
This definitional fragmentation matters. Unlike many countries, the United States does not criminalize “domestic terrorism” as a stand-alone offense; the relevant statute (18 U.S.C., § 2331) defines “international terrorism” and “domestic terrorism” descriptively but does not by itself create a prosecutable offense. As a result, the FBI does not report a simple annual count of domestic terrorism incidents. Instead, the statistics reflect investigations, disrupted plots, arrests, and threat assessments organized around ideological motivation, such as racially and ethnically motivated violent extremism, antigovernment or antiauthority extremism, and hostile acts against government structures. The absence of a single metric has fueled public confusion and partisan cherry-picking, with critics on all sides accusing the FBI of either exaggerating or minimizing particular threats.
Despite these constraints, a consistent picture emerges from FBI testimony, annual threat assessments, and congressional reporting since 2016. Across political administrations, FBI directors have warned that domestic violent extremism is a persistent and elevated threat, with particular emphasis on right-wing ideologies—especially white supremacist and ethno-nationalist violence—as the most lethal category among domestic violent threats. This assessment is grounded not in ideology per se but in outcomes: The majority of fatal attacks tied to political or ideological motives in recent years have originated in right-wing ecosystems, often carried out by lone actors inspired by online propaganda rather than formal organizations.
At the same time, federal reporting makes clear that political violence is not monopolized by the right. The FBI and DHS have also documented significant spikes in violence associated with mass protest movements, assaults on law enforcement, arson, and attacks on government facilities during periods of intense unrest—most notably in 2020, when protests following the killing of George Floyd were accompanied by substantial violent confrontations in many cities. These events are more commonly linked to left-wing or anti-authority contexts, tend to cluster geographically, and are far less likely to result in mass casualties. The distinction federal agencies draw is therefore not between “violent” and “nonviolent” sides but between forms of violence that differ in frequency, lethality, and strategic orientation.
A further frustration is temporal. Much of the FBI’s publicly accessible data lags behind current events. Detailed breakdowns often stop several years short of the present, while ongoing investigations limit transparency about more recent trends. As a result, scholars and policymakers must rely on testimony, qualitative assessments, and partial datasets to infer patterns after 2021—a gap that has widened in the wake of intensified threats against public officials and institutions. This delay has created a disconnect between the lived experience of escalating threats—particularly against elected officials—and the statistical record available to the public.
These limitations should not be mistaken for insignificance. On the contrary, the persistence of the same core warnings across multiple administrations, political contexts, and leadership teams suggests institutional continuity rather than partisan distortion. While the FBI cannot provide a clean annual count of “political violence,” its threat assessments provide something arguably more important: a comparative judgment about which forms of violence are most likely to kill, destabilize institutions, and undermine democratic governance.
When federal threat assessments are read alongside terrorism databases, incident-level coding, congressional security data, and survey research, the contours of political violence since 2016 come into focus—even if the exact numbers remain contested. The challenge is not the absence of evidence but the difficulty of integrating imperfect sources into an honest and comprehensive account.

A tropical storm off the south-west coast of Mexico has intensified into a category 5 monster in fewer than 24 hours, fueled by stronger than usual El Niño weather patterns in the Pacific Ocean.
Hurricane Polo was sending out maximum sustained winds of 165mph (266km/h) on Tuesday as its center churned about 215 miles (346km) south of the coastal city of Zihuatanejo, in Guerrero state.
On Monday, Polo was only a tropical storm with winds below 74mph (120km/h). Its rapid and sudden growth is testament to the dominance of this year’s so-called super El Niño, which set a record on Monday as the most extreme on record, and has amplified a number of extreme weather events globally.
Forecasters at the National Hurricane Center in Miami said Mexico was likely to avoid a direct hit, but warned that further intensification was likely, and that life-threatening flooding and mudslides were possible inland, along with dangerous surf and rip current conditions.
El Niño occurs when extended ocean temperatures in the eastern and central Pacific, and near the equator, rise above their historical average.
Meteorologists say the phenomenon increases disruptive winds and curtails other conditions favorable to storm development in the Atlantic basin, which remains quiet with less than three months to go in this year’s hurricane season.
Conversely, it promotes increased activity in the Pacific, where the 2026 El Niño remains one of the strongest on record.
“The water temperatures in two separate areas, the north-central Pacific and off the Mexican coast, are running well above average,” Paul Pastelok, AccuWeather’s lead long-range meteorologist, said in the online weather service’s fall hurricane outlook last month.
“We are seeing a strong impact in both the Atlantic and Pacific basins, with extreme wind shear limiting Atlantic storm development, while the Pacific remains quite active, as we expected back in the spring.”
Hurricane Polo’s single-day intensification also fits into the assessment of University of Miami senior research associate Brian McNoldy on his tropical Atlantic blog that El Niño, which he said was only “moderate” towards the beginning of September, was “forecast to become very strong, likely the strongest on record, by later this fall and into winter”.
Polo is the 18th named storm, and seventh hurricane, of the 2026 Pacific season, which runs from 15 May until 30 November.
By contrast, the Atlantic basin, which has a six-month season from June until November, has seen only six named tropical storms and no hurricanes so far.
It is the first time in 112 years that no Atlantic hurricanes have formed by 21 September, and 2026 could join 1907 and 1914 as the only years without one being recorded.

Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington on Wednesday for a three-day state visit, receiving a rare airport welcome from US President Donald Trump as the two leaders prepare for talks on trade, technology, artificial intelligence, military ties, Iran, Taiwan, the Russia-Ukraine war and other geopolitical issues.
Xi and Chinese First Lady Peng Liyuan arrived at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, where Trump and First Lady Melania Trump were waiting to receive them. The visit marks Xi's first trip to Washington since 2015 and the second summit meeting between Xi and Trump in less than six months.
The high-profile visit combines elaborate ceremonial events with closed-door discussions on issues that have kept Washington and Beijing at odds. The programme includes a White House arrival ceremony, troop review, a black-tie state dinner and a visit to the National Archives.
Rare airport welcome for Xi
Trump personally travelled to Joint Base Andrews to receive Xi, rather than waiting for the Chinese president to arrive at the White House.
The aircraft carrying Xi and Peng touched down at 5.39 pm local time on Wednesday. Trump and Melania were waiting at the foot of the aircraft ladder when Xi and Peng disembarked at 6.01 pm local time.
The welcome featured a 21-person honour cordon, a 100-foot red carpet, the US Air Force Band and ceremonial cannon fire. Two US Air Force B-1 bombers also flew over the airbase as the national anthems of the United States and China were played.
After a brief welcome exchange, Xi and Peng walked down the red carpet before leaving the airbase in a motorcade. Trump and Melania returned to the White House aboard Marine One.
According to the material provided, it was the first time since 1962 that a US president had welcomed a foreign leader at an airport. Then-president John F Kennedy had welcomed British prime minister Harold Macmillan at the airport that year.
Why Trump is giving Xi such a high-profile welcome
The elaborate reception is intended to reciprocate the ceremonial grandeur surrounding Trump's visit to China in May.
Xi was not at the airport when Trump arrived in Beijing. Chinese Vice President Han Zheng received Trump instead. However, Air Force One was welcomed with a red carpet, military honour guard, military band and about 300 Chinese youths carrying Chinese and American flags and chanting, “Welcome, welcome! Warm welcome!”
Trump has also made clear that he wants to give Xi an elaborate reception in Washington.
Melania Trump said her husband decided to personally greet Xi because “they have a great relationship.”
“He’s coming on our soil, and we need to welcome them with the most respect,” she said during an interview with Fox News Channel's “Fox & Friends.”
Trade and tariffs
Trade tariffs are expected to be among the key issues during the Trump-Xi discussions.
The visit comes against the backdrop of continuing disagreements between the world's two largest economies. A US-China trade agreement reached last year is also set to expire in November, adding another issue to the discussions.
The two leaders are expected to discuss the broader economic relationship as they seek to maintain what has been described as “strategic stability” between Washington and Beijing.
Artificial intelligence and technology
Technology and artificial intelligence are also expected to feature prominently in the talks.
The visit comes as the US and China compete over advanced technologies and AI capabilities. Technology executives are also expected to be present at the White House state dinner.
The dinner will feature tech industry leaders including Nvidia's Jensen Huang and SpaceX's Elon Musk.
Trump's previous China visit also included prominent US technology executives, including Apple's Tim Cook, Musk and Huang.
Military ties and China's military buildup
Military relations and China's expanding military capabilities are expected to be another subject of discussion.
Sen. Roger Wicker, chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, criticised what he described as the “lavish welcome” being extended to Xi.
Wicker said Trump should not have invited the Chinese leader “based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party.”
Wicker suggested that Trump should discuss “the purposes of China’s massive military buildup, or about China’s clear support for Iran” during the state dinner.
He said that “during every minute of dialogue” Trump should keep in mind that “his guest is a brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America.”
Taiwan and US arms sales
China's designs on Taiwan and US arms sales to Taiwan are also expected to feature in the discussions.
Taiwan remains one of the major points of disagreement between Washington and Beijing. The US-China talks are therefore expected to cover military issues connected with the island, including US arms sales to Taiwan.
The issue comes alongside broader discussions on military ties and China's military buildup.
Iran and Middle East conflicts
The war in Iran and conflicts in the Middle East are also expected to figure in the talks.
Wicker urged Trump to raise what he described as China's “clear support for Iran” during discussions with Xi.
The two leaders are expected to discuss the broader regional security situation as part of their talks, alongside other geopolitical issues.
Russia-Ukraine war
The Russia-Ukraine war is another international issue expected to be discussed by Trump and Xi.
The war has become part of the wider strategic relationship between Washington and Beijing, with the two countries taking different positions on the conflict.
The issue is expected to be discussed alongside the Middle East, Taiwan and military relations.
Arms race in space
The two leaders are also expected to discuss the arms race in space.
The issue forms part of a broader agenda covering military ties, advanced technology and strategic competition between the United States and China.
Human rights and detained Americans
Trump is expected to raise the cases of US citizens detained in China, although it remains unclear how extensively broader human-rights issues will feature in the talks.
A US official said Trump was likely to bring up cases of people wrongfully detained in China with Xi.
Trump is expected to ask Xi to free Youlin Chen, a Chinese-born expert on North Korean nuclear tests who has been imprisoned since late 2024, and Min Zin, a scholar arrested in June. Both are US citizens.
Trump had raised Chen's case during his meeting with Xi in Beijing in May, but according to Chen's wife, Yufang Rong, there has been no change since then.
"We hope to see Dr. Chen and Zin come home after this meeting," said Elizabeth Richards, research director of the James Foley Foundation, a hostage advocacy group.
Broader human-rights issues involving Tibet, the Uyghur Muslim minority and Hong Kong may also come up, although the White House has not said whether Trump will directly raise them.
China warns human rights are a 'red line'
Beijing has indicated that human rights and democracy are sensitive issues in the bilateral relationship.
China's ambassador to the US warned on Wednesday that democracy and human rights are "red lines" that cannot be crossed.
Human rights groups and Democratic lawmakers have called on Trump to raise China's treatment of Tibetans and Uyghurs and speak up for Hong Kong pro-democracy protesters.
"We cannot abandon human rights in our foreign policy," Democratic Representative Jim McGovern of Massachusetts said. "China's record is beyond debate and it is atrocious."
Human rights groups say China has detained Uyghurs on the pretext of countering extremism and confined them in re-education camps. US secretaries of state from both parties have labelled the treatment of Uyghurs as genocide.
"Xi's visit to Washington is a strategic moment to move beyond words of condemnation on the Uyghur genocide," World Uyghur Congress President Turgunjan Alawdun said.
Beijing says it has established "vocational training centers" to curb extremism and denies abuse allegations.
Tibet issue and Dalai Lama dialogue
Tibet is another issue that could add to the human-rights discussion.
Rights groups and exiles have described China's rule in Tibet as "oppressive", an accusation Beijing rejects. China has exerted greater control over the region since Xi became chief of the Communist Party in 2012.
Beijing has said Washington should stop using "Tibet-related issues to interfere in China's internal affairs."
The International Campaign for Tibet called on Trump to ask Xi "to resume substantive dialogue without preconditions" with the Dalai Lama, the spiritual head of Tibetan Buddhists and a Nobel Peace Prize laureate.
China's ethnic unity law
China's new law concerning ethnic unity is also part of the broader human-rights debate surrounding the visit.
China passed a law this year to create a shared national identity among the country's 55 ethnic minority groups. The legislation includes penalties for people outside the country for "inciting ethnic separatism."
The US State Department has described the law as problematic.
Katie LaRoque, director for policy and advocacy at Freedom House, urged Trump to condemn the legislation himself.
"President Trump must make clear that Beijing’s domestic law has no jurisdiction over those exercising their fundamental freedoms on US soil," she said.
Marco Rubio defends high-level engagement
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington and Beijing must continue to engage at the highest levels despite their disagreements.
Rubio described the US and China as “the two largest economies in the world” and “probably the two most powerful militaries in the world.”
“The idea that we would not interact with them at the highest levels is irresponsible. It’s outrageous. We have to,” Rubio told reporters Wednesday while he was in New York.
He later said: "The relationship between the United States and China will define the 21st century."
Rubio also acknowledged strong disagreements between the two countries and said continued engagement was necessary.
"I think it's an obligation to be able to interact at the highest levels now. I think that's what this visit reflects, is the president's belief that no matter what our disagreements and differences may be with the Chinese government, this is not some small country," Rubio said.
Thursday: White House ceremony and state dinner
Xi's airport welcome will be followed by a more formal programme at the White House on Thursday.
Xi will be accorded a ceremonial welcome and a review of troops before the two leaders move into closed-door discussions.
The day will culminate in a black-tie state dinner at the White House.
The dinner is expected to include leading technology executives such as Nvidia's Jensen Huang and SpaceX's Elon Musk.
The visit is expected to combine diplomatic discussions with extensive ceremonial events, even as expectations remain low that it will produce any major breakthroughs in the US-China relationship.
Friday: Private tea and National Archives visit
The final day of Xi's visit will focus on a more private and cultural programme.
On Friday, Xi and Peng will return to the White House for a private tea with Trump and Melania.
The two couples will then visit the National Archives in Washington.
The White House has said they will view historic documents underscoring the relationship between the United States and China.
Melania has also planned a visit to the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art with Peng Liyuan to showcase cultural connections between the two countries.
Who is travelling with Xi?
Xi is travelling with Peng Liyuan and senior Chinese officials including Cai Qi, a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and director of the General Office of the Central Committee, and Foreign Minister Wang Yi, a member of the Political Bureau of the Central Committee.
The exact names of Chinese business executives accompanying Xi were not confirmed in the material provided.
Xi and Peng are scheduled to return to China on Friday.
Xi's first Washington visit since 2015
The visit is Xi's first trip to Washington since 2015, when he was received by then-President Barack Obama.
It is also the second summit meeting between Xi and Trump in less than six months, following Trump's visit to China in May.
The three-day visit brings together an extensive agenda covering trade, tariffs, technology, AI, military ties, Taiwan, Iran, the Russia-Ukraine war, space security and human rights.
While Trump has sought to project warmth towards Xi through an unusually elaborate welcome, the talks will take place against a backdrop of major strategic and economic disagreements between Washington and Beijing.

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

The EU and Canada, Ursula von der Leyen said last week, “see the world with the same eyes”, with shared stances on everything from AI to the climate crisis, the Ukraine war and the unholy chaos unleashed by the current occupant of the White House (OK, she didn’t actually say that last bit. But I like to think she almost certainly thought it.)
So, the European Commission president went on, Canada should become “the first associate member of the EU”. In the audience, Mark Carney beamed with delight. The next day, Canada’s prime minister enthusiastically embraced the idea of an “alliance for the future”, to build “collective resilience” through “deep cooperation”.
Cue standing ovations, warm handshakes – and a great deal of head-scratching in Brussels and assorted EU capitals. Because “associate membership” of the EU is not, in fact, a thing. Nor, as a Guardian editorial pointed out, is there “any blueprint for what such a thing might involve”.
The term was, the editorial argued, “a political hypothesis”, describing “a relationship of intimate strategic alignment with the EU, stopping short of actual membership, in ways that are significant but undefined”. So what exactly are the commission and Canada playing at here, and where might it lead?
You can see where they’re coming from. On paper, in a world of unpredictable and increasingly aggressive great powers, it makes perfect sense. For Canada – which already has the Ceta free trade agreement with the EU – the catalyst for even closer cooperation is clearly Donald Trump: incessant tariff threats, an escalating trade war, bullying talk of Canada as the “51st state”, the renaming of Lake Ontario – all have left Ottawa eager to diversify its relations.
Aligning with European industrial strategy, working together on defence and AI, and joining EU scientific research and student exchange programmes would offer Canada a reliable counterweight to its all-too-unreliable southern neighbour. (Unsurprisingly, Trump called the tie-up “laughable”, and threatened more tariffs.)
For the EU, meanwhile, Canada is a dream partner: a stable, like-minded “middle power” rich in critical minerals, rare earths and – as Carney couldn’t resist noting – good manners. Plus, Canada’s unbridled EU-enthusiasm is a pleasing boost to the bloc’s bruised ego after Iceland’s recent rejection of more EU accession negotiations.
There’s only one problem: “associate membership” is not a status in the EU treaties, and creating such a status would mean treaty reform, which member states won’t contemplate. There are things called “association agreements”, such as with Ukraine, Moldova or Georgia, but those are essentially stepping stones to full membership – which Canada can’t aspire to, for the very good reason that it isn’t in Europe.
But if “associate member” sounds vaguely familiar, that’s because the EU has been talking about a “second circle” since the days of Jacques Delors: an outer ring of countries bound by shared values, free trade and security cooperation to an inner core of members, but without full voting rights or complete regulatory integration.
Emmanuel Macron’s European Political Community is a variation on this theme, and Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, recently floated “associate member” status for Ukraine. Indeed, non-EU nations in the European Economic Area (EEA) and European Free Trade Association, such as Norway, Iceland or Switzerland, already function as quasi-associate members, enjoying single-market access while being largely “rule-takers”: adopting EU rules without having a vote in Brussels.
Writing in the Guardian, Fabian Zuleeg suggested that Canada and Europe actually need more of an “integrated partnership” – a model that leaves single market access to one side, focusing instead on concrete collaboration in areas such as defence, supply chains and EU programmes like Horizon and Erasmus+.
Alberto Alemanno, a professor of EU law, noted that a realistic EU-Canada landing zone would have to go further than Ceta and might more resemble the kind of tailored framework of the EU-Swiss relationship. But the real significance of any formal new status, he said, was that it could make the EU “an institutional hub around which other democracies organise strategic autonomy – but without joining the union”.
What that might actually look like is anyone’s guess: visa-free work access, shared military procurement, Canadian seats on EU regulatory committees? For the moment, Canada’s hypothetical “associate membership” is more of a mood than a reality: the expressed intent of a democratic bloc and a middle power to deepen ties in the face of mounting global uncertainty.
Does it, all the same, hold any hope for Brexit-regretting Britain? As Jill Rutter of the Institute for Government highlighted, the EU’s sudden willingness to display “institutional imagination” at least shows that the bloc is willing to think about adapting when geopolitical pressures demand.
But a new deal for Canada won’t automatically fix the UK’s issues. As Joël Reland of UK in a Changing Europe pointed out, the vagueness of the EU offer to Canada might look promising for the UK. But Canada wants “deep cooperation” without touching single-market rules, and the UK’s main problem is that it is now shut out of that same market. Whatever Canada eventually gets, it’s unlikely to work for the UK.
A miserable time for Merz
Friedrich Merz is in trouble. A fortnight after the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) swept to a crushing victory in one state election in Saxony-Anhalt, the German chancellor’s centre-right CDU failed to clear the 5% threshold needed to enter the state parliament in another, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
It fared a little better in Berlin, where it was the incumbent, but was still beaten – by a clear five-point margin – by the far-left Die Linke. And the AfD made headway in the capital, too, surging to a double-digit result. The embattled chancellor has vowed to fight on, but faces an uncomfortable choice: revise the unpopular economic reforms he insists are essential, or risk oblivion defending them.
Meanwhile, as long as he refuses to step aside and no one is actively seeking to replace him, a volatile and damaging deadlock will reign in Europe’s biggest economy. After 16 months in office, it is becoming increasingly clear – as a Guardian editorial noted – that Merz is “ill-suited for the job” of defending Germany’s democratic future against the far right.
