Nika’s story
No one would tell the shackled detainees onboard the US immigration plane where they were going. The officers in charge would taunt them when they asked, they said. It was only when the seat-back video screens finally showed a map that the 18 migrants worked it out.
Their destination was Central African Republic (CAR), a country few of them had even heard of.
Nika, a 32-year-old Iranian woman, recalled how the handcuffs dug into her wrists. She begged the officers to loosen them, but they did not. Other passengers had it worse, she said. Some of the men were restrained in black and yellow body wraps, as if mummified, after resisting orders to get on the plane.
Nika, who had fled Iran 18 months earlier after protesting against its regime, had imagined the US as a place of sanctuary. Iran was already one of the most repressive countries in the world when she left, and its horrors had only deepened since then: security forces gunned down thousands of other demonstrators this year, then Donald Trump’s administration launched the war there.
After more than a year locked up in a US immigration detention centre, Nika, whose name the Guardian has changed to protect her family in Iran, was granted legal protections and freed on a judge’s orders. Within two weeks, the Department of Homeland Security had rearrested her, and days later she was on the plane heading 7,000 miles east.
“They never told me they were going to deport me [to] this country,” she told the Guardian. “I don’t know anything about Africa.”
The Department of State warns US citizens not to travel to CAR because it says it is too dangerous. Nika spends most of her days there under a form of self-imprisonment, too scared to venture out from her small bedroom as she waits for an answer to the question on which her life depends: will she be sent back to Iran, and to a regime that could kill her?
Nika is one of more than 25,000 people deported by the Trump administration to countries that are not their own. About 20,000 people have been bussed to Mexico, according to a count by Refugees International and Human Rights First. And more than 5,000 others have been put on flights to countries in Africa, Latin America, the Caribbean and central Asia to which they have no connection, and then, often, returned to the countries where US immigration judges had ruled their lives or liberty were at risk.
Human rights lawyers describe these so-called third-country national arrangements as part of a “show of force” by the US intended to discourage migrants and asylum seekers from entering. People from Peru and Colombia have been sent to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). On 20 August, four Cubans, a Brazilian and a Cameroonian refused to disembark in Liberia, and were sent to Equatorial Guinea instead.
In order to compile the most comprehensive account of a policy that has mostly operated behind closed doors, the Guardian joined 23 other media organisations in the Deportation Project, a joint investigation coordinated by Paris-based Forbidden Stories. The consortium interviewed more than 100 people affected by, or involved in, the US drive to extinguish unauthorised immigration, and reviewed documents outlining details of the agreements made by US officials with governments around the world.
It has tracked more than 100 flights that have carried migrants and asylum seekers to 28 different countries. This is likely to be an undercount as the consortium’s dataset only includes flights it was able to independently verify.
The pace of flights is increasing. After an initial wave during the opening months of the second Trump administration, the number of deportations spiked in August again when, according to a count by Human Rights First, a record 16 flights carried people to 13 different countries that were not their own.
A US federal appeals court ruled on Friday that third-country removals were unlawful, arguing that they violated due process because people are not notified with enough time to mount a legal challenge to the decision to send them to another country. Human rights lawyers suggested this should immediately ground third-country deportation flights. The government is expected to appeal against the judgment, and to press ahead with its policy.
A state department spokesperson said implementing the Trump administration’s immigration policies was a “top priority” and “we are unwavering in our commitment to end illegal and mass immigration and bolster America’s border security”. They added: “The US government will use all legal means to remove those with no right to remain in our country.”
The Trump administration has said the people it deports are criminals. Yet documents obtained by the Washington Post as part of this project show that a majority of the 35 countries that have signed deals with the US have said they will not accept migrants with violent criminal records.
 The people forced on to planes include those who spent most of their lives in the US, parents detained on the school run, the adult children of elderly relatives who depend on them for care.
Many are people whose fear of returning home was deemed so credible that immigration judges barred their removal from the US. Nika had been granted “withholding of removal”, a protection for individuals who may face severe harm in their country of origin but are ineligible for asylum. On 28 May, not only was she released from US Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s custody, but she was eligible to find a job, to work, and to stay.
Image credit: Guardian Design/Getty Images/Reuters
The rug pull
Nika’s lawyer, Sahar Jalili, is Iranian and, like her client, studied in Tehran. She took the case when she was pregnant, and often worked past the point of exhaustion. “That could be me,” she said of Nika.
Combing through the case file, Jalili was shocked to learn ICE had officially decided to send Nika to CAR’s capital, Bangui, just eight days before a judge ordered her release from the detention centre. Her uncle’s family had prepared a room for her in Los Angeles. It took her two days to get there, and she spent a week with them, unfurling, after 18 months of hell.
Her re-arrest on 8 June, during what ICE officers had presented as a routine check-in, felt like cruelty for cruelty’s sake, Jalili said.
Nika said she had finished her appointment and left when an officer called her uncle and asked him to drive her back to pick up some papers.
This time there were new questions. A man took Nika’s fingerprints, then her photograph, Jalili said. “Then he came back accompanied by a female ICE officer, and they said put your hands above your head.” She said she was arrested, handcuffed and led to the basement.
Nika felt numb, she said, as she was transferred out of the detention facility that evening. Anti-ICE demonstrators smacked their palms on the side of the van as she passed through protests that had become a regular feature in LA.
For Jalili, the previous two days had already been a blur, as she and her colleagues battled to save two other Iranian women from being put on the same plane for Bangui. The lawyers managed to get the other two women off the plane, but not Nika. The only difference between them was that Nika was detained last, so by the time a network of immigration lawyers had learned of her case, there was not enough time before the flight departed.
Jalili said she begged every ICE officer: “Give me two days. Just two days.” She recalled: “They told me that they had respected the judge’s order to release her. But they’d never promised not to send her to a third country.”
Image credit: Guardian Design/AP/Reuters
African deals
When Rabbiatu Kuyateh, 58, learned that the country she had been sent to, Ghana, was deporting her to her childhood homeland, she was so scared it took a scrum of people to force her into the waiting van.
A video captured the moment last November when she was dragged, shoeless and distraught, by her hair. She still remembers the crack of her head on the stone steps as she begged not to be returned to Sierra Leone, screaming: “I’m not going.”
Kuyateh was a nurse and had spent most of her life in the US with her parents, after fleeing Sierra Leone. She cared for American coronavirus patients during the pandemic and had looked after disabled adults and children in the years since.
She had scrapped hard for the life she built, she said. She had raised her son, Mohamed, alone and they had bought a house together. By the time Trump was re-elected in 2024, her parents were so frail she began each day by checking on them before her shift, and then returning to make sure they were ready for bed.
In order to accelerate its expulsion of people such as Kuyateh, the Trump administration has remade the very institutions that were once intended to protect migrants who fled persecution.
“I would describe [this] as the Trump administration’s way of trying to undermine the concept of asylum and refugee protection,” said Alma David, one of the leading immigration lawyers tracking the policy. “While the US understands that they can’t deport them to their home country legally, what they can do is basically send them through this third country that perceives itself as a transit hub.”
 The drive is being led by Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff, who has been open about his desire to end most migration to the US. In interviews with the Washington Post as part of the Deportation Project, current and former US officials said Miller had rolled out the third-country removals policy by pushing key appointments inside the state department that have allowed him to overrule other foreign policy objectives in service of his agenda.
Among them is Christian Ehrhardt, a career state department official who heads the newly formed Office of Remigration – its name incorporating a term adopted by the far right to describe the forcible expulsion of minority ethnic immigrants. Ehrhardt has helped secure at least 13 third-country deportation agreements in Africa, after diplomatic tours through the continent.
Internal records reviewed by the Washington Post show the Trump administration has pledged at least $410m (£307m) to secure such agreements with 35 different countries, almost a third of them in Africa.
They indicate that $30m was earmarked for Cameroon, in order to support UN operations in the country, in return for accepting 1,000 migrants. The US has so far sent only 44. The DRC was promised $75m towards UN operations there, in return for accepting 2,000 migrants. It has only received 15, and flights to Kinshasa are on hold due to the country’s Ebola outbreak.
The arrangements differ from country to country. A handful, including Eswatini, have agreed to accept people with violent criminal histories. But many have said they will not take anyone with a record of violence or other types of serious crimes. The state department did not respond to questions about details of these agreements.
Ghana will only take people from west Africa; CAR did not specify nationalities, and the passengers on Nika’s plane were from places including Afghanistan, Iraq and Kyrgyzstan. Most of them had no ties to Africa at all, she said.
On 1 July 2025, Kuyateh’s son, Mohamed, had accompanied her to a routine ICE check-in, as her immigration status required. He remembered his mother feeling anxious that the cuffs on an officer’s belt were for her. “I doubt it,” Mohamed told her. But when they called Kuyateh into an interrogation room, he was told to wait outside.
“That’s the last time I saw her,” he said.
During Kuyateh’s four months in ICE custody, Mohamed spoke to her often. He had not heard from her on the day in November when he said he was called by another detainee who told him she had been sent to Texas. “And I was just like, why is she going to Texas?”
Two days later Kuyateh called him in tears. She was in Ghana, about to be sent to Sierra Leone.
The footage of her being dragged into a bus, beginning the onward deportation, appeared to anger the Ghanaian authorities when it spread across social media, according to Malick, the Senegalese man, also deported from the US, who filmed it. The Guardian has given him a pseudonym out of concern for his safety. “They got angry,” Malick said. “They came in the evening, at night, with two trucks full of soldiers.”
He said the troops drove his group to a remote military camp with faltering electricity and little contact with the outside world. The Ghanaian government did not respond to questions from the Guardian.
One woman sent to the camp said she grew so scared of what might happen if she was returned to her native Senegal that she attempted suicide by drinking bleach. She was treated in hospital, then sent back to Senegal anyway. “I drank the bleach because I wanted to die,” she said. “Because they wanted to force me to go back to my country.”
Image credit: Guardian Design/Rabbiatu Kuyateh
Malaria
Onboard Nika’s flight on 11 June this year, the inflight video showed Ghana as its initial destination, so the passengers assumed that was where they were going. But their stop in the capital, Accra, was brief. The 18 passengers then landed in Bangui at 9.45pm, flight monitors said. The officers onboard removed their cuffs, but did not get off the plane.
For several hours, the group did not meet anyone who spoke English. “They were communicating with hand gestures, like, get on a bus, and then they put us on a bus. And then they took us to give us some vaccinations, and I didn’t know what they were going to inject me with,” Nika said. It turned out to be for yellow fever.
Her room was in an apartment block. She was told she could stay for three months. But the idea of returning to Iran was unfathomable.
US-based Iranian rights groups say they have been unable to determine the fates of hundreds of other Iranian nationals deported back home during the course of the US-Israeli war on Iran. A recent lawsuit filed against ICE alleges the administration has shared the records of Iranian asylum-seekers with the very regime they had fled, further elevating the risk for those sent back.
When a headache started clouding her brain, Nika thought it was a migraine. She felt sick, her body hurt. She had been bitten by so many mosquitoes that her skin looked bruised, she said. A medical report, seen by the Guardian, confirmed she had malaria. Speaking by phone, Nika said: “I didn’t even know what that was.”
 Back in Los Angeles, Jalili waited anxiously on updates about Nika’s situation. There were injections every 12 hours to clear her bloodstream of parasites. The bad news did not stop when she was well enough to return to her accommodation. Jalili was horrified to learn Nika had been deported from the US without her passport, meaning she had neither identification documents, nor a visa, and on trips to the hospital and vegetable market, police officers used her lack of papers to make threats.
The CAR government did not respond to a request for comment.
The second time she was stopped, Nika said, the police officer mimed the action of putting cuffs on her. The message, she said, was: “I can take you in, unless you pay us.”
Image credit: Guardian Design/Getty Images/Reuters
Old tools to grease the wheels
As the Trump administration accelerates its third-country deportations, CAR is one of 13 host countries where the deported are being supported by the International Organization for Migration (IOM), a UN agency, which provides them with food, lodgings and psychological counsel upon their arrival.
Although the Trump administration has announced sweeping cuts to its funding for UN agencies, there seem to be exceptions where the funds enable this deportation programme.
In March last year, the state department spelled out the logic. From now on, it said, humanitarian funding would be used to “reduce mass and illegal immigration, such as funding voluntary returns of illegal aliens, incentivising governments to implement safe third-country agreements, and building the migration management capacity of other countries”.
According to a federal government database that tracks spending, more than 60% of US grants to the IOM during the second Trump administration have gone to programmes in countries that accept deported migrants. In CAR, that meant an allocation of $85m. The highest US contribution to IOM in CAR under the Biden administration, according to the database, was $14m.
 Nika said she had been treated well by the agency. “The people here are doing their best,” she said. The accommodation was secure and transport was provided when needed. “But at the same time, it’s not living. I’m breathing here, I’m not dying. But I can’t leave the house without a driver they provide here. I can’t find jobs. I don’t speak their language.”
The potential for a negative perception of its involvement in the programme is something the IOM has grappled with. An internal risk assessment for a programme supporting third-country nationals sent from the US to one African country, seen by the Guardian, warns it could lead the agency to be “perceived as complicit”.
An IOM spokesperson said in a statement that such assessments were conducted in order to ascertain whether host nations were able to commit to safeguards for the migrants, but added: “We are fully cognisant that states use financial assistance to advance their national priorities. However, IOM’s decisions to accept funding, provide post-arrival assistance, or support assisted voluntary return are guided by our own mandate and principles, and rest on a single question: whether our engagement will improve the lives of the migrants affected. In these instances, we believe strongly it does.”
Many in the human rights field are uncomfortable the UN is easing the process for governments that agree to cooperate with the Trump administration.
“It just feels very incongruous for IOM to be the organisation in charge of these men and women,” said Alma David. “These aren’t migrants in your typical sense. These aren’t people who chose to migrate,” she said. “These are people who were kidnapped, essentially.”
Image credit: Guardian Design/Getty Images/Alamy
Life in the shadows
People who had been returned from third countries to the places they were born describe a life now lived in the shadows. Kuyateh left Sierra Leone within days of being sent back there. The Guardian is not naming her location. “I don’t sleep at night,” she said. “Sometimes I just wake up. I’ll be sitting down like, what am I doing here? Why am I here?”
She called her family every day. Sometimes, she said, she felt too sad to turn on the video and see their faces. She could get through the conversation with her mother without tears, she said, “but whenever I talk to my daddy, I’ll be crying. And when I sit here, I think about them. It hurts so much.”
She was not sure what scared her more: the thought of dying alone in a foreign country, or knowing that her parents might die without her at their bedside.
Annan, a gay man who fled Ghana after he was outed, and then hunted, by members of his family, said he was terrified when he touched back down in Accra. He had refused to disembark during his initial deportation from the US to Sierra Leone, and had to be forcibly removed from the plane, he said. He later begged authorities not to return him, he said, but they did not listen.
In a statement, the Sierra Leonean government said it took its “international obligations seriously” but that questions relating to immigration protections afforded by an American court were for the US government to address.
It added: “So far, no individual returned to Sierra Leone under the TCNA [third-country national arrangement] has requested to remain in Sierra Leone or not to be returned to his or her country of choice either in west Africa or beyond.”
Annan’s mother had used her savings to pay for his escape to the US. She was distraught when he called to say he was back. “She knew she couldn’t protect me,” he said.
He shared footage of where he lived now: an abandoned building with no electricity or running water in a neighbouring country, he said. He spent his daylight hours hiding, and walked almost an hour to find food when darkness fell. His bed was a blanket on the floor, although he barely slept, he said, too scared of being infected by one of the insects that crawled or buzzed around him. He said the loneliness felt crippling.
In recent weeks, someone had texted him anonymously, saying that his survival, as a gay man, would not be tolerated. The message made him feel hopeless: he could run, it said, but he could not hide for ever.
Image credit: Guardian Design/Getty Images/Rabbiatu Kuyateh
Exhaustion
In Los Angeles, Jalili is getting more calls about clients bound for deportation flights. In June, a 30-year-old Iranian woman with a blood disorder that made her so weak she needed a walker was told she would be sent to the landlocked south African nation of Eswatini.
Another client was “going crazy”, Jalili said. “They’re coming up with a new country for her every week.”
Immigration lawyers said that while their jobs had always been hard, the scale of the efforts to obstruct those opposing the Trump administration’s drive to quash all types of irregular migration was unprecedented.
When a client is detained, avenues of accountability have largely been shut, including the office of an independent ombudsman for immigration detention, which was responsible for investigating abuses and misconduct.
In court, immigration lawyers can face hostile judges after the Trump administration purged some of those deemed insufficiently loyal to the deportation agenda. Meanwhile, the cost of even filing a case has risen steeply, under the terms of a bill passed through Congress in July last year.
Jalili, like many others, spent much of the first Trump administration mounting legal challenges against a policy of separating children from their parents at the US-Mexico border. Knowing that what would follow might be worse, she decided on the eve of Trump’s re-election to start her own firm to fight the coming storm
It was not uncommon for calls from the desperate families of new ICE detainees to wake her in the night.
One of the biggest challenges, said Erica Reilly, an immigration attorney based in Washington DC, was basic communication with ICE officers.
“You send all these emails to deportation officers, and you’re like: ‘Hi, just following up again on the email I sent you last week, and the week before that, and the week before that, and the week before that, that you haven’t responded to,’” she said. “And they know they don’t have to because there’s no accountability.”
The worst thing, she said, was the powerlessness. But the cruelty and the lack of access, she had come to believe, “that’s all the point”.
“I think that the administration is doing what they can to get enough people to say, well, the alternative is too scary or too uncertain or too bad. I’ll just leave on my own.”
Getting through the day meant reformulating the wins, Reilly said. “Getting a call back from a deportation officer shouldn’t be a win, but in this environment it is.”
Jalili said she did her best to focus on the battles she could win. When she heard Nika’s flight had left for Bangui, she sank to the floor, called her mother, and began to cry. “It’s not a situation where you can just say: ‘Oh, I did my best.’”
Nika had lost the life she knew in Iran. The US offered little better. Jalili listed the cost.
“Being detained for 17 months. Being released from the federal judge’s order for 10 days. Being stripped away from her uncle’s hands. Being put in a car and then on a flight in shackles, and for 24 hours, sitting on that flight. She must have felt so lonely.”

After U.S. President Donald Trump banned CNN, Politico and MS NOW (archived) from the White House reporting pool in September 2026, several television networks — Fox News, ABC, NBC and CBS — said they would halt television coverage until he lifted restrictions. This is in part because networks pool their resources and take turns providing sound and images for live coverage of the president.
Trump's decision sparked a fierce debate about free press access to the White House. The three banned outlets said they would seek to return to covering the president via legal means. As a result of the networks' boycott of live coverage of the White House, Trump inaugurated the presidential residence's new helipad without any sound on Sept. 21. Meanwhile, rumors abounded, claiming Trump was hardly the first president to impose restrictions on the press.
Over the years, Snopes has examined several claims about the White House press corps and its relationship to successive presidents. Here are five of them.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. gave the keynote address Thursday at a conference of an anti-vaccine activist group he once chaired, telling the hundreds in attendance that they had a friend in President Donald Trump's White House.
It was Kennedy's first time appearing at the Children's Health Defense conference since he became secretary. Kennedy took leave from the group when he launched his bid to become president in 2023, but his speech Thursday served as a sort of homecoming, offering him a platform from which to hail the administration's steps to scale back vaccine guidance and reassure the activists in attendance that he was working to turn their priorities into policy.
“Let me be clear: You have a strong and steadfast friend in the White House. We've accomplished in 19 months things that would have seemed unthinkable two years ago,” he said.
The speech, peppered with questions about long established vaccine safety, also highlighted how once fringe views on vaccines have been given a prominent pulpit under the Trump administration.
Kennedy boasted about the administration's moves to downsize the childhood vaccination schedule and reshape a key vaccine advisory board — steps that have since been halted by a judge.
Kennedy lauded Trump for pushing ahead with attempts to overhaul vaccine guidance, including an executive order last month calling for spacing out the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, against medical groups' recommendations.
That executive order and now Kennedy's keynote speech at the Children's Health Defense conference mark a pivot by the White House and the Department of Health and Human Services, who earlier this year had appeared to be moving beyond vaccine efforts and toward a less contentious agenda on healthy food ahead of November’s midterm elections. HHS promoted the speech on its social media channels.
Kennedy, a longtime anti-vaccine activist, chaired Children’s Health Defense for years. He served as the group’s chief legal counsel and expanded it. After becoming health secretary last year, Kennedy moved at a blistering pace to overhaul public health guidance and revamp long-held precedents in vaccine policymaking.
Critics, among them many of the country's top medical associations, have said the moves risk stoking vaccine hesitancy and sowing confusion among Americans who endured a crisis of trust in their public health agencies following the COVID-19 pandemic. That public confidence continues to erode.
“We have not taken vaccines away from anybody. We have preserved access. But we have started asking the questions that you and millions of American parents have been asking for years,” Kennedy told the group.
Mary Holland, the CEO of Children’s Health Defense, referred to Kennedy as “Bobby” and said the group has “gratitude beyond words” to the HHS secretary for “recognizing there are real consequential issues around childhood vaccinations.”
Kennedy's appearance Thursday comes as the country faces its worst year for measles since 1991 and has seen seven reported measles-associated deaths in the last two years — more than the combined total of reported deaths over the previous three decades.
Pennsylvania officials have reported four measles-associated deaths this year. None of the four were vaccinated, according to the state health department. When state officials last month announced the first two of those deaths, it ignited a public feud between Gov. Josh Shapiro and Kennedy.
Shapiro blasted Kennedy's appearance on the social media site X Thursday, saying Kennedy “chose to spend his time today addressing the premier vaccine-denial conference in America.”
Shapiro said the HHS secretary should have encouraged people to get vaccinated for measles, "yet he couldn’t bring himself to do it. Instead, he pushed a narrative that continues to stoke fear and mistrust.”
A representative from the White House did not respond to an Associated Press request for comment on Kennedy’s appearance at the event.
Following Kennedy onstage Thursday was Andrew Wakefield, an author of a since-discredited study that linked the MMR vaccine to autism, which has fueled the anti-vaccine movement even though it was retracted.
Widespread scientific consensus and decades of studies have firmly concluded there is no link between vaccines and autism.
Shaughnessy Naughton, founder of 314 Action, a group that recruits scientists to run for public office, said Kennedy's decision to give a speech at the conference shows “the lack of seriousness he brings to HHS.”
"With a deadly measles outbreak killing people in Pennsylvania, the best thing Kennedy can do for Americans is step aside.”

Is Nepal's flood a harbinger of what's to come in the Himalayas?
KATHMANDU, Nepal — On a recent September day, Sumana Shrestha Amatya stood alongside other protesters in the Nepali capital, urging the government to work faster to find their loved ones, trapped inside hydropower plants since flash floods devastated miles of a river valley in late August.
Amatya says she hasn't heard from officials about her husband, Sunil, a geologist. Still, she acknowledged the scale of the disaster that the government was grappling with: "It was like a Himalayan tsunami."
It's a description other Nepalis have used for the events of Aug. 26, when a glacier and its bedrock spanning more than 3,800 feet in width collapsed into a river valley, some 4,000 feet below.
That triggered 30-foot-high waves of boulders, water and ice that surged for miles downstream. It swept away a multistory border building and some 70 bridges and miles of highway, and buried 12 hydropower plants under mud and boulders along the Trishuli River, which was badly impacted by the floods.
Some 1,400 bodies have been recovered in Nepal, and more than 5,000 remain unaccounted for.
The dead and missing include 121 people who were trapped in hydropower plants, according to Brig. Gen. Subas Jung Thapa of the Nepali army, which is leading rescue efforts. He spoke in early September.
It took days just to find the power plants under the mud. It was like "a bomb's gone off," said Arnold Dix, a tunneling expert helping with rescue efforts. "It's removed the power stations from the surface, like they're just not there." Only three men were found alive in the plants since rescue efforts began.
Did hydropower projects add to the risk?
It is those hydropower plants that have received the most scrutiny in regional media since the floods, with experts reviving questions about whether developers had properly assessed the risks of building them in the Himalayas.
"We need to understand what is happening now in Nepal can happen in other parts of the Himalayas," says C.P. Rajendran, an Indian geoscientist who has been critical of big construction works in the Himalayas. (Rajendran, like many Indians, uses initials for his first name.)
Critics have also focused on the role of international institutions like the World Bank, which has long supported some of these hydropower projects and their associated dams.
They include one of the biggest hydropower projects in the river basin, known as the Upper Trishuli-1, which cost Nepal over half a billion dollars. It was backed by about $300 million in loans and equity by two arms of the World Bank.
The Upper-Trishuli-1 was under construction. Now it's under the mud. Thapa of the Nepali army said in his press briefing that he estimated some 50 people were trapped inside. On Wednesday, the Kathmandu Post reported the bodies of five men were recovered from the plant.
"Why did it have to happen in the first place?" asked Parineeta Dandekar, an expert on rivers who has written critically about these projects for the advocacy group South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers and People.
Dandekar accuses the World Bank of producing a flawed risk assessment report for the project from the get-go. Its many omissions, Dandekar says, included ignoring "the cumulative disaster risk that can happen after having so many projects across the same river."
Experts say the Trishuli river basin has 36 hydro power projects — including the dozen now under the mud.
Dandekar says the constant blasting of mountains to build these projects, including for miles-long tunnels, has its own impact.
It's a region where earthquakes and landslides are common, and where climate change is causing its glaciers to melt more rapidly, making them — and their slopes — more unstable. Initial analysis suggests global warming exacerbated the melting of the glacier that snapped off in August, triggering flash floods.
There's no clear evidence that the construction of these projects had a role in causing the severity of the Aug. 26 disaster. But experts like geoscientist Rajendran say construction has caused damage in other communities where hydropower projects are being built, including damaging mountain springs, causing homes to crack and even landslides.
In this case, though, says Dipak Gyawali, a hydropower engineer with the Nepal Academy of Science and Technology, "compared to the tectonic forces at play that caused this event, dynamiting is minuscule. This is almost nothing. It's like scratching your skin."
But he and other experts said developers were not seriously investigating the risk caused by so many projects built in the same zone. "These risks have to be properly studied and assessed. Unfortunately, they have not been," Gyawali said.
Retired Indian ambassador Shyam Saran, who served as the Indian prime minister's special envoy for climate change, says developers typically look at risks that could be triggered by their project, alongside environmental risks to it, and they appear safe. "But if you do actually a cumulative environmental impact assessment of the whole river system," he says, "then a different picture emerges."
And the Trishuli river "is a really high-risk area to build [hydropower] dams, says Austin Lord of the Stimson Center, who works on disaster risk reduction in the Himalayan region at the Stimson Center. In events exacerbated by climate change, there's been deadly flooding three years in a row in the Trishuli basin. In 2024, it was extreme rainfall. In 2025, a glacial lake burst. This year, a glacier snapped off.
A pre-flood warning
Days before the August flood, Lord and others authored a paper warning that the area was particularly vulnerable to glacial lakes bursting. "Recurring landslides, and prolonged closures," they wrote, "had all highlighted its vulnerability."
In a statement, the World Bank told NPR that the hydropower plant's design reflected assessments that looked at the risk of flooding and landslides using evidence available when the assessment was made in 2018. The statement said that as more information becomes available about the August floods, "the World Bank Group will consider any implications for risk assessment, monitoring, early warning and emergency response measures in hydropower projects."
Another major funder for the Upper Trishuli-1 was the Asian Development Bank, which loaned $60 million for the project. In 2024, independent experts who visited the site reported that no climate resilience assessment was undertaken. They described that as a "significant gap." The bank did not immediately respond to NPR's question as to whether that assessment was ultimately undertaken.
Arnold Dix, the tunneling expert, defended the hydropower plants' construction. "They were built properly to start with," he said, noting the underground infrastructure, including tunnels, was still intact. He said the collapsing glacier that triggered the August flash floods was an unforeseen new threat that "will change the way we do the designs of the power station."
Rethinking hydropower in the Himalayas
Advocates say they hope this devastating flood might prompt a rethink of how hydropower is constructed across the Himalayas. Reuters reported in 2025 that China and India, the world's most populous countries, have built 68 major dams in the Himalayas and another 101 are in the pipeline.
Most prominently, China is constructing one of the world's largest dams and hydropower plants in Tibet, costing around $170 billion. It's estimated that it will provide power to 300 million people.
In July, Chinese geologists reported that the dam is being constructed over an active fault line, risking the integrity of the project's infrastructure. Chinese officials have maintained that the project is safe and that they had considered downstream communities.
"If something happens, it is going to be a monumental disaster," says retired ambassador Saran. He says Chinese authorities have assured their neighbors that the hydro project is safe. "But as we see," he says, "those precautions which supposedly had been taken don't mean very much when you have nature's fury to deal with."
That Chinese hydropower plant and dam is being built some 30 miles from the border of the Indian state of Arunachal Pradesh, according to the state's Chief Minister Pema Khandu. In 2025 statements to the media, he described two possible threats: It could hold back much of the water that presently passes downstream, and it could inundate downstream areas, whether by negligence, design or natural disaster.
For now, India's strategy appears to be building its own dam in Arunachal Pradesh in case China releases — perhaps deliberately — enormous quantities of water, as Chief Minister Khandu suggested in June last year to the outlet, Press Trust of India. "Setting aside the military threat from China, it seems to me that this is a far bigger issue than anything else. It is going to cause an existential threat to our tribes and our livelihoods. It is quite serious because China could even use this as a sort of water bomb," Khandu was quoted as saying.
Many in the local community have opposed the dam, even damaging bridges to prevent surveyors from entering the area. On Wednesday, local media reported that India's premier criminal investigation agency filed a case against Bhanu Tatak, the adviser to a group resisting the hydropower project, accusing her of illegally taking funds from foreign entities. She's previously said the Indian state has been trying to find ways to stop her advocacy.
Rajendran, the geoscientist, said both China and India needed to undertake smaller projects that are less politically attractive but less disruptive to people and their environments. "The kind of construction they are doing," he says, "it might happen probably 25 years later, or maybe 30 or 40 years later, but there will be a huge tragedy
Bhandari reported from Kathmandu. Hadid reported from Mumbai.

Soon after the news of Hindutva fanatic Swatantra Bhardwaj getting interim bail for three weeks went out, a 1.16-minute video of him got viral, in which he is with another person who boasts about Bhardwaj’s release and compares him with a lion on the hunt. Bhardwaj then threatens those who had attacked his supporters while he was in detention. He says (in Hindi), “You are like insects.. why did you target my brothers? if they wanted they could have beaten you up.. but for some reason, they followed the law… I will not do anything to you.. tell your father Chandrashekhar Azad (Bhim Army chief whom Bhardwaj compares to Ravana), that this Brahmin lion (referring to himself) will avenge the attack. It is an open challenge…”
Bhardwaj faces criminal charges under Sections 115(2), 126(2) and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, along with provisions of the POCSO Act and SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act and an attempt-to-murder charge for an alleged assault on the father of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) activist Nishu Azaad. On September 7, he had been sent to 14-day judicial remand.
An X user named Gen-Z of India shared the said video on September 17 and wrote (in Hindi), “As soon as Swatantra Bharadwaj stepped out, he started up again, even though the court had imposed the condition that he would not make any grandstanding statements in the media, but listen to what he is saying.” The post has received close to 1 million views. This post was reshared by several influential and verified handles, including Trinamool Congress MP Mahua Moitra, journalist Vir Sanghvi, CJP leader Ratna Singh and others, making it go viral. Others like film writer Darab Farooqi and verified X user @tanmoyofc shared the video as well.
Media outlets Prabhat Khabar and The Mooknayak published reports on the video presenting it as recorded after Bhardwaj’s release on bail in the assault case.
Fact Check
First of all, we found that India Today posted a video on September 17 stating that Bhardwaj came out of Tihar Jail around 9.45 pm on that day (September 17). The caption of India Today’s Instagram post said, “Although he was granted bail two days ago, he was released around 9:45 pm after the remaining procedures were completed. He immediately ran towards a taxi and left without speaking to the media.”
View this post on Instagram
Several other media outlets reported that Bhardwaj walked out of jail late at night on Thursday, September 17, and rushed into a car avoiding media persons.
Next, a reverse image search with some key frames from the viral video led us to a Facebook post and a YouTube video from September 7. This makes it clear that the video was not recorded after Bhardwaj’s release on September 17. Check the screenshots in the gallery below:
By scraping our database of active Right-wing vigilantes, we then identified the other individual in the video as Vaibhaw Kumar alias Vaibhaw Pandey. While going through his Instagram timeline, we found the now-viral video uploaded on June 26.
According to another video posted by Vaibhaw, Bhardwaj was detained on June 22 for threatening CJP leaders at Jantar Mantar.
To sum up, the viral video of Hindutva fanatic and attempt-to-murder accused Swatantra Bhardwaj threatening Chandrashekhar Azad was not recorded after his release on interim bail on September 17. It was shared on social media by another Hindutva vigilante on June 26.

Is produce from a home garden safer than store bought? 'It depends'
Many consumers responded to this summer's record foodborne illness numbers by buying more produce from farmers markets or growing their own at home. A third of Americans — 44 million households — grow some type of fruits or vegetables, up about 4% every year for the past five years, according to the National Gardening Association.
But is buying from small farms or growing your own safer?
"As with anything, it depends," says James Rogers, director of food safety for Consumer Reports, which regularly tests retail produce. What shapes safety is the farming practices, and has less to do with the operation's size, he says.
On one hand, large operations are regulated by cleanliness standards, and can track produce using bar codes, which can help to quickly trace back contamination. But co-mingling huge volumes of produce in washing and processing warehouses can also lead to big outbreaks
"You can have a problem if you have one batch that's contaminated, it will contaminate the entire batch," Rogers says.
Most small growers, he notes, are exempt from Food and Drug Administration rules, dealing with irrigation or testing for microorganisms. So their practices vary widely, which is how you end up with contrasting food-safety approaches like those of Phil Tocco and Dave Whitinger — both veteran gardeners growing lettuce in their own home gardens.
The fastidious gardener
Tocco, who lives in Jackson, Mich., is a Michigan State University agricultural food-safety expert who advises farms of all sizes. He considers himself more fastidious than your average farmer: "Some backyard gardeners don't understand the risks – the fecal risks."
Tocco's wife contracted amoebic dysentery — a painful intestinal parasite — from lettuce grown at a small farm 25 years ago. He says she still suffers from aftereffects of the infection. So Tocco keeps his garden free of animals and small children, who might track feces and pathogens like salmonella, E.coli, or Cyclospora that may be in it. He won't, as some gardeners do, use water from barrels collecting rainwater in his garden, because they might harbor bacteria.

"If then someone uses water from that rain barrel that's going to go into their mouth in a day, it's kind of like bacterial soup," he says.
Tocco replicates what he can of the sanitary practices he preaches: He harvests with sanitized hands and buckets, won't harvest food near bird or other wild animal droppings, and uses a commercial form of hydroxyacetic acid to rid any pathogens on his leafy greens. He says washing with water alone eliminates only about 90% of most pathogens – leaving enough to still potentially sicken a person.
A different approach
Meanwhile, Westlake, Texas, gardener Dave Whitinger is no less concerned for food safety.
"I told my wife to stop buying lettuce from the store," he says. "I was like, 'Hey, we're going to make sure that we're growing lettuce this fall because I don't want to buy any store bought lettuce until this whole thing dies down,'" he says, referring to the record-breaking caseload of the parasitic cyclosporiasis outbreak, traced back in large part to contamination with Taylor Farms lettuce grown in Mexico.
Whitinger runs a family seed business and is director of the National Gardening Association, an organization that has educated and surveyed home gardeners since the mid-1970s. He says his belief in growing his own food is shaped in part by a mistrust of large agricultural operations, especially when it comes to handling manure as fertilizer. That isn't an issue in his fenced garden: "I know what I'm fertilizing with; I know where the seeds came from."
Although microbes are invisible to the naked eye, Whitinger says he feels safe picking and eating leafy greens from his garden — even without washing: "If it's coming in from my backyard and like, for example, lettuce: I don't want to get wet," he says. "You know how hard it is to dry lettuce if you get it wet."
So how should most consumers deal with fresh produce?
Rogers, at Consumer Reports, says it's best to wash everything — just with water — no matter where the produce came from.
He and other food safety experts note contamination can also occur in the kitchen, when raw meats aren't kept separate from produce, for example. The FDA advises consumers to keep hands and cooking surfaces clean, including cutting boards when preparing different foods. Also, home chefs should heat food to the right temperature to prevent foodborne illness.

Jesse Lyu doesn't think the Rabbit R1 was a flop.
Lyu's gadget was among the first in the gold rush to create dedicated AI hardware that acted as a virtual assistant. You could speak into the R1 and ask it to complete tasks for you—book an Uber; order food on DoorDash. After a buzzy launch at CES 2024, it earned scathing reviews. All the agentic stuff on the R1 just didn't work that well. WIRED gave it a 3/10.
Since those early days, the capabilities of AI assistants have vastly improved, and now the tech is all the rage. So Rabbit is banging the drum again.
On Tuesday, Rabbit announced OS3, a standalone “agentic operating system” designed to run across multiple screens. It also arrives as a software update for the company's R1 gadget, though you don't need an R1 to use it. Instead, you can access OS3 through a desktop browser, Telegram on your phone, or even iMessage.
It’s a striking pivot for a company that once championed the handheld hardware over smartphone apps, but the environment for this type of software has ripened.
Agents that handle tasks for you are all anyone in Silicon Valley talks about. Meta's new Muse agent was just banned from crawling Amazon to shop on a user's behalf using a virtual machine. Lyu smirks as he brings it up, saying, “We've been through all of this a year and a half ago,” calling back to the R1's controversial use of a virtual machine to execute app actions on your behalf. So was Rabbit just too ahead of the curve?
Lyu says from a monetary perspective, the Rabbit R1 was tremendously successful, especially considering the company doesn't offer a subscription for its AI features, unlike many competitors. He claims the company delivered more than 100,000 of the orange-red, Teenage Engineering-designed gadgets worldwide, with return rates of less than 5 percent, and earned roughly a 45 to 50 percent margin on the hardware.
"Internally, from an engineering perspective—we didn't make the wrong bet," Lyu says. “I think the challenge is really being extremely limited in resources, team-wise and money-wise, compared to other AI studios that raised billions of dollars.” He says Rabbit has raised around $60 million in total and currently employs 15 people.
But after dismal reviews upon the R1's launch, the company had to make tough decisions. Rabbit decided against expanding the team and chose to stay lean, but things were dire around this time last year. A planned launch in India was stymied by regulations, putting the company in financial strain, so much so that a handful of employees went on strike and claimed they weren't getting paid. Lyu says he respected their decision, adding that the company secured more funding and is on stronger footing. “There are no issues with the company's health,” he says.
Lyu says the team decided not to rush into new hardware, and instead focused on delivering software updates to polish the R1 experience—to date, Lyu says Rabbit has deployed around 50 updates in the past year and a half. He points to a dedicated Discord community of more than 12,000 users that provide feedback on what new features to add to the R1, like opening up the hardware. For example, you can integrate OpenClaw or Hermes AI agents into the R1 instead of using Rabbit's proprietary models.
“Today, if you look at our R1 device, it's completely different from day one,” he says. “We're more open; the device is yours, you decide what to do with the device.”
And people are supposedly still buying the R1 right now. Lyu raised his phone screen into his webcam to show me four or five orders that came through that morning for the R1 sold through Rabbit's website. (He points out that it doesn't include sales data from Amazon, Target, or Best Buy, where you can also buy the R1.)
For now. Rabbit is no longer manufacturing the R1, and the existing stock is dwindling. The company is focusing on the new OS3 software platform, which is designed to work on the other hardware you already have. If you own an R1, you can use it as an input/output gadget for OS3. Lyu says Rabbit has no plans for an R2. Instead, its next hardware release, slated to arrive within “months,” is what he describes as a Cyberdeck—a dedicated “vibe coding” machine that will run OS3.
So what exactly is OS3? Lyu pitches it as an open, cross-platform agentic system that operates across the devices you already own. The platform lives in the cloud, but connects directly to desktop software, files, and web pages through a local agent node you install on Windows, Mac, or Linux. Using Rabbit’s DLAM (Direct Large Action Model) technology, it can execute local software tasks and autonomously write and debug code. One account links up to five machines, with OS3 determining behind the scenes which device should execute a given task.
The interface is a single, continuous chat stream—no sidebar of disjointed chat threads. Lyu repeatedly calls it a “brain dump” interface: paste your intent, and the system coordinates the models and tools needed to pull it off. It supports universal skill compatibility—paste a public URL for any third-party agent skill into the chat, and OS3 can install it automatically without users needing any technical know-how.
Rabbit uses a “Bring Your Own Key” (BYOK) approach to power OS3. There's no monthly subscription fee, but users supply their own API keys from providers like OpenAI or Anthropic—or link local open source models.
Lyu has been using OS3 to handle plenty of tasks. For example, he says vendors send him an Excel report for R1 sales every week. He'll check it on his phone, but he always returns to his PC to open the document and manually add the data into a master sheet. But with OS3, since the Rabbit agent is deployed on his PC, he can send a message through Telegram on his phone asking it to handle the task, and it'll complete the routine action.
Just the other day, Lyu was heading to a video shoot that would take up most of his day. That meant he wasn't reachable on Slack. So, he asked OS3 to represent him on Slack, and the agent supposedly had a 50-minute conversation with an engineer (it announced itself as Lyu's agent, so the engineer was aware) and could even access files on Lyu's computer to help answer the engineer's questions.
Rabbit says the local agent doesn't store, copy, or sell data. While conversations and memory logs reside on Rabbit’s servers, file contents stay on your machine. The caveat is that when a task requires model reasoning, the relevant prompts pass through Rabbit’s servers to your model provider, which then processes that data under its own terms.
Anyone can try OS3 starting today, which in itself quietly refutes the premise that launched Rabbit into the spotlight in 2024. It turns out people never really needed another gadget in their pocket to chat with AI. They’ve already got the best tool for the job.

BYJU'S has reportedly reached a settlement with Aakash Educational Services Limited (AESL) over the dispute over the latter’s rights issue. As per a report by LiveLaw Biz, BYJU’S senior advocate Abhinav Vasisht and senior advocate C K Nandakumar on Aakash’s behalf, informed the NCLT’s Bengaluru about the settlement today. The proceedings relate to Aakash’s rights issue, which BYJU’S had challenged before the NCLT, alleging oppression and mismanagement. Amid a financial strain, Aakash had proposed to undertake a ₹500 Cr rights issue. The proposed rights issue could have diluted BYJU’S stake in Akash from 26% to less than 5%, which prompted BYJU'S to contest the rights issue before the NCLT, the NCLAT, and the Supreme Court. The development comes months after BYJU’S creditors approved a proposal to settle the long-running dispute over AESL’s shareholding before the Bengaluru bench of the NCLT. Earlier this month, BYJU’S founder Byju Raveendran proposed relinquishing his shareholding in Aakash to settle Qatar Holding’s arbitration claim of more than $235 Mn against him. The latest proposal further places Aakash at the centre of overlapping disputes over ownership, creditor recoveries, and the future of BYJU’S, which once commanded a valuation of $22 Bn. Creditors have been separately exploring a broader settlement centred around Aakash as it remains the most valuable surviving asset of the edtech startup. Global lenders who extended BYJU’S $1.2 Bn term loan B, represented by GLAS Trust, are said to be in advanced talks to acquire a 30% stake in Aakash, valuing the coaching chain at around $2 Bn. BYJU’S acquired Aakash in April 2021 for about $1 Bn in a cash-and-stock deal to expand into offline test preparation. Aakash, one of India’s largest test-prep brands for engineering and medical entrance exams, has since been entangled in the broader financial and legal troubles at the BYJU’S group. On the financial front, the test-prep major managed to narrow its net loss for FY26 by 15.5% to ₹186.5 Cr from ₹220.8 Cr loss incurred in the previous fiscal. Operating revenue rose marginally by 0.4% to ₹2,040.5 Cr in FY26 from ₹2,032.1 Cr in the previous year.

From leaving Rangers to La Liga - Scotland is next step for Ure
- Published
Robbie Ure, cool and confident and 22 years old, played 90 minutes for Sevilla against Barcelona at the weekend; 90 minutes of being marked by Pau Cubarsi, man of the match in the World Cup final, 90 minutes of pitch-time with Rodri, player of the tournament, 90 minutes of breathing the same rarefied air as Lamine Yamal.
Ure is a part of a new-ish wave of Scotland striker, uncapped but hopeful of making a debut on Saturday away to Slovenia in the Nations League.
There is no Lyndon Dykes in Sebastien Pocognoli's squad and no George Hirst. Injury has ruled out Che Adams, Lawrence Shankland and Ross Stewart. Those five were all at the World Cup in the United States during the summer.
Now, it's Ure alongside James Wilson of Hearts and Kieron Bowie of Sassuolo, who both have two caps, and Oli McBurnie of Hull, with the last of his 16 international appearances coming five years ago.
There is an intriguing freshness to this and nowhere is that buzz more obvious than in the story of Ure, the boy who wanted to play for Rangers but couldn't force his way in, the young man who in his seven games for Sevilla since his move from IK Sirius in Sweden has already played against 12 of Spain's World Cup winning squad.
Just over three years ago, Ure left Rangers as a teenager, his last forays with the senior team being one minute against St Mirren in November 2022 and another minute against Hibs in May 2023.
He is the poster boy in the Scottish FA's campaign to persuade clubs to give youth more of a chance. Ure wasn't given that opportunity in Glasgow and left for Anderlecht, then IK Sirius and now Sevilla, who paid £5.5m for him, plus another £2.5m in add-ons.
He calls the past few months "busy" which is an understatement. He's operating at a different level now. Sevilla lost that Barcelona game 3-1 - he has yet to score for his new club - but this is an education he's receiving, a critical part of his development.
"The first half, we were good," he says. "But as the game goes on, they wear you down. Raphinha at the moment. I mean…"
There's a knowing smile there, an indication of the kind of class he is now witnessing. "I really enjoyed it," he adds. "But against these players, you give them one chance and most of the time it's a goal. For me, it was a really good experience. I'm only going to get better as a result of it."
Ure is a Rangers boy - one that got away. Was it difficult having to leave? "Yeah, it was," he explains. "All I'd ever known was Rangers. Going in every single day since I was probably eight years old but it was something that I felt I had to do.
"I felt like I wasn't good enough to play for Rangers at the time, which is normal for many 18-year-olds. It was nothing that affected my confidence. I would have loved to have stayed but I knew myself that I wasn't going to play, which I accepted.
"At a club like Rangers, it's difficult for any 18-year-old to play. I needed a change of scenery and a fresh start, somewhere that I could go to play at a level that would be good enough for me at the time. Anderlecht provided that."
- Well-travelled Binks eager to make mark for Scotland 
  - Published14 hours ago
Belgium was the first step on his road to the Scotland team but Sweden was when it all started to happen. In 2025-26, he scored 11 goals in 30 games, a mere warm-up for what was to follow.
Between April and July this year, Ure played 14 games for IK Sirius and scored 15 goals, including four in one game against Mjallby.
"I was scoring near enough every game, so that was probably the happiest I've been," he says. "Every week I was scoring and we were top of the league. I was improving and that interest in me was getting bigger and bigger.
"At a young age it's really important you're playing. I was playing 90 minutes every week, getting trust from the manager and from the club. I was given time as well. The day I scored the four goals, it was my first hat-trick. I felt like every time I shot it was going to be a goal. I've not had a feeling like that before in football. It was pretty special."
Player pathway is a hot topic in Scottish football and Ure is an example of what can happen when a kid is given a proper chance.
"Everyone's different," he says. "You have to give players patience and give them time to develop but the way to do that is, of course, playing minutes at a level where you can develop at. I couldn't find that level in Scotland, so I had to look elsewhere and I'm happy that I did that."
The level he has found in Spain is stratospheric. No goals yet, but it's a savagely tough school.
He will have his moment under Pocognoli in the coming weeks. Four games in quick succession - he will get his first cap and his first chance to shine on another stage. And he's earned it.

In March this year, the American College of Cardiology (ACC) and the American Heart Association (AHA), both globally recognised premier organisations in cardiovascular medicine, handed down their newest dyslipidemia guideline, and gave universal Lipoprotein(a) screening in every adult a ‘Class I’ recommendation -- the strongest tier there is. The High-Sensitivity C-Reactive Protein (hsCRP) test got a lighter endorsement: checked selectively, alongside coronary calcium scoring, to sharpen risk estimates when they’re uncertain. These two long-debated biomarkers, were both freshly blessed by the field’s governing societies.
Then arrived the irony. On July 31, pharma major Novo Nordisk’s ziltivekimab — a drug built to block the inflammatory pathway behind elevated C-Reactive Protein (CRP) — fully hit its target in a Phase 3 clinical trial and still didn’t move the needle on heart attacks or strokes. Five weeks later, pelacarsenm, a drug that lowers high levels of Lp(a) failed the same way. Within six months of the guideline telling every clinician to start checking these numbers, the two flagship drugs built to act on them came up empty.
It’s a familiar shape for cardiology. Heart disease mortality fell almost every year through the back half of the last century — statins, blood pressure control, smoking cessation, better acute care — and that decline has visibly slowed this past decade, even as the drug arsenal has never been more sophisticated. LDL (’bad cholesterol’) is already driven remarkably low in anyone on a serious statin; medicine needed a new lever, and reached for the two candidates the guidelines had just endorsed. Neither has delivered yet.
What actually happened
On September 4, Novartis announced pelacarsen missed the primary endpoint of Lp(a)HORIZON, the first cardiovascular outcomes trial ever run for a drug built to lower lipoprotein(a). Pelacarsen is an antisense drug — a short, lab-made strand of genetic material injected monthly, designed to intercept the liver’s instructions for building Lp(a) before it’s ever made, rather than mopping up what’s already circulating. In 8,323 patients with established heart disease, it cut Lp(a) by roughly 80%. And yet, there was no reduction in heart attacks or stroke.
What we were taught
Lp(a) was drilled into me in medical school as one of the ‘unfair’ risk factors — a number you’re essentially born with, indifferent to diet or willpower, and loaded disproportionately onto South Asian patients, who as a population carry some of the highest mean Lp(a) levels of any group studied. It helped explain a pattern every cardiology rotation eventually shows you: South Asian patients with premature, multi-vessel disease and normal LDL numbers. That teaching isn’t wrong, and this trial doesn’t overturn it — Lp(a) is a real, heritable, biologically active risk factor. What it disputes is narrower: whether lowering it, this late and this fast, changes what happens next.
What Lp(a) actually is
Here’s the plain version of how a heart attack builds. LDL particles, commonly known as ‘bad cholesterol’ work their way into the artery wall and get stuck there. Once trapped, immune cells chemically alter them and swallow them up, ballooning into fat-filled ‘foam cells.’ Over years, those dying cells pile up into a fatty core, and the artery seals it off with a cap of scar-like tissue. When that cap eventually cracks or wears thin, a blood clot forms on top of it — that’s the heart attack.
Statins, ezetimibe, and the newer PCSK9-inhibitor injections all lower LDL through different mechanisms, but the trial data lines up the same way every time: about a 22% drop in heart attacks and strokes for every 39-point drop in LDL, no matter how you get there.
Lp(a) is an LDL particle with one extra piece stuck to it — a protein called apolipoprotein(a), built from the same molecular parts as the protein your body uses to break up blood clots. But it’s a decoy, not a copy: it fits into the same docking spots on a forming clot, without carrying the working part that actually gets activated into a clot-dissolving enzyme. So instead of helping to break clots down, it crowds out the real thing and makes clots a little harder to clear. That’s what makes Lp(a) different from LDL: it builds plaque the same way LDL does, but it also nudges the body toward clotting rather than away from it. And unlike LDL, your Lp(a) level is almost entirely set by your genes at birth — diet, exercise, and statins barely move it.
Why did the trial fail?
A floor effect: Mean background LDL in the trial was 66 mg/dL as most patients were already on aggressive therapy. Whatever risk Lp(a) adds on top of that may be smaller than older, less-treated cohorts suggested, offering little room for an 80% reduction to matter.
Too late in the game: Every patient entered with 50-plus years of Lp(a) exposure already built into their arteries. Lowering the level for three or four years in someone’s sixties, after a cardiac event, may be too late to undo a lifetime of exposure the genetic data actually measured.
This isn’t cardiology’s first time at this wall. The CANTOS trial suggested a decade ago that quieting the immune system could work, independent of cholesterol reduction. Hitting the biomarkers still doesn’t seem to be enough: Lp(a) may just be writing the newest chapter of the same story.
Back to basics
The interventions with the deepest trial evidence are still the boring ones: eat well, move, don’t smoke, stay lean. LDL, blood pressure, glucose, and tobacco remain the pillars with decades of reproducible data behind them.
Lp(a) will likely still matter — as a flag for who needs those basics enforced hardest, and maybe eventually as a target that is treated decades earlier than this trial tried. But for now, the fanciest number on the panel failed its biggest test, and the oldest advice in medicine didn’t.
No antisense drug, no anti-inflammatory antibody, has found a way around the same wall. In Greek mythology, Icarus didn’t fall because he was foolish — he flew exactly as high as anyone reasonably could, and the sun turned out to be closer than he’d been told. Despite everything medicine can now measure, alter and silence, the quest for a healthy long life perhaps rests on the same principles it has rested on for centuries: eat well, move well, sleep well.
(Dr. Dinesh Arab is director, interventional and structural cardiology, AdventHealth Daytona Beach and clinical assistant professor of medicine, Florida State University. dinarab@yahoo.com)

A day before the rowing finals at the Nagoya Asian Games, India are assured of their worst-ever performance in the sport at the continental event. Of the six men’s events India entered in Nagoya, only four will have Indian boats in the final. It is the first time since 2002 that India will not have a boat in every men’s rowing final at the Games.
Regardless how the four finalists do, India will not match the 5 medals won at the last edition of the Asian Games in Hangzhou.
Several rowers attributed India’s performance to the team management’s decision to change crews just two days before their events. As reported previously by Sportstar, Navdeep Singh and Kulwinder Singh, originally entered in the men’s double sculls, were moved to the quadruple sculls, while Salman and Satnam, members of the original quadruple, were shifted to the double. Balraj Panwar was moved from the quadruple to the single sculls, with Arvind Singh moving in the opposite direction.
“The reason we did not make it to the final is that the people we were practising with for a long time were moved to a different boat. The new guys who came with us, we have never practiced with them so they are not at fault either,” a player who did not make the final told Sportstar on condition of anonymity.
ALSO READ | The final piece of the puzzle: Mirabai turns obsession into reality with Asian Games silver
Another player told this publication that they had tried to convince the team management to change their decision but was berated instead by the Rowing Federation of India (RFI) president Balaji Maradapa.
“We tried to request them them (the team officials) so much. We asked them to fix the team back to its formation but nothing was done. The President of RFI shouted at us yesterday morning a day before our qualification round. He said, ‘if you don’t race nothing will happen to me. I have two children, they both are settled in life. I will enjoy life. Your future will be spoiled. If you don’t want to race, then book tickets and go back to India.’ We couldn’t say anything in response,” a player told Sportstar.
Although disappointed returning to India was out of the question. “We have been working for four years towards this medal. For the last eight months, we didn’t even go home. We never told anyone our problems because we were fighting for a medal. This is the hardest we had worked. We trained sometimes four times a day. We did everything that was asked of us. Is it possible that any person doesn’t try his best in a race?” the player said.
“The morale of the entire team is broken. The team that was chosen by the selection committee, that has been changed completely. All of us are saddened and disappointed by what has happened at the last minute. We had hoped to get a good color of medal. But our dream has been broken,” a player who did not make his final told Sportstar on condition of anonymity.
He further added that while his crew had tried their best, there was no coordination in their boat.
“Rowing is such an event that till the time there is no coordination in the boat, nothing happens. If there is no coordination, how will the boat run? We are in such a depression that we don’t know what to do. We haven’t had any appetite to eat because we are so upset,” another player told Sportstar.
ALSO READ | India coach Ronak Pandit: ‘This performance is unpardonable’ after 10m air pistol disappointment
RFI president Maradapa, however, denied claims that he shouted at his players, saying the rowers were being instigated to make such statements.
“It’s all false allegations. Two days ago, I spoke to about eight fellows. I told them,you have a long future ahead. I am talking to you like you are my children. I will speak to you the way I speak to my children. I’m telling you, please go ahead and discuss and think what is good for you and don’t get monitored by somebody who’s 10000 kilometers away. Do what is right for yourself so that if you win money you will get it to your account, you will get it around your neck. You will get all the benefits so look out for yourself so that your future is good. There was nothing heated about our discussion,” he said.
On Thursday India will feature four boats – Balraj Panwar in the men’s single sculls, Satnam Singh and Salman Khan in the men’s doubles, Ujwal Singh and Rohit Kumar Singh in the men’s lightweight double, Jakar Khan, Kulvinder Singh, Navdeep Singh and Arvind Singh in the men’s quadruple sculls.
Vipul Ghurde, Saurav Kumar, Babu Lal and Yogesh Kumar in the men’s four , Jaswinder Singh and Nitin Kumar in the men’s pair have missed the cut for the final.
