When an “Amadeus” revival opened at Pasadena Playhouse in February, it was such a spectacular success on every level that you wouldn’t have minded if the keepers of the venerable San Gabriel Valley venue just turned over the keys to the place for a while to the two Tony winners most responsible for making it a smash: star Jefferson Mays and director Darko Tresnjak. And that’s kind of what the Playhouse has done. That dynamic duo is already back in Pasadena with “The Visit,” which has opened a mere seven months after “Amadeus” first hit the boards there. With a good number of cast and crew members carrying over from the previous production to rock us again after “Amadeus,” this looks, for the moment, like as close a thing to an official house company as you can get in a major theater nowadays.
But is “The Visit” as much fun as “Amadeus”? Let’s just say for the moment that this followup production is destined to be more polarizing than that across-the-board crowd pleaser, although it’s not even a bit less lively. Like Peter Shaffer’s play before it, it is a vintage black comedy — even more vintage, as it was written by Swiss playwright Friedrich Dürrenmatt in 1956, although it’s been subject to a lot of Engligh adaptations and re-writes in subsequent decades. It loosely belongs to the theater of absurdism, which means that there is increasing room as the tragicomedy proceeds for Tresnjak to play around with the initially realistic trappings and have some fun with surrealist, grotesque and/or anachronistic elements. But what it really belongs to is the theater of fatalism, where things line up along the way to increasingly convince us that society, government and individua people themselves are inevitably subject to corruption and venality. So your enjoyment of the play may finally be subject to how much you feel you already do or don’t know that.
Popular on Variety
Given that Mays is widely regarded as one of the most charismatic and capable actors in modern theater, would it surprise you to learn that he is not really the star of “The Visit”? Well, he is, certainly in billing, and in the fact that he is the clear protagonist, as Anton Schill, a humble shopkeeper in postwar (or is it 2020s?) Europe whose past comes back to haunt him. But Mays is playing almost more of a mouse than a man. So, talk about a turnaround from Salieri. As much scenery-chewing as the actor was doing in “Amadeus” — and it was a glorious meal — that’s how little he’s doing here. Mays admitted in a recent interview that he wasn’t sure he was right for the role, and you can see why he might have thought so, given the character’s passivity. But it takes a skilled actor to successfully put his mojo on mute, too. So if you know what he’s capable of, there’s some pleasure in watching him at first seem to embody the milk of human kindness, before he succumbs more of an emblem ofBut the the milquetoast of human depravity.
But the obvious centrifugal force of “The Visit” is the female lead, a character named Claire Zachanassian who may be the richest woman in the world, and who has an even greater surfeit of personality than money. She’s played here to perfection by Melinda Page Hamilton, whose stage appearances and recurring TV roles have not made her a household name — yet she has such presence that, from her first scene forward, you’re convinced that she must be one anyway. She gets off a train and breezes into the downtrodden European town where she spent her impoverished girlhood like she is some charming ane cunning combination of Lauren Bacall, Madonna and a demonically possessed Daisy Buchanan. Her intentions for the hometown she is nostalgically revisiting are cloaked at first, but her barbed banter is so much fun, you can almost half-wish she doesn’t mean anything sinister with her visit, even if she clearly does. After all, her musclebound handlers have brought along with them an empty casket, and this is the sort of play where a coffin that appears in the first act is definitely going to go off in the third. (Not literally; although “The Visit” has been produced in as a hefty three-parter in some productions, it’s mercifully cut down to a single act in Pasadena.) You can never take your eyes or ears off Hamilton, even when the plot gives her increasingly schematic things to say and do in the second half.
About that plot. There is a big revelation less than halfway into the show, one that might even count as a plot twist, and thus something not to be spoiled… if not for the fact that virtually every synopsis in the last 70 years has included it in the first sentence. So we’ll assume most patrons know it going in and won’t hold a discussion of it against us here, though stop right now if you think you might. Cutting to the chase, Claire has earmarked the aforementioned casket for Anton, despite the fact that he was her lover in their youthful days, and they are sharing sweet memories of their lusty romps in the woods within minutes of her arrival. After some more talk of the bucolic days gone by, Claire suddenly announces at a town meeting that she will rescue this on-the-skids burg with a donation of one billion (what the currency is goes unspecified), with one condition: that they deliver her a dead Anton. For reasons eventually to be revealed, she represents pure vengeance, even if she does talk like someone out of a ’30s screwball comedy, or “Truth or Dare.”
Up to the point that she delivers the townspeople this ultimatum — a deal with the devil, or with an especially cocktail-party-friendly Cruella de Vil — “The Visit” has kind of been a rollicking good time. For much of the audience, it will remain that all the way to the end, even with some somber moments along the way that aren’t played for laughs. But the basic problem with the play — if you’re spoilsport enough to see it as one — is that once Claire makes her modest proposal to save the town, there won’t likely be any doubt in a single audience member’s mind that things are going to pan out exactly as she wants them to. Because it’s that kind of a show: one that is just a little too self-pleased with itself for offering the bleakest possible vision of what civilized people can and probably will do, offered a way out of their misery or mundanity. So there’s not that much to happen in the last two-thirds of the drama than for your ribs to be constantly nudged with the idea of how easily the most respectable citizens among us will give in to modest proposals and, indeed, murder. It rings true, don’t get me wrong! But it also rings awfully predictable, in a way that maybe it didn’t in the late ’50s and ’60s, when it was a little easier for defiantly grim morality tales to seem transgressive in the mainstream.
The story might have at least a modicum of suspense if any of the upstanding townspeople were seen as struggling with the idea of murdering a trusted friend. But after an initial vote of “no way” to Claire’s offer, everyone seems to have become completely transformed by the next morning. The program notes reference “Invasion of the Body Snatchers,” which seems like an apt analogy, except that that film would be a lot less riveting if the entire city turned into pod people instantly, followed by an hour of Kevin McCarthy slowly deciding he should accept his fate. To give some credit here, there is one scene in which a cleric openly debates with himself whether to go along with the greedy mob or not, but within a couple of minutes he’s come to terms with the creeping evil, too. It’s realistic, sad to say, that a population would find a way to justify throw all of its collective principles away and commit a horrific crime; it’s just a little less realistic — or good for the purposes of a full-length drama — that this would all happen in a virtual instant.
There are other huge dramatic implausibilities, if we want to get picky about it. The opening scenes of “The Visit,” when it is in its most realistic mode, have the townspeople convinced that Anton is actually their ticket to riches, not a future scapegoat, because of his past romance with Claire. And he seems to be firmly convinced of this, too, as they get together alone in the woods and share reminiscings of those tender or erotic moments of yore. But once Claire reveals the backstory of why she is out to bring the wrath of God down on him, her reasoning seems… well, still a little psychopathic, but somewhat justified, by the standard of modern feminist morality tales. To say he did her wrong is an understatement. So is Anton supposed to be mentally compromised or deranged, rather than the harmless soul we first meet him as, to have imagined that Claire would have come back after all these decades with a positive picture of him, instead of a lust for blood? It makes no sense. Maybe that’s a fault of the condensation, and the picture would be clearer in the three-and-a-half-hour version (!) Tony Kushner adapted for the London stage at the turn of the decade. But there’s some basic sense missing here that can’t be explained away with the idea that it’s just a surrealist fable.
With all that said, there are still a lot of pleasures in this production that remain failsafe, even after the ride toward a way-too-inevitable outcome is firmly on its tracks. For instance, the way that Tresnjak, wardrobe designer Charlotte DeVaux Shields and set designer Alexander Dodge have conspired to make sneakers into the embodiment of complicity and evil is fairly ingenious. Somehow, the show’s supporting cast members manage to make their way onstage without giving away their footwear until, at some key moment, their colorful shoes are lit up in what looks like a flurorescent glow, revealing that they, too, have gone along with the body snatchers. (Everyone should see it coming a mile away, but even I LOL-ed when the town cleric showed that he, also, has succumbed to the Air Jordan pandemic.) There are an increasing number of moments like that throughout the production in which it seems to have suddenly jumped into the present day, and some work, some don’t. It is a little jarring when, still pretty early in the show, you hear the first example of disco bumper music, like they suddenly piped in a little bit of David Byrne’s score for “Here Lies Love” to cover the scene change. But by the end, the use of modern-day cameras and video screens to bring the action fully into the 2020s seems justified enough, if you buy into Tresnjak’s time-tripping aesthetic at all.
The show’s creepiest characters — no contest here — are a couple of aging, balding, blind eunuchs (played by Jake Levy and Lauren Worsham)who seem to be part of Claire’s entourage for no good reason, other than to figure into the tale of woe she eventually tells, which finally explains why they know their way around the town so well despite being sightless visitors. Their presence brings “The Visit” almost right up to the edge of horror, which is where thematically it kind of belongs, despite all the zingers, smirks and guffaws. The play seems to want to flirt with the idea of Grand Guignol, even if remains more firmly rooted in the land of Samuel Beckett.
But the swing being taken here is bold enough that there’s no reason to want to take the Playhouse keys back from Tresnjak, if he has more offbeat revival aspirations where this one came from. And with lead performances like Mays’ and Hamilton’s, the production is — sorry to do this here — worth your visit. If the initial impulse is that Mays doesn’t have as much to do here as is worthy of his talent, he is so firmly enmeshed in the character of a nebbish caught up in a sub-Kafkaesque nightmare, he makes you feel deeply for his fate, even if Maurice Valency’s adapted script kind of seems to want you to not feel so bad about it. And Melinda Page Hamilton? She’s so captivating, in both her rages and her funnier, more casual cruelty, that I’d follow her Claire to just about any soiree where the multi-billionaire elite meet, even if I did spot a coffin there with my name on it.
“The Visit” runs through Oct. 4 at Pasadena Playhouse, located at 39 South El Molino Ave. in Pasadena. Phone: 626-356-7529. For tickets and more information, visit http://www.pasadenaplayhouse.org.

Herpetologists first discovered in 1933 that rattlesnakes are immune to their own venom. Native to the Americas, rattlesnakes are pit vipers, a family of vipers with a heat-sensing pit organ between each nostril and eye.
Venom resistance in snakes comes in two forms: either the targets in their bodies have evolved such that the venom doesn’t attack them, like in cobras, or they possess specific molecules in their bloodstream that serve as “toxin sponges”, like in vipers, Sean B. Carroll, chair of biology at the University of Maryland, U.S., said.
In 1972, Japanese researchers discovered the first example of a so-called toxin sponge — a serum protein dubbed Fetuin-A — from Okinawa habu (Protobothrops flavoviridis), a pit viper endemic to the Ryukyu Islands. Fetuin-A could inhibit metalloproteinases, a class of venom toxins that could cause haemorrhage, damage tissue, and disrupt the coagulation system.
Metalloproteinases are the most abundant toxin family in rattlesnake venoms, and researchers have studied metalloproteinase inhibitors such as Fetuin-A in great detail. However, only recently did they discover that Fetuin-A belongs to a larger family of FETUA proteins.
In a 2022 paper, Dr. Carroll and his team identified four FETUA proteins from the western diamondback rattlesnake (Crotalus atrox).
Curiously, understanding the principles of venom resistance from C. atrox led the researchers to leverage these antitoxins, which had evolved over millions of years, for human benefit.
In a new study in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the team at Maryland has shown that specific combinations of C. atrox FETUA proteins can fully neutralise rattlesnake venom lethality in mice, with roughly 10-times the potency of commercial antivenom.
‘String of surprises’
On discovering metalloproteinase-inhibiting FETUA-2, 3, 4, and 5 proteins from C. atrox, the research team studied their antivenom potency. By injecting various protein combinations preincubated with C. atrox venom into experimental mice, they found that some combinations successfully blocked haemorrhaging, while some even staved off death.
“Rattlesnake venoms have 10-15 different kinds of toxins,” Dr. Carroll said. “So it was entirely unexpected that just blocking metalloproteinases would block the lethality of the venom.”
The test results that followed were a “string of surprises”. Encouraged by the success of FETUA proteins against C. atrox venom, the team tried them against the eastern diamondback rattlesnake (Crotalus adamanteus), which proved successful. Then they tested them against two Asian snakes: the Malayan pit viper (Calloselasma rhodostoma) and the Chinese moccasin (Deinagkistrodon acutus). The proteins could protect against those as well.
The team then moved to candidates outside of pit vipers. Of the two true vipers they tested against, the proteins protected significantly against the Sochurek’s saw-scaled viper (Echis carinatus sochureki) — but none against the puff adder (Bitis arietans).
“Our surprises ran out, you could say,” Dr. Carroll said.
According to him, an antivenom needs potency and broad reactivity. And not only could these proteins recognise and neutralise the venom of a spectrum of distant species, when tested against CroFab, a commercial antivenom obtained from animals immunised with four pit viper venoms, including C. atrox, the proteins proved tenfold more potent.
The findings are a “real advance” for antivenom development, according to Kartik Sunagar, an associate professor at the Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru; he was not involved in the study. “The paper shows convincingly that a combination of naturally evolved FETUA proteins can fully neutralise rattlesnake venom lethality by inhibiting metalloproteinases alone.”
However, Dr. Sunagar also pointed out that the study did not exactly measure clinical capacity.
“Every efficacy experiment premixed venom and inhibitor before injection,” he said. “So the study measures neutralising capacity, not treatment of an animal already envenomed, which is the clinically relevant scenario.”
Next-generation antivenom
According to Dr. Carroll, unlike lab-made compounds, FETUA proteins have been tested in nature.
“Rattlesnakes have evolved these proteins for 50 million years, with remarkable specificity and potency to inhibit their own venom, which gives me the sense that it is worth exploring,” he said.
Manufacturability and purity are added advantages, he added: “We can make recombinant FETUA proteins in the lab in unlimited quantities — whereas traditional antivenom requires animals to be immunised, and then the obtained antibodies have to be purified.”
Dr. Sunagar also shared the view that the recombinant and defined nature of FETUA proteins will help sidestep the low purity of animal-derived products.
While the study showed that these proteins can protect experimental mice from venom lethality, toxins other than metalloproteinases will have physiological effects on humans, Dr Carroll said: “What we don’t know is what else we will have to use in conjunction with these proteins to make an antivenom” for humans.
“FETUAs do nothing for the neurotoxins that dominate many medically important venoms,” Dr. Sunagar said. “The honest reading is that these proteins form the metalloproteinase-neutralising component of a next-generation antivenom, but it is not yet a standalone therapy.”
Dr. Carroll also said his team has found a new component that could aid human antivenom development, but did not elaborate on ongoing research.
Implications for India
In countries like India, which host both vipers and elapids such as cobras, FETUA proteins alone cannot provide a complete antivenom solution, Dr. Carroll said.
Although the study revealed partial protection against saw-scaled vipers (Echis carinatus sp.), one of India’s ‘Big Four’ and a major cause of death and disability, partial cross-reactivity need not translate into clinical protection, Dr. Sunagar added.
But India’s bigger takeaway is the strategy: “The logical path for India is to identify and test FETUAs from our own vipers rather than relying on rattlesnake versions, and to pair them with agents covering the neurotoxic elapids the FETUAs cannot touch,” according to Dr. Sunagar.
Nikhil Sreekandan is an independent journalist.

Trump’s new arch plan: snipers and drones
If you give the president his national security ballroom, he’s going to ask for his national security arch.
Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump’s proposed triumphal arch is going in a new direction: drone port and sniper platform.
What’s happening? Trump has been pushing to build a 250-foot-tall “triumphal arch” near the National Mall since at least this January. Relative to some of his other projects, however, it’s been slow going, and now he has a new plan.
Trump announced the updated design in a Sunday morning post, writing, “At the strong request of the United States Military, and for National Security purposes, I have agreed to convert” the arch into “a top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch.”
In addition to drones, Trump said, the new arch will have “snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage.”
Really? Maybe. We don’t yet know if this version of the arch will happen, or even if the military actually requested it.
For that matter, we don’t know if the arch will get built at all — though the administration appears prepared to move forward, despite a National Park Service determination that the arch would harm nearby historical sites, including the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.
What’s the big picture? Trump’s plan for a “Military Complex/Triumphal Arch” sounds an awful lot like his “Ballroom/Military Complex,” which got a stamp of approval from the Supreme Court last month after multiple lower courts ruled against its construction without permission from Congress (which Trump also does not have for his arch).
Like the arch, the ballroom acquired its “military complex” label after running into obstacles (though unlike the arch, there’s a clear connection: The ballroom does in fact sit on top of a secure bunker).
The unifying theme, though, is Trump’s instinct to reach for “national security” as a cudgel whenever he’s thwarted. He also accused the media of being a “threat to our National Security” on Monday amid backlash to his press ban.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

Lisa Marie Wilson matched with a man on a dating app who claimed to be 5-foot-10 and to live on the beach. Only one of those facts turned out to be true. When she showed up to the date, Wilson observed that she and her date were the same height — and she isn’t 5-foot-10. She wasn’t planning to mention it, but her date did: “He told me I wasn’t really 5-foot-9,” Wilson, a 51-year-old author, told Vox.
It’s not your imagination — dating has gotten way more combative lately
Here’s how to find love (or just have fun!) when everyone has their guard up.
Even though he accused her of lying about her height before he even said hello, Wilson told Vox she still gave the man the benefit of the doubt. But as they continued on with their planned walk along the beach, Wilson sensed her date was suspicious of her. “The whole time it was like he was an investigative reporter asking me questions, but kind of like if you were interviewing someone you didn’t like,” she said.
By the end of the date, Wilson was sure she didn’t want to see this guy again, so she turned down his offer to give her a massage and left. She couldn’t get past his accusatory comment about her height. “I was like, ‘I’m not a liar,’” Wilson said. “But I think he was — because he obviously wasn’t as tall as he was saying he was.” (To add insult to injury, Wilson’s date emailed her the next day breaking things off with her.)
Why I reported this
Lately I’ve noticed an outright antagonism among singles, online and off. They want to find love, but have been so burned by past relationships (or situationships) that they have a pessimistic view of dating. As a result, some singles cast blanket judgments about the very people with whom they hope to foster a relationship: They’re all bad. It turns out the reason why dating is so negative now is the pressure we put on strangers to fulfill our every fantasy, when that’s not how people have historically become attracted to one another.
If you’ve been on a date recently, the phrase “love is a battlefield” might seem a fitting descriptor for the sordid state of romantic affairs.
According to this year’s Kinsey Institute Singles in America Survey, the percentage of singles with a “checklist” of what they’re looking for in a partner rose from 25 percent in 2021 to 34 percent in 2026. Dating has also become even more partisan this year, another survey found: A date’s political affiliation, especially if it conflicts with their own, is a major dealbreaker. This year, traditional gender roles and values have made a return, hardening some people’s idea of what romance looks like — a dynamic where a woman is pursued by a man with an absurdly strong jaw — and warping the expectations that women have of men and vice versa. Daters are also increasingly using AI to chat with matches on apps and bots’ infiltration of dating apps might have you questioning who you’re even chatting with in the first place.
It stands to reason that we’ve forgotten how to be human — and some of the basic rules of human decency — in our love lives. Relationship experts, historians, and critics agreed: Dating feels different now.
TikTok has only added fuel to the fire. A popular outlet for singles to share their gripes, the platform has given rise to new dating vernacular — rosters, breadcrumbing, goblintimacy. These new dynamics seeped into the dates themselves, with people openly antagonistic and confrontational from the jump.
Experts say that if your goal is to find love, or even just have a night of fun, assuming the worst of others — as so many seem to do right now — isn’t an effective strategy. “If you’re eternally suspicious, that tends to be a boundary to attraction,” Paul Eastwick, a psychology professor at the University of California Davis and author of Bonded by Evolution: The New Science of Love and Connection, told Vox.
The consequence of such hostility in dating is less tolerance — for ordinary friction, for learning lessons, for romance itself. So, what’s a single in 2026 to do?
The problem with dating right now
Most of modern dating followed a predictable pattern: Two singles met at church or at school or at work or at a party hosted by a mutual friend or through family. They might continue to see each other in social settings, gradually growing accustomed to one another’s personality, quirks, interests, until one person (usually the man, if they were straight) asked out the other on a date. Because they had mutual friends or coworkers in common, there was someone to vouch for them, to give some context to their life.
Since the early 2010s, the most popular way to meet a potential romantic partner has been through online dating. App users are exposed to swaths of people they might not have ordinarily met without having to leave the comfort of their homes, meaning they are going on dates with virtual strangers. The sussing-out phase — where your perception of a person grows from simply “hot woman” to “Amy, the funny blonde from my dodgeball team” — has been condensed or eliminated altogether. “It’s not like, I got to know this person naturally,” Eastwick, also the co-host of the podcast Love Factually, said. “When somebody is a stranger, it’s maybe a little easier to come in with whatever negative assumptions you’ve gleaned from these online spaces.”
Life as a whole in the US has become more combative and tense in the past decade, from political polarization to increasingly rude behavior. At work, our labor and time is extracted until we’re laid off; at home, we’re suspicious of our neighbors. And dating is inherently vulnerable, rife with rejection and negative consequences.
Dating apps have played a huge role in this dramatic shift in tenor. While effective at connecting users with multiple eligible singles, apps don’t encourage slow-burn connections, which is how humans have historically grown attracted to one another. And when a date goes awry, terrible tales can be mined for engagement online, where commenters are quick to validate a unique experience as universal, often reinforcing gendered stereotypes, like “all men are toxic” and “all women are shallow.”
People have historically commiserated over their romantic lives as a way of bonding: Think of men in bars with their buddies bemoaning the old ball and chain, women lamenting their husbands not shouldering their share of household labor. During the feminist movement of the 1970s, women gathered to validate each other’s experiences and consider political responses to sexist issues, according to Rebecca Davis, a professor of history and women and gender studies at the University of Delaware. Social media now fulfills many of the same functions as these in-person conversations, Davis told Vox; people can take to TikTok or Reddit to share their frustrating or traumatic experiences, and comment sections are populated with others sharing their own similar stories. But unlike in the relatively private spaces of the past, these gripes now spread from individual to individual with little context, follow-up questions, or nuance.
Instead, posts beget more posts. Algorithms reward extreme content and creators may embellish details to encourage engagement. Whether intentionally or not, TikToks about how coffee dates signify low effort and Reddit threads parroting misogynist language perpetuate harmful stereotypes. “People are good at finding a reason to externalize the difficulty of dating,” the writer Asa Seresin told Vox. It’s much easier to assume the people you date are altogether bad than it is to assess your own actions.
In a viral essay published in 2019, Seresin gave the outward disdain with heterosexuality a name: heteropessimism. Since then, dating culture has only gotten more dismal, he said, in large part due to a national regression toward conservative views of gender and sexuality. The overturning of Roe v. Wade, contentious debates over transgender rights, and a generation of young men who believe a woman should obey her husband have become a dark cloud over the world of romance.
Some of these more traditional beliefs have filtered into 33-year-old Brittni Kristine’s dating life. After only a few weeks of dating, a man Kristine had met on an app asked her to be exclusive, but his actions suggested he wasn’t fully invested. Whenever Kristine inquired about their plans for the week, the guy would get irritated. “His defense mechanism was essentially like, ‘Well, I didn’t tell you I wasn’t seeing you next week, so why would you assume?’” Kristine told Vox.
Over the course of the month they dated, Kristine and the man got into multiple arguments of this nature until she’d grown exasperated with his stonewalling. His antagonism, Kristine suspected, stemmed from a puritanical view of sex and romance, where casually dating is seen as a moral failure. “I’ve had so many people tell me, ‘If I go on a first date with you and I find out that you have gone on another date in the past two weeks, basically I would never talk to you again because you’re promiscuous,’” she said.
These off-putting experiences fuel heteropessimism. A key aspect of heteropessimism, the pervasive embarrassment with which some young women express being attracted to men, only adds to a cycle of shame that makes people feel guilty for who they’re attracted to, Davis said. This has led some to internalize the idea that queer relationships are easier or more ideal. “When women talk about division of labor…it makes sense that there’s a longing for a relationship where the gender division of labor isn’t at play,” Seresin said. “I actually do think that is one way in which queer relationships are a lot easier, but I wouldn’t say that overall queer relationships are easier.”
Negative stereotypes and preemptive defensiveness plague queer relationships, too, Seresin said. “A lot of gay men also say, ‘I wish I wasn’t into men,’ and will blame a culture of very casual intimacy on being unable to find a boyfriend,” Seresin said. “A lot of lesbians will blame there not being enough queer women out there or enough of their type.”
The result is a population of singles, regardless of who they’re attracted to, walking into dating scenarios with strangers who they might already be suspicious of.
Dating with walls up
As soon as his date walked through the coffee shop doors recently, Alex Alberti told Vox he sensed an air of negativity. “Literally from the jump, he kind of felt on the defensive and a little bit guarded from just buying coffee,” the 35-year-old education researcher said. Even a change of scenery on their walk around a nearby lake did not help matters. Alberti remembered his date venting about his dating troubles: how shallow and rude and awful the men were. About halfway through the get-together, Alberti decided there would not be another.
It was clear to Alberti that his date was letting past negative experiences color his current one. But instead of protecting him, drawing attention to bad behavior only pushed Alberti away. “I think people believe that if they can just beat the bad thing to the punch by calling it out, they’re going to make themselves safer,” he said. “When someone approaches a first date being highly skeptical and highly guarded and even a little bit combative, they think that it’s going to serve as a helpful filter.”
When you approach other people with distrust and ire instead of openness and curiosity, forging genuine connections turns into a monumental undertaking. People tend to like folks they feel comfortable opening up to, and the gradual revelations and bits of your interior life you show each other are what foster attraction. Fearing someone will weaponize your vulnerability against you turns dating into a surface-level endeavor at best, or, at worst, a contentious battle no one can possibly win.
The walls people put up are meant to be protective: You can’t hurt me if I never let you in to begin with. And the youngest prospective daters are dating even less in 2026: One recent study found that more than half of single young adults, ages 22 to 35, said past breakups made them more reluctant to pursue new relationships. Those are just the ones who’ve had previous romantic experiences. A Pew Research Center survey found that about a third of singles who have never married have never been in a committed romantic relationship to begin with.
When daters lack experience and are primed to see the worst in each other, the very normal aspects of courtship — negotiating boundaries, establishing trust, navigating conflict — are seen as dealbreakers. “There’s a growing discomfort with the normal friction, that if you say or do the wrong thing, it’s cringe, it’s disqualifiable; there’s no appetite for any kind of misstep,” Daniel Cox, the director of the Survey Center on American Life and author of Generation Uncoupled: America’s New Gender Divide and the Crisis of Human Connection, told Vox.
This is an impossibly high bar to clear and runs contrary to how many relationships form, Eastwick, the psychology professor, said. Most people’s affection for another person grows the more they get to know them. But if you’re meeting a stranger from an app who you assume has nefarious intentions, that first date isn’t likely to turn into a second.
Letting your guard down
Trauma and past negative experiences, both your own and others, can be a helpful teacher, a useful framework for what to avoid, and what lessons could be gleaned from pain. But it can also be distorting, Seresin, the writer, said. One bad relationship or date doesn’t mean all future relationships and dates with a similar type of person will be doomed. “It’s almost like if you’ve had a bad experience and you want to protect yourself, that’s almost morally good,” Seresin said.
Instead of focusing on avoiding any bad feelings (an impossible task), singles should question their own assumptions and operate from a place of curiosity. Resist the urge to cast judgment based on what little you know of someone. Even couples who have been married for decades can still discover new things about their partner. “It’s very easy to think, ‘I know exactly how this person thinks. I know what they want. I know how they’re trying to manipulate me,’” Seresin said.
The process of getting to know someone is a risk. All relationships come with potential disappointment; there will always be a person who ghosts or makes a bad joke or minimizes your accomplishments. But it doesn’t mean that person represents all men or all women, that they’re the enemy, that these connections are inherently toxic or not worth pursuing in the first place.
To find love, we have to turn down the instinct to protect ourselves and open ourselves to the possibility that the person across the table might also be a flawed human who’s been hurt before. And they might want the same thing, too.

Congressman says Venezuelan man shot by ICE then taken into custody told he needs surgery
A Democratic congressman says a Venezuelan man shot by a federal immigration officer in Texas has been told by a specialist he needs surgery to remove a bullet near his spine

A Democratic congressman said Wednesday that a Venezuelan man shot by a federal immigration officer in Texas and then taken to a detention center has been told by a specialist he needs surgery to remove the bullet still lodged near his spine.
U.S. Rep. Greg Casar visited a federal detention center in south Texas where Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, was taken into custody after being shot Sunday in Austin by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent.
Casar said Garces Perez was in a wheelchair and still in pain, but did not say whether the family had decided that he should undergo surgery. The Department of Homeland Security has said Garces Perez, who has been taken to a hospital twice since the shooting, is receiving around-the-clock medical care and pain medication.
"If they want to say it’s great medical care, they should start providing great medical care today by having him leave the detention center, go to a hospital or to a doctor, and do not delay his surgery if that’s what his family chooses to do,” Casar said.
Garces Perez remains in Texas detention center
Casar, whose district includes Austin, was the first member of Congress to visit Garces Perez in person since the shooting. He said the wound in Garces Perez's back remains bloody and medical staff change his gauze two or three times daily.
Following Casar's visit and a press conference, DHS issued a previous statement denying claims that Garces Perez was forced to sleep on a floor or that he was prevented from having the bullet removed, saying ICE would not advise on a medical procedure for a detainee.
Garces Perez was making a DoorDash delivery when ICE officers in an unmarked truck sideswiped his car twice, his attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, said. He was shot and taken to a hospital, then released into ICE custody with a bullet still in his back, she said.
ICE and DHS haven't said what led to the shooting beyond that Garces Perez was “the subject of a targeted vehicle stop."
ICE has not said if the agent who fired was wearing a body camera. At the beginning of September, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said he expected all field agents to have them by the end of the month.
Austin police released body camera footage from its officers who arrived just after the shooting. Garces Perez is seen hunched over in the front seat of his car and grabbing his shoulder and rocking back and forth. An officer later cut off Garces Perez’s shirt, and a wound can be seen in his upper back.
Garces Perez entered the U.S. in 2024 using CBP One, a program begun under President Joe Biden that allowed migrants to make appointments with U.S. authorities to be considered for asylum, Lincoln-Goldfinch said. President Donald Trump ended the program on his first day in office.
Garces Perez was an asylum seeker and had a valid work permit, according to Lincoln-Goldfinch. She said a judge issued a deportation order after Garces Perez missed an immigration court hearing because the notice was sent to a former address.
ICE crackdown in Austin sees more than 1,000 arrests
Garces Perez's shooting came at the end of a summer in which ICE notably ramped up enforcement operations in Austin and surrounding suburbs and increasingly targeted immigrants without criminal records in public places.
In all, ICE made more than 1,000 arrests in Austin, Pflugerville and other nearby cities during June and July, more than an 80% increase from a year earlier, which had been the previous peak, according to ICE data provided to the Deportation Data Project at the University of California, Berkeley, and the University of California, Los Angeles, and analyzed by The Associated Press.
Unlike some other places, the increases in Austin were not driven by partnerships with local law enforcement agencies or by picking up jail inmates. Instead, the data shows that ICE officers made the vast majority of arrests in the community through traffic stops and other enforcement methods.
Nearly 2 out of 3 people who were arrested in the Austin area had no criminal convictions and no pending criminal charges, the data shows.
___
Foley reported from Iowa City, Iowa. Jeffrey Collins in Columbia, South Carolina, contributed to this report.

Disney+ got its fourth price hike in four years today. Hulu prices also went up.
Disney+ and Hulu’s respective standalone, ad-free plans (which also support 4K and HDR) are each increasing 13 percent from $19 per month to $21.50/month.
Disney+ and Hulu’s respective standalone plans with ads increased from $12 to $12.50.
The Walt Disney Company also increased prices for bundles of the streaming services, including those with ESPN.
The price for the Disney+ and Hulu bundle without ads increased from $20/month to $22/month. The Disney+ and Hulu bundle with ads ($13) didn’t get more expensive.
However, prices increased for the Disney+, Hulu, and ESPN Select bundles with ads (from $20 to $22) and without ads (from $29 to $33).
Monthly subscription prices for Hulu + Live, which adds cable channels delivered over the Internet to Hulu’s on-demand options, went up by $10.
For comparison, Netflix is currently $9/month with ads and starts at $20/month without ads. There’s also a $27/month ad-free plan for premium features, like 4K. That means Disney+ and Hulu are both more expensive than the most popular streaming service now, unless you want 4K or HDR.

New Delhi, Sep 23: Expansive red flags raised by two Election Commissioners within the poll panel over the Special Intensive Revision of voters list triggered a massive political storm on Wednesday, with the Opposition accusing CEC Gyanesh Kumar of indulging in "one-man autocracy" and demanding his removal.
Officials said Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had flagged multiple issues, including deletion of names, in various states during the voter roll cleanup but the poll body was unanimous in its decisions related to the pan-India Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voters' list.
The reactions poured in after a report in The Indian Express revealed that questions were raised on issues related to the SIR of electoral rolls within the three-member Election Commission (EC) itself, time and again by two of the three Election Commissioners.
The national rollout of the SIR has been under the supervision of all three Commissioners. But Sandhu and Joshi have formally objected, on record, at least 14 times over the last 10 months -- four times on a single day -- to decisions taken and orders issued, they say, without their knowledge, the report in the English daily said.
Congress general secretary in-charge communications Jairam Ramesh shared the screenshot of the media report on X.
Ramesh said that on behalf of the party, his colleague Abhishek Singhvi will be speaking in detail to the media on the sensational revelations made in the leading national newspaper on the way "the CEC has destroyed the credibility and integrity of the Election Commission of India".
Congress general secretary in-charge organisation K C Venugopal said there is no doubt remaining that Kumar has no right to remain in office.
"How the hell can one man, acting on His Master's orders, strike off names at whim? How can he sideline fellow Constitutional officers to only take blatantly illegal steps that put our democracy in danger?" he said.
"The right to vote is an essential Constitutional power given to every citizen, the fundamental bedrock of our democracy. If it is to be taken away, due process must be followed with utmost probity," he said.
"Today, when we are staring at crores of genuine voters being excluded and a similar number of bogus voters being added to the rolls, it is clear that Gyanesh Kumar was the Chief Architect of the nationwide 'Vote Chori' exercise, with the the Modi top brass pulling the strings," he alleged.
"We demand Gyanesh Kumar's immediate removal and a Supreme Court-monitored impartial investigation to expose the rot that has destroyed the ECI's credibility," Venugopal said.
If Kumar remains in office, the people of India will come forward and make sure that our democracy is not destroyed by a mere bureaucrat, he added.
Congress' media and publicity department head Pawan Khera lashed out at Kumar, saying he is "planted" and being "protected" by the BJP to hollow out the Election Commission of India from within.
"It was already known that things were not exactly well within the ECI. But just how messy, dysfunctional and, frankly, disturbing things had become is laid bare by this brilliant expose by @IndianExpress," he said on X.
Kumar has to be the single most sold-out bureaucrat of the Modi era who has disenfranchised crores of Indians, and he must face the law, he alleged.
Congress MP Manish Tewari also reacted to the media report, saying that if the ostensible facts as reported are correct then it seems to suggest that there is an "invisible hand" running the Election Commission.
"If rules were not allegedly followed and decisions were taken that were not unanimous or by majority then all the decisions of @ECISVEEP are per -se arbitrary and capricious if not completely illegal," Tewari said on X.
"This is perhaps a fit case for serious considering an impeachment proceeding but more importantly the fundamental question is as to how will the credibility of @ECISVEEP be ever resurrected," he said.
Rajya Sabha MP Kapil Sibal demanded Kumar's suspension and filing of an FIR to probe who is behind his actions.
Former chief election commissioner O P Rawat said changes to the statutory voter registration Form 6 are "absolutely wrong and illegal", while describing revelations of differences within the Election Commission as "very serious" and "unfortunate".
CPI(M) MP John Brittas said this is no longer an Election Commission, it is a "one-man autocracy" under CEC Kumar.
"Two Election Commissioners have formally objected 14 times in 10 months. They branded the addition of new voters and mass deletion 'unauthorised and illegal'. They recorded objections to secret deletions, restorations, and form 6 changes that harass young first-time voters - all while being kept in the dark," he said.
This is the open subversion of the EC and our democracy too, Brittas said.
"Parliament must immediately start the process for the removal of the CEC. We had in fact submitted a notice for removal on 24th April, 2026 as per the constitutional stipulations - solid grounds and around 70 members signing( 50 in the stipulated number)," he said.
The Constitution provides this power for precisely such moments of institutional capture and subversion, he said.
"The Supreme Court must annul the entire SIR process without delay. When two of the three Commissioners put on record that the exercise is illegal and destructive of the electoral roll's integrity, judicial silence becomes complicity," Brittas said.
What Kumar is doing is the death knell of a democratic nation, he said.
"Remove the CEC. Strike down the SIR. Or accept that free and fair elections in India are already being buried," the CPI(M) MP said.
Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Sanjay Raut also cited the media report, and said "A-Gyanesh Kumar will go to jail! He will have to go! His masters will flee the country and run away!"
TMC Rajya Sabha leader Derek O'Brien said on X, "Five months ago, 60+ Rajya Sabha MPs (50 needed) wrote to Chairman RS moving Motion to remove CEC Gyanesh Kumar. After big news break today that two Election Commissioners objected to many of CEC's actions, it's time to bring out the RS Motion today. Impeach CEC to save democracy".

Finance and technology usually spring to mind when thinking of the world's most lucrative industries.
And that's for good reason. They have been the source of wealth for nearly half of America's 400 richest people, as ranked and categorized by Forbes.
However, billion-dollar fortunes have been made in other sectors, too, ranging from trucking to pest control.
Business Insider has compiled data from the 2026 Forbes 400 list, which is an estimated snapshot of the 400 richest people in America as of September 4.
Forbes estimated each member's net worth using a variety of sources, including interviews, asset valuations, and deductions for debt, charitable contributions, and fund donations.
The following ranking is based on the 16 industries into which Forbes categorized each individual. Business Insider calculated how many individuals went into each category to find which industries have minted the most of America's richest people. It also compiled the richest person within each industry.
Some of the members featured an "& family" tag, which means wealth held by a founder or heir's immediate family. The totals, therefore, count Forbes entries, not necessarily individual people.
Here are the industries that featured the most on the Forbes 400 list, from most to least prevalent.
1. Finance & investments — 108 members
Richest: Warren Buffett — $144 billion
The finance and investments industry has been the biggest maker of fortunes. Most of the wealthiest individuals in this category are founders of hedge funds, mortgage lenders, VC, and investment firms.
Some are heirs to founders, such as the grandchildren of Fidelity founder Edward Johnson II.
2. Technology — 91 members
Richest: Elon Musk — $908 billion
Technology has been a massive maker of fortunes; the nine richest in this category are wealthier than Warren Buffett.
Many are founders of big-name tech companies, as well as software and computer hardware firms. The AI boom has brought several newcomers to the list, including OpenAI cofounder and president Greg Brockman.
3. Food & beverage — 35 members
Richest: (Tie) Jacqueline and John Mars — $50.3 billion
From Chick-fil-A to Tito's Vodka, there are plenty of household-name brands in this category.
Others made their fortunes in the non-consumer parts of the food and beverage industry. These include J. Christopher Reyes and Jude Reyes, who cochair the food and beverage distribution firm Reyes Holdings, or Harry Stine, who made his fortune licensing soybean and corn genetics.
4. Fashion & retail — 26 members
Richest: Rob Walton & family — $132 billion
Like food and beverage, household names dominate the fashion & retail category. Walmart alone is listed as the source of wealth of eight people in this industry.
Other sources of retail wealth are less obvious. Jimmy and Bill Haslam's fortunes largely derive from the truck stop chain Pilot Flying J, which their father founded.
5. Energy — 23 members
Richest: Lyndal Stephens Greth & family — $30 billion
Oil tycoons and their families make up the bulk of this list. And it's not just those with stakes or roles in companies involved in production, but also pipelines and refineries.
6. Real estate — 18 members
Richest: Stephen Ross — $21.5 billion
America's wealthiest real-estate magnates built their fortunes through all kinds of properties. Jeff Greene, for example, made billions investing in credit default swaps tied to subprime mortgage-backed securities before the financial crisis.
With an estimated net worth of $7 billion and much of his wealth tied to real estate, President Donald Trump is also included in this category.
7. Media & entertainment — 17 members
Richest: Rupert Murdoch & family — $25 billion
Legacy media, such as cable and satellite television, continue to dominate this category. However, some billionaires built their fortunes through other kinds of media, including Gabe Newell, who cofounded video game developer Valve.
Movies have minted others, such as award-winning director Steven Spielberg and "Star Wars" creator George Lucas.
8. Sports — 16 members
Richest: Stanley Kroenke — $27.6 billion
For many people in the sports category, team ownership is more of a second act, rather than the original source of their wealth.
For example, before they bought teams, Arthur Blank cofounded Home Depot, Stephen Bisciotti made his fortune in talent management, and Arturo Moreno made his money from billboard advertising.
There are some exceptions, such as Michael Jordan, whose basketball career was the origin of his wealth.
9. Healthcare — 15 members
Richest: Thomas Frist, Jr. & family — $33.6 billion
Aside from the category's richest entry, Thomas Frist Jr. and family, whose wealth comes from hospitals, most of the others made or inherited their fortunes in pharmaceuticals, medical devices, and medical equipment.
One, Patrick Soon-Shiong, developed the chemotherapy drug Abraxane.
10. Manufacturing — 15 members
Richest: Steven Rales — $8.7 billion
Manufacturing spans a variety of industries, from packaging materials to defense.
Some big fortunes come from everyday products you might not expect. Cleaning products alone account for four people on the list, all of whom are heirs to SC Johnson, whose products include Windex and Glade.
11. Service — 11 members
Richest: Micky Arison & family — $11.5 billion
Aircraft leasing, cruises, and self-storage are just some examples of services that have turned people into billionaires.
Lucrative service companies aren't necessarily the most glamorous. Gary Rollins, for example, is executive chairman emeritus of pest control firm Rollins, which was founded by his father.
12. Automotive — 8 members
Richest: Ernest Garcia, II — $24.3 billion
In the US, automotive fortunes are less about manufacturing cars and more about selling, servicing, and moving them.
Forbes 400 member Dan Friedkin, for example, owns Gulf States Toyota, while Shahid Khan owns auto parts supplier Flex-N-Gate.
13. Diversified — 8 members
Richest: Julia Koch & family — $84.6 billion
Diversified means fortunes that don't neatly come from one industry. Members of the Koch family, which has stakes in the conglomerate Koch, dominate this segment.
14. Logistics — 4 members
Richest: Brad Jacobs — $13.3 billion
The businesses that move products through the supply chain are among the most essential to day-to-day life, and can be worth billions.
For example, Johnelle Hunt, who cofounded transportation and logistics firm J.B. Hunt Transport Services, is worth $6.6 billion.
15. Construction & engineering — 3 members
Richest: Diane Hendricks — $23.6 billion
All three members of the Forbes 400 in the construction and engineering industry are self-made billionaires.
Diane Hendricks cofounded building-supply distributor ABC Supply with her late husband, Ken Hendricks. Mike Hollingshead founded concrete maker Smyrna Ready Mix, while Robert Clark founded construction firm Clayco.
16. Gambling & casinos — 2 members
Richest: Miriam Adelson & family — $33.5 billion
With just two members categorized in the Forbes 400, gambling and casinos are the smallest category.
Miriam Adelson's late husband, Sheldon Adelson, was the founder of casino company Las Vegas Sands, while Jon Yarbrough founded casino producer Video Gaming Technologies.
Phil Ruffin, who Forbes categorized as diversified, made his wealth from a mix of casinos and real estate.

The high-ranking military position of Aide-de-Camp has been the subject of discussion ever since ‘national crush’ Major Rishabh Singh Sambyal (Retd.) took premature retirement as Aide-de-Camp (ADC) to President Droupadi Murmu.
Aide-de-Camp (ADC) is an honorary position in the Indian Armed Forces. ADCS are appointed from the three wings — the Indian Army, Indian Navy and Indian Air Force — and are responsible for coordinating and supporting the President’s day-to-day activities and ensuring protocol is maintained.
The President of India has five Aides-de-Camp: three from the Army, and one each from the Navy and Air Force.
In a podcast, ex-ADC Major Sambyal revealed the gruelling training that soldiers have to undergo to become Special Forces operatives. He described the Balidan Badge as a symbol of sacrifice, and said: “You have to give your blood, your sweat, and your sleepless nights to earn this… . It is a symbol that you have given balidan [sacrifice] of your soul - you have given what it takes to be the best towards the organisation and towards this cause."
Sambyal spoke about the demanding training and selection process that soldiers must complete before qualifying as Special Forces operatives. He also referred to a Discovery documentary released a few years ago that offered viewers a glimpse into the rigorous probation process.
“For roughly 90 days, you are put into a completely cut-off world under controlled stressful situations to assess your capabilities... For 90 days, it is rigorous training, sleepless nights, tasks, and missions,” Sambyal said in a podcast with Raj Shamani.
“Basically, they don't let you sleep during these 90 days-you hardly sleep in your classes when you're about to doze off…,” he said, adding that a candidate is pushed to human limits to see whether the individual breaks or not.
“Because we are looking for a human who doesn't break.”
In one of Raj Shamani's podcasts, Sambyal spoke at length about the vigilance required to ensure the President of India's safety.
The ex-ADC shared why no one is allowed to touch the feet of the President or shake their hands. "You don't know the intentions of the individual," said Sambyal. He added, "How can you trust the person who is on the other side?" He went on to share that he was even concerned about the glass from which she would have water. "You don't know who has kept it there. You don't know if something is there..."
He explained that an area extending up to 1 km around the President is kept sanitised, which means no arms, metal or other dangerous materials are allowed.

Electric vehicle (EV) manufacturer Zelio E-Mobility’s board of directors approved a proposal today to raise up to ₹167.95 Cr via a preferential issue of equity shares and convertible warrants to fund its growth initiatives. The BSE SME listed company will issue up to 9.73 Lakh equity shares at an issue price of ₹853 per share to four non-promoter institutional and private investors, aggregating to nearly ₹83 Cr. The allottees would be Motilal Oswal Financial Services to get ₹40.1 Cr, Calliope Capital Advisors LLP (₹31.4 Cr), Param Value Investments (₹8.5 Cr), and Hem Growth Opportunities Fund (nearly ₹3 Cr). Simultaneously, the board approved issuing over 9.96 Lakh convertible warrants at the same issue price to three promoters, Niraj Arya, Deepak Arya, and Kunal Arya, to raise an additional sum of nearly ₹85 Cr. For the warrants, the promoters will pay 25% or ₹21.24 Cr at the time of allotment, while the remaining 75% (₹63.72 Cr) will be payable when the warrants are converted into equity shares. The warrants can be converted within 18 months of allotment. Following the full conversion of warrants and allotment of equity shares, the promoter group’s stake in Zelio will dilute from 72.8% to 70.9%, whilst public shareholding will rise from 27.2% to 29.1%. As the total issue exceeds ₹100 Cr, the board appointed SEBI-registered Brickwork Ratings India to monitor how the proceeds of the fundraise would be utilised in accordance with regulations. The company will seek shareholder approval via an EGM, which is scheduled for October 20. Separately, shareholders will be asked to approve related-party transactions of up to ₹50 Cr each with five entities — Torque Innovation EV, AVR Auto Industries, Jai Bharat Engineering Tools, Jai Bharat Auto Components, Rajdhani Machinery Store. Zelio says these transactions will be conducted in the ordinary course of business and on an arm’s-length basis. Founded in 2021 by Neeraj Arya, Hisar-based Zelio manufactures electric vehicles, primarily low-speed electric scooters. It operates in over 25 states with a network of more than 300 dealers. The startup made its debut on the BSE SME platform in 2025, raising ₹78.34 Cr. The EV manufacturer operated manufacturing units in Ladwa, Hisar, Alarpur, Cuttack and a warehousing facility in Chandan Nagar. It claims to have a footprint across 400 cities and towns across India. In July, the company also inaugurated a manufacturing plant in Coimbatore to expand its presence in Southern India. With the establishment of the Coimbatore factory, Zelio is now looking to enhance its manufacturing capabilities from 1.8 Lakh units per annum to 2.4 Lakh units per annum in Q2 FY27. "Coimbatore facility has an installed production and assembly capacity of 60,000 units per annum. During its initial phase of operations, the plant is expected to manufacture and assemble approximately 24,000-30,000 E2Ws annually, with production gradually scaling in line with market demand and operational ramp-up," the company had said. By the end of FY27, Zelio is looking to expand its dealership network to 550 from 400 in 25 states at the end of FY26. On the financial front, Zelio’s standalone profit soared 75.4% to ₹28 Cr in FY26. The EV maker set up a new auto components manufacturing subsidiary, Zelio Auto Components, in May 2025. Including the financial performance of the newly set up subsidiary, Zelio’s consolidated operating revenue for FY26 stood at ₹310.7 Cr. Meanwhile, Zelio is not the first listed new-age tech company to return to the capital markets to raise fresh capital. Among other listed competitors in the EV space, Ola Electric raised ₹780 Cr in June and Ather raised ₹1,300 Cr in July, both utilising Qualified Institutional Placements (QIPs). Ola Electric is mulling another QIP as of now, with its board approving the raise of ₹1,500 Cr via the markets three months after raising fresh funds. Shares of Zelio ended today’s trading session 4.99% higher at ₹986.90.

Morning opening: Zelenskyy to present Ukraine's case to UN leaders
Jakub Krupa
Ukraine is set to feature prominently on Day 2 of the UN general assembly in New York, with leaders first joining the UN security council meeting on Ukraine, before presidentVolodymyr Zelenskyy takes to the podium to deliver his address to the assembly.
It will be a key opportunity to rally international support behind Kyiv, bolstering Ukraine’s position ahead of any potential peace talks with Moscow.
Zelenskyy did not get a chance to say much during his last night’s meeting with US president Donald Trump.
“I hope we will end this war, and president Trump will help us end this war. We need to do it as quick as possible, before winter,” he said at the beginning of the meeting before Trump dominated the Q&A with reporters.
He later said on social media that the pair discussed ending “the senseless war” before winter, with “potential de-escalatory steps that can open up the way to diplomacy.”
He also said Ukraine was “ready for any kind of format of energy ceasefire” if Russia agrees to “not attack out energy system”
Before we get to Zelenskyy late afternoon, we will hear from some other European leaders from Latvia, Romania, Czech Republic, Estonia, and Cyprus. I will monitor their speeches for any key lines.
Lots to cover.
It’s Wednesday, 23 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
New UK agency to fight ‘information warfare’ from likes of Russia, Burnham tells UN
There was also lots of focus on UK prime minister Andy Burnham’s first UN speech, late at night in Europe.
In his speech, Burnham was keen to speak about how “Britain is back” after 10 years of Brexit, “restoring our stability” and “building a more dynamic economy.”
On Russia, he said the UK will be “will be relentless in building up our hard power and deterrence,” but “we will not play Russia’s game of trading escalatory rhetoric.”
“Unlike Russia, we do not seek confrontation. Instead, we will be prepared, but not panicked. Clear-eyed, but cool headed. And unflinching in defending our people and our allies.”
In particularly eye-catching paragraphs, he said Britain has been “under attack” with years of “an industrial-scale assault by hostile actors on the information environment in the UK and that of many of our allies.”
“Russian agencies have used every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people’s fears. They’ve used bots and fake websites. Falsified newspaper articles. Forged the branding of 28 British organisations – including universities and the BBC. They’ve amplified far right narratives,” he said, adding that Moscow “tried to interfere with the 2019 general election.”
In response, security chiefs will set up a new national centre to tackle disinformation and deepfakes from hostile states such as Russia, he said, saying the government had a duty to “stem the poisonous tide” from damaging British interests.
Burnham said the country would have to go into the next decade “eyes wide open” about “insidious” campaigns, many of which had been orchestrated by Russia, which “twisted” what people at home felt about their own country and community.
Macron's final UN speech condemns 'return to the law of the jungle' with focus on Ukraine, Gaza, West Bank
Catching up with what happened at UNGA last night, France’s president Emmanuel Macron delivered his last general assembly speech as he is firmly in the last year of his presidency.
And he did not hold back, warning against a global “return to the law of the jungle,” as he said “we cannot accept the new order of impunity that some would like to build.”
He warned that “in the Middle East, in Ukraine, in Africa, the industrialisation of war crimes, violations of the law, and the destruction of civilian infrastructure is ushering in a new age of barbarity.”
He assured leaders of France’s “unwavering support” for Ukraine, and urged leaders to “defend the Ukrainian people … more than ever before the coming winter.”
Separately, in what was seen as a swipe at Trump, Macron also said the world was witnessing a spectacle that should shame everyone, rebuking Trump’s portrayal of his Gaza peace plan as a diplomatic triumph, Reuters reported.
“A year ago, here in this very hall, about a dozen states had recognised Palestine. I hear the cynicism of some people: ‘Recognition is just a piece of paper, look at the reality.’
What credibility do we have if we continue to remain inactive in the face of Gaza? Some boast of a supposed peace. But that peace has not reopened humanitarian access for a single second. Are we simply to stand by and watch this spectacle that should shame us all?”
Macron also opted for tough language on settler violence against Palestiniansin the West Bank, saying:
“Look at what is happening in the West Bank, where every day violations are committed. In whose name? Hamas has never operated in the West Bank …
What is happening there is building, day by day, the impossibility of a project that should be based on respect for the legitimate right of the Palestinian people to exist.”
At least one dead, seven injured in Russian strikes on Kyiv this morning
Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said at least one person died and seven were injured in this morning’s Russian attacks on Kyiv.
In a series of updates, he said Russian drones struck a business centre, a transport facility, and a “non-residential building,” among others.
Separately, Ukrainian oil company Ukrnafta said Russia hit one of its petrol stations in the capital, the sixth such facility attacked in recent weeks.

When Bellamy watched on as Ronaldo caused lockdown
- Published
With five Ballon d'Or wins, eight league titles, five Champions Leagues, a European Championship and a pair of Nations League triumphs among his glut of honours, Cristiano Ronaldo's status as one of football's all-time greats is not in doubt.
But a chance encounter with the Portugal legend helped Wales boss Craig Bellamy appreciate that the 41-year-old is significantly more than just a footballing icon.
Bellamy was on a pre-season trip to Lisbon during his time as an assistant to manager Vincent Kompany at Burnley when the Portuguese capital's airport was effectively put into lockdown.
It led to the Welshman describing Ronaldo as "beyond a superstar" after he realised the vast presence of police and security officials were to help escort the global icon.
"So we got to the airport and the police were everywhere. It was on lockdown," Bellamy said.
- Ronaldo spurred on by 1,000 goals and Portugal glory 
  - Published7 hours ago

Nations League Group A4
Thursday, 24 September, 19:45 BST
Estádio José Alvalade, Lisbon

"We're Burnley and we had a little bit of VIP. We were on a coach, we were chartered but still had to go into the airport a certain way.
"It was like rows of police with police cars everywhere. We thought, 'something has happened, there must be a warning here'.
"Everything was locked off. People in the terminal, you name it. We couldn't get off the coach and we had to wait for what we thought was a security breach or something.
"We are stuck on the coach for 10, 15 minutes and suddenly this car turns up, it parks and a guy walks out, goes in the boot, grabs a rucksack and someone else gets out and puts the rucksack on and who is it? Ronaldo."
Bellamy added: "He is walking on his own with police everywhere and Lisbon airport locked off. Even the police were taking pictures. No-one could bother him.
"It was the coolest walk I have ever watched for a minute.
"We were all on the coach and our jaws dropped. Everyone who had been moaning quickly shut up. It was like presidents stuff."
Bellamy last shared a pitch with Ronaldo in October 2008 as the Portuguese scored twice for Manchester United in a 2-0 Premier League win over West Ham United at Old Trafford.
He is now set to manage his country against the 233-cap international as Wales kick-start their Nations League A campaign in Portugal on Thursday night.
As he bids to conjure up a plan to nullify Ronaldo and the rest of the star-studded Portugal squad at the Estadio Jose Alvalade, Bellamy was eager to fully reflect on the experience of the forward he witnessed at Lisbon airport.
"How can you lock off a whole airport?" added Bellamy.
"I would not be able to get my computer through customs in Cardiff airport. What have I just seen?
"The reason I'm telling the story is because that's how big this guy is.
"It was like, 'wow'. I'm so glad I saw that moment because he is beyond a superstar."
- What will 'greatest captain' bring to Bellamy's Wales? 
  - Published2 days ago
- FAW chief questions Infantino's Fifa reform claims 
  - Published1 day ago
During the summer, Ronaldo confirmed the 2026 World Cup would be his last.
However, the Al-Nassr frontman has so far not revealed when he will finally bring his glittering career to an end.
Despite the uncertainty surrounding Ronaldo's future, Bellamy says he can fully understand why the forward - now in his 24th year as a senior Portugal international - is still operating at an elite level.
"I'm not surprised he is still playing with the professionalism he has shown," added Bellamy.
"It's also how clever he is, he knows how to protect himself, he knows not to waste his energy at certain times and he's still got the habit of goal-scoring, and you never lose that.
"We're talking about not just one of the greatest players of our generation, we're talking all generations with what he has been able to do. He's beyond a superstar."
For all of the spotlight on Ronaldo and his team-mates, Bellamy knows his full focus - along with that of his players and staff - must be on how Wales can leave the City of Light with a positive result.
The head coach's already tough task has been made harder by the fact he will be without players including Harry Wilson, Joe Rodon, Karl Darlow, Nathan Broadhead, Dylan Lawlor, Rubin Colwill and Isaak Davies in Lisbon.
But Bellamy has urged his players to show the right kind of fight as they bid to upset the odds and remain in the top tier of the Nations League over the coming months.
"We have to be excited, but not too excited," he added.
"We have worked hard to get into League A, so what can we do to stay in it? If we do then it will help us massively and that's the motivation.
"You want to be in these moments. I'm telling you, when your playing days finish, you won't remember Bury away and all that. These moments you will remember and will live with you.
"But you also want to remember how you performed. You don't want this to get too much.
"I want my players to go out and give everything. They should love every second of it. That's the drive for this."

Dr Oz and Trump’s health team shredded for ‘shameful’ reason behind bouncing 760,000 from medical coverage
‘So you pay for insurance, stay healthy enough not to use it, and somehow that makes your coverage suspicious?’ one user asked

Trump administration officials said they booted thousands of people from their health coverage because they never filed claims and could not be contacted — and the internet had a field day pointing out the problem with the thinking.
On Tuesday, Vice President JD Vance and Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz announced that 760,000 people had been kicked off health insurance purchased in the federal Affordable Care Act marketplace, arguing those individuals were either enrolled fraudulently or did not exist. They said the initiative — part of a broader effort to crack down on fraud — would save about $2.2 billion in taxpayer dollars.
“We call them phantoms because we believe most of them either don’t exist or had no idea they had coverage,” Oz said during a press conference. “We believe that because we’ve been writing them, Telexing them, you know, walking to them, Fedexing, whatever we could possibly do to get in touch with them. They won’t answer.”
“And they have never filed a claim, so it meets all the criteria for us to pretty, as much as any government can, say you actually don’t know you have this or you don’t exist,” he added.
Oz’s remarks, which drew millions of views on social media, quickly prompted criticism from people who insisted that his reasoning was flawed.
Some said they routinely ignore government outreach.
“Could be me. I dodge all spam calls. Especially Healthcare ones,” one X user wrote. “Cause I already pay for my insurance and don’t have anything they need. Or so I thought.”
But much of the backlash focused on the Trump administration’s suggestion that not filing an insurance claim could itself be evidence of fraud. Typically people who do not file claims are welcomed because they are paying into the insurance pool, but not receiving services that end up costing money.
“So you pay for insurance, stay healthy enough not to use it, and somehow that makes your coverage suspicious?” one user asked. Another wrote: “So car insurance will kick us off next b/c we never got into a car wreck? Or life insurance kicks us off b/c we never died?”
One commenter said Oz’s rationale misunderstands a basic premise of health insurance.
“But that's how insurance works,” they wrote. “The majority of healthy people paying their monthly bill funds the people who are sick or injured and need assistance. What are we even doing here?”
“How is it fraud if they aren’t even filing claims?” another user asked.
Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi wrote: “The Trump Administration's shameless decision to rip away health insurance from thousands will leave working families unable to get the care they need. Using the false pretext of fighting fraud to strip Americans of their healthcare is as cynical as it is cruel.”
Melanie D’Arrigo, executive director of Campaign for New York Health, tweeted: “Your reminder that private health insurance companies defraud taxpayers by at least $80 billion per year, and no one is holding them accountable because the insurance industry spent over $100 million in the last election.”
And Dean Baker, senior economist at the Center for Economic & Policy Research, reacted to a clip of Oz explaining the policy on Fox News by writing: “Can a person be this stupid and breathe? I have had homeowners and car insurance for decades and never used them. In fact, in many years I didn't use my health insurance. I'm very glad for that.”
The centers insinuated that the losses were not primarily tied to claims spending. Instead, officials said, fraud stemmed from bad actors, such as brokers, enrolling consumers in coverage without their knowledge in order to collect federal premium subsidies.
Government data does indicate the Affordable Care Act marketplace faces fraud risks. In a report last year, the Government Accountability Office said the federal marketplace approved subsidized coverage for most of the fictitious applicants it submitted as part of a covert test.
Still, some health policy experts have raised concerns about the Trump administration’s approach to combating fraud.
“I think there’s no question that somebody who was fraudulently enrolled should have their coverage canceled,” Cynthia Cox, a vice president at the healthcare research nonprofit KFF, told The Associated Press. “I think the question is whether this was the appropriate process by which to identify fraudulent enrollees, and also whether all of them were indeed fraudulently enrolled.”
“There’s a lot of work to be done, and the Trump administration has done some good things that are targeting the actual fraudsters,” Ellen Montz, a former CMS official who served under former President Joe Biden, told the outlet. That said, she added: “I would imagine we’ll hear from some subset of consumers that ask: why did my enrollment get cancelled?”
This latest effort to root out fraud in the health care system comes as the price for ACA insurance has soared following Congress’ failure to extend pandemic-era subsidies last year.
According to a June Gallup survey, fewer than half of Americans can now consistently afford healthcare, marking the first time this threshold has been passed in five years.
The Independent has contacted the centers for comment.
