Donald Trump welcomed Xi Jinping on Wednesday evening, taking the unusual step of greeting the Chinese leader on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews to kick off his state visit to Washington.
Xi’s plane was met with a lavish arrival ceremony that included a 100ft long red carpet flanked by US service members, a military flyover by two B-1 bombers and a presentation of the flags and national anthems of both countries. US presidents typically welcome foreign leaders at the White House, but Trump and first lady Melania Trump traveled to the the military base in Maryland, just outside Washington, to personally shake Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan’s hands upon their arrival in the US.
It came as Scott Bessent, the US Treasury secretary, announced that the US and China agreed on Wednesday to extend the so-called “Busan agreement” – a temporary trade truce between the rival superpowers.
Bessent, who met Chinese vice-premier He Lifeng earlier on Wednesday, told Fox News the agreement would be extended until 10 January, two months after it was originally due to expire.
When Xi arrives at the White Hous Chinese president will receive a 21-gun salute on the South Lawn of the White House, private tea with the US president and first lady, and a tour of the National Archives, among other special events.
For the world leaders’ second meeting this year, Trump and Xi must confront a range of thorny issues such as the race in artificial intelligence development and geopolitical instability during the two-day visit.
On Thursday, the White House has invited major tech leaders, such as executives from OpenAI, Apple, xAI, Microsoft, Nvidia, Meta and others, to a state dinner being held for Xi.
The US and China have long been competing to develop increasingly powerful technology, but the race to further AI has become a major topic among tech companies – especially after several executives came forward to warn about the dangers of rapid development.
Trump has dismissed concerns that AI development could harm people, instead promoting more investment in the technology so the US can beat China in the race.
“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so,” Trump wrote on Truth Social last week.
The president and members of the administration have insisted that leading AI development also means leading the world militarily and economically – further raising the stakes for the US and China.
Xi’s visit is expected to be filled with pageantry, reciprocating the treatment Trump received when he visited China earlier this year.
Trump’s decision to greet the Chinese leader at his plane, rather than at the White House, shows how far the US president is willing to go to indulge Xi.
“He’s coming on our soil, and we need to welcome them with the most respect,” Melania Trump said of the visit to Fox & Friends on Wednesday morning.

Major insurers are pushing back on a Medicare proposal that would significantly disrupt how many doctors bill for tracking the health of patients using devices like connected blood pressure cuffs, scales, and blood glucose meters. These remote monitoring services help patients manage a range of medical conditions, including hypertension, diabetes, and heart failure.
UnitedHealth Group, CVS Health, and Kaiser Permanente all wrote letters to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services opposing a proposal that would require that remote patient monitoring care be delivered by direct employees of the practice that is billing for them — effectively banning providers from using contractors for the care. All of these groups operate both insurers and care organizations.
The opposition from UnitedHealth Group is notable in particular because the company’s insurance subsidiary, UnitedHealthcare, recently attempted to stop paying for most remote patient monitoring “due to insufficient evidence of efficacy.”

There's legal drama swirling around Dolly Parton's estimated $450 million estate.
Nearly a month after Parton's death in August, her nephew and longtime head of security, Bryan Seaver, was fired and sued by Parton's manager and one of the entities established to oversee Parton's business affairs, She's Alive LLC.
In court filings, Parton's manager, Danny Nozell, and She's Alive LLC allege that Seaver made violent threats against employees and vowed to damage her business empire unless his demands were met.
Seaver confirmed he was fired but disputed that he made threats, saying the language was taken out of context.
Seaver, Nozzell, and Parton's estate did not respond to requests for comment from Business Insider.
The dispute casts a spotlight on the business empire Parton built over her decadeslong career and on the people now responsible for protecting it.
Here's what you need to know about the fallout and what, exactly, is at stake in this conflict.
Dolly Parton died on August 25. She was 80.
Parton died after a private battle with cancer, though she had referenced unspecified health issues earlier in the year.
Her death sent shockwaves around the world. There were tributes across the US, including a heartwarming one to her at the 2026 Emmys, with a song performed by Reba McEntire.
President Donald Trump ordered all the flags to be lowered to half-mast, a rare honor for a private citizen.
Her death was announced on Instagram by her nephew, Bryan Seaver. He was her head of security for over 20 years.
"This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago, before I fully absorbed it as a future reality. As her head of security for more than two decades, a role my father Larry held before me, I have imagined the heaviness of this moment, but haven't truly felt it until now," said Seaver in the video.
"Rest in peace, Aunt Dolly, Aunt Granny, Gigi. My God bless Dolly Parton, and may God bless you all. She will always love you," he concluded.
Seaver is the son of Parton's younger sister, Cassie, one of her six surviving siblings.
About a month after Parton's death, Seaver was fired from his role as her security.
The New York Times reported that Seaver was fired from his role as head of security for Parton's estate and properties. His firm was replaced by new security personnel.
On September 22, Nozell and She's Alive LLC filed a lawsuit against Seaver and sought a temporary restraining order. On September 23, a judge granted the temporary restraining order.
Variety reported that Nozell alleges Seaver "engaged in a campaign of coercion, extortion and violent threats."
The joint filing for the suit and restraining order says that Seaver referred to himself as "literally an international arms dealer and mercenary" and said he's "not an entertainment person. I'm a killer."
The next day, Seaver confirmed he had been fired but disputed Nozell's version of events.
"The restraining order is spurious and simply a publicity stunt," Seaver told ABC News.
"I was fired. After the estate negotiated with me and my company for services in perpetuity and agreed to that service provision from my company," the statement continues. "A week later, they fired me for these contrived 'threats.'"
"Dolly called me her killer. It was a joke we used around her camp," he added. "Danny Nozell took that text out of context to somehow imagine that I was threatening him. He's always called me The Killer."
Nozell and She's Alive LLC, an entity set up by Parton before her death to protect her legacy, allege that Seaver demanded money or else.
While Nozell (pictured with Parton above) is acting on behalf of She's Alive LLC (SAL), dedicated to overseeing Parton's posthumous legacy, it's separate from the DP Dean Trust, the entity controlling Parton's estate.
Variety reported that the suit alleges Seaver threatened to interfere with his aunt's businesses unless he was paid. One filing said Seaver said he would start a podcast "dedicated to ruining Dolly's brand partnerships" without financial compensation.
The suit also contains text messages that it says were sent by Seaver. One reads: "I am about to become the hand of retribution for my entire family."
Seaver disputed the characterizations of his texts to The New York Times.
"This is a contrived out-of-context explanation of how this went down, and it is being done in an effort to solidify me as some sort of opposition to her brand in her legacy," he wrote, "and that is not the case."
He added, "I trusted Danny, and that's what those messages were, two friends and brothers commiserating on the people that have screwed Dolly over for many, many years."
Parton had an estimated net worth of $450 million.
Forbes reported Parton's net worth was $450 million in June 2025, about a year before her death.
Parton didn't come from money — in fact, she had humbler beginnings than most. She and her 11 siblings grew up in a two-room log cabin in Sevierville, Tennessee. It had no electricity or running water.
But decades of iconic songs and smart business decisions led to her wealth growing.
Dollywood was her biggest asset.
Dollywood is an amusement park located in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee. It opened in 1986 and has been a popular attraction in the area ever since.
According to a 2021 Forbes report, Parton retained a 50% stake in the park, worth about $165 million.
There's also the adjacent water park, Dollywood's Splash Country.
Splash Country, adjacent to the theme park, opened in 2001. Her shares in Splash Country were worth about $20 million, per the 2021 Forbes report.
Her songwriting catalog is estimated to be worth about $120 million.
Parton recorded 49 studio albums (plus more compilations and live albums) over the course of her career, and thousands of songs — and she owned the publishing for most of them.
Famously, Elvis Presley wanted to record a cover of "I Will Always Love You," but, as his (infamous) manager Colonel Tom Parker told her, Presley typically took 50% of the profits from covers he recorded.
Parton refused, later allowed Whitney Houston to cover the song while retaining ownership, and, as she famously said, earned enough money from that one cover to purchase Graceland itself.
As Forbes reported in 2021, her catalog was worth about $120 million.
Her likeness and brand have been licensed to everything from Duncan Hines baking mixes to pet gear.
Parton had restaurants, cookware, jewelry, cookbooks, boxed mixes, home decor, and more, all of which bear her name and earned her a profit.
There are also multiple charities bearing Parton's name.
Parton was famously very giving. The Dollywood Foundation was founded in 1988 and has been responsible for efforts such as the Imagination Library, which distributes 3 million books a month to children from birth to age 5.
She also established the Dolly Parton COVID-19 Research Fund to support the Moderna vaccine, and funded the Dolly Parton Center for Women's Services and Dolly Parton Birthing Unit at the LeConte Medical Center in Sevierville.
Nozell has asked for a jury trial.
In the request for the temporary restraining order, Nozell also requested a jury trial to resolve the matter, so we'll have to wait and see what happens next. A hearing is scheduled for October 7.

In September 2026, people shared an image purportedly showing U.S. President Donald Trump leaving a brown stain on a chair during his trip to Ireland that month.
One X post (archived) featuring the alleged photo had amassed roughly 4 million views as of this writing.
(@StillADog via X)
Trump visited the country on the weekend of Sept. 12-13, during which he met with Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin. The U.S. president sparked controversy following that meeting after calling for Irish unification, an act that would merge the United Kingdom's Northern Ireland with the Republic of Ireland. Trump also met with Ireland President Catherine Connolly and attended the Irish Open at his golf course in Doonbeg.
Several Snopes readers asked if the image of Trump leaving the stain — which also spread on Bluesky, Facebook, Threads, TikTok and YouTube — is authentic.
One Threads user claimed artificial intelligence was not used to create the alleged photo, though it was not clear whether or not this was said sincerely.
(@becca_reptile_and_human_momma via Threads)
Some users commenting under the posts seemed genuinely unsure whether the image was real, while other remarks of bewilderment were possibly written in jest.
In sum, the image is fake and originated from an AI-generated video. That AI-generated clip originated from a prompt seemingly using an authentic photo that did not display a stain.
Creator Tom Adelsbach first posted the content as a fake video on Facebook, Instagram and X on Sept. 12, as confirmed by a reverse image search. His posts' captions read, "BREAKING: Donald Trump causes an international incident during his meeting with Ireland President Catherine Connolly."
In an email, Adelsbach told us he was responsible for coming up with the fake video. We also emailed the White House to request comment and will update this article if we receive additional details.
Adelsbach's 22-second, AI-generated video features a fake depiction of Trump sitting next to Connolly. The U.S. president appears to sigh, stand up and shake Connolly's hand. The sound of photographers taking pictures can also be heard. As the inauthentic clip continues, Trump exits left, revealing the brown stain on his chair. The stain then grows in size and drips on the floor, leaving Connolly's AI depiction audibly reacting in horror.
Adelsbach previously labeled similar content with disclaimers about comedy, parody and satire. His posts featuring the fake chair stain do not show the same disclaimer. However, Meta's "AI content" label does appear on Facebook and Instagram.
The original photo
Another reverse image search revealed that the Northern Irish Belfast Telegraph newspaper published an authentic photo that Adelsbach appeared to use when creating the AI-generated video. The newspaper credited the picture of Trump and Connolly to photographer Tony Maxwell. The caption says the pair were seated inside Áras an Uachtaráin, the Irish president's residence. The full caption reads, "President Catherine Connolly and President Donald Trump at Aras an Uachtarain (Tony Maxwell/Maxwells/PA)."
President Connolly's social media accounts also feature a similar photo of her sitting next to Trump.

'I don't even know if my parents are alive' - the war heroes jailed 25 years ago
- Published
Hanna Petros Solomon breaks down in tears as she recalls how she and her siblings effectively became orphans 25 years ago when their father was arrested in Eritrea and jailed without trial. Their mother was subsequently detained - and no-one has heard from either of them - or of them - since.
"He had a towel on his shoulders like a sportsman," she tells the BBC about the last time she saw her father when she was 10 years old, and he had gone out for a jog.
"He used to work out every morning."
Her parents met when they both fought in the long liberation war that saw Eritrea gain independence from Ethiopia in 1993.
Her father Petros Solomon had been one of the senior leaders during the war and is regarded by many as a national hero for his critical role.
After independence, he had served as defence minister, then foreign minister and had been heading the fisheries ministry when his troubles began.
That was in May 2001 when he and 14 other high-profile politicians signed an open letter to President Isaias Afewerki calling for the implementation of a constitution that was ratified after independence and demanding national elections. They became known as the G-15.
Isaias, the leader of the Eritrean People's Liberation Front (EPLF) which had fought against Ethiopia, did not take the criticism well.
Unbeknown to Hanna, her father had been dismissed as a minister, though he still went out early to get some exercise each day.
It was not until a few days after 9/11 - when the world was distracted by the al-Qaeda attacks on the US - that the country was to discover the full extent of Isais's displeasure in what became a watershed moment in Eritrea's history.
In the early hours of 18 September, the security forces positioned themselves outside the homes of 11 senior government officials in the capital, Asmara, on the president's orders.
Petros was picked up by security agents as he left in his tracksuit.
The family had no idea what had happened to him. Hanna and her three siblings went to stay with their paternal grandmother as their mother, Aster Yohannes, was away studying in the US.
It was only some days after Petros had disappeared that things became clearer, says Hanna about the painful memories.
"My classmates told me that my father sold out his country.
"That is when I understood how serious the situation was, and how people framed my dad and his colleagues who fought for the independence of their country. I was hurt."
In the US, Aster was shell-shocked by what had happened - and was in a very bad way. She asked government officials if they could issue the children with passports - but they refused, telling her to come home.
After agonising about the situation for two years and reportedly receiving assurances from government officials, she packed her bags to return.
Hanna and her siblings desperately wanted her back - but they were also worried.
"I told her on the phone: 'What if they arrest you?'" Hanna remembers.
"She insisted nothing would happen to her, saying: 'I haven't done anything wrong, and am only coming to raise my children.'"
Hanna says she learned later that President Isaias himself had promised Aster that she would be safe. But while the family waited at Asmara International Airport on 11 December 2003, she failed to emerge through arrivals with the other passengers.
Their hopes began to wilt along with the flowers they had brought: "It was a long, long wait. Eventually we gave up and went back home.
"First we called to the US, friends and relatives told us they saw her off at the airport."
Then ominously an official called from the airport asking Aster to collect her luggage. That is when they realised she had arrived in the country but would not be coming home.
All pleas and requests for information fell on deaf ears in the months that followed. Instead Hanna's grandmother was warned by authorities to stop inquiring.
The family later heard that Aster was being held in the infamous jail known as Karshelli in the heart of Asmara.
Hanna's father is believed to be detained, with the others arrested on 18 and 19 September 2001, in the remote, hostile and highly secretive prison known as Ela-Ero, located in eastern lowlands north-east of Asmara. Accused of treason, none of them has ever been brought to trial or allowed to see their relatives.
At around the same time, the government also shut down all the fledgling independent newspapers and detained their editors and journalists - also believed to be imprisoned in Ela-Ero.
The Eritrean government - including its embassy in the UK - has not responded to the BBC's request for comment regarding the whereabouts of the prisoners or whether or not they are alive.
Hanna, like many thousands of young Eritreans fleeing conscription and in search of better opportunities, left the country - travelling secretively over the border without a passport.
Now 35 years old, she is married and lives in the US, working as a trauma specialist - but still feels traumatised herself by how she lost her parents.
As she stares at old pictures of her parents, she worries her memories will fade of the happy times before their arrest - the laughter, the family gatherings, the birthday parties: "My dad always wanted to gather people in the house, they were good days."
She also hankers after her mother's "unmatched" egg and potato sandwiches.
On trips down to the coast when her father was the minister of fisheries, Hanna remembers him organising singing competitions in the car: "He would ask us to sing one by one and whoever won would get a present."
One of his favourite songs included the lyrics: "I had a sweater, a blue sweater, that my sister took" - which reminded him of his sister who was also a freedom fighter and had been killed during the war.
She also has memories of her mother loving music - playing and singing hits by Abba, Dolly Parton and Whitney Houston.
Until her father's arrest, Hanna remembers September as being full of hope with its three big Orthodox Christian festivals, including the Geez New Year. Now the month brings her no joy.
Ibrahim Sherifo knows exactly how she feels. Both his parents, who were senior members of the ruling People's Front for Democracy and Justice (PFDJ), were among the G-15 people arrested 25 years ago.
He was 13 years old at the time
"For me 18 September 2001 is a dark day, but not only for me, it is a dark day for Eritrea and its people, because it is the day when law and democracy was detained," he tells the BBC.
He is now 38 and living in exile in the Netherlands, where he was granted asylum, and is pursuing an MA in political science - following in his father's footsteps.
His dad Mahmoud Ahmed Sherifo was the local government minister and de facto deputy president before his detention.
Ibrahim was with his mother, Aster Fissehatsion, staying with her sister when he remembers security agents knocking on the door early in the morning and taking her away in her pyjamas.
Worried about his father, Ibrahim immediately ran to his nearby house but was told he had already been picked up when he had gone out for exercise.
Both Hanna and Ibrahim say they are forever grateful to the friends and family who offered them care and supported them as they grew up without their parents, despite the risks.
They are also proud of what their parents stood for and daring to call for reforms.
"They had conscience and couldn't observe idly while what they fought for what had been hijacked by Isaias and his coterie," says Ibrahim.
"As a family, we should be informed whether they are alive or not," he adds, accusing the government of wanting to erase all memory of the political prisoners.
Hanna also wants the plight of the many others whose relatives have disappeared over the years to be heard too.
Sometimes it is calm and you can float, but other times the sorrow comes back to you like a wave and drowns you deep down"
Human rights groups, including the UN, consider the G-15 prisoners of conscience and have been calling for their release.
President Isaias, now 80, has still not implemented the country's first constitution - approved in 1997 - and remains in power without ever holding an election.
Hanna recalls that on the eve of her father's disappearance, she had a "bad feeling" - and had crept into his bed and tied his legs to her own with string while he slept.
"In the morning he woke up to find he was tied up and to release himself he pulled my legs and I woke up. I begged him not to leave but he assured me that he would return [after his run]."
Describing the years of sorrow since, she says it is like living in the deep sea.
"Sometimes it is calm and you can float, but other times the sorrow comes back to you like a wave and drowns you deep down.
"Sometimes you lose hope and you are out of breath."
Asked what she would say if she could get a message to her parents, she replies: "Don't worry about us.
"Like you survived the struggle through sheer steadfastness, we hope you can pull through this too and return to us."

Storm alert: Are schools in Odisha, Andhra Pradesh open or closed today?
Educational institutions in several districts of Odisha have been ordered to remain closed till September 24, Thursday.
Authorities in several regions of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh were on alert on Wednesday as a Bay of Bengal depression intensified into a deep depression, triggering heavy rainfall in coastal and southern areas.
The weather conditions have prompted local administrations to take precautionary measures.
Follow live updates on Cyclone 'Arnab' here.
Odisha schools - open or shut?
Deep Dive
Coastal and southern Odisha witnessed heavy rainfall on Tuesday, prompting authorities to take precautionary measures, including the closure of educational institutions in several districts, news agency PTI reported.
Schools closed: Educational institutions in Nabarangpur, Puri, Jagatsinghpur, Ganjam, Gajapati, Koraput and Khurda have been ordered to remain closed till September 24, Thursday, the report added.
Malkangiri also declared that schools would be shut till Thursday. Anganwadi centres will also remain shut till September 24, Thursday. Despite the closure, teachers and other staff will report to schools.
Meanwhile, the Puri district administration hoisted red flags across the beach and completely banned sea bathing till Thursday.
Also Read | Cyclone ‘Arnab’ threat: Which states will be affected as Bay of Bengal weather system nears coast
What the IMD said
According to the update by the India Meteorological Department (IMD), the system is moved westwards at a speed of 7 kmph during the past several hours.
"The Deep Depression over Westcentral & adjoining Northwest Bay of Bengal, moved westwards with a speed of 07 kmph during past 06 hours, and lay centred at 2330 hrs IST of yesterday, the 22nd September, 2026, over the same region near latitude 18.0°N and longitude 85.0°E, about 100 km east-southeast of Kalingapatnam (Andhra Pradesh), 150 km south of Gopalpur (Odisha), 220 km south-southwest of Puri (Odisha), and 180 km east-northeast of Visakhapatnam (Andhra Pradesh)," the weather department said in a post on X (formerly Twitter).
"It is very likely to move west-northwestwards, and cross North Andhra Pradesh - South Odisha coasts between Vishakhapatnam & Gopalpur, close to Kalingapatnam as a Deep Depression by night of 23rd September 2026," it added.
According to the roster that lists the names of cyclonic storms, the next cyclone that forms in the North Indian Ocean will be named ‘Arnab’, as HT reported earlier.
Are Andhra Pradesh schools open?
A holiday has been declared for all schools in Vizianagaram district on September 23, Wednesday, according to an official statement from the Vizianagaram District Education Officer (DEO), as reported by Moneycontrol.
Schools in Srikakulam have also been ordered to remain shut, it further reported.

India's manufacturing story is entering a new era. After years of policy support and incentives, capital is now flowing into factories, production lines and specialised industrial technology. The semiconductor industry offers the clearest signal of this shift. At Semicon India 2026 earlier this month, the Centre said it has received investment commitments totalling ₹1 Lakh Cr under the recently notified Semicon 2.0 mission. Global suppliers are also beginning to treat India as part of their production strategy. At Semicon India 2026, Applied Materials alone committed $5 Bn to the country – an investment that reinforces India’s evolution to a potential manufacturing hub. The funding momentum is also picking up across manufacturing-intensive sectors. Advanced hardware and technology startups, spanning aerospace, defence, semiconductors and robotics, raised $365 Mn across 66 deals in the first half (H1) of 2026. And the momentum is percolating into the second half as well. Pixxel recently bagged $100 Mn to expand satellite manufacturing, while DheyaTech mopped up capital to develop indigenous gas turbines. Then, there is Aeron Systems, which secured funding to scale navigation and weather-monitoring systems. Yet, the manufacturing opportunity is not limited to strategic technologies. New regulations are creating demand for domestic capabilities in materials and industrial components. Simultaneously, India’s energy transition is creating another market, driving investor interest in manufacturing required to support electric mobility. Taken together, these developments point to a growing manufacturing ecosystem that is broadening beyond conventional assembly. As a result, a new wave of startups is building products and technologies for the next phase of India’s industrial growth. Against this backdrop, Inc42 is back with the latest edition of its 'Five Manufacturing Startups To Watch'. This edition features startups building low-carbon metals, power electronics, MEMS devices, metal additive manufacturing systems and EV charging hardware. With that said, here are the five manufacturing startups that caught our eye in September. Editor's Note: This list is not a ranking. It is a curated selection of manufacturing startups that have stood out to the Inc42 editorial team this month. Alteon | Builds Ultra-High-Endurance Autonomous Aircraft Conventional aircraft need to land for refuelling and maintenance, making continuous monitoring of oceans, borders and remote infrastructure both expensive and intermittent. Albatrosses, a large sea bird, however, can stay airborne for long periods by harnessing wind energy. The same principle is now being applied to aircraft. Alteon is a Bengaluru-based aerospace startup building autonomous aircraft that fly on dynamic soaring instead of conventional propulsion. It operates in India's UAV market, valued at $470 Mn in 2025 and projected to reach $1.39 Bn by 2030, with defence and surveillance use cases expected to drive growth. Founder Samay Sanghvi began working on the technology with radio-controlled aircraft in 2023 and incorporated the startup in 2025 without a formal engineering degree. It has since grown to a team of 20 and raised $2.5 Mn in pre-seed funding led by Lachy Groom, with Together Fund participating, after earlier grants from Emergent Ventures and 1517. Alteon recently completed an offshore flight test in which its aircraft autonomously flew consecutive loops less than a metre above the ocean surface, and it is now working towards aircraft that can stay airborne for over a year, enabling continuous monitoring of illegal fishing and drug trafficking. Grevoro | Leading India’s Low-Carbon Industrial Shift The carbon emissions embedded in steel and aluminium are now adding to export costs. The European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism entered its payment phase in January 2026, meaning exporters must report a shipment’s emissions or face an additional cost. Grevoro is a Bengaluru-based industrial manufacturing startup producing low-carbon steel, aluminium and allied metals through a network of contract manufacturing partners, with every tonne carrying auditable emissions data. It operates in India's green steel market, where demand is projected to reach 4.49 Mn tonnes by 2030, with construction and infrastructure absorbing most of it. Founded in October 2025 by former Zetwerk executives Vijayanand K and Raghav Jaju, its manufacturing intelligence platform GREMI quantifies embedded carbon at product and lot level from live plant data, built to satisfy CBAM and green steel certification requirements. Its steel line spans scrap-route billets, flat products, structurals, transmission towers and solar mounting structures, and a recycling vertical covers PET bales, rPET flakes and granules. Grevoro raised ₹43 Cr (about $4.7 Mn) in seed funding from the family offices of the Atha and Misra groups, and supplies structural steel for renewable energy projects and construction chemicals. INFAB Semiconductor | Fabricating MEMS Devices In India Sensors that run aircraft, medical devices and industrial machinery, and the microfluidic chips used in diagnostics are largely imported, which means higher prices and long lead times. INFAB Semiconductor is a Bengaluru-based deeptech startup that designs and fabricates micro-electro-mechanical systems (MEMS) pressure switches, transducers and lab-on-chip platforms. Founder and CEO Muthuraman Swaminathan spent years working hands-on with pressure sensors, accelerometers and inertial sensors, incorporating the startup in December 2021. Working out of the cleanroom at IISc’s Centre for Nano Science and Engineering, where it was incubated, INFAB supplies qualification-stage pressure switches and transducers to aerospace and defence programmes, with DRDO, ADA and HAL among its customers, and a revenue run rate of ₹1.5 Cr in FY26. It operates in India's sensors market, projected to grow from $8.5 Bn in 2025 to $17.2 Bn by 2034, and in India's microfluidics market, forecast to grow from $1.08 Bn in 2025 to $1.83 Bn by 2030. Leanwatts | Building Chargers For India's EV Boom India's electric two- and three-wheeler market is scaling faster than the components that keep the vehicles running, and much of the charging hardware is still imported. Leanwatts is a Hyderabad-based power electronics manufacturer building chargers and converters for electric vehicle makers. Founded in October 2023 by Pradeep Chowdary, Sujith Kumar and Abhilash Reddy, the startup designs and produces portable and on-board chargers between 500W and 6.6kW for electric two- and three-wheelers and electric tractors. Its in-house capabilities span hardware design, embedded firmware, product engineering, validation and testing, and it runs a manufacturing facility in Hyderabad. Leanwatts operates in India's EV charging station market, projected to grow from $0.71 Bn in 2025 to $2.48 Bn by 2030. The country had 29,151 charging stations as of December 2025, including 8,805 fast chargers. With $2 Mn (about ₹18.15 Cr) in seed funding, the startup plans to expand into public charging solutions, rectifiers, and hybrid inverters, targeting an annualised revenue run rate of nearly ₹60 Cr by March 2027. ThinkMetal | Advanced Material Manufacturing Solutions Factories rely on custom-made tools such as moulds, dies, jigs and fixtures to make products. These tools can take two to four weeks to produce, often overseas, slowing manufacturers down when they need to quickly test and refine a new product. ThinkMetal is a Chennai-based metal additive manufacturing startup building compact industrial printing systems for these parts. Founded in March 2021 by Sabyasachi Ghosh and Arushi Sharma, the startup's SistemT1 machine uses a process it calls metal fused additive manufacturing, in which it deposits wound metal feedstock layer by layer, then debounds and sinters it to reach full strength. It pairs the hardware with its own FuseX materials and Thinkware software, and claims manufacturers can produce metal parts up to 10X faster and at half the cost of conventional routes. It operates in India's additive manufacturing market, projected to grow from $677.4 Mn in 2023 to $3.75 Bn by 2030. The startup’s customers include Ants Ceramics, ZeQube Technologies and Hosur CNC, and its parts go into automotive, aerospace and defence applications. ThinkMetal has raised about $1.1 Mn so far, including a pre-Series A round led by YourNest Venture Capital, and is scaling production of its first-generation system. ShinyHunters hackers claim to have 2-3TB of sensitive information about FBI employees
Financial extortion doesn’t seem to be the group’s goal this time.
Hacking group ShinyHunters has allegedly stolen extensive amounts of sensitive information from the US Federal Bureau of Investigation that includes details about its employees and job applicants. Reuters reports that it has seen a sample of the data obtained by the attack on the agency, and 404 Media also said it received confirmation of the action from a representative of ShinyHunters. The hackers also appeared responsible for an unauthorized takeover of the FBI website earlier this week.
"We hacked the FBI. We hold data on all FBI employees and applicants," the spokesperson told 404 Media. According to that source, ShinyHunters got the information by using a zero day exploit in the PeopleSoft program from Oracle to obtain access to Amazon Web Services' GovCloud servers.
A statement from the FBI shared with Reuters said that the agency was aware of "a cyber-criminal enterprise group claiming a compromise of the FBIJobs.gov portal and alleged impact to FBI employee personally identifiable information" and that it is "actively and aggressively investigating the matter."
The attackers claim to have 2-3TB of data, but the sample shared with the media appeared to contain names, addresses, telephone numbers, dates of birth, social security numbers and emergency contact details for 5,000 employees at the FBI. The group may also have gathered details about some work assignments for agents and about some FBI units that are working on intelligence, security and counter-espionage efforts, including operations focused on both China and Russia.
Many of ShinyHunters' previous hacks have been aimed at extortion, with actions against parties ranging from Ticketmaster to Rockstar Games in recent years. However, the rep who spoke with 404 Media claimed this move against the FBI was "not financially motivated" but rather aimed at coercing the government agency to remove or amend a previous statement made about ShinyHunters. In a report from May, the FBI said the hacking group "exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims."

When Gloria Steinem’s plane touched down in Bombay in 1957, she could not have known that her stay in India would become what she later called a “pivotal, life-dividing event [that] made me who I am”.
She was 22, with a degree in government from Smith college and was travelling on a Chester Bowles fellowship.
India was “not only a place I’d always wanted to go, but (also) an escape from a very kind and tempting man to whom I was engaged and knew I shouldn’t marry,” Steinem later wrote. The prospect of marrying Blair Chotzinoff, a pilot from a well-connected New York family, depressed her “enormously because marriage meant the end of life to me”.
Funds were short, so she wangled a free airline ticket in exchange for an article “that I still feel guilty to this day because I never wrote”.
While in London waiting for her Indian visa, she discovered she was pregnant and obtained an illegal abortion – an experience that underpinned her conviction that, without control over reproduction, women could not control their own lives.
Steinem, who died this week at the age of 92, arrived in Delhi with romantic expectations of “ageless beauty and jewelled elephants”. They were quickly displaced. Driving from the airport, she had what she called her “first glimpse of Asian poverty”, seeing people sleeping on pavements and doorsteps.
She lived at Miranda House, one of Delhi University’s leading women’s colleges, immersing herself in student life.
“At night in our rooms we have long sessions and are asked everything: the Christians’ conception of God, the intricacies of western lingerie, the dating system, how much milk the American cow gives,” Steinem wrote.
Steinem’s Indian years have been extensively documented by Rashida Shafiq of Southern Methodist University, who drew on her fellowship reports and other archival material for a recently published PhD thesis.
She adopted the sari as everyday dress, writing: “Saris make one stand straighter and walk more slowly and worry less about time and efficiency.”
India was not entirely unfamiliar territory. Her mother and paternal grandmother had been Theosophists, part of a spiritual movement that drew heavily on Hindu and Buddhist ideas such as karma and reincarnation, and at college Steinem had written a paper on the Communist party of India.
When her fellowship money ran out, she supported herself by writing for Indian newspapers, doing advertising work and taking occasional modelling jobs – including posing in saris.
Wider travel in the country brought some of her most important encounters.
She met Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, the former princess and follower of Mahatma Gandhi who became independent India’s first health minister, and spent two hours with Indira Gandhi, whom she described as “shy to uncertainty, gentle and a little whimsical”.
At a Radical Humanist study camp in Mussoorie, followers of the former communist MN Roy debated democracy, individual freedom and political organisation. Steinem later said she learned there that “radical” need not mean violent or extremist, but could mean “going to the root,” and that “the means we choose dictate the ends we achieve”.
But some of her most lasting political education happened on the road.
On a journey from Calcutta to Kerala, Steinem travelled third class in a railway carriage reserved for women, which she later described as “a dormitory on wheels”.
Women settled in with children and food, nursing babies, sharing tiffins and talking. They wanted to know everything about her and conversations ranged across marriage, childbirth, contraception and family life. “Had I been isolated in a car, this talking circle could never have happened,” Steinem wrote later.
Years before American feminist “consciousness-raising” groups brought women together to discover that supposedly private problems were widely shared, Steinem had watched women in India exchange intimate experiences among themselves.
But the experience she regarded as most important came after caste violence erupted in what was then Madras state in 1957.
Steinem joined workers associated with the movement of Vinoba Bhave, a leading disciple of Gandhi, who were walking from village to village trying to counter rumours, discourage revenge and bring people together to talk.
She travelled with little more than “a cup, a comb and the sari I wore”.
In settlements scarred by violence, meetings were held beneath trees and in village courtyards.
“I listened as villagers narrated burnings, murders, thefts and rapes, with fear and trauma needing no translation,” she wrote.
The lesson was to listen before offering solutions. “Ask the people what they want, don’t tell them what they need,” was how Steinem later described it.
She remembered “the ancient and modern magic of groups in which anyone may speak in turn, everyone must listen and consensus is more important than time”.
“If you want to know how people live, you have to go where they live; if you want people to listen to you, you have to listen to them,” she later said. “I believe I learned that in India.”
Steinem returned to the United States in 1958, more than a decade before she became one of the leading figures in the women’s movement.
“I couldn’t integrate into the rest of my life these two very, very crucial years,” she recalled. “It was only after the women’s movement started that links began to be forged.”
She repeatedly connected her later organising methods with India. “The first organising I did was in India, though I didn’t realise it then,” she said.
Her years travelling across America as a feminist activist, she later wrote, were “just a western version of walking in villages”.
And when Ms. magazine, which Steinem co-founded, produced its spring 1972 preview issue, its cover featured an American housewife depicted as the many-armed Hindu goddess Kali, pregnant with her hands clutching a frying pan, duster, telephone, iron and other symbols of the domestic demands placed on women.
Steinem said the image “had come out of my Indian past”.

A Zoom call today with 500 senior Warner Bros. staffers about the Paramount-AGs settlement did little to dissipate the Mordor-like gloomy clouds over the Burbank, CA lot, to use a Lord of the Rings reference.
Today’s Zoom, which has been routine since Paramount won the bid for Warner Bros. Discovery, was led by WBD Studios Chief Operating Officer Simon Robinson, who is running point on the merger integration, as well as Chief Legal Officer Priya Aiyar, WBD Chief Comms Robert Gibbs and HR Boss Amy Girdwood. The four conceded that they didn’t have that much visibility into Paramount’s plans for the new company but indicated that the anticipation is for the deal to close in about 10 days, in line with Paramount CEO David Ellison‘s two-week timeframe provided on Monday.
The name and the leadership structure of the new company would likely be announced ahead of close, the executives reportedly said, though they weren’t clear as to when exactly that would be. We heard that Girldwood told leaders to take a moment to reflect on the great work accomplished during their tenures.
Watch on Deadline
“It feels like a scramble,” one source said.
To say staffers were surprised by the attorneys general settlement Monday doesn’t really cover it.
“It was a big shock,” one person said. “If you were riding the rollercoaster, you felt like things were not progressing.”
Still, even if the settlement and its timing came as a surprise, the ultimate result seemed inevitable as WBD CEO David Zaslav has been hellbent on selling the studio. David Ellison’s takeover of the Albert, Harry, Sam and Jack Warner founded cinematic institution “was always bound to happen,” one insider exclaimed.
Zaslav, who is likely to walk away with more than $600M from the $110B merger, was not on today’s Zoom, we’re told.
The Ellison-run Paramount has said that the Warner Bros. acquisition will yield $6B in synergy savings, and that doesn’t necessarily translate into job cuts, rather inefficiencies in other structural areas (i.e. real estate portfolio, data servers).
But Warner Bros staffers aren’t buying that.
“We’ve been here before. We know what it looks like,” said one insider about the changeover in ownership of Warner Bros. over the last decade. It was only four years ago that AT&T dumped Warner Media into the hands of Discovery.
Myriad people inside Warner Bros. are cynical about the capping of severances and the fact that only a few at the top are bound for a windfall. There’s also ire over the pausing of contract renewals due to the merger, as well as irritable infighting between departments about theatrical failures this year; No one title has cleared $100M at the domestic box office — the highest-grossing movie stateside is Wuthering Heights at $84M. Home entertainment and data analytics divisions were none too happy about DC’s Supergirl tanking. With its $186M net production cost and a global gross of $126.3M, key staffers believe that DC chose the wrong comic-book character to adapt.
On the immediate horizon as the Paramount-Warner Bros. marriage comes together is the $125M Tom Cruise starring, Alejandro Iñárritu directed, Legendary-produced Digger, opening on Oct. 2. While domestic debut prospects are around $20M, Warners is hoping to get past any sour headlines about box office-to-cost ratios on the film, much like they did on One Battle After Another, as the 4x Oscar winning filmmaker’s latest Doctor Strangelove-like epic is being primed as an awards season contender; a chip that Paramount really doesn’t have on its year-end schedule.
The new Paramount could also inherit another awards contender and its first billion dollar grossing title since Skydance took over the Melrose Ave lot in Legendary/Warner Bros’ Dune: Part Three. That opens on Dec. 18.
At Paramount, the epic would fall into the arms of global marketing and distribution guru — and former WB senior ranking theatrical suit — Josh Goldstine, who led the Dune franchise across two movies to a $1.12B global gross and eight Oscar wins.
We’ve heard on the Paramount side, that it’s still TBD in regards to how the merger will handle duplications in marketing and distribution.
“There could be more fear on the Paramount side,” says one source in the know when it comes to marketing. How’s that? Goldstine will be back together with the team he built at Warners, meaning Dana Nussbaum and Christian Davin in global marketing and Creative Advertising EVP John Stanford.
There’s also a thick fog around those staffers who were bound to decamp from Warner Bros. proper in the previously planned Gunnar Wiedenfels led spinoff Global Networks.
Yes, Warner Bros. staffers are already putting themselves out there for other jobs. Some of them have already found new gigs — read: Former EVP of Comms Katie Martin Kelly. Prized by De Luca and Abdy, Martin Kelly high-tailed it for Netflix as VP of Comms as her contract ended, rather than wait for the Russian roulette the new conglomerate could bring. Former HBO Max EVP Originals Marketing Pia Barlow found a new job at Amazon MGM Studios as their Series Marketing VP, a gig that triggered WBD to sue the shooting site/streamer for poaching.
The deal closing would likely trigger more voluntary departures as many WBD executives had been waiting to cash out stock options post-transaction and had been bound by contracts that typically provide a way out in case of change of ownership.
“Since David Zaslav took control of Warner Bros, there’s just been thousands of jobs lost,” one former Turner publicist emphatically told us. “Those are jobs that the entertainment industry is never going to get back.”
And therein lies the ultimate piercing wound for any Warners or Paramount employee in the danger zone: The fact that there are not a lot of jobs out there is a big deal.
What’s more, adds a source, “People are very concerned about the survival of the Warner Bros. brand.”
Counters a senior ranking insider at the conglomerate to us: “There’s a feeling of relief from senior executives to junior staff about the possibilities that the new company can bring. They were very excited by David Ellison’s note.”
For now, Paramount is inheriting at least 39 Warner Bros. theatrical releases on the calendar dated between Oct. 2 this year and the end of 2028. That output reps 56% of what will be a current combined 70 features between the two studios. During the agita of Netflix and Paramount courting Warner Bros., the studio’s greenlighting of productions has been at a loud hum. Assumptions were made by some that Warner Bros. Motion Pictures would be in purgatory during the merger talk time, that filmmakers and reps would be wary of taking projects to them. That’s not really an option for content creators at a time when it’s a miracle for any major motion picture to get off the ground.
Something to look forward to: While a Barbie sequel hasn’t been greenlit yet due to constant talks with top tier talent such as director Greta Gerwig and stars Margot Robbie and Ryan Gosling, expect that to be one of the first orders of business in the new David Ellison-owned Paramount-Warner Bros.
Beams one optimistic Warner exec, “The new merger gives us the all the financial resources to compete on a level with the big streamers.”

Trump’s push to acquire Greenland almost broke NATO. The winner of it all may be ... Greenland
In the end, it was all kisses and laughter as President Donald Trump hailed his “fantastic” relationship with Denmark and Greenland

In the end, it was all kisses and laughter as President Donald Trump hailed his “fantastic” relationship with Denmark and Greenland after signing a new security deal that America’s European allies hope will close one of the most dangerous chapters in transatlantic relations.
Trump’s territorial ambitions over Greenland almost broke the NATO military alliance and shattered trust with one of America’s oldest and closest partners. The new defense agreement puts an end to the standoff. But was it worth the cost?
While the new defense agreement is a bit broader, the United States already had extensive military access under an existing 1951 deal and all the gains laid out in the agreement signed on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday could, ostensibly, have been achieved by asking nicely a year ago. The trans-Atlantic distrust created since the end of 2024 seems a very high price to pay for what may ultimately be a fairly incremental gain.
Interestingly, one place may emerge from this standoff as the real winner: Greenland itself.
The promised investments and contracts may never fully materialize, but the episode marks a major step forward in its push for greater autonomy and a more influential seat at the table. Greenland is no longer merely the subject of foreign policy decided by its former colonial rulers. Increasingly, it is helping to shape it.
There's been progress toward self-determination
“A notable change is Greenland itself at the table today, signing this agreement," said Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen speaking to a room cram packed with journalists and officials at the UN to witness the signing of the deal.
That's an understatement. The world’s largest island, home to about 56,000 mostly Inuit people, was still considered a colony until the early 1950s. Progress towards greater self-determination has been slow and it wasn't until 2009 that Greenland became a self-governing country within the Kingdom of Denmark.
Even then, while the Self-Government Act recognized Greenland’s right to independence when requested by local voters in the future, Denmark retained control of defense and foreign affairs.
“I cannot stress it enough: This is the first time that we are venturing into a binding agreement as a country," Naaja Nathanielsen, one of Greenland’s two lawmakers in the Danish parliament and a former government minister in Nuuk, told The Associated Press. “That is a huge step forward in our quest for more self-autonomy.”
Denmark and Greenland confront their own troubled past
Like most former colonial powers that discover history keeps receipts, Denmark's ties with Greenland are complicated. Greenland's economy is heavily dependent on Denmark, families and students often live between the two territories and the cultural linguistic ties are strong. Yet underwriting modern relations are centuries of Danish policies that dehumanized Greenlanders and their families.
They included forced contraception, the removal of Inuit children for reeducation by Danish foster families, and controversial parental-competency tests that led to children being separated from their parents.
“For many, many years you believed that you were a good colonizer,” Múte Bourup Egede, then Greenland's prime minister and now its foreign minister, reminded Danish journalists early last year, shortly after a newly elected Trump made his first military threat against the island. “But time has also caught up with us, and ... cruel things have come to light.”
The abuses are not distant history; many victims remain alive. Hundreds of Inuit women have claimed compensation from Denmark, alleging that health authorities violated their rights by fitting them with intrauterine devices — often when they were teenagers and without their informed consent. Danish authorities estimate that as many as 4,500 women and girls received IUDs between the 1960s and mid-1970s.
While the first official apology for the historic mistreatment had long been coming it was finally delivered in the summer of 2025.
The standoff with the United States “has been applying pressure and focused some of the Danish attention” on reconciliation with Greenland said Ulrik Pram Gad, a senior researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies, but “perhaps, some Greenlanders feel that it’s not as credible as it could have been without Trump.”
Trump's involvement changed the equation
While Denmark moved to address past grievances, anger with Trump's tactics also helped shore up support for its sovereignty and take the edge off calls by some in Greenland for quick moves to independence.
At the height of the crisis over Trump's ambitions in January, Nielsen said that “if we have to choose between the United States and Denmark here and now, we choose Denmark. We choose NATO."
For Denmark, the main victory is no doubt getting the US president off its back and succeeding in framing the crisis as a European security problem.
Danish and Greenlandic diplomats “have been working very hard to have European allies be part of this," Pram Gad said. "The result is an attempt to patch together the NATO alliance.”
And while Denmark has accepted some limitations to its sovereignty, investments by adversary countries such as Russia had long been off the table.
“The benefit of keeping the transatlantic alliance, or patching it together, or at least not allowing Greenland to be the occasion for Trump to blow it up, I think that counts heavily on both the Danish and the Greenlandic cost-benefit analysis here,” he said.
After Tuesday’s signing ceremony, relief was palpable. But while the Danish and Greenland delegations celebrated with a cold beer on a rooftop bar in Manhattan, the Greenland crisis has scarred a once undefiable bond. It leaves leaders in Copenhagen, Nuuk and other European capitals now assessing the reliability of the United States — and whether a signed agreement can repair trust once it has been broken.

Meta could be beating OpenAI to the punch on the hardware front.
The social media giant announced that it has put its viral new AI agent, Muse, into a small device you can speak to.
The gizmo is called "Charm," and only a few have been made so far, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced Wednesday at the company's Connect event. He said it should be ready to ship in time for the holiday shopping season.
"We've packed a lot of technology into this little guy," Zuckerberg said onstage. "If you're not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the best way to talk to your Muse and show it what's going on around you."
It signals that Meta is becoming a serious competitor in the race to build an AI device that goes beyond smartphones. It's also a shot across the bow at OpenAI, which has created a lot of buzz around its own efforts to build an AI device.
Last year, OpenAI bought legendary Apple designer Jony Ive's startup to work on a physical device. So far, little is publicly known about that device.
Zuckerberg only teased Charm at the very end of the conference. Charm has a screen, which showcases "Jolly," the mascot of Muse, which Meta launched earlier this month.
While the overwhelming majority of Meta's revenue comes from its ads business, it's making a big bet on hardware. Getting people to use Meta products through its own devices would unlock major advantages for the tech giant.
Charm was born out of Meta's new design lab, led by former Apple interface design chief Alan Dye, Bloomberg reported. Meta didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on the report.
Meta has been expanding its hardware efforts elsewhere.
Earlier this year, Meta tapped Rui Xu, a veteran with years of experience at China's top tech companies, to lead a hardware effort inside its superintelligence division, Business Insider previously reported.
OpenAI didn't immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider.

'This is our company': Nigerians show off oil wealth after share-buying frenzy
- Published
Every Nigerian is now an oil magnate.
At least that is what the social media memes would have you believe as investor fever hits the country.
Nigerians have been eager to have a piece of the energy business that was built up by the country's – and continent's – richest man: Aliko Dangote.
More than four billion shares in his giant oil refinery – representing just over 3% of the company - went on the market on Monday in Africa's biggest-ever sale of its kind.
The minimum purchase was 10 shares for about $4 (£3) and despite this only representing a miniscule portion of the firm, many are now celebrating and joking about their new-found (part-)owner status.
One popular social media video has a Nigerian narrating how he stopped a speeding Dangote company lorry driver, telling him not to be reckless with company property.
Other memes show investors trying to phone up Dangote to discuss business matters.
And the term "Yangote" – a pun in the Hausa language essentially meaning "we all have a share now" - has been trending on social media.
On the first day of the Initial Public Offering (IPO), investment apps crashed as they could not handle the high demand.
Bamboo, which runs one of the most popular investor tools here, later apologised, saying: "We know we let you down."
Public affairs analyst Jamil Ubah said he had rarely seen Nigerians as excited about something as this. He argued that it fed the dream that it could lead to greater riches for a population that is often battling to make ends meet.
"I think the hope for the common man is that his money will grow into something big, and don't forget this is coming at a time when many are struggling as the economy is not doing great," he told the BBC.
Dangote wanted this to be "the people's IPO" with drivers, cooks, cleaners and servants having the chance to be part of something big.
And they took him at his word.
Twenty-five-year-old clothes seller Idris Lawal Musa made his first-ever stock exchange purchase and told the BBC he was happy after investing 21,000 naira ($16; £12) in 40 shares.
"It is no longer Dangote but 'Yangote', the company belongs to us now," he said while laughing.
But he may make a quick sale.
"I am a trader by profession and when I see that the shares have increased in price I will sell," he noted.
The popularity also reflects a growing investment culture among younger Nigerians who have embraced mobile trading platforms, cryptocurrencies and digital savings products.
But fear of missing out may have also pushed some to get into the investment business.
In the build-up to the IPO, social media platforms were awash with financial conversations. People shared subscription guides, debated valuation metrics and encouraged friends and family to participate.
But amid the frenzy, experts have warned that there are risks – shares can go down in value, as well as up, meaning people could lose some, or all, of their investment.
Financial analyst Shuaib Uwais said prospective investors should avoid thinking of the IPO as a guaranteed route to wealth.
He urged people to consider a number of factors that could impact the refinery's future performance, including disruptions to crude oil supply, operational challenges, regulatory changes and fluctuations in demand for refined petroleum products.
"If for any reason the company experiences difficulty in sourcing its raw materials, there could be challenges," he told the BBC.
Nevertheless, the IPO has given people the chance to be part of this home-grown success story.
Dangote's sprawling refinery on the outskirts of Lagos, which began operating two years ago and now processes around 700,000 barrels of crude a day, has transformed the fortunes of Nigeria's oil sector.
Until recently, Africa's largest crude oil producer had no refining capacity and had to import the finished product. Now the Dangote refinery is feeding much of the domestic demand.
But for Dangote, the share offer is about raising cash to fund the growth of the business, something that the country's mini-magnates may now be able to get behind.

‘Proud to have Trump’s endorsement’ post gets MAGA rep slapped with community note
With the president’s favorability at record lows, a Republican gubernatorial candidate locked in a heated race wiped nearly all references to Trump from his campaign site — and then got called out for it

Rep. Byron Donalds was hit with a community note on X after attempting to un-distance himself from President Donald Trump, who gave him his endorsement in Florida’s nail-biter gubernatorial race.
Donalds, long a staunch proponent of Trump and MAGA, wrote on the platform that he was proud to celebrate Trump’s endorsement, and took a swing at journalists and political junkies alike for making a big deal out of his campaign’s decision to strip references to that endorsement from his website. “I am proud to have President Trump’s endorsement,” wrote Donalds. “While everyone is focused on our website, check out our policy proposals to make life more affordable for Floridians.”
But the X post quickly received a community note claiming that the Trump endorsement only reappeared after news sites reported it had been stripped from Donalds’ website, previously having been featured on the homepage on donation buttons, banners and other widgets. The site also previously featured a photo of Donalds and his wife Erika posing with Trump.
A third-term congressman, Donalds is now running against Democratic candidate David Jolly, a former member of the House, in the general election. Jolly’s bid would be an uphill battle for any Democrat in increasingly red Florida, but it has become a surprisingly competitive race as the Republican brand has suffered nationally in recent months at the hands of Trump, whose unpopular war with Iran continues to drag on and push prices for average Americans higher and higher. The state is also home to a Senate race this cycle which has Republicans sweating for the same reason.
Jolly and Donalds were in a dead heat in a poll released last week by Florida Politics, separated by just one percentage point. The close margin seen in the polling is part of a bigger picture this cycle where candidates in red-purple states like Texas, Florida, Iowa, Ohio and others are finding themselves in a rapidly worsening political environment for conservative candidates and particularly those closely aligned with the president.
With that in mind, more than half a dozen references urging users to “Chip in to Support Trump-Endorsed Byron Donalds” and labels calling him a “TRUMP-ENDORSED Proven Conservative Fighter”, or otherwise highlighting Trump’s endorsement were stripped from the website in the days following the Florida Republican primary in August. Trump’s sole references now appear on the endorsements landing page — far from hidden, but also a marked shift for a candidate who was previously running with close association with the president.
"Our campaign website reflects Byron's focus on the issues that matter most to Floridians -- affordability, insurance costs, and government transparency. He's running to be the next Governor of Florida, is proud to have President Trump's endorsement, and has real policy proposals to tackle those issues," a campaign spokesperson told ABC News.
The removal of multiple references to the president comes as Trump’s approval rating still hovers in the mid-thirties, and support for the war in Iran is plunging to new lows.
A CNN/SRSS poll this week found that three in four U.S. adults are opposed to the war, and polling has found for months that as many as seven in ten Americans do not believe Trump has a plan to get the U.S. out of the conflict.
Donalds won the August primary in a factional GOP contest that pitted him against a top ally of Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, Trump’s 2024 primary rival. Jay Collins has since endorsed Donalds’ bid for governor. Another candidate in the race was James Fishback, who ran an insurgent bid that was criticized by many for leaning heavily into overtly racist language against Donalds and his supporters.
A defeat of Donalds in November would be a massive blow to Republicans in Florida, who are highly organized and better funded than Democratic rivals in the state. It would also be a personal blow to the political capital of the president within the Republican Party, as Donalds’ opponents warned that he was a weak candidate for the general election and are generally looking for any opportunity to weaken Trump’s grip on the party.
n Florida, Trump’s adopted home, the president’s dominance in Republican Party politics is well-known; in 2024, he successfully won endorsements from the majority of the state’s congressional delegation, dealing a blow to DeSantis out of the gate.
Donalds is far from the most vocal Trump loyalist in D.C. but has not wavered from the president’s side publicly. He was previously floated as a candidate for speaker by a coalition of pro-Trump representatives during the ousting of Kevin McCarthy from the role in 2023.

Actor Swaroopa Ghosh has opened up about her experience of working with Manoj Bajpayee in Last Man In Tower, describing the collaboration as a deeply rewarding experience. She praised the actor for his ability to create a comfortable working environment while also bringing a rare intensity and spontaneity to his performances.

Last Man In Tower brings together Manoj Bajpayee, Divya Dutta and Boman Irani in a story that explores human relationships and conflicts. For Ghosh, working alongside Bajpayee became an opportunity to experience first-hand the spontaneity and emotional depth he brings to a performance.

Following the recent reports of a Houthi drone being intercepted south of Mecca (here, here), a video showing a missile intercepting in the night sky is being widely shared on social media with the claim that it shows Saudi Arabia’s air defences intercepting a Houthi drone near Mecca in September 2026 (here, here, here). Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: The viral video shows Saudi Arabia intercepting a Houthi drone that attempted to enter Mecca’s airspace.
Fact: The viral video does not show the recent alleged Houthi attack on Mecca. The video is from September 2025 and shows Saudi forces intercepting a missile fired by Yemen’s Houthis towards Israel near the Prophet’s Mosque in Medina. Recently, Saudi Arabia claimed that its forces destroyed a Houthi drone south of Mecca on 15 September 2026. However, the Houthis denied targeting Mecca. Hence, the claim is MISLEADING.
According to reports, Saudi Arabia said its air defence forces intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone south of Mecca on 15 September 2026, before it entered the restricted airspace over the holy city. The Houthis denied targeting Mecca (here, here, here, here).
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to several older posts carrying the same visuals. We found that the video was shared as early as September 2025, nearly a year before the current incident. Greater Kashmir published the video on 13 September 2025 with a caption claiming that it showed an alleged Houthi missile being intercepted over Medina, near the Prophet’s Mosque. We also found that The Times of India had published the same visuals on 12 September 2025, reporting on an alleged missile interception near the Prophet’s Mosque in Medina.
The Yemeni news outlet Belqees TV had posted these visuals on 12 September 2025, with a caption stating that a missile had been intercepted over Medina while Saudi authorities remained silent. More reports related to this can be seen here, here.
To sum up, an old video is being shared as recent visuals of a Houthi drone attack near Mecca.

U.S. health regulators will review the scientific evidence on testosterone use in menopausal women on Thursday, including its benefits, risks, dosing and role in female health, as well as perspectives from doctors and patients.
The public meeting, which the U.S. Food and Drug Administration said could help guide future research and drug development, comes as a growing number of women are turning to testosterone to manage menopause symptoms.
There is no FDA-approved testosterone therapy for women, despite years of off-label use to treat low sexual desire, known as hypoactive sexual desire disorder, or HSDD.
Last year, the FDA removed the boxed warning about increased cardiovascular risk from testosterone products for men after reviewing post-marketing studies, though the products still carry warnings about increased blood pressure.
Physicians who prescribe testosterone to women typically rely on low doses of products approved for men, often dividing existing products such as AbbVie's AndroGel and Keenova Therapeutics' Testim, or on compounded formulations.
The lack of a female-specific product creates practical challenges for clinicians, said Diana Tordoff, an instructor in obstetrics and gynecology at Stanford, noting that an approved product could provide standardised dosing, labeling and safety-monitoring guidance and potentially improve insurance coverage.
Still, some experts say key questions remain unresolved. More long-term safety data are needed, said Stephanie Faubion, director of Mayo Clinic's Center for Women's Health.
The United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa have approved or licensed testosterone products specifically for women.
The FDA's request for public comments ahead of the meeting attracted hundreds of submissions, many from women describing improved libido, energy and quality of life while using testosterone.
Evidence and safety gaps
Interest in testosterone among menopausal women has grown alongside claims on social media that it can improve energy, muscle mass, bone health and cognition, though specialists say the evidence is strongest for HSDD.
"We do not have any evidence in women that it will improve muscle mass or bone density or mood or well-being or really any other metric," Faubion said.
Karen Adams, director of Stanford Medicine's Program in Menopause and Healthy Aging, said testosterone has been reviewed by the FDA four times for use in women but has never been approved because of a lack of long-term safety data and concerns about cardiovascular and breast cancer risks.
The FDA has approved non-testosterone options like Sprout Pharmaceuticals' Addyi and Cosette Pharmaceuticals' Vyleesi for certain patients with HSDD.
Testosterone is generally not recommended for women with a history of breast cancer because it can be converted to estrogen in the body that can drive some cancers.
Excessive testosterone exposure can cause acne and increased hair growth, physicians said, while rarer effects such as voice deepening and hair loss may be irreversible.
Studies show that testosterone therapy is generally considered safe for men with medically diagnosed low levels of the hormone when prescribed and monitored by a doctor.
Tordoff and Adams are leading Stanford's MIX-T pilot study examining how low-dose testosterone affects vaginal health and the vaginal microbiome in postmenopausal women. Results are expected within the next two years.

Asian shares were mixed Wednesday after Wall Street held near its record and oil prices fell following U.S. President Donald Trump’s remarks that United States and Iranian officials had a “very good” meeting Tuesday on the sidelines at the United Nations.
U.S. futures were higher.
South Korea’s Kospi rose 0.5% to 7,052.75. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng lost 0.8% to 24,896.04. The Shanghai Composite index slid 0.4% to 3,938.08. Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 added 0.3% to 8,779.80.

Japan’s Nikkei 225 was closed on Wednesday for a holiday and will resume trading Thursday.
Oil prices fell and remained below $100 a barrel on Tuesday after Trump said U.S. and Iranian officials met on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York following his threat during an address to the annual gathering that the U.S. might “annihilate” the Islamic Republic if a deal couldn’t be made.
“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world,” Trump said. “Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”
