Colombia's president sends troops to a Caribbean city after an outburst of violence
Troops are patrolling the streets of Santa Marta, Colombia, as President Abelardo de la Espriella tries to restore order after violence erupted there
SANTA MARTA, Colombia -- Troops patrolled the unusually empty streets of Colombia’s Caribbean resort city of Santa Marta on Wednesday as President Abelardo de la Espriella tried to restore order a day after an outburst of violence blamed on a drug-trafficking gang.
Residents in a working-class neighborhood in the city’s northeast lined up outside the few supermarkets that remained open as police officers carrying rifles stood guard.
“We woke up this morning afraid to go out and see what the situation was, but you have to go out to stock up on supplies,” taxi driver Antonio Ochoa said.
On Tuesday, arsonists set ablaze at least three vehicles, including a taxi and a public bus, and armed men threatened merchants in broad daylight, plunging the city into fear. De la Espriella blamed the Sierra Nevada Self-Defense Forces and ordered troops to the city in response.
The president said the group planned to “set fire” to parts of the Caribbean region in retaliation for a military operation that killed José Pérez Villanueva, known as “Cholo” and identified by the government as the group’s second-in-command.
“I swear by Colombia and by my life that I will finish them off,” de la Espriella warned Tuesday night from Santa Marta, wearing a bulletproof vest while touring the city in an armored vehicle. “I will leave no stone unturned until I find them... and if they do not surrender, I will send them to hell in a body bag.”
De la Espriella took office last month after vowing to wield an “iron fist” against illegal armed groups. His deployment of troops to Santa Marta, a city of about 480,000 people, is the first of his administration.
The president also has halted all peace talks with armed groups begun by his progressive predecessor, Gustavo Petro. Those included negotiations with self-defense forces like the Sierra Nevada one, which emerged following the demobilization of paramilitary groups in the early 2000s.
According to the police, the group operates in the departments of Magdalena — where Santa Marta is located — La Guajira, and Cesar, and has been implicated in crimes such as drug trafficking and extortion.
Magdalena Gov. María Margarita Guerra toured the public market Wednesday where all vegetable, fruit and meat stalls were shuttered. She and her team handed out flyers reading “Extortion doesn’t pay” and encouraged vendors to reopen.
“I know it’s hard to trust. There have been decades of violence, but we have to do our part and say, ‘Let’s unite,’” Guerra told reporters. She called reopening the public market vital, describing it as the “heart of commerce.”
Guerra estimated that more than 1,500 additional police officers and military personnel had been deployed across the region.
Meanwhile, hundreds of tourists relaxed on Santa Marta’s beach, listening to music, drinking beer and sunbathing, even as most nearby restaurants and shops remained closed.
Orlando Andrade, 64, said he was caught off guard by the armed strike in the city center Tuesday when he noticed public transportation was scarce. When he asked why, a street vendor told him to “hide.”
“The strike did affect us because we couldn’t enjoy other beaches,” said Andrade, a journalist vacationing with his family.

As respiratory virus season nears and fall vaccination drives get underway, more than half of US children are facing uncertainty over access to this year’s COVID-19 shot. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has unexpectedly delayed the distribution of the shots to a key federal program and some states.
Usually, the CDC would allow states to order the newly available seasonal COVID-19 vaccines through the federal Vaccine for Children (VFC) program, which provides vaccines at no cost to children who are uninsured, underinsured, Medicaid-eligible, or Indigenous people in the US. Approximately 52 percent of all US children are eligible for vaccines through the program.
Additionally, The Guardian reports that at least 11 states and one US territory are part of a universal vaccine purchase program, in which they buy all vaccines for children—regardless of their ability to pay or insurance status—through contracts otherwise for the VFC. The 11 states and one territory include: Alaska, Connecticut, Hawaii, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Rhode Island, Vermont, Washington, Wyoming, and American Samoan.
“The delay in VFC means delays in these states’ ability to get vaccine for all children,” Demetre Daskalakis, former director of the CDC’s National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases and chief medical officer at Callen-Lorde Community Health Center, told The Guardian.
Kennedy’s track record
In a statement, the Department of Health and Human Services told Ars Technica that “CDC has not yet finalized procurement decisions for COVID-19 vaccines through the Vaccines for Children and Section 317 programs.” The department—currently run by ardent anti-vaccine activist Robert F. Kennedy Jr.—declined to answer the question of why there was a delay in the decision. But the statement suggested that Trump officials were questioning whether children should get the vaccine.
“HHS and CDC are committed to … ensuring that vaccines purchased through federally funded programs are appropriate for the populations those programs serve,” the department said in the statement. It added that additional information about the decision will be released “soon.”
The unexplained delay fits with Kennedy’s well-established disdain for COVID-19 vaccines, which he has falsely called “the deadliest vaccine[s] ever made,” and has actively tried to blame them for the deaths of children, despite no evidence to support the allegations.

Anthony Albanese says OpenAI agent hacked Medicare
Anthony Albanese has revealed an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare in June.
The prime minister made the comments at the UN summit in New York.
This incident occurred in June this year and involved an Open AI agent gaining unauthorised access into the public-facing Medicare statistics reporting service portal, which is administered by Services Australia.
The AI agent accessed both public and non-public files.
A forensic investigation, aided by the Australian Signals Directorate, is now under way to ascertain more information, including what other government systems were affected.
The Medicare statistics reporting portal is a public-facing statistics portal that contains non-sensitive Medicare information relating to data and statistics, such as spending.
No personal information is believed to have been accessed at this stage but investigations are ongoing.
Evidence currently available is there is no broader compromise to the Services Australia network.
Nonetheless, this situation is obviously unacceptable.
Today, I spoke with the CEO of Open AI, Sam Altman, to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident.
And I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred.

OECD says Australia will struggle to get underlying inflation below 3%
The OECD says Australia will struggle to bring underlying inflation back below 3% in 2027, despite sub-par economic growth in this year and the next.
The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development in its interim economic outlook flagged that the world economy had, once again, proved more resilient than expected to the global energy shock triggered by the ongoing Iran war.
The artificial intelligence boom had papered over many of the cracks, the report said, adding that “global economic prospects remain heavily dependent on whether a durable resolution to the Middle East conflict is achieved”.
With fuel costs here jumping over recent weeks and inflation proving more persistent than hoped, there is a strong consensus that the Reserve Bank will deliver another interest rate hike next Tuesday – the fourth this year.
The OECD projected Australia’s headline inflation would drop from 4.1% this year, to 2.8% in 2027.
But “core” inflation – which removes the effects of big price swings, like for fuel – would prove harder to shift back into the RBA’s 2-3% target range.
The OECD expected the underlying price growth measure to ease from 3.5% in 2026 to 3.1% in 2027.
“Faced with renewed energy price shocks and stronger than expected demand pressures, and at a time when inflation is already above target in many economies, central banks need to ensure that underlying inflation pressures are durably contained,” the OECD said.

India needs firms that can grow, integrate into global value chains and compete internationally. To make this happen, the Quality Control Order (QCO) reassessment exercise needs to move forward.
Concerns over India’s QCOs and other non-tariff barriers also surfaced during the WTO’s eighth Trade Policy Review of India, held in July 2026, and were raised not only by major trading partners such as the European Union and the United States, but also by fellow BRICS members, including Brazil, China and Indonesia.
The number of products covered under QCOs expanded rapidly after 2019, from 88 products in 2019 to 765 by the end of December 2024. However, the pace of expansion slowed considerably towards the end of 2025. This was driven by an important shift in the government’s approach, with several QCOs being revoked or suspended, particularly those covering intermediate goods, as mandatory certification had raised concerns about input availability, costs and potential supply-chain disruptions.
The government’s new order
Recently, the government introduced the Transition Facilitation (Quality Control) Order, 2026, notified by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) on June 25, 2026. The order seeks to ease regulatory bottlenecks by allowing eligible firms facing difficulties in obtaining BIS Scheme-I certification to source products temporarily from BIS Scheme-II-licensed suppliers in specified sectors, including toys, footwear and air conditioners. Access to this transition mechanism is subject to prescribed eligibility criteria and approval by a committee constituted by the DPIIT.
These developments are welcome steps towards reducing the risk that quality regulations inadvertently disrupt supply chains or constrain domestic manufacturing. More than 600 QCO-covered products remain to be reassessed, including several critical intermediate inputs used across key manufacturing sectors such as chemicals, steel, textiles, machinery and electronics, and rubber and plastics.
Existing regulations can place a disproportionate burden on smaller industrial players, both by constraining their access to critical inputs and by imposing relatively high compliance costs. Given the extensive downstream linkages of these inputs, the next phase of QCO rationalisation should focus particularly on regulations affecting intermediate goods and assess their implications not only for product quality but also for input availability, costs, competitiveness and domestic value addition.
Findings of a recent study
In this regard, a recent CSEP study examined this question in detail for firms that use chemicals. Chemicals are critical intermediate inputs for downstream sectors such as rubber and plastics, pharmaceuticals and electronics, among others. The first QCO for a chemical product was introduced in 2018, and the number of chemical products covered rose to 52 by 2024. Consequently, the share of chemical-using firms exposed to regulation on the input side rose from 11.8% in 2019 to 56.6% in 2024.
When examining the impact of QCOs on chemicals on downstream user industries, the study finds that the effects vary considerably by firm size. Among larger firms, input QCOs are associated with a 9.6% increase in production alongside a sharp 37% decline in gross value added (GVA). This suggests that while larger firms can sustain and even expand output, this comes at the cost of lower value addition, potentially reflecting higher input costs and their ability to pass on at least part of these costs through higher output prices.
For smaller firms, input QCOs have no statistically significant effect on production or GVA but are associated with a steep 47.6% decline in profitability. This points to their more limited ability to absorb rising input costs and bear the additional compliance costs associated with QCOs.
The empirical evidence makes it clear that the adverse effects of QCOs on key inputs are not confined to smaller downstream firms. Even larger firms, which are better placed to absorb regulatory and input-cost shocks and are often able to sustain production, can experience significant declines in value addition. Supply-chain implications should therefore become an integral part of both the design of new QCOs and the reassessment of existing ones. Finally, the disproportionate burden on Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) requires specific policy attention. Smaller firms need dedicated assistance to meet certification and compliance requirements, alongside appropriately designed exemptions or transition periods where compliance costs are particularly burdensome.
Quality standards, greater scale
As India works towards the ambition of Viksit Bharat 2047, achieving greater scale in manufacturing will be critical. Quality standards have an important role to play in that journey, but their success should ultimately be judged not by the number of products brought under mandatory regulation, but by whether they improve quality without constraining the scale, efficiency and competitiveness of Indian manufacturing.
Prerna Prabhakar is a Fellow at Centre for Social and Economic Progress (CSEP); Nancy Gupta is a Visiting Fellow at the Crawford School of Public Policy. The views expressed are personal

The FBI is now investigating claims from a hacker group that thousands of current and former employees’ personal data was stolen after the group exploited a previously unknown bug found on an agency jobs website.
On Tuesday, 404 Media reported that ShinyHunters took down the agency site, FBIJobs.gov, then posted a banner on the homepage that said “THIS SITE HAS BEEN SEIZED BY SHINYHUNTERS.”
About two to three terabytes of data were taken, ShinyHunters told The New York Times. None of the data has been leaked yet, but it included “names of current and former agents as well as applicants and corresponding home addresses, phone numbers, names of spouses, certain medical information, and other data.” According to Bloomberg, the data could be used to potentially retaliate against agents, with one sample appearing to include “potentially sensitive professional information on the FBI employees’ work focus such as counter-intelligence work on China, Russia and Iran, as well as work against street gangs.”
The group’s motive was not to extort the FBI or seek a ransom, it claimed. Instead, the strike was meant to force the FBI to either remove or edit a May advisory warning about ShinyHunters that the group said circulated “disinformation in an attempt to ‘disrupt’ our operations.”
In a message posted on the dark web that was reviewed by Ars, ShinyHunters said it was “severely offended” that the FBI alleged that they sometimes use “exaggerated claims” to extract payments from victims. “We wish to state unequivocally our threats and claims are very real,” the group said. “Not exaggerated and never a bluff.”
ShinyHunters was also upset that the FBI claimed the group conducts swatting attacks against corporate workers and makes sextortion threats. That “never” happens, ShinyHunters said.

A Punjab consumer commission has ordered a training company to refund an MBA graduate’s fees. The dispute concerned a course advertised with a promise of “100% guaranteed placement”. The Gurdaspur district consumer commission passed its order on 16 September. It directed Eduinx Education Services to refund ₹84,960 to Harish Malhotra, The Times of India reported. The commission also awarded ₹10,000 for mental tension and harassment. Another ₹5,000 was granted towards his legal expenses, according to TOI. Malhotra joined an online programme covering artificial intelligence (AI) in product management. According to his complaint, an advertisement promising guaranteed placement influenced his decision. The MBA graduate paid ₹84,960 through a credit card on 12 July 2025. He completed the course and received his certificate on 24 November 2025. However, Malhotra alleged that the promised job had never materialised despite repeated follow-ups. He said the company had kept extending its timelines. He then approached the commission, seeking a refund and compensation. Malhotra claimed he had remained unemployed for more than 10 months. He sought ₹6 lakh for financial losses and damage to his career continuity. He also requested ₹30,000 towards legal expenses. Eduinx denied the allegations and described itself as a training and career-support platform. It argued that employers, rather than the platform, made hiring decisions. The company said its guarantee covered interview preparation, profile improvement and contact with employers. It also claimed Malhotra participated in recruitment processes involving several companies. Eduinx alleged that he had rejected opportunities outside his preferred locations, Gurugram and Delhi-NCR. The commission examined whether these recruitment efforts fulfilled the advertised promise. President Lalit Mohan Dogra and member B S Matharu found that they did not. The bench distinguished between arranging interviews and actually securing placement. It said any limits on the guarantee should have been clearly disclosed during enrolment. The commission also rejected unsupported claims linking the outcome to Malhotra’s interview performance. Eduinx did not produce employer assessments or communications establishing rejection on that basis. WhatsApp messages showed that some vacancies were shared with him. However, the commission found these messages did not establish definite employment offers or successful placement. “A mere suggestion of a vacancy cannot be equated with an employment offer as promised. Nor can a recruitment lead, screening call or interview be treated as equivalent to a successful placement,” TOI quoted the commission as stating. “Therefore, even after taking the WhatsApp conversations at their face value, the evidence falls short of establishing that the opposite parties fulfilled the substantive placement representation,” it added. It held that the unfulfilled commitment amounted to deficient service. The inadequately-qualified placement guarantee also amounted to an unfair trade practice. However, the commission rejected the ₹6 lakh compensation claim because supporting documents were insufficient. Payment must follow within 45 days of receiving the order’s copy. The Confrontation That Broke New York
A new book sheds some light on the death of Jordan Neely and the trial that divided a post-pandemic city.
In the spring of 2023, a young Black man stepped onto a subway car in Manhattan. He screamed, threw garbage at passengers, and announced that he was prepared to die. New Yorkers often encase themselves in psychological armor on the subway, but for many of the riders in that car, this was too much.
Terror flooded in. A woman hid her face in a friend’s chest; a mother tried to hide behind her stroller with her toddler. One man began to pray. Then a 24-year-old white man, an ex-Marine, grabbed the screaming man and put him in a neck lock, and five minutes later—by mistake? Intentionally?—left that man dead on the floor of the subway car.
To read the new book on that killing, Man in the Mirror: Hope, Struggle, and Belonging in an American City, by Anand Giridharadas, is to recognize that the membrane separating safety and fear on the New York City subways appeared in danger of rupturing by 2023. In the preceding few years, dozens of people had been pushed onto subway tracks, suffering injury or death. Murder and assault had risen sharply. The tension between chaos and order—often evident in New York—could be acute. And in those five minutes, it snapped.
Before anyone could sort out the facts, too many people rushed to impose narratives. Jordan Neely became the homeless Black man with the too-disposable life; Daniel Penny became the muscular vigilante who grew up in the white-bread suburbs. Leftist activists howled racism; right-wing sorts adjusted their ties and talked tough. “In a civilized society, the strong protect the weak,” a member of The Wall Street Journal’s editorial board wrote. “A Marine uses his strength to fight for those unable to fight for themselves.” Liberal politicians divined morality tales. Brad Lander, at the time the city comptroller, who lives in a prosperous liberal precinct in Brooklyn, proclaimed: “We must not become a city where a mentally ill human being can be choked to death by a vigilante without consequence.”
I wanted to say: Stop, please. Forgo reading your political catechisms. Try not to talk of consequences and militarization and the menace of the streets until we have a clue about how to prevent this from happening again.
There is pathos enough to be found in basic facts. In his book, Giridharadas takes on the considerable challenge of telling a story that encompasses conflicting narratives and the voices of nearly every player: defense attorneys, people living on the street, public-health officials, both Neely and Penny. His writing is most powerful when he traces the threads of tragically entwined lives. Whereas some in the media reduced Neely to a trope—the mentally ill homeless man—Man in the Mirror invests his life with complication and nuance. His mother was killed by her boyfriend; in a gothic twist, that boyfriend cross-examined young Jordan while representing himself at his trial. In time, Neely drifted further and further away from those who wanted to offer him succor. The reader learns about outreach workers and prosecutors who were ambivalent on how to treat his illness, and about well-meaning bureaucrats whose actions fell short.
Here and there, the author stumbles when inserting liberal punctuation points. He argues that addressing crime is an inescapable fact of life for Democrats, even if the fear that crime is out of control is “based in nonreality.” The biggest problem, he writes, is a nation “awash in anxiety and fear: of change, of the social advancement of marginalized populations, of losing control of children, of losing control of the border, of losing cultural status and centrality, of the Other, of chaos.” This strikes me as too easy.
Change, demographic and otherwise, has swept through and revitalized New York City for centuries. And the subways are arteries that give life to us all. I grew up riding the rails to see girlfriends and basketball games. My schoolmates and I rode to a Bronx public high school in train cars so encased in graffiti, we had to peer out of the opening doors to see if we’d reached our stop. Slowly, however, that system grew cleaner and safer.
When the coronavirus pandemic overtook New York City, that momentum seemed to reverse, and the subways began to feel menacing again. My claim here is reality-based, drawing on statistics and personal experience. Assaults on the subway increased by 65 percent from 2020 to 2025, and the number of murders in the system spiked as well. And a year after Neely died, a man shoved a friend of my family onto the subway tracks. He suffered multiple fractures, and his rehabilitation stretched across brutal months.
One morning in the spring of 2023, I was riding the Q train to the Upper East Side when I heard a booming voice and saw a great block of a man enter the subway car and ask for money. I returned to my reading. As the man approached, the timbre of his voice grew agitated. I fixed a side eye on him. When the train stopped in the middle of a tunnel, the panhandler stood over a young man who sat across from me. He put out a massive hand.
“You’re giving me money,” he announced. Silence followed as the young passenger kept eyes downcast. “Mutherfucker, I’ve got a big-ass knife”—the man patted his shaggy overcoat—“and I’m going to gut you from your balls to your throat.” I made eye contact with other men on the train. What the hell do we do if he pulls out that knife? If we are lucky enough to pull him to the floor, how do we keep him there?
I offer none of this to sound macho. I’m a 60-something man with a strong desire to remain alive. I harbored no illusions about my ability to wrestle this man to the ground. As it happened, the train started and pulled into the next station and he got off, but not before loudly vowing to gut us all.
I can venture a reasonable thumbnail sketch of this man. He was probably homeless. He was likely known to social-services caseworkers and to police. If he had been prescribed medications, he did not seem to be taking them. His inner resources had been eroded by life’s dysfunctions and the brutal reality of too many days on the street.
In a 2024 column about Neely and Penny in The New York Times, Emmett Rensin noted that the prevalence of “madness”—“those serious and spectacular forms of mental illness”—on the streets and in the subways “creates a dilemma between two principles of a liberal society: the sovereignty of individuals and the collective right to public order.” When those values can’t be reconciled, the city can feel perilous. I have a desperate desire not to live in a Death Wish version of New York, in which residents take it upon themselves to mete out justice, but what happens when you are caught in a moral pincer without a third party to adjudicate? Had that man on the Q pulled a knife, and had we hurt him before he hurt us, would we have been branded vigilantes?
The worst of those times appear to have passed. Murders and shootings in New York City have plunged in the past few years, and it remains one of the nation’s safest big cities. But statistics comfort only to a point. The continuing presence in public of so many people with seemingly untreated mental illness—including those who still push strangers onto the tracks—is unignorable.
To read Man in the Mirror is to inoculate yourself against the belief that the larger crisis is over. Giridharadas’s book illuminates the conundrum posed by those with Neely’s behavioral profile. On a good day, he could be a gentle busker. He was the Michael Jackson impersonator with a moonwalk step and a sweet smile. But Neely’s mental illness most often went untreated, and it had festered as he evaded caseworkers. He was becoming dangerous. In 2019, he punched someone on a subway platform. Two years later, he slugged a 67-year-old woman as she emerged from a subway station, breaking her nose and fracturing her eye socket; for this, he served a sentence at Rikers Island.
Locking away the Neelys of our cities in Kafkaesque asylums was a more common solution until the 1960s and ’70s; the practice was ultimately rejected for urgent and humane reasons. Yet discerning which mentally ill person poses a threat has not gotten any easier, and letting the most afflicted roam the streets untreated does not constitute a sustainable policy.
Giridharadas writes sensitively about this, and illuminates debates between hopeful public-health officials who yearn to transform society—changing “everything ‘out there’”—and hardheaded pragmatists. The latter group supports a sensible program in New York, now in its early stages, to pair public caseworkers with police officers, marrying the compassion of the former with the practical authority of law enforcement—the better to offer the right kind of help in any situation. There is also an effort to make it easier for families to commit mentally ill relatives for care.
Unfortunately, when Giridharadas moves away from the man who died in the confrontation and the questions that arise from the incident, his analysis grows less subtle. He devotes substantial pages early in his account to the Black activist Al Sharpton without mentioning the extent to which the reverend is a sometimes-unreliable narrator. Sharpton can speak movingly of the lives of the Black forgotten and of those who suffer from police abuse; he also has served as an FBI informant, been on a first-name basis with mobsters, and embraced an outright hoax about a racist conspiracy. And in his politics, he is in some ways an outlier. Many Black New Yorkers, as well as Latinos and Asians, have told pollsters that they favor more, not less, police presence, and that safer subways are an urgent concern. That perspective could have enriched the book.
The author also succumbs in places to class-based stereotypes, particularly when writing of Penny and his family of white suburbanites, people who are unlikely to share his political priors. Such missteps limit rather than expand our understanding of Penny’s background and worldview. Penny grew up in West Islip, on Long Island, a town where, Giridharadas writes, “you had your little yard, your little fence, your little deck, maybe you had your little boat.” He adds that “nothing was beautiful and nothing was ugly.” He casts a cold eye on Penny’s mother, Gina, mocking her working-class accent and writing that she had “so much to express” on Facebook, “but not necessarily the skill or will to express those things in any personal, authentic, or original way.”
The book reaches a crescendo with Penny’s trial. Defense lawyers portrayed a city lost to dysfunction; the police were too late to show up, and only Penny was left to put his life on the line to save “perfect strangers.” The prosecutor—who several times during the trial referred to the former Marine as “the white man” and “the white defendant”—acknowledged what activists and liberal politicians could not: Penny had “started out trying to do the right thing,” until he kept his choke hold in place too long and Neely died. A majority of the jurors were white, but at least four were not. They took 24 hours—not very long, given the case’s complexity—to acquit Penny of criminally negligent homicide.
Afterward, Lander warned that the verdict would “valorize vigilantism.” The left-wing Working Families Party called it a “modern-day lynching.” But all of the jurors rode the subway at least semi-regularly; several had spoken before the trial of their own upsetting experiences on the train, and in the end they appeared disinclined to punish a man who acted to forestall what might have been imminent violence.
It is a virtue of this book that Giridharadas, even while seeming to harbor sympathies for the prosecutors, applies an empathy for New Yorkers who try to thread their way through the divides created by this case. “They shared the sense of being undefended. They shared the sense that the calvary was not coming,” he writes. “They shared a sense that the system was rigged,” and so “shared the sense of their own powerlessness.”
Just hours after the verdict, Penny walked along 30th Street, and people recognized him. “Almost to a person,” Giridharadas notes, “they shook his hand and thanked him.”
It’s tempting to think of this, three years after the incident, as a snapshot of a more turbulent city. But as I finished this essay, I learned of a new horror: Early this month, Erin Piacenti was walking through Times Square, having freshly returned from maternity leave, when Pamela Cisneros, a middle-aged mother of three who appeared lost to madness, fatally stabbed Piacenti in the abdomen. Cisneros, who had suffered decades of mental-health issues, then tried to stab police officers; they shot and killed her. And for Piacenti, the young, innocent woman who lost her life, no one was there to save her.

Synagogue shooting suspect's online username alluded to killing Jews weeks before attack, friend says
Sean Ward, who was a former Armed Forces member, died Monday after the weekend shooting in Belleville, Ont.
The man who died following a Sunday shootout with police outside a synagogue in Belleville, Ont., alluded to killing Jewish people using a slur and railed against immigrants in interactions with a friend in the weeks leading up to the fatal attack, CBC News visual investigation team has learned.
According to a childhood friend CBC News spoke to, Sean Ward — a former member of the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) — tried using a slur for Jewish people combined with the word "killer" as a username for an online game, but settled on "kitekiller" after it was censored. The friend was with Ward online on Sept. 2 while they waited to play the video game Once Human when Ward attempted to use the username.
"There was that one game we played … he tried to name himself the k--e killer, and it changed to 'kitekiller' because you can't obviously have that on there," said his friend.
The word is a deeply offensive term used against Jews.
- Questions swirl as members of Belleville, Ont., synagogue return after shooting
- Suspect in Belleville, Ont., shooting is dead, SIU says
CBC News is not naming the friend due to his fear that he will lose his job because of his association with the suspect.
Using text messages, online usernames and social media accounts, and an interview with the childhood friend, CBC News was able to put together a partial profile of Ward — a person who not only routinely engaged in antisemitic speech, but who more recently espoused anti-immigrant sentiments, blaming them for his lack of employment.
"He said he was depressed," said his friend, recounting a conversation with Ward earlier this month. "He was saying, 'F--k the immigrants', like … 'I can't find work.' "
"I just didn't think he would do anything to that extreme."
A spokesperson with the Special Investigations Unit, the civilian agency that investigates police conduct during shootings and other serious incidents in Ontario, said Ward, 29, died from injuries sustained during the exchange of gunfire outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville on Sunday night, where congregants gathered for Yom Kippur services.
According to the SIU, Ward is alleged to have fired at Belleville Police Const. Jeff Smith with a shotgun, then Smith and a second officer on scene returned fire, with dozens of shots exchanged.
Smith was injured in the confrontation.
Both were taken to hospital, where Ward died on Monday night.
So far, police have not released any information about the suspect's potential motivation for the attack.
'Don't do anything stupid'
The friend CBC spoke to said he noticed a change in Ward over a period of months this summer. His appearance changed, the friend said, noting Ward went from bulky to slim, with long, greasy hair.
"He just looked different. Felt different. I could feel a different vibe on him," the friend said. "Usually we talk more. So that's why I felt odd because, like, he wasn't shooting the shit like we usually did. Like, he was like, in his head kind of thing."
The friend said the last time he saw Ward in person was Sept. 2, roughly three weeks before the shooting.
"When he was leaving … I was like, 'Don't do anything stupid, bro.' I was like, 'I know times are tough, but don't do anything stupid.' "
Following news of the shooting Sunday, the friend messaged Ward.
"I immediately texted Sean," he said. "And the message never sent. So that kind of clicked to my brain that he probably did do it."
The friend said Ward always had his phone on. "Like always. He'd always answer pretty quick."
CAF confirmed Tuesday that Ward had served in the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry from 2017 to 2022. CAF did not comment on the reasons for Ward's release, but multiple people CBC News spoke to, including the friend, said Ward refused to be vaccinated.
The CAF vaccine policy required all members to be vaccinated against COVID-19 or face potential release. That requirement ended in October 2022.
A number of violent attacks have been directed against Jewish-owned businesses and places of worship in recent years, with several instances of firebombings or buildings being shot at.
Jewish advocacy group B'nai Brith Canada recorded more than 6,800 antisemitic incidents in 2025, the highest number it has recorded since 1982.

Brad Bird has directed some of our all-time favorite animated films: The Iron Giant (1999), The Incredibles (2004), and Ratatouille (2007), with the latter two snagging well-deserved Oscar wins. He’s back with a new animated feature, Ray Gunn, coming to Netflix in December, described as a neo-noir science-fiction mystery. Netflix recently released the official trailer, chock-full of retro-futuristic elements, like flying cars, jet packs, laser guns, aliens, and yes, a sultry femme fatale. Color us among those now eagerly awaiting the film’s release.
Bird has been kicking around the idea for Ray Gunn for the last 30 years, working on his many other film projects while the Ray Gunn script—co-written by Matthew Robbins, who also co-wrote 1987’s Batteries Not Included with Bird—“stayed in a filing cabinet at Warner Brothers,” the director said earlier this year.
The film’s inspiration came when Bird heard the opening of the B-52s’ “Planet Claire” (a personal favorite) and initially thought it was a cover of Henry Mancini’s theme music from the classic TV show Peter Gunn. Bird is a longtime fan of film noir and hard-boiled detectives, and he came up with the idea of a futuristic detective named Ray Gunn (a pun on raygun, of course). “It’s film noir and a hard-boiled detective story, but it’s got a lot more comedy and a lot more action than the average film noir,” said Bird.

'Alarming' - does WSL have a homegrown problem?
- Published
When London City Lionesses beat Manchester United on the opening night of the 2025-26 season, it suggested times were changing in the English women's game.
For some, that had become clear about an hour before kick-off in Bromley when the team news revealed a starting XI without any English players - the first time a Women's Super League side had done so on the first day of the season.
Two days later it happened again, when Scotland striker Kirsty Hanson was the only British player to start for Tottenham in their win over West Ham.
Both instances speak to the increasing ability of WSL clubs to attract top talents from across the globe, creating a league many now view as the world's best.
But, with the Women's Champions League returning this week, is what's good for the WSL good for homegrown players, and by extension the home nations?
Or is it, as The Guardian's Tom Garry puts it, "alarming" for the hopes of the home nations?
Arsenal v HB Koge, Women's Champions League
Tuesday, 22 September, 20:00 BST
Listen to BBC Radio 5 Live commentary and follow text updates of the matches featuring English teams on the BBC Sport website as the Women's Champions League returns
The changing make-up of the WSL
Ten years ago when current champions Manchester City last won the WSL title, they did so with an all-British starting line-up.
Much has changed since.
In 2018, the WSL went fully professional, the subsequent success of the Lionesses in the 2020s rapidly grew the game's audience and revenues have increased accordingly.
As a result, clubs have expanded their scouting pool and been able to attract players from a wider variety of nationalities - with transfer fees exploding since the turn of the decade.
Over recent windows, WSL clubs have recruited heavily from Germany and Sweden, while two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas exchanged the trophies of Barcelona for big-spending London City this summer.
The proliferation of players from Japan and Australia also highlights the WSL's attractiveness for those at the top of the game as those clubs with the deepest pockets pack their squads with players from across the globe.
"Our league has grown significantly and attracted world class athletes from all over the world," says Birmingham City manager Amy Merricks. "Unfortunately that blocks some of the pathways for the youngsters coming through.
"We need [this] talent in our league because our league is growing, but at the same time we have got to try and address this issue."
Looking at the proportion of homegrown players (English, Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish) to start 11 or more matches, half of a WSL season, the data shows a steady decline over the past three seasons to under a third.
The first three weeks of 2026-27 have offered a bump on last season, but that can partly be attributed to the WSL's expansion from 12 teams to 14 teams and the greater proportion of homegrown talent in the promoted trio of Birmingham City, Crystal Palace and Charlton Athletic.
It is a downward trend that is not mirrored across other major European leagues.
For 2025-26, 61% of those to start half or more of Premiere Ligue matches in France were French, 63% of those in Frauen Bundesliga games were German, and 69% of Liga F players in Spain were Spanish.
And, while WSL managers say they appreciate the importance of cultivating homegrown talent, the reality of the job ensures it is not their first priority.
"The club has a responsibility to raise young players, give our own talents possibilities to be in the squad and compete every week," says Manchester City boss Andree Jeglertz.
"But when it comes to team selection, I always need to pick the team that gives us the best chance of winning the game. If that contains eight young and promising English players or zero, I don't care. I just want to win the game."
What is the potential impact on the national team?
1 of 4
It feels like a crossroads has been reached between clubs wanting to be competitive, the WSL continuing to grow, and the need to regenerate an England squad that has not changed much over the past three major tournaments.
After all, England are the two-time European champions but seven of the team that started against Spain in June also played in the Euro 2022 final against Germany - while two of the remaining starters in this year's game were on the bench four years ago.
Sarina Wiegman's side were outclassed in Majorca, losing 4-0 to miss out on automatic qualification for the 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil. They must now navigate two rounds of play-off matches, starting against Greece next month.
Discussions on England's future is pertinent given the biennial Women's Under-20s World Cup is ongoing in Poland.
Last Thursday, Lydia Bedford's young side were dismissed 3-0 from the last 16 by Nigeria, albeit with the caveat a number of players such as US-based Erica Meg Parkinson and Laila Harbert were not released by their clubs to play.
Nevertheless, in 2022 and 2024, like the other home nations, they did not even qualify.
It is a far cry from the class of 2018 where the likes of Alessia Russo, Lauren Hemp and Georgia Stanway led the Lionesses to third place in the Under-20s World Cup, setting the tone for the incredible subsequent success.
Wiegman has handed debuts to 21 players since her arrival in September 2021, but only Lauren James, Hannah Hampton and Lucia Kendall have become established starters.
When England kick off in Crete on Friday, 5 October (20:00 BST), it is likely to be the same faces once again.
- Young Lionesses win European trophy 
  - Published17 April
To try and facilitate the pathway to top level football for young academy players, Football Association rules require WSL sides to include eight homegrown players in their squad lists.
The quota for WSL 2 clubs is higher and works on a sliding scale depending on squad size.
Former England striker Ellen White told the Women's Football Weekly podcast this was insufficient, saying: "We should be updating that quota of eight players, tweaking it to best help and complement our international structure, our homegrown talent."
"I would love to see them go much further - something mandated, a minimum on the pitch at any one time," the Guardian's Garry told BBC Women's Football Weekly. "London City's line-up was alarming.
"It's great for the product over here, but will we see pain in 15 years' time if England are struggling to go deep in major tournaments because we're not developing players?"
Last month, the FA approved a controversial plan to allow some WSL academy sides to play in the National League from 2027-28, saying it would "strengthen the women's football pyramid, raise standards across the league, and improve the development pathway for young players".
The FA believes this reform will address the relative lack of competitive minutes young English players receive.
Chelsea have already confirmed they plan to enter an academy side in the third tier and Manchester City women's managing director Charlotte O'Neill has previously said she would want to enter a team too.

Workers came across human remains – and unearthed a mass grave of 572 people
- Published
When a mass grave was unearthed in northern Sri Lanka last February, it was not by design.
Workers were digging to extend a cremation ground in the Chemmani area of the Jaffna region when they suddenly discovered human remains, prompting an investigation.
By August, archaeologists had completed the third phase of the excavation at the site, during which they found the skeletal remains of 572 people, including children and infants.
Among the dead were artefacts from their lives – bangles, a school bag, a milk bottle.
It is believed to be the largest mass grave site ever uncovered in Sri Lanka.
There had been whispers of its existence before - a soldier on trial for the rape and murder of a young woman during the country's devastating civil war, had spoken about a mass grave which contained hundreds of bodies. Rights groups said they were disappeared civilians
But there was no proof - until now.
And while the discovery is devastating, it has offered hope to people like Jeyaruby Jeyabalan, whose father was among thousands of people who disappeared during the decades-long war. Jeyabalan and families like his hope that answers about what happened to their loved ones lie among the bodies.
Many Tamils believe the grave holds the victims of extrajudicial killings carried out during the civil war. They are calling for an investigation – and for justice.
But the excavation process at Chemmani has moved slowly, testing the patience of families searching for answers about their disappeared loved ones.
The discovery of hundreds of remains near a previously identified mass grave has fuelled anger among the Tamils, who have long-demanded a thorough inquiry into disappearances.
Many fear the mass grave will eventually fade from public attention because of a lack of political will to pursue the truth – and so the grave has become a rallying point for renewed protests in Sri Lanka's north.
Two decades waiting for answers
Sri Lanka, particularly the Tamil-dominated north and east, suffered decades of conflict. The war, which lasted from 1983 to 2009, divided the island-nation along ethnic lines. Tamil Tiger rebels fought for an independent state in the north-east of the country due to what they called systematic discrimination by the Sinhalese-dominated government.
The conflict lasted 26 years and the fighting killed an estimated 100,000 people. It also left about 23,000 – mostly Tamils – missing.
Both the security forces and Tamil Tigers are accused of atrocities and crimes.
In 1995, after a bloody conflict, the Sri Lankan army wrested control of the Jaffna Peninsula from the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE). It was seen as a key turning point in the war, which ended with the defeat of the Tigers in 2009.
As they extended control in the late 1990s, the entire Chemmani region became part of a high-security zone and was dotted with army camps, check points and security posts. There was an army camp in Chemmani close to the cemetery as well.
Some at that time described the Jaffna region as an "open prison" - and the security forces were accused of causing the disappearance of thousands of civilians, something Sri Lankan governments have always denied.
"I was 12 years old when my father was picked up by the Sri Lankan army at a checkpoint close to Chemmani area in September 1996. We still don't know what happened to him," Jeyaruby Jayapalan, who now lives in Jaffna, tells the BBC.
She recalls how, after learning of his disappearance, the family panicked and visited military camps and police stations across Jaffna in a desperate search for information without any luck. He never came back.
Her father, Kandaiah Jayapalan, was a government employee who also ran a roadside café not far from Chemmani.
"I went to Chemmani mass grave with many others hoping that I will find some answers. But we didn't find any material evidence. We want a detailed forensic analysis of the human remains," says Jeyaruby.
Two weeks before Kandaiah Jayapalan vanished, an 18-year-old Tamil school girl, Krishanthi Kumaraswamy, disappeared in the same area.
In 1998, a court in Colombo sentenced five soldiers to death for the rape and murder of Kumaraswamy and for killing three of her family members. The case drew global attention at that time. Their bodies were later found buried in Chemmani area.
It is among the most infamous cases from the conflict – and the grave currently under investigation is within 100 metres of the remains of Kumaraswamy and others were found.
In a startling court testimony, one of the convicted soldiers, Somaratne Rajapakse, alleged that between 300 and 400 people who had been killed in the mid-1990s were buried in Chemmani.
His claim led to the first excavation at Chemmani a year later, during which investigators unearthed more than 10 human skeletons. Human rights activists believed those remains were linked to people who had disappeared during the civil war, but there was little judicial follow-up.
Activists say that because the war with the Tamil rebels was ongoing, the then government didn't pursue the investigation and did not explain why.
The discovery of another mass grave in the same area has revived calls for accountability.
"Preliminary inspections suggest this was not a normal burial site and not consistent with ordinary Hindu burial practices," says Gehan Gunatilleke, a commissioner with Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka, which conducted inspections at Chemmani last year.
Activists and experts say that while a few dozen bodies appeared to have been formally buried, the vast majority told a different story.
Most of the human remains were found without clothing, packed tightly together and, in some cases, stacked on top of others. The graves were shallow, with bodies buried just one to two metres below the surface.
"There is a reasonable likelihood that the burials were unlawful and pursuant to extrajudicial killings," the Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka said in a report last year.
Past investigations haven't led to prosecutions
The families of those disappeared during the conflict have responded to the discovery by holding protest meetings and remembrance ceremonies.
Among them is Suseela, a 65-year-old woman who is looking for her son, Gnanaseelan Ravi, who was picked up by the Sri Lankan military in 2007, when he was 24.
"He was my only son, and I keep crying every day remembering him. My life is empty without him," she tells the BBC.
She went to Chemmani grave but couldn't find any evidence, likes clothes or personal jewellery, that suggested her son was buried there. DNA tests on the human remains are yet to be carried out.
All the remains recovered so far from Chemmani have been kept in the Forensic Department of the University of Jaffna campus under court custody.
"We are preparing an interim report, and it will be submitted to the court by the end of September," Prof Raj Somadeva, the chief archaeologist of the mass grave told the BBC.
Some of the samples are expected to be sent abroad for detailed examination to help determine the age of the remains. Separate medical analyses will be needed to establish the possible causes of death.
More than 20 mass graves have been found across Sri Lanka in recent decades, but none have been conclusively linked to enforced disappearances or alleged extra-judicial killings in the north and south of the country – and none have led to prosecutions.
Given the failure of the authorities to investigate previous mass graves, there is scepticism among many Tamil people over what the new investigation might achieve.
They point out to the outcome of the investigation on another mass grave was unearthed in the north-western town of Mannar in 2018 in which more than 350 skeletal remains were found. Investigations proved inconclusive, leaving many families disappointed.
They want Sri Lanka to be referred to the International Criminal Court.
The government of President Anura Kumara Dissanayake insists that it is fully cooperating with the investigation.
After coming to power in September 2024, Dissanayake promised to work towards justice and ethnic reconciliation. But his government vehemently opposes any international mechanism to investigate alleged war crimes committed during the ethnic conflict, disappointing Tamils.
"We will continue with the excavation work at Chemmani," Harshana Nanayakkara, Sri Lanka's justice minister told the BBC.
"We need to analyse the skeletons and find out how these people died. Then we have to carry out DNA tests," he said.
The government, he insists, has also asked the families to give their DNA so that it can be analysed later with the remains.
During his inspection at Chemmani in June, the minister promised investigations to find justice and truth to bring an end to the matter. He also promised that necessary funding will be allocated for the excavation.
The Sri Lankan army spokesman, Brigadier Waruna Gamage rejects allegations that security forces buried civilians after massacring them.
"All the allegations should be proved in court," he told the BBC.
Calls for international assistance
The delays in investigating past crimes have attracted stringent criticism from rights groups.
After years of international pressure, in 2018 the government set up an independent body, the Office of the Missing Persons (OMP), to investigate the disappearances. But those affected say it hasn't made much progress in finding their missing relatives.
"Many cases of forced disappearance, torture and killing remain stalled, while families of victims and human rights defenders face threats and intimidation," Human Rights Watch said in a report earlier this month.
The United Nations has urged Sri Lanka to seek international help in identifying the victims, to find out how they died, and who is responsible.
"This is a situation where victims are deeply frustrated, have lived with pain for decades, have come to distrust past investigations," Rory Mungoven, the Asia-Pacific chief at the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights tells the BBC.
"I think involving international assistance would help to bolster confidence in these investigations," he points out.
Successive Sri Lankan governments have strongly resisted calls for international investigations into alleged wartime atrocities.
During earlier reporting trips to Sri Lanka, I met parents and family members of the disappeared who campaigned for decades to the search for truth. Some have since passed away without ever discovering the fates of their loved ones.
Human rights groups say that President Dissanayake's government now has an opportunity to break from a long-standing pattern of delay and denial and deliver accountability for grave abuses committed during the conflict.
Suseela is determined to know the truth.
"I don't know how long I will live with such uncertainty, but I want closure," she says.
Additional Reporting by: Ranjan Arun Prasadh, BBC Tamil Service in Kandy and Kumanan Kanapathippillai in Jaffna.

Russia's parliamentary election result underscores public support for Kremlin policies, Putin says
President Vladimir Putin says Russia’s first wartime parliamentary election, which further strengthened the Kremlin’s already-overwhelming legislative control, was a sign of public support for his policies
President Vladimir Putin said Wednesday that Russia's first wartime parliamentary election, which further strengthened the Kremlin's already-overwhelming legislative control, was a show of public support for his policies.
With over 97% of the vote counted from three days of balloting that ended Sunday, election officials said the main Kremlin party, United Russia, will get more than three-fourths of the seats in the lower house, the State Duma, a record high. The tightly orchestrated vote excluded virtually any genuine opposition.
Voter turnout exceeded 59% of the 111 eligible million voters, the most for a parliamentary election in over a decade. Authorities had spread the voting over three days to boost attendance at the polls and included illegally annexed parts of Ukraine. Online voting also took place in some regions.
“Such a record number of people who come to cast ballots shows that the people of Russia support our efforts aimed at strengthening the country,” Putin said in televised remarks at a meeting with top government members, his first public remarks on the outcome.
The election took place against the backdrop of incessant Ukrainian drone attacks. On Sunday, Russia's Defense Ministry reported it downed 1,110 drones overnight.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 450 drones were downed while flying toward the city in what he described as “the largest ever” attack on the capital in a failed attempt to disrupt the vote. The attack, which damaged an oil refinery and a residential building, also killed three people and injured 38 in the wider Moscow region, officials said.
“They tried to hamper our efforts, to derail the election, as evidenced by the enemy’s continuous efforts to breach air defenses around Moscow and in other regions,” Putin said. “But lines at polling stations have shown that Russia can’t be intimidated.”
The parliamentary election was the first since Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and the first to include residents of four regions of that country that were seized and illegally annexed by Moscow later that year. At a polling station in the Russian-held part of the Donetsk region, voters dropped their ballots in a box under the gaze of an armed Russian soldier.
Voting also was held in Crimea, which was illegally annexed by Russia in 2014. Kyiv denounced the voting in those regions as illegal.
Putin also addressed Russian soldiers fighting in Ukraine.
“Comrades, I want you to know that it was the vote for you. People trust you, they believe in our victory, believe in your courage, heroism and your devotion to the Motherland,” he said.
“I have no doubt that all the goals we set for the special military operation will be fulfilled,” Putin said, using the Kremlin term for the war in Ukraine.
A massive state media campaign and tight control over the election allowed the Kremlin to strengthen its political dominance despite economic troubles and long-range Ukrainian drone attacks.
The preliminary results indicated that United Russia would get between 347 and 355 out of 450 Duma seats. It received just under 58% of the vote for the 225 seats apportioned by parties and also won 208 single-seat races that fill the other half of the chamber.
Several smaller parties representing the “systemic opposition” that vote in sync with the Kremlin on all key issues are set to fill most of the remaining seats. Just a handful will go to candidates who ran without a party affiliation.
The liberal Yabloko party, the only registered political entity that dared to publicly criticize the war, was removed from the ballot last month by Russia’s Supreme Court, and only had a few dozen candidates in the single-seat races. Preliminary results indicated that no Yabloko candidates won a seat.

There isn’t much that we Indians agree on these days. GDP numbers are no exception. Last week, India released glowing GDP numbers for the latest quarter – 7.8% growth – higher than the forecast 7%. It sparked a furore.
Subhash Garg, a former finance secretary under Narendra Modi’s government and now a critic, reframed what Modi called a “herculean feat” as mere smoke and mirrors. According to Garg, the government revised last year’s current-price GDP downwards to inflate this year’s number – he believes the real growth is only 2.6%.
The assertion, made on a television channel, immediately went viral. A flurry of op-eds and hot takes have been published since. Supporters of the government, predictably, rejected the claims. Those who have questions agree on a more fundamental problem: a lack of transparency and statistical credibility in India’s economic data. So why is there no consensus?
Over the past decade, critics say, the government has systematically hollowed out the integrity of its own data infrastructure, weaponising economic data for political gain and creating a trust deficit. Methodologies have been changed, crucial surveys have faced long delays and there have been attempts to suppress inconvenient findings.
In November, the International Monetary Fund rated India’s national accounts data a ‘C’ on a four-point scale, the second-lowest grade. In its report, the IMF said some of the methodologies are outdated, including relying on an old base year, unexplained discrepancies between GDP calculated from the production and expenditure side, as well as a lack of seasonal data.
India’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous. There might have been disagreements on the quality of estimates but their independence was widely accepted. That trust appears to have eroded in recent years.
“There seems to be a systematic effort by the government to hide the truth,” said R Nagaraj, an economist who taught at the Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, adding that some of the other contested datasets include employment numbers, poverty numbers, health data and consumption data. “Over the last 10 years, the government has changed the methodology for many of these, raising questions. They have apparently also removed critical officials who headed some surveys. All of this adds to the scepticism.”
In one of the most prominent examples, from 2019, a Business Standard journalist revealed that the government had not published an official report showing unemployment at a 45-year high of 6.1%. Two expert members of the National Statistical Commission resigned in protest. The government initially denied it, calling it a draft. The figures were only released months later.
Then there is the census, which for the first time since independence, was delayed in 2021. Economists say relying on outdated demographic data means, among other things, inequitable allocation of welfare entitlements. (The first phase of the latest census finally began in April 2026.)
Nagaraj has witnessed some of this first-hand. He served on a subcommittee in 2014 whose report forms a part of the GDP. “The [numbers] we had discussed in the committee and what came out in the final report were different. So, I had to raise a red flag,” he said. The difference was notable: one figure in the published report had been inflated by 108%.
But government economists reject the ongoing criticism of the GDP numbers. Shamika Ravi, a member of the Economic Advisory Council to the prime minister, described it as a “noisy and very ill-informed debate” arguing that political leanings, not data, are behind the criticism.
The IMF rating was expected, she said. “The IMF rating of ‘C’ is the same rating that China has for its statistics. Several large developing or just developed economies have data issues.” Revisions to its calculations that the government was accused of having manipulated, she added, were precisely the sorts of changes the IMF had recommended.
The sticking point, as some including India’s former chief statistician Pronab Sen have pointed out, is the trustworthiness of the underlying data used.
Complicating this debate is the reality for many Indians. This year, young people have taken to the streets in frustration. Protests, which first began over leaked examination papers, have crystallised into a broader reckoning over systemic failures in education, jobs and the promise of a better future.
Almost 40% of graduates under 25 are unemployed, a recent report by Azim Premji University concluded. An estimated 87 million (8.7 crore) Indians between 15 and 29 are neither working, studying, nor doing skill training, a government thinktank reported last month.
That is why we should care about data quality, economists say. Incorrect data means bad policy. As economist Reetika Khera wrote in her recent book, Freebies or Rights: “Data shines the light to guide policymaking and is important for informed public debates.” As evidence, she points to gaps in basic statistics such as urbanisation and literacy numbers due to the delayed census. The consequences, she argues, are not abstract. Because the government still relies on outdated population numbers to decide who gets food subsidies, she estimates approximately 100 million (10 crore) people who should be covered are being deprived.
The controversy is making waves further ashore. In Sri Lanka, where second-quarter GDP figures are expected, the Daily FT newspaper wrote: “One hopes Sri Lankan policymakers and experts are not watching the theatrics in India with watering mouths and dreaming up smart arguments. Spare us such theatre!”
What else we’re reading about
Lollapalooza | British pop star Olivia Dean is to perform in India for the first time in January when she headlines Lollapalooza 2027 in Mumbai. Limp Bizkit is another headline act at the two-day event. Indian artists on the lineup include Ricky Kej (performing with Stewart Copeland) and Aditya Gadhvi.
The price of gold | Prime Minister Narendra Modi asked Indians once again to refrain from buying gold and travelling abroad. He had first made an appeal to self-reliance in May, in part to conserve India’s declining foreign exchange reserves amid a rise in import prices and global energy shocks.
Census 2027 | The new and expanded questionnaire for the 2027 census is raising concerns, reports Scroll’s Anant Gupta. The questionnaire asks respondents for details about their identity documents, as well as their parents’ religion and place of birth. Several of these questions were part of the controversial National Population Register that has remained in abeyance since 2020 and was controversial due to fears that the data might be used to target minorities through a citizenship registry.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Singer Prateek Kuhad (@prateekkuhad), whose latest album, Full Moon Chamber, was released in July, shares an indulgent treat: “I’m a big fan of artisanal Indian chocolate makers. I really like Manam, Carra and Naviluna, and there are many others. Although India has been growing cacao [commercially] since the 1960s, its craft bean-to-bar movement is more recent. Even a plain chocolate bar from one of these makers can be remarkably complex and delicious. More people outside India should know about it and try it.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
4,756,000
One-third of the electorate in Delhi, about 4.76 million voters, have been deleted from the draft voting list as the Election Commission carries out a contentious revision of its rolls across states. So far, about 130 million names have been dropped from draft rolls in 30 states and union territories, the Indian Express reported.
Vibe check
Earlier this year, Shakira’s concerts in India was postponed. But Rajasthani folk musicians the Ismail Langa Group (@ismaillanga_official) decided the music had to go on, in their own way. Their mashup of the Colombian star’s Hips Don’t Lie with the traditional folk song called Moruda has got everyone grooving (42m views and counting).
It took two months to pull off, says creative director Jagirdar RV. Most artists in the group, aged between 23 and 60, don’t speak or read English and learned the lyrics by rote. The song choice was simple, he said, because it “has a very nice vibe which matched our vibe”.
It’s been a breakout year for the group, which had a semi-final run on India’s Got Talent and are becoming known for taking folk songs to gen Z audiences on Instagram. They are working on their next English mashup – just not spilling which song, yet.

How Kenya won its bid for 2029 World Athletics Championships
- Published
Kenya's President William Ruto says the World Athletics Championship will be "coming home", with Nairobi set to make history after being selected as the first African city to host the event in 2029.
Ruto hailed the winning bid as a "victory for generations of athletes" who have made the nation "synonymous with excellence" on the track and road.
Nairobi beat London and Rome to the hosting rights, with Munich selected to stage the 2031 edition.
After missing out on the 2025 World Championships to Tokyo, a series of factors helped Kenya see off its European rivals this time around.
A sport 'woven into the fabric' of the nation
When World Athletics president Lord Coe announced the decision in Budapest on Tuesday, he described Kenya's bid as "compelling and emotional".
The East African nation is the second-most successful nation in the history of the World Championships with 72 gold medals, placing it behind the United States.
The vast majority of those glories, alongside 38 Olympic gold medals, have come in middle- and long-distance running.
Lord Coe said that athletics is "woven into the fabric" of the nation and that Kenyans have helped "shape the history" of the sport.
He name-checked several runners including two-time Olympic champion Eliud Kipchoge - who was involved in the lobbying for Kenya's bid - men's 800m world record holder David Rudisha and multiple world and Olympic medallist Faith Kipyegon.
A passionate fanbase is also one of the country's great strengths.
Some 68% of Kenyans surveyed by World Athletics rated their interest in athletics as high, compared with a global average of 39%.
Athletics is the country's second-most followed sport, behind only football, and when World Athletics assessed its social media channels, Kenya was the fourth-highest nation in terms of followers.
Upgraded facilities
Kenya's previous bid for the 2025 edition fell down largely on the facilities which the country possessed.
This time around, the Kasarani Stadium will have gone through a complete structural upgrade well before the world's top athletes descend on Nairobi.
The 48,000-capacity venue will be used when Kenya co-hosts football's 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) next June and July alongside Tanzania and Uganda.
"We learned from the 2025 bid because there were areas that we did not score well," Barnaba Korir, who worked on the successful bid, told the BBC World Service.
"Because of that, we managed to improve on those areas.
"I'm happy that the infrastructure that we have already developed will also meet the standards that we have seen all over the world."
Hotel space is one area not expected to be a problem, with Nairobi a regular host for large conventions.
"Kenya is also known for its very dynamic hospitality, the tourism sector," Elijah Mwangi, principal secretary at the State Department for Sports, told the BBC.
"It has a game park within the city, so we are waiting to welcome everybody."
President Ruto made financial and security guarantees in order to secure the Championships.
"We thank World Athletics for the confidence it has placed in Kenya," Ruto said.
"We will honour that confidence by delivering an unforgettable championship worthy of our athletes, our country and our continent."
Expanding athletics
Lord Coe became president of World Athletics (then known as the IAAF) in 2015 and has pledged to grow the sport around the globe.
During his time in office the World Championships have been hosted in Qatar (2019), the United States (2022) and Tokyo, while China's capital Beijing will stage them in 2027.
Kenya has successfully hosted age-grade events in Nairobi and the World Cross Country Championships in Mombasa, while the World Athletics Relays were held in Botswana's capital Gaborone in May.
With Coe's third term in office coming to an end next year, one official involved in Kenya's bid, speaking before the host announcement, said it was "unthinkable" that Nairobi would not succeed.
"With this decision we continue to fulfil our mission of growing athletics worldwide," Coe said.
"It was important that the World Athletics Championships should come to Africa when we had the right host, the right bid and the right circumstances.
Coe hailed the "quality, ambition and commitment" of all four bidding cities.
London, Munich and Rome have all previously held the Olympics, with the World Championships in London as recently as 2017, but the chance to break new ground in Africa was clearly compelling.
UK Athletics chief executive Jack Buckner said his team was "deeply disappointed" to see London miss out.
What is needed next?
Kenya now faces logistical and organisational challenges over the next three years as it prepares to deliver Africa's first World Championships.
With the 2027 Afcon looming large on the horizon, Nairobi will have a chance to test-run getting fans in and out of the Kasarani Stadium, which lies about a half-hour drive from the city's central business district.
The venue does not have any rail connections but Korir says World Athletics officials were "very satisfied" by Kenya's transport plan.
There were instances of overcrowding when the stadium hosted Kenya games at football's African Nations Championships last year, which led to the capacity being reduced for some matches.
Delays in preparations for Afcon have raised concerns, and the funding for the World Championships will come entirely from the Kenyan government.
Mwangi revealed that $78m (£58.5m) is the current estimate for the government's contribution, with sponsorship deals also playing a role.
"We are prepared to ensure that whatever is expected to be paid, it is paid in the due time," he added.
Presidential elections are scheduled for next year, but Korir is confident organisers will secure the "huge" and "legally binding" figure earmarked even if there is a change in government.
"Whatever the government assigns now will be observed by the next government. It is an international agreement," he said.
Then comes ticketing, first to make sure the local population are not priced out and then to ensure the stands are filled.
The cheapest tickets for the Under-18 World Championships in 2017 were priced at 200 Kenyan shillings ($1.15, £1.14) but attendances were low until entry was made free.
World Athletics generated $522m in revenue from Tokyo 2025, with a total of 619,000 tickets sold over the nine days of competition, while London sold a record 705,000 tickets in 2017.
In passing up the opportunity of returning to the British capital, World Athletics has chosen expansion over guaranteed ticket sales, but attendances will be scrutinised - especially after the sparse numbers seen in the stands in Doha in 2019.
Korir, however, is confident the Kasarani Stadium "will be full" on "every day" of competition, including morning sessions, if sales begin early enough.
Meanwhile, Kenya has endured a spate of doping scandals in recent years, with 11 individuals banned by the Athletics Integrity Unit so far this year alone.
The pressure is now on the East African nation to deliver on its promises in the build-up to Nairobi 2029 and ensure the Championships pass off without any major issues.
Additional reporting by Ian Williams and Celestine Karoney.

Tokyo International Film Festival (TIFF) has announced that Australian director Rolf de Heer will serve as president of the International Competition jury at this year’s edition of the festival.
De Heer’s 2022 film The Survival Of Kindness, which was selected for competition at the Berlinale, will screen in Tokyo as part of an Australia Spotlight, a special showcase of Australian cinema presented in cooperation with the Australian Embassy in Japan.
Based in Tasmania, de Heer has a career spanning more than 40 years and widespread international acclaim, starting with Bad Boy Bubby (1993), which won the Special Jury Prize and FIPRESCI Prize at Venice. Other early career highlights include Dingo (1991) with Colin Friels and jazz legend Miles Davis; The Quiet Room (1996) and Dance Me To My Song (1998), both selected for Competition at Cannes.
In total, four of his films have screened in Official Selection at Cannes Film Festival, including Ten Canoes (2006), which won the Special Jury Prize in Un Certain Regard.
Watch on Deadline
Mid-career highlights also include The Tracker (2002), which also played in Venice competition and marked de Heer’s first collaboration with Australian Indigenous actor David Gulpilil; Alexandra’s Project (2003), which won best actress at San Sebastian for Helen Buday’s performance; The King Is Dead! (2012); and Charlie’s Country (2013), which won Gulpilil a Best Actor award at Cannes.
De Heer said: “For any of us attending the Tokyo International Film Festival, it is a privilege. For me, as a filmmaker, it is even more so. The more films I manage to make, the fewer films I manage to see, especially on the big screen.
“But as a part of this jury, I have the duty, the obligation, to see at least 15 films and talk about them with other filmmakers! And not just any old 15 films, but the 15 films in Competition, drawn from films made all over the world by all sorts of extraordinary filmmakers! And to do this in a city that plays host to one of the most formidable film cultures in the world! Can life ever get much better than this?”
Tokyo Festival Director Takeo Hisamatsu said: “We are delighted to welcome Rolf de Heer as President of the International Competition jury at the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival. With his distinctive perspective and unwavering commitment to filmmaking, de Heer has spent decades opening up new possibilities in cinema. We look forward to the fresh dialogue and discoveries that his wealth of experience and deep insight will bring to this year’s Competition and its diverse selection of films.”
Tokyo International Film Festival will take place October 26 to November 4, with the TIFFCOM contents market running October 28-30.
