Like many at that time, the O'Phalen family was at a crossroads in 2020.
Kate and Daniel were living in Brooklyn with their two kids and had a third on the way. Kate was in grad school, and Daniel had a demanding job. It was the bustling life that many people dream of when they think of moving to New York.
Then, the pandemic hit, and suddenly, everyone's in-person commitment vanished. The O'Phalens made it work in their apartment for a few months, but their lives weren't as fulfilling as they once were.
"Everyone was kind of cooped up and miserable," Kate, 40, told Business Insider.
Their lease was up in June 2020, so the O'Phalens decided to rent an Airbnb in Maine for the summer.
They couldn't have anticipated their decision would lead them to leave New York for good and embrace RV living, even if it comes with the occasional expensive challenge that can cost thousands of dollars to solve.
The O'Phalens were ready for a change of pace.
Kate, who is her kids' homeschool teacher and a content creator, told Business Insider that she and her family were eager to spend time outdoors after months in their apartment.
They put their belongings in storage and planned to return to New York for the school year, hoping the summer would offer some respite.
However, after three months of hiking, beach days, and a slower pace of life, the O'Phalens didn't want to go back.
They decided to keep traveling for another year.
Since Daniel's job as a recruiter remained remote, there was no reason they couldn't keep traveling.
"We decided to do a loop around the country for a year, and we did it in Airbnbs," Kate said. "We did monthly Airbnbs combined with a few short hotel stays."
They spent much of that year on the West Coast, visiting every National Park they could, before looping back to the East Coast. They had a blast.
In fact, the O'Phalens had so much fun that they wanted to find a way to make the nomadic lifestyle work more permanently.
They decided to buy an RV that they could live in full time.
The O'Phalens knew they loved traveling, but an RV would be a big change for them. They had never towed a vehicle or driven a truck.
"We had only recently even bought a car, living in New York," Kate said. "We didn't even have a car for 10 years."
Still, in 2021, they bought a truck and spent $18,000 on a used RV that Kate renovated. The family rented an Airbnb in Alabama, where Kate has family, while she worked on it for six months.
"It was what I like to call granny hunting cabin chic when we purchased it," she said. "It was sort of camo floral all over the place and brown everywhere, but it had good bones."
Kate didn't have much experience with home renovations aside from painting, but she was excited for the challenge.
The RV needed some TLC.
Kate and Daniel were most drawn to the RV's layout. The door opens into a living space with a couch, a kitchen, and a loft. A primary bedroom sits at one end, and a "toy hauler" room is at the tail end. The bathroom is inside the primary bedroom.
Kate didn't take down any walls during the reno, but she did gut pretty much everything else, both because of the decor style and the shape it was in.
"The layout was really good, but it was absolutely hideous. And it had not been used a whole lot recently, so it was absolutely filthy," she recalled. "So, we started by just demoing a lot of it."
Everything they ripped out, they took to the dump and had it weighed, making sure they knew how much weight they could add to the RV without affecting its function.
Kate focused on making the living space feel airy.
Kate didn't want to sacrifice coziness in the 400-square-foot RV, so she focused on making the small space beautiful and functional.
She splurged on their flooring, choosing a dark, durable vinyl that would withstand her active kids.
There is also a wall in the living room covered in floral wallpaper. It cost about $200, but Kate loves the pop of color it adds to the space.
She offset the cost by using the couch from her family's apartment in Brooklyn as their main seating area.
"When we lived for a year in Airbnbs, there were only two things I really missed," Kate said. "One was my sectional, and two was a good vacuum. So now we have both."
Surprisingly, the kitchen needed the least work.
Kate said she didn't have to demo much of the kitchen because the cabinets and appliances were in good shape.
She painted the cabinets a soft green and added brass hardware to give them a more luxurious look. The kitchen also has a fold-up counter extension, giving the O'Phalens more space to prep food, and she uses baskets for additional storage above the cabinets.
"I feel like the paint in our renovation really did a lot of heavy lifting," Kate said, adding that she thinks the kitchen is one of the most beautiful spaces in her home.
You can also see Kate's eldest child's bedroom, a loft that sits above the room, from the kitchen. It's covered by a curtain during the day and accessible by a ladder.
The bedroom has to be able to transform on travel days.
The primary bedroom has a queen-size bed, a dresser, and a closet.
However, the bed sits on a slide-out that must be pulled in when the O'Phalens are driving so it fits in a highway lane. Because of that, some pieces of the bedroom have to be taken off the walls when they drive.
"In an RV…your house goes through an earthquake every time you move," O'Phalen said. "Everything has to be really secured, or it has to come down."
They use the bed to store larger items that need to come down on travel days, such as large mirrors or other art pieces.
The O'Phalens also have a washing machine in their bedroom, so they don't have to stop at laundromats on the road.
The RV's sole bathroom is in the primary bedroom.
The shower and toilet sit separately in the RV, with the toilet in a private room on one side of the bedroom entrance and the shower on the other.
The orange paint and artwork make the bathroom cozy, and Kate said she ended up completely redoing the shower.
"It was the hardest part of the renovation, and I discovered exactly why plumbers make good money," she said. "I sat on the floor of the Home Depot for so long trying to figure out what fittings I needed that an employee came over and brought me a cushion."
She's happy with how the shower turned out, though, with its skylight and tile walls.
The kid's bedroom was originally a storage space.
"Our RV is called a toy hauler, which means it's designed to haul side by sides or motorcycles or big kid toys, essentially," Kate said.
They don't need to haul those kinds of items, but they did need additional bedroom space for their two younger children.
Kate installed lofted queen beds in the space, which can be raised during the day to create extra living space for the family.
The back wall of the room also opens completely, allowing them to enjoy indoor-outdoor living when the weather is nice.
The O'Phalens spent about $7,000 refurbishing the RV.
Kate did her best to keep the RV renovation costs low, saying the aesthetic upgrades cost only about $5,000.
In addition, they had to make some safety upgrades, including $1,000 for new tires. They also spent around $600 on their washer-dryer.
A lot of the decor was budget finds, like a dresser they found on the side of the road, which Kate altered to fit the RV. She made a DIY version of a light fixture; it would have cost $400 online, but she made it for $30.
Kate also said her kids helped paint and make the space feel like home, so they felt invested in the RV too.
They hit the road in early 2022 and haven't looked back.
When the RV was finally done, the O'Phalens were excited to start traveling in early 2022. Kate said she and Daniel weren't worried about living nomadically, since they had already done so for a year in Airbnbs. It was the idea of driving a truck and an RV that intimidated them because of their lack of experience.
"The first time we hitched up the truck and trailer, it took us two hours because we could not figure out why it wouldn't hitch up," Kate said. "We're city people. There was so much to learn about things that seem obvious to people who have grown up outdoors."
Overall, though, Kate said her family adjusted to RV life pretty quickly.
"We had gotten really flexible and resilient," she said. "It felt like home immediately. And every time we've talked about moving out of it, my kids are really upset. They don't want to move out of it."
The O'Phalens have traveled all over North America in their RV.
The O'Phalens typically travel every two to three weeks, staying at campgrounds or on public land. They have traveled all over the US, including Alaska; seen 53 of the 66 National Parks in the US; visited 11 provinces in Canada; and spent six months in Mexico this past winter.
Kate said living on the road was initially a little lonely until they formed friendships with other people who live the RV life.
"We have a traveling community that we have caravanned with for years now," she said. "We have friends that are like my kids' cousins at this point."
She also said she's been surprised by how much her kids get out of RV life, particularly through hands-on learning experiences. For instance, her eldest daughter is an aspiring veterinarian, and she has been able to spend time with a variety of animals thanks to their lifestyle.
"She just got to do the veterinary camp at UC Davis this summer, and we have been to vet camp on a farm in North Carolina," Kate said. "We went to the monarch butterfly migration in Mexico. We went to a jaguar sanctuary for her birthday in Oaxaca. We released baby sea turtles on the beach."
"We just have had such incredible, deep lifelong learning experiences because of the way that we live," Kate said. "It's hard to give that up."
It's also brought their whole family closer.
Kate and Daniel were both always involved parents, but traveling together has only brought them closer. Daniel, in particular, said being home with his kids has made a huge difference for him.
"I went from seeing my kids only an hour or two a day to never missing a moment, and I'm very grateful to this lifestyle and the time that I've been given with them," he told Business Insider.
"He knows his children in such a deep way now," Kate agreed, saying the time her family gets to spend together is something they never take for granted.
RV life also saves the O'Phalen family money.
Kate said that she knows people who live very affordably on the road and people who spend a lot of money on vehicle payments or luxury resort stays on RV life.
Her family falls more in the middle. They live mostly off of Daniel's income, with Kate providing some additional income through her content creation. They have a Thousand Trails subscription, which costs them a little under $1,000 a year for nationwide campground access.
"When my husband was laid off a couple of years ago, it really helped us weather that," Kate said of their lifestyle. "We said multiple times, 'My gosh, if we were living in New York, this would be so stressful right now.' And we were able to just really dial back our spending and make it through that."
Still, RV living isn't always easy. It can be expensive.
Kate told Business Insider that they have had plenty of problems with their vehicles, from their truck's heater pump hose popping off in Yosemite to a tire falling off in Mexico.
Plus, when those issues come up, they're not just managing their truck; they also have to handle their home and family.
"It's not just like my road trip has gone wrong, but it's like, where do I park my house while I figure out how to fix the vehicle that tows my house?" Kate said. "And do I have enough groceries and water? And are the police going to knock on my door and say, 'You can't park here?' There's just so much of that. That's the hard part."
Those issues often cost thousands of dollars, making them even more stressful. For now, those expenses are worth it for the O'Phalens, particularly since their daily living costs are so low, but they are still stressful.
Kate also said the "logistics" of RV life can be tough, particularly because she is raising young children.
For instance, when they first started living in an RV, her youngest child was an infant, and it was difficult to find doctors while traveling to keep up with the baby's vaccination schedule. They find solutions, but living on the road can make day-to-day life more complicated.
Because of their lifestyle, they were able to save enough money to buy land.
In 2026, the O'Phalens used some of the money they had saved to buy an acre of land outside Bend, Oregon. They don't plan to stop traveling anytime soon, though.
"We really have done a lot of the United States at this point," she said. "And the cultural experience in Mexico was so amazing that we'd like to do more of that."
They hope to slowly build a house that can serve as their home base, then embrace international travel.
"My vision is that at some point the RV stays here for good and we do more international flying for maybe three to six months at a time," she said. "I have a dream that at some point we build out a sprinter van and ship it either to Europe or to South America."
Kate said RV life has been "magical" for her family.
Kate said her family's nomadic lifestyle has completely changed their family forever.
"It is magical in a way that almost defies description," Kate said of their life on the road. "It is extremely transformative. I would say we've become outdoorsy and really conservation-minded in a way that we never were."
Kate said she knows RV life can be challenging and that it's not for everyone, though she hopes sharing her experience can show people it's more accessible than they think.
"I would encourage anyone who is on the fence to try it out because I really do think even if you do go back to the same life that you were living before, you will go back with such an interesting perspective, and you'll be changed," she said.

“Have a scrumdiddlyumptious day!” is how Rusty Goffe, who played an Oompa-Loompa in the 1971 adaptation of “Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory” opposite Gene Wilder, signs off our Zoom call after we speak earlier this month.
With such Wonka-isms rolling off his tongue with ease, it’s no surprise that when Netflix, which acquired the rights to Roald Dahl’s literary estate five years ago, planned to make a Wonka-inspired game show Goffe was clearly top of their list to bring back.
In “Wonka’s Golden Ticket,” which launched on Sept. 23, he stars alongside his son Ben Goffe — also an actor who has appeared in “Artemis Fowl,” among other titles — as well as a host of new Oompa-Loompas. (Unlike in the original film, these Oompa-Loompas “come in all shapes and sizes now,” as the contestants are told during the show.). Also back is Wilder, albeit only his voice, which has been, somewhat controversially, recreated in AI with the blessing of his wife, Wilder himself having died in 2016.
Popular on Variety
Over the course of nine episodes, viewers will see 12 contestants take part in a series of increasingly wacky challenges in the hopes of winning a “lifetime’s supply of money” (approximately $3 million, calculated as an annual six-figure salary over 30 years), all played out on Wonka-themed set pieces, including the famous elevator and, of course, the edible candy room, complete with chocolate waterfall.
Ahead of “Wonka’s The Golden Ticket” launching, Goffe, now 77, spoke with Variety about how he came to work on the competition show, what it was like to step back into the world of Wonka — and his feelings at hearing Wilder’s voice recreated by AI.
How did this come about? Did Netflix reach out to you?
Well, I just had a phone call from my agent in New York saying they want you in Netflix, talking about “Wonka.” [I said] “Being in ‘Wonka?’ That was a long time ago.” And they said “Yeah, they still want you.” So that’s how I got into it, and I really loved the new one.
Once you knew it was a game show, were you wondering what that format might be?
I was wondering how is this going to happen. But after a couple of days, I got used to it. The contestants were in their own bubble, so when they came on, you just nodded to them, because they were trying to get answers from your face, how they’re doing. So we’re not giving anything away. I was really pleased — thrilled — this time to have my son with me, Ben. [He’s] 33 years of age, an Oompa-Loompa!
What was it like for him to step into that iconic role?
Well, he’s grown up with “Wonka” through me, and he loved the first one, and when [Netflix] said about Ben being in it, he jumped at the chance. “Yeah, yeah, I’m going to be an Oompa-Loompa,” you know, because he’s an actor. He’s done Shakespeare, many, many movies.
Did you give any give him any tips?
No. None whatsoever. I was an Oompa-Loompa. You’re the new one. Learn — on the job!
What was it like for you stepping back into the world of “Wonka”?
It was bizarre, going into the studio, into the chocolate room, in fact. And it was all modern. They still had a river. They still had a waterfall. It was absolutely fantastic, it was. And the river — last time, it was just dirty water, it smelled because we were pouring real cream and real sugar into it, and with the hot lights, it was melting. It was melting, and poor Michael Böllner, who played Augustus Gloop [in th 1971 film], he had to fall in it when he was a kid. And they ask him now, “What was it like, Michael? What was the river like?” [In a German accent] “It vas stinky vater!” in his best German. But it was lovely. But unfortunately, he wasn’t there, it was just myself and my young son, who wasn’t there in the original.
Did you keep anything from the set of the original film?
Mmmmmm, yes. I might have a golden ticket, a real one or two. My children’s inheritance.
Would you have wanted to be a contestant on “Wonka’s Golden Ticket” if you weren’t part of the cast?
No. It was great being the Oompa-Loompa just watching them, because I knew what they were going to win, lose, what’s going to happen if they lost [a challenge]. Which is not good on some occasions.
Did you ever think that the original film would have such a lasting impact that you’d still be revisiting that world so many years later?
I am still absolutely amazed how big it still is. I get to go and do conventions, mainly in the States, and people say, “Yeah, we loved it. We came out the theater, when we saw the new ones. We came out the theater, but we were still singing ‘Oompa-Loompa doompa dee do’ — your movie.” They loved it. But I was surprised how big it still was and still is! And I thank the people for keeping it alive. If it wasn’t for the fans, it’d be gone.
This time round there seems to be more diversity among the Oompa-Loompas…
[These] Oompa-Loompas, they weren’t just short. We had one bodybuilder, big guy, a tall guy, three ladies, a small man, and Ben. It was wonderful to have this diverse [cast of] people.
Netflix has also brought Gene Wilder’s voice back for the show with AI, which has prompted some discussion. Was it weird hearing his voice again after so many years?
Well, “weird” is not the word. It was lovely hearing his voice again, because I loved that man. He was a gentle, fantastic character, very funny, very, very kind, and to hear him in the show, I was so pleased that Netflix had done it. He is Mr. Wonka. He is Willy Wonka. Gene Wilder is Willy Wonka.
Was it uncanny hearing him again, or is it just like he’s standing there?
It’s just him standing there. I did shed a tear when I first heard it, because I loved the man so much. But then I thought he wouldn’t want me to do that. He’d want me to be an Oompa-Loompa, get out there, do the job. Yeah, that that was Gene. He was a lovely, lovely man.
Did you have a favorite moment of filming this new show?
Yes, the breaks! It was one of the best moments of my life to do “Wonka” again. I started my career on “Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory” and now I am pleased to announce to Variety that I’ve ended my career on “Willy Wonka’s The Golden Ticket.”

A video showing a group of people removing and breaking metal barricades near a water body is being widely shared with a claim that it shows people in Karnataka vandalising barricades after authorities restricted Ganesh idol immersion (here, here, here). Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: A video shows devotees in Karnataka vandalising barricades after authorities restricted Ganesh idol immersion.
Fact: The video is from Hyderabad. It shows members of the Bhagyanagar Ganesh Utsav Samithi removing barricades at Tank Bund while protesting restrictions on Ganesh idol immersion. Hence, the claim made in the post is MISLEADING.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to an Instagram post by South Matters featuring the same visuals. According to the post, the visuals show tension at Tank Bund in Hyderabad, where representatives of the Bhagyanagar Ganesh Utsav Samithi staged a protest against restrictions on Ganesh idol immersion. We also found a post by the BNN channel on X stating the same.
Based on this, we conducted a relevant keyword search and found multiple media reports about the incident (here, here, here). According to these reports, the barricades were installed to prevent devotees from immersing Ganesh idols along the Tank Bund stretch. Members of the Bhagyanagar Ganesh Utsav Samithi (BGUS) protested against the restrictions and demanded that devotees be allowed to continue idol immersion at Tank Bund.
The comparison between the viral visuals and the visuals reported by the media can be seen below.
To sum up, this viral video of devotees removing barricades is from Hyderabad, not Karnataka.

ICC convicts former Central African Republic militia commander of torture
Judges at the International Criminal Court have convicted former Seleka rebel commander Mahamat Said Abdel Kani of persecution and torture as crimes against humanity committed while he ran a prison in Bangui, the capital of the Central African Republic
THE HAGUE, Netherlands -- Judges at the International Criminal Court on Wednesday convicted rebel commander Mahamat Said Abdel Kani of persecution and torture as crimes against humanity committed while he ran a prison in the Central African Republic.
Said, 56, wore jeans and a blue sweater and remained expressionless for most of the hourlong hearing as presiding Judge Miatta Maria Samba described the conditions prisoners endured at the facility in the capital, Bangui.
During the trial, witnesses described cramped cells with walls marked by “bullet holes and blood” and said they were whipped “until they soiled themselves,” Samba said. Other victims testified that they were confined in a windowless room under the floorboards of Said’s office.
The charges stemmed from fighting more than a decade ago between the predominantly Muslim Seleka rebels, who had seized power from then-President Francois Bozize, and a mainly Christian militia called the anti-Balaka.
Said pleaded not guilty to all charges when the proceedings began in 2021. His sentence, which could be as long as life in prison, will be decided at a later date.

Throughout 2026, people shared a rumor alleging Denver Broncos quarterback Bo Nix responded to U.S. President Donald Trump calling a reporter a pig. According to social media users' posts, the NFL quarterback publicly rebuked Trump, saying that "staying silent makes me part of the problem."
For example, on Sept. 20, a Facebook post (archived) read, "BREAKING NFL NEWS: Broncos star Bo Nix breaks his silence in shocking video response after 'Little Pig' comment to a female reporter shocks T.r.u.m.p — NFL superstar condemns disrespect towards women and sparks nationwide outrage."
The post featured a meme showing side-by-side images of Nix and Trump, with a purported Nix quote reading as follows:
When I watched that clip, something in me snapped. I play this game with fire and pride, but I was raised to respect every woman who cheers, works, and sacrifices behind the scenes. If a man with that much power can mock and demean them in front of the world, then staying silent makes me part of the problem. And I refuse to be part of that.
Other examples of the claim appeared on Facebook, Instagram and Threads. Snopes readers also searched this website in September 2026, specifically asking, "Did Bo Nix stand up for a female reporter?"
We first used search engines such as DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo to locate possible evidence from credible sources about Nix publicly commenting on Trump. If the story was true, journalists with reputable news outlets, such as The Associated Press or Reuters — or sports blogs — would have widely reported on it. That was not the case.
The rumor about Bo Nix responding to Trump was fictional, and as a result we've rated the claim false.
The claim appeared to take inspiration from a real remark Trump made in November 2025 while aboard Air Force One, when he told a female reporter asking a question, "Quiet. Quiet, piggy." 
People.com, citing a journalist's X post, reported the female journalist Trump addressed as "piggy" was Bloomberg reporter Catherine Lucey. The subject matter of Lucey's question pertained to asking Trump about his past relationship with deceased convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
We emailed the Denver Broncos to ask if the organization would like to address the fake Nix quote and will update this article if we receive further details.
Digging into the rumor
In addition to social media posts, the untrue rumor about Nix publicly rebuking Trump appeared on a handful of generic-looking WordPress blogs. Those blogs lacked author names and credible information about their founding. An examination of the blogs found they were not reputable outlets, for example such as well-known newspapers or established news websites, or websites for local or national TV channels.
A scan of the text in one blog article with the artificial intelligence detection tool Pangram displayed the results, "We believe that this entire text is AI," as well as, "100% of this text is AI."
Snopes doesn't depend solely on AI detection tools, which vary in reliability, and instead considers the tools' results as one of several data points toward judging an image's authenticity. For Pangram, we bear in mind the platform's strong performance in third-party and internal evaluations, as well as criticisms of the tool.
Creators of content like the fabricated Nix quote capitalize on social media users' willingness to believe and share the made-up stories, profiting from advertising revenue on external websites to which the posts link. (Snopes has previously reported on the business strategy.)
The fictional story about Nix standing up for women resembled glurge, which Dictionary.com defines as "stories, often sent by email, that are supposed to be true and uplifting, but which are often fabricated and sentimental."
For further reading, we previously reported about whether Broncos head coach Sean Payton fired two players for refusing to stand for the U.S. national anthem.

- Amy Hennig's original version of Uncharted 4 portrayed Sam Drake as a villain to his brother and the series hero, Nathan Drake.
- According to former Naughty Dog VFX artist Matt Redford, Sam Drake was "not the same guy" as he is in the final 2016 release.
- He confirmed that a different actor was planned to play Sam before the role ultimately went to Troy Baker.
The Uncharted 4: A Thief’s End we played in 2016 differed vastly from the version Amy Hennig originally developed at Naughty Dog. The PlayStation title remains one of the best adventure games of all time, but it originally had Sam Drake as a villain.
According to former Naughty Dog VFX artist Matt Radford, Amy Hennig’s Uncharted 4 was “very different” from the official release.
Sam Drake Was “Not the Same Guy” in Amy Hennig’s Uncharted 4
Speaking on the latest Kiwi Talkz episode, Radford said he worked alongside Hennig on the original version of Uncharted 4 while he was still new to game development. However, Naughty Dog’s final release a decade ago didn’t match Hennig’s original vision for the ambitious sequel, which made Nathan Drake’s own brother a villain.
“Amy’s vision for the game that I saw didn’t have the same characters, like Sam, and I mean Sam was in it, but he was not the same guy. It was like a very different, very different; like Sam was the villain,” said Radford.
The former Naughty Dog VFX artist also revealed that the team originally planned to cast a different actor for Sam. Troy Baker ultimately played Sam Drake in the final release, making the character central to Nathan’s journey to search for Avery’s treasure.
“There was a bunch of differences: different actor, and that actor used to hang around Naughty Dog,” said Radford. “The original guy they had cast, he was really nice, and he works with Amy still on the Star Wars game.”
Sam helps Nathan in Uncharted 4, despite deceiving him with a false plan to save his own life by helping the main antagonist, Rafe Adler. But he never becomes a villain himself. Whether Hennig’s Uncharted 4 would’ve been better than the one we got remains unanswered, but Radford says it “seemed cool.”
However, he admits, “But then again, Uncharted 4 was amazing. So, you know, you can’t kind of fault Neil and Bruce’s vision because I loved that game and I loved the story they came up with.”
Speaking of Bruce Straley, the Uncharted 4 director recently shared his AAA gaming thoughts, while Naughty Dog head Neil Druckmann is currently working on their next flagship release, Intergalactic The Heretic Prophet.
That said, would you have preferred Sam as a villain alongside Rafe in Uncharted 4? Let us know in the comments section below.

- A video shared on social media in September 2026 by the conservative pundit Rob Smith featured an interview with a woman who claimed to live on the South side of Chicago andsaid that immigrants who entered the United States without authorization ("illegals") were receiving $20,000 in benefits from the Democratic-led governments of Chicago and Illinois.
- Snopes found that the interview was originally conducted by Brooke Shirley (the mother of the conservative social media personality Nick Shirley, who is herself a conservative social media personality) in August 2024, while the Democratic National Convention was happening in Chicago.
- The woman interviewed in the video made several claims that closely resembled major Republican talking points at the time. Some of those claims referenced policies that have become outdated, while others were misleading or exaggerated. As a result, we have not rated the claim.
- We contacted Smith for comment on the fact that his posts sharing the video never mentioned that the interview took place in 2024, and will update this story if we learn more. We also reached out to the Illinois Housing Development Authority to confirm that a program that provided up to 6 months or $15,000 in renter's assistance for asylum seekers was no longer active; it said that program stopped processing applications in June 2024.
In September 2026, a video posted by the conservative pundit Rob Smith appeared online claiming that Democrats were giving $20,000 in benefits to "illegals" in Chicago.
Snopes readers asked us to verify or disprove the claims made in the video, the latest in a long stretch of Republican-promoted rumors suggesting Democrats give large amounts of money or other benefits to immigrants living in the country without authorization. (Snopes fact-checked a version of that claim from the White House here).
Oftentimes, as is the case here, such claims are accompanied by the idea that these payments are the first step in a Democratic-led plot to permanently control the federal government.
The video presents its narrative without providing any additional evidence to support any of its claims, which are as follows:
Immigrants living in the country illegally receive $15,000 in food stamps from the government; - These immigrants receive $5,000 in cash from the government;
- These immigrants receive free, government subsidized Wi-Fi;
- The government covers these immigrants' rent for two years;
- Democrats give immigrants living in the country illegally these benefits as a sort of "bribe," with the later goal of granting them the right to vote. The immigrants would then repay the favor by voting for Democrats in large numbers, effectively diluting the voting power of non-immigrant Americans and giving the party long-term control.
We have refrained from rating this article because of the complexity of the claims in the video. Our research indicated that the first two claims were unfounded at best, while the third and fourth are exaggerated, though the fourth might have been the source behind the $15,000 figure. (The fifth claim is also unfounded, since it depends on the other four being true.)
We also noted that much of the rhetoric resembled common claims made during the last two years of President Joe Biden's administration, when Texas Gov. Greg Abbott made a show of busing migrants entering the U.S. to cities like Chicago. Much of the reporting around these issues also came from that time, leading us to suspect that the interview took place in the lead-up to the 2024 election, rather than in 2026.
We were able to confirm the theory using a reverse image search. The original video first appeared on the Instagram (archived) and TikTok accounts of conservative social media personality Brooke Shirley in late August 2024. Shirley, the mother of conservative social media personality Nick Shirley, originally posted the video in the days following the 2024 Democratic National Convention, which was held in Chicago. She has reposted the video at least twice since then.
As part of reporting this story, we contacted the Illinois Housing Development Authority, which ran a program that paid some rent costs for immigrants legally seeking asylum, though not to the extent suggested in the video
We also contacted Smith seeking clarification on the time discrepancy, since his September 2026 video never mentioned that the interview originally took place two years prior. We also asked whether Smith believed the policies described in the interview were active in 2026, but had not heard back.
Wealso attempted to confirm that the interview featured in the video, conducted with a woman who said she lived on Chicago's south side, was real — if it was instead generated using AI tools, for instance, the person who generated it 
Immigrants did not get $15,000 in food stamps
Immigrants who are in the country without authorization have never been eligible for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, and the video's assertion otherwise is not based on concrete evidence.
SNAP eligibility is extended to some non-citizens, but there are strict requirements, which were made even more strict after the passage of the Trump administration's much-touted "One Big Beautiful Bill" budget act in July 2025.
The principal requirement is that an immigrant must have a permanent residency card and have lived in the U.S. for at least five years, or be under the age of 18. Prior to July 2025, however, there were exceptions for refugees and individuals granted asylum. Even before these exceptions were eliminated, however, the claim would still have been untrue. SNAP benefits are calculated using the number of individuals in a household (in 2024, for instance, a family of four could receive a maximum of $973 each month, or just over $11,500 per year, with money subtracted based on an individual's household income. Immigration status does not factor into the calculation at all.
Immigrants are not getting $5,000 in cash
This claim also spread significantly around the time the video was originally shared.. It, too, is not based on any evidence. Snopes disproved a claim that immigrants got roughly $3,800 in 2017, and many prominent fact-checking organizations have disproved the claim that immigrants are getting $5,000 in cash or gift cards.
Furthermore, although exposing and cutting alleged wasteful government spending has been a major policy platform of the second Trump administration, there was no evidence the administration has identified or targeted programs matching the claims in the video.
Chicago has a free WiFi program ... for families of students
It's worth noting that many libraries in 
However, we found that the city does offer a free home internet program that immigrants can access. The program is eligible for families of students enrolled in Chicago Public Schools who receive free or reduced meals, and there are no eligibility requirements based on immigration status.
According to a city fact-sheet about the program, the internet access is valued at $10 per month — a drop in the bucket compared to the alleged $20,000 in benefits each immigrant allegedly receives.
Chicago did pay some immigrants' rent ... for up to 6 months, or $15,000
Snopes found that in the fall of 2022, months after Greg Abbott's busing program began, the state of Illinois did implement a program through the Illinois Housing Development Authority to cover the housing costs for the influx of migrants seeking asylum entering Chicago. (It should be noted that migrants are legally entitled to claim asylum, and therefore the description of these individuals as "illegal immigrants" is suspect at best).  
However, contrary to the claim, this program did not cover rent for two years. Several outlets have separately investigated a similar claim about the government of Michigan, too.
Instead, it covered a security deposit and rent for three months, with an optional extension for another three months, making six months in total. Applicants could receive a maximum of $15,000, which we suspect may have been the source of the food stamps figure.
According to an IHDA document detailing the program's accomplishments, it gave $3.7 million in grants to 681 families by the beginning of 2023, and another $1.4 million went toward additional three-month extensions. The authority claimed households received an average of $6,369, which is significant, but still below the fictitious $15,000 in food stamps described previously.
The program provided $53 million in rental assistance to 6,623 asylum seekers and families over the course of its lifespan, meaning that each successfully applicant received an average of just over $8,000.
One last note on this program: the IDHA's program paid landlords directly wherever possible — the money for rental assistance offered through the program was not given to immigrants.
Conclusion
In sum, the claims were a combination of 
It is true that immigrants were eligible for some welfare programs in Chicago during the later years of Joe Biden's presidency. However, the emergency housing program ended in 2024, while the additional restrictions on SNAP implemented by the Trump administration specifically bars refugees and asylum seekers — the individuals generally being incorrectly described as "illegal immigrants."
For more reading, we previously investigated a rumor that the government of Massachusetts gave $100 million to non-citizens.

Cristiano Ronaldo walked into a packed room, claimed to be nervous, then did what he has done for more than two decades: taking centre stage, swatting away critics and insisting the final whistle is not yet in sight.
The 41-year-old Portugal captain, speaking on Wednesday at the Portugal Football Summit main stage before Thursday’s UEFA Nations League match against Wales, said he still had plenty to offer his country as Jorge Jesus prepares for his first game as national team coach.
Jesus replaced Roberto Martinez after Portugal’s disappointing World Cup campaign ended in the round of 16 against eventual champion Spain.
Ronaldo, now on 979 career goals — 833 for clubs and 146 for Portugal — is 21 short of the 1,000-goal landmark he has openly targeted. Asked whether winning the Nations League or reaching four figures mattered more, he grinned and chose both.
“One goal is to achieve both – reaching 1,000 goals and the national team trying to win this Nations League,” Ronaldo said.
“It’s a new era with manager Jorge Jesus, whom we all know well; I just hope things go well for him.”
Ronaldo said reaching 1,000 in Portugal colours would be “the icing on the cake”.
“Scoring my 1,000th goal for the national team would be the culmination of something – a beautiful story,” he said. “It wouldn’t be the end of it, but it would be a beautiful story.”
Ronaldo insisted, however, that he was not consumed by the chase.
“I’ve already admitted that I want to get there, and I will get there,” he said. “An obsession? No ... The rest is about enjoying it, enjoying every day.”
PRODUCTIVE TALKS
Ronaldo acknowledged he had considered his international future after Portugal’s World Cup exit, but said talks with the Portuguese FA and Jesus convinced him to continue.
“They count on me. I still believe that I’m able to help the national team,” he said. “The most important point is to be able, inside the pitch, to score goals and help the team to win games.
“If the manager doesn’t count on me, I can leave today – no problem at all... When I feel that I’m not doing anything here, that I’m not contributing on the pitch, not scoring goals, creating a bad atmosphere, or that they don’t want me here, I’ll be the first to pack my bags.”
Pressed on retirement, Ronaldo refused to draw a clear line under his career.
“I learnt something from my late 30s onwards, which is to live in the moment, don’t think about tomorrow,” he said.
“Is it possible? Yes. Highly likely? Yes. But will it happen? No, I don’t know.”
Ronaldo also bristled at criticism, saying media outlets had been trying to “kill” him for years.
“That’s not going to happen under any circumstances – not even with a shotgun,” he said. “And even so, I still manage to dodge the bullet.”
Ronaldo may be 21 goals from four figures and perhaps closer to the exit than he cares to admit, but for now he remains exactly where he likes to be: in Portugal’s shirt, in front of the cameras, and dodging bullets with a smile.

Judge considers restoring journalists' access to White House after Trump's ban
Sign up for alerts on breaking news and exclusive reporting from NPR
A federal judge appeared inclined to order the White House to restore — at least temporarily — the press passes of journalists for CNN, Politico and MS NOW (formerly MSNBC).
On Wednesday afternoon, U.S. District Judge Timothy J. Kelly, who was nominated by Trump in 2017, held an emergency hearing after the news outlets filed a lawsuit seeking to undo the ban.
In his introductory remarks, Kelly said it appeared the White House had violated the news outlets' constitutional right of due process — which was set out in previous court decisions — when it abruptly blocked the access of journalists who held permanent credentials to work in the building.
Theodore J. Boutrous, a lawyer representing the three news outlets, said the White House ban took place " without a semblance of due process."
He also argued that the move was in violation of CNN, MS NOW and Politico's First Amendment rights and called it a form of retaliation for their coverage of the president, adding that it was "probably the clearest case in history" of viewpoint discrimination.
In threatening to ban the news outlets on Friday, Trump had told reporters at the White House, "They purposely write negative news, and they do that because they want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration."
Boutrous further contended the news organizations were suffering irreparable harm by being locked out of the White House at a time of war, and on the eve of Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House.
" The constitutional violation is against the public interest," he said.
Justice Department lawyer Michael Velchik, on the other hand, argued that access to the White House was a "privilege," not a right. He also cited national security concerns as a reason for the continued ban. In its legal filings, the department had included White House letters to the three news organizations taking issue with stories on a variety of topics, including construction of a "top secret" bunker under the White House ballroom, talks with Iran and whether there were "very bad" vibes at the recent Republican convention in Dallas.
Boutrous pushed back on the claim, asserting that the first mention of national security came only days after the ban was imposed.
" I guess the light bulb went off and they all decided 'Start talking about national security,'" Boutrous said.
Kelly did not rule from the bench, adding that he will consider both sides and make a decision as soon as possible.

The 50th episode of The Health Wrap by The Hindu explores longevity, healthspan and factors that influence health as people age.
Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, The Hindu, speaks to Navin Gnanasekaran, longevity physician and head of Radiology, Apollo Hospitals, Chennai, about healthy ageing and the distinction between lifespan and healthspan.
India’s population is ageing. According to the United Nations Population Fund’s India Ageing Report 2023, the share of people aged 60 and above is projected to increase from 10.5% in 2022 to 20.8% by 2050. The episode discusses what this demographic change means for maintaining health and functional ability in later life.
The conversation covers racquet sports as a key form of physical activity, along with nutrition, sleep, muscle strength, stress, metabolism, inflammation and cognition. It also examines the importance of establishing sustainable health habits.
Physical activity is a key part of the discussion. The World Health Organisation recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity or 75 minutes of vigorous activity a week for adults, along with muscle-strengthening activities on two or more days. For older adults, the guidelines also recommend activities that improve balance and help prevent falls.
Racquet sports are discussed as one form of physical activity. Dr. Gnanasekaran looks at how they can combine exercise with social interaction and cognitive engagement.
The episode also discusses whether longevity advice needs to account for Indian lifestyles and health needs, including food habits, physical activity and other aspects of daily life.
The discussion focuses on the practical aspects of maintaining health and physical function as people live longer, and on the difference between simply extending lifespan and maintaining health during those additional years.

The Press Is Not the Root of Trump’s Problems
He’s in a predicament of his own creation.
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
President Trump is going through a rough patch—in foreign relations, in the economy, in the courts, and in election outlook—and he believes that he has found the culprits: CNN, MS NOW, and Politico. On Friday, Trump said he was banning the three outlets from the White House “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS” and warned that more bans could come. When he feels beleaguered, he tends to lash out at familiar enemies, especially reporters. The idea that negative coverage is to blame for his predicament is perversely flattering. But Trump’s true scourge is reality, not how the news is covering it.
Although the decision is part of a gradually intensifying attack on free speech, as I noted last month, it has drawn particular pushback. This morning, five major TV networks (including Fox News) agreed to suspend pool coverage of the president and White House events after CNN was blocked from its previously assigned spot in a pool rotation today. The three banned outlets also sued over their exclusion. How such a suit will fare is unclear; Trump banned the Associated Press from the White House press pool last year after it refused to adopt his renaming of the Gulf of Mexico, and a lawsuit challenging the ban is still pending.
After Trump committed a Kinsley gaffe on Friday by calling his move “the ban on the free press,” he tried to clean up his spin this morning. “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS,” he wrote, claiming that it “is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!” This is nonsense. Trump has every right to hate the way he’s covered, but if the government has the power to decide what is fake and what is true, then the press is not free.
Trump’s post demonstrates his talismanic belief in the power of news coverage. The president himself has been obsessed with attention—how to get it and how to shape it—for his entire life, and he is a relic from an era when the media were so dominant, and had such control over the means of reaching an audience, that they seemed to shape reality. They are much diminished today, occupying a strange, unstable role: strong enough to be blamed for both Trump’s rise and his downfall, yet weak enough that they can be threatened with relative impunity. Though Trump’s attacks on free speech are unlike any in living memory, his is not the first administration to believe that its problems are about messaging and coverage. In 2012, Barack Obama said that the biggest mistake of his first term “was thinking that this job was just about getting the policy right,” because “the nature of this office is also to tell a story to the American people.” A decade later, Joe Biden’s administration was convinced that negative coverage of inflation and Biden’s age were bigger problems than inflation or the president’s evident frailty.
Now Trump is making the same misjudgment. He is not unpopular because of Politico, an outlet that focuses largely on Washington machinations, or because of MS NOW or CNN, two cable channels that—as he is fond of pointing out—have relatively small audiences for television. The media cannot be “failing” and all-powerful at the same time. Trump is unpopular because (to name a few big reasons) he is losing a war of choice to Iran, making inflation worse without seeming to care how voters feel, overreaching with draconian immigration enforcement, and focusing on vanity projects that don’t matter to voters.
Ironically, Trump is committing the same error as many liberal critics of the press, who seem to believe that popular support for the president would have collapsed long ago if the media had used harsher words to describe him. But the idea that tougher coverage would have stopped him is fantasy. Although the press has made many mistakes in how it has reported on the president, including giving him hours of uninterrupted TV air time in 2016, downplaying bigoted remarks, and “sanewashing” some statements, Trump has also received more intensive investigation and negative coverage than any president in American history.
Some of that coverage has surely been hackish partisanship—which is protected by the First Amendment too—but much of it has been earned. Newspapers, magazines, wire services, and TV networks have turned out a series of scoops about the chaos inside the administration, Trump’s policy errors, and the pervasive corruption around him. In late 2023, The Atlantic published a set of prescient essays considering what would happen if Trump won back the White House. Voters had even lived through one Trump presidency already. They had access to the relevant information before they voted him in again.
Believing that Americans might have chosen differently if only The New York Times had abandoned its obtuse headline conventions is comforting to some Trump critics, because it puts the blame on the press rather than acknowledging that a majority of those who voted wanted Trump. By the same token, Trump would rather blame news outlets he does not like than confront the reality that some of those same voters are rejecting him because of his choices.
The president faces an additional risk in trying to ban these three outlets. He detests adversarial coverage, but he desperately desires attention. This afternoon, Trump spoke with reporters outside the White House. Usually, his comments are captured by the boom mics from the pool TV team, but without their presence today, he was inaudible. Censorship can silence anyone, it turns out—even the censor.

By Ayad Akhtar
When I was 20 years old, I started to sense a hole inside me. The feeling was utterly concrete, though the result of no medical condition that any of the various doctors I saw could identify. The hole felt like a viscous emptiness—a paradox, admittedly, as any real emptiness should have felt like nothing. This was a nothing, but its nothingness very much felt like something—and something that was growing …
My friends found my behavior disturbing. I was missing class in college, showing up to theater rehearsals drunk. A caring young woman I was dating could take no more of my savage, ranting mood swings and persistent despair. She broke up with me over tea at the student union and implored me to seek help. I knew she was right. Even sleep was now fraught with violent, terrifying dreams—of rocket ships out of control, conflagrations and invasions, and, yes, holes into which I would disappear. But exactly what sort of help I might need, I didn’t know.

Trump set to greet Xi for high-stakes state visit
BEIJING/WASHINGTON — Chinese leader Xi Jinping is set to arrive in the United States on Wednesday evening for his first state visit in 11 years, opening high-stakes talks with President Trump at a pivotal moment for both men.
It is the second time the leaders are meeting this year after the Beijing summit in May, when they agreed to build a more stable bilateral relationship.
Both leaders are trying to shore up power at home. For Trump, the visit comes just over a month before the midterm elections, and for Xi, preparations for an all-important Party Congress start when he returns to Beijing.
But despite both countries projecting a willingness to build what China has dubbed a relationship of "constructive strategic stability," fierce negotiations over weighty subjects such as AI and trade are underway.
"Under the water, the Chinese seem to have done a lot of kicking lately. And you know, if we have to, we'll kick back," U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a Fox News interview in July.
A "fragile" detente
Trump has frequently spoken warmly about how he was treated during his recent visit to China, which included pageantry and a state banquet at Beijing's Great Hall of the People.
One of the banquet attendees, Wu Xinbo, who directs the American Studies center at Shanghai's Fudan University, said it was the warmest he had seen in the U.S.-China relations in years.
But since then, Wu said, things have been more "fragile."
"In the last several months, the U.S. has continued to contain and pressure China in economic, technological [and] people-to-people exchanges," he said.
For example, the U.S. imposed extra tariffs on Chinese exports over forced labor claims, and the Pentagon added Chinese tech giants on a military blacklist. The Federal Communications Commission banned new imports of Chinese humanoid robots and robot dogs over national security concerns.
Ups and downs are to be expected in a relationship as complicated as the U.S. and China's, said international studies professor Zhang Yun at Nanjing University.
The key is to build high-level channels to deal with problems as they emerge and "mitigate the negative impacts," he said.
Zhang said Taiwan, tech and trade are high on Xi's agenda this trip. Discussions on the wars in Iran and Ukraine, plus tensions along the Korean peninsula, are also expected.
The U.S. is expected to reciprocate the high level of pomp and circumstance for Xi regardless of the tough negotiations expected — and Trump has publicly held Xi in high regard.
Rare earths and AI
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said this week that the two countries are still negotiating the potential extension of a rare earths truce that would ensure continued flow of Chinese rare earth products for the U.S.
China dominates the refining of rare earths and other critical minerals that are important to manufacture a range of products, from cellphones to weapons.
However, American officials have complained that China has not upheld its end of the bargain. NPR reporting shows that mutual distrust scuppered an offer from Beijing to extend the rare earths truce to the end of Trump's term, in January 2029.
The NPR Politics Podcast
Trump takes the world stage
Trump and Xi are also expected to talk about AI governance.
China has "been trying to figure out, in talking to the United States, what kind of so-called guardrails or controls can be put on artificial intelligence," said Rose Gottemoeller, a former NATO official who attends regular dialogues on nuclear proliferation with retired Chinese military officials.
"So it's a combination nowadays of the older issues related to nuclear stability and new issues related to new technology," she said.
China is interested in imposing safety measures, according to Zhang, but he said there is a lot of "mistrust" between the U.S. and China on the proposed solutions.
Taiwan on the table
In their previous meetings, Xi has repeatedly emphasized to Trump that Taiwan, a self-governing island Beijing claims as its own, is a red line and if mishandled could put the U.S.-China relations in "jeopardy." Trump told reporters later that he was not interested in a war thousands of miles away.
"Let's see if the United States can make [a] clearer statement opposing Taiwan independence," said Zhang.
This spring, the Trump administration paused a $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan. Experts say Xi is expected to press Trump to maintain this momentum when he sits down with Trump on Thursday.
On Wednesday, as Xi departed for the U.S., China's state news agency published a statement from the country's cabinet-like State Council excoriating Taiwan's president, Lai Ching-te. Lai is despised by Beijing, which suspects he is trying to lead Taiwan to declare formal independence.
"The most important issue that the Chinese always raise in preparation for these high-level visits is the topic of Taiwan," says William Klein, acting deputy chief of mission at the U.S. Embassy in Beijing until 2021.
Trade discussions underway
Trump and Xi also agreed to create trade and investment boards back in May. Among the discussions is a reciprocal tariff reduction framework on products worth $30 billion or more.
China is expected to announce purchases of American agricultural products, and the U.S. is expected to announce tariff reductions on what are called 4A consumer goods, which include footwear and apparel, according to two people in the U.S.-China business community who requested anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
However, no details of who will be on either trade or investment boards have been announced yet.
During Trump's visit to China this spring, the U.S. said China agreed to purchase American beef, soybeans and 200 Boeing jets.
But data shows China is already behind schedule on its promises to buy American agricultural goods.
Jasmine Ling contributed to this reporting.

Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda
- Published
Teenage brothers Olly and Seb Fisher are closing in on their dream of international recognition - but it won't come from their homeland of Scotland.
Instead, the Partick Thistle duo are in line to play for Uganda.
They believe they would become the first white players ever to represent the African nation, thanks to their mother Kate being born there.
"My gran and grandad lived out here for, I think, four or five years," Olly, 18, tells BBC Sport Scotland. "My grandfather came out here to teach in a school then my mum was born here. So, it's a bit of a strange one."
The siblings became aware of interest from Uganda about six months ago, following a chance conversation some time before between their father and a football consultant at a game in Nigeria.
And, at the start of August, they were invited to attend under-20 and under-17s training camps.
They spent last week in Jinja in the country's eastern region and will stay on for one more week, with the pair saying they're "shocked" and "honoured" at the call-ups.
"I couldn't believe it," 16-year-old striker Seb said. "It's one of those things you look at and you're shocked. You can't believe it. Most other people couldn't as well."
Goalkeeper Olly had a similar reaction. "A real mixture of emotions," he said. "I was quite shocked. I didn't really think that this was a possibility but I was honoured to be asked to represent Uganda. I thought it was a real big opportunity."
Mum Kate is "ecstatic" and "thinks it'd be a great experience for us", adds Seb.
'The other boys have been brand new'
There is another Scottish link with Uganda, with former Hearts and Ghana midfielder Laryea Kingston currently coach of Uganda's under-20s.
And he is the one who believes the Fisher brothers are on the verge of making history.
"Coach Kingston was saying we'd be the first white boys to play for Uganda, which would be history in the making," Seb explained. "It is very special."
And Olly added: "It's never been done before, so definitely it is very special."
The pair feel like they're making connections with the African nation, having been reared on stories about Uganda from their grandparents.
And even though they have been training in oppressively warm conditions, they are embracing the opportunity.
"Everyone has been brilliant, welcoming, really great," Seb said. "The other boys have been brand new with us. Some of the boys actually come from the same area where my mum was born. So, they were all talking about that."
The boys will return to Scotland soon, combining training and playing with Thistle with university and school, but are planning to rejoin their new international team-mates in the near future.
Olly hopes to be part of his squad if they qualify for the Under-20's Africa Cup of Nations early next year, and Seb could be in the Under-17 squad for November's World Cup in Qatar.
"That's what you want as a footballer, being in an international environment," Seb said. "It makes you a better player and hopefully it does for the two of us, and I think it will, and benefit us very much going back to Scotland playing at Thistle."

The 51st episode of The Health Wrap by The Hindu explores what constitutes a healthy diet amid the growing focus on protein, along with recent developments in osteoarthritis research, corneal donation and rabies prevention.
Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, The Hindu, and Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, The Hindu, discuss nutrition, weight management, osteoarthritis, corneal donation and transplantation, and rabies prevention.
Protein has become a major focus of nutrition advice, particularly on social media. The episode discusses the role of protein in the diet and why a healthy diet needs to be considered as a whole rather than through the lens of a single nutrient or product.
The conversation also looks at what happens to protein consumed in excess of the body’s requirements. Unlike carbohydrates and fat, protein is not stored in the body as a dedicated reserve. Amino acids from protein are used for functions including tissue repair, muscle maintenance and the production of enzymes and hormones, while excess intake can be used for energy or other metabolic processes.
The episode examines the role of diet and exercise in weight management, including research suggesting that combining dietary changes with physical activity can help support sustained weight loss. It also discusses why overall dietary patterns matter when assessing healthy eating.
Another segment looks at new research into osteoarthritis and cartilage regeneration. The research involves stromal-cell extracellular vesicles derived from menstrual blood and their potential role in cartilage repair. The findings are preliminary and are discussed in the context of ongoing research into new approaches to osteoarthritis care.
The episode also examines challenges in corneal donation and transplantation. Despite the potential of donated corneas to restore vision, some donated tissue does not reach patients who need it. The discussion looks at gaps in the process and the need to improve the use of donated corneal tissue.
Rabies prevention is another focus of the episode. The discussion looks at dog vaccination as an important part of preventing human rabies, given the role of dogs in transmission of the disease.
The episode can also be viewed here at The Hindu health page along with the full playlist of The Health Wrap .

Ex-ED official Niranjan Singh joins Akali Dal Waris Punjab De ahead of Punjab polls
Asked about allegations of the misuse of central agencies including the ED, Niranjan said there is no government which does not misuse it a "little bit".
Former Enforcement Directorate deputy director Niranjan Singh on Wednesday joined the Akali Dal Waris Punjab De ahead of the Punjab Assembly elections here.
Former deputy superintendent of police Balwinder Singh Sekhon also joined the party in the presence of MLA Manpreet Singh Ayali, Tarsem Singh, the father of jailed Khadoor Sahib MP Amritpal Singh and Faridkot MP Sarabjit Singh Khalsa.
While welcoming the former ED officer into the party fold, Ayali said Niranjan Singh's joining will boost the Akali Dal Waris Punjab De.
Deep Dive
Asked about allegations of the misuse of central agencies including the ED, Niranjan said there is no government which does not misuse it a "little bit".
"For the past some time, allegations are being levelled that the ED is getting more active, but these allegations are to be replied to by the ED," he said.
Niranjan, however, said that he always worked as per the law when he was serving in the ED.
Also read: Differing views are normal but decisions unanimous: Election Commission amid row
On his joining, he expressed concern over the "worsening" situation in Punjab as he was referring to the drug problem and corruption.
He also spoke about the alleged "deteriorating" law and order situation and further alleged that mafias have been running for a long time with the protection of police and politicians and stressed that there was a need to raise voice against it.
Speaking about the Akali Dal Waris Punjab De, he said it is fighting against the drug menace.
"They need support of Punjabis in their campaign against drugs. It is a secular group of people. It is a group against drugs and corruption. I came here to support them," he said.
"If I could do something for Punjab, fight against the drug menace, that is why I came here," he added.
Also read: 'Go counsel Pakistan': India hits back at OIC over Kashmir remarks
Asked about fighting elections, Niranjan said it is the party which is to take a call.
"Fighting elections is not the primary purpose. My purpose is only that I can contribute on the basis of my experience," he said.
On drug investigation when he was serving in the ED, Niranjan said he had earlier written the names of the persons who did not allow investigation.
"I had even resigned in protest. If authorities are protecting those involved in drugs, then who is Niranjan Singh? I had written the names of three directors of the ED who were not allowing investigation," he said.
He said he had submitted eight to nine secret reports in drug cases in sealed cover and these were given to the anti-drug Special Task Force and on this basis, FIRs were registered.
On the ₹1,200 crore irrigation scam, Niranjan alleged that the Punjab Vigilance Bureau had "hushed it up".
"Everybody knows about those who were involved in it. No action was taken on it," he alleged.
Punjab Vigilance Bureau (VB) this year gave a clean chit to three retired IAS officers, including the former chief secretary, in the multi-crore irrigation scam after not finding concrete evidence. It involved the fraudulent allotment of state water projects worth over ₹1,000-1,200 crore during the SAD-BJP regime (2007-2017).
Singh decided to join the party after Ayali and Tarsem Singh met him at his Jalandhar residence on Tuesday.
Niranjan Singh, who retired from service in May 2021, had probed several high-profile drug cases, including the multi-crore Jagdish Bhola drug racket case.
He had questioned senior politicians, including former ministers Bikram Singh Majithia and Sarwan Singh Phillaur, in connection with the case, which he probed under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act.
Singh was later transferred from Jalandhar to Kolkata, a transfer later revoked by the Punjab and Haryana High Court.
Akali Dal Waris Punjab De is led by MP Amritpal Singh, who is currently lodged in a jail in Assam in the 2023 Ajnala police station attack case.
Punjab will go to polls early next year.

The Manipur Police arrested two persons, including a 40-year-old woman, from Thoubal district’s Lilong on September 14 in connection with the seizure of addiction-causing pharmaceutical drugs. The police found in their possession 50 boxes containing 15,000 capsules of “Tramadol Hydrochloride Tramanil”, weighing about 7 kg.
Also Read: Highest prevalence of opioid use disorders in eastern parts of India: UNODC report
The consignment, allegedly for illegal distribution to specific clients, was seized almost a month after a youth died at a drug rehabilitation centre in the State’s capital, Imphal. He had reportedly been injecting crushed tablets of Tapentadol, an opioid analgesic thrice as potent as Tramadol.
These incidents and the admission of another Tapentadol user at the drug rehabilitation centre with a serious infection due to injections confirmed what anti-narcotic officials and counsellors suspected — drug addicts were shifting to opioid analgesics available as prescription pain management medication from heroin and other narcotic substances made costlier by the ongoing ethnic conflict in Manipur.
“We are investigating to ascertain the source and intended destination of the Tramadol capsules and to determine the extent of involvement of the arrested duo in the possession or distribution of the pharmaceutical drug,” a Manipur police officer said.
The police and drug enforcement agencies in Manipur said data on seizures of opioid analgesics sold or ferried illegally in the State were not immediately available. They, however, said the price factor could have dictated the shift from methamphetamine and heroin, locally known as No. 4.
High prices
The prices of narcotic substances increased sharply after Manipur spiralled into seemingly unending violence in May 2023. According to reports in the local media, a vial of heroin, for instance, costs almost ₹5,000. A strip of Tramadol or Tapentadol costs between ₹40 and ₹400 depending on strength, brand, and manufacturer.
“Tramadol and Tapentadol are painkilling compounds derived from opium alkaloids. Taken for pain relief, they cause a sense of well-being, but can develop dependence if these are taken continuously for a few weeks,” Krishanu Krori, a Guwahati-based medicine specialist, told The Hindu.
“Addicts increase the dosage through injections after typically starting with 50-100 mg. Apart from a sense of euphoria, they develop disinterest in daily activities, withdrawal from family and society, and a craving for violence,” he said.
Counsellors in Manipur said pharmacists should strictly observe prescription requirements and health authorities should monitor emerging patterns of Tramadol and Tapentadol misuse. Hospitals and rehabilitation centres also need updated guidance on dependence, withdrawal, and complications associated with its misuse and injection, they said.
Opioid analgesics have become a worry for enforcement agencies beyond India’s northeastern region too. In August, the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) unearthed an organised network involved in the clandestine manufacture, concealment, and illegal export of such drugs, a scheduled psychotropic substance, to African countries.
The seized items included 1 lakh Tramadol Hydrochloride tablets, 1 lakh Tapentadol tablets, machinery, and raw materials. The DRI sleuths arrested three key members of the syndicate during the operation at the Mumbai Air Cargo Complex.
