Pocognoli has 'positive nervousness' for Scotland debut
- Published
Nations League: Slovenia v Scotland
Stadion Stozice, Ljubljana
Saturday 26 September, 14:00 BST
Scotland head coach Sebastien Pocognoli admits to feeling a "positive nervousness" before his first game in charge of the country, a Nations League tie against Slovenia in Ljubljana on Saturday.
The Belgian was appointed in August, replacing Steve Clarke, whose seven-year tenure ended after Scotland's exit at the group stages of the World Cup.
Pocognoli starts with four Nations League matches across 11 days, with the trip to Slovenia followed by Switzerland at Hampden, a fixture in North Macedonia, then a return meeting with the Slovenes in Glasgow.
"If we talk about nerves, yes, but it's a positive nervousness," he told BBC Sport Scotland. "We have a job with responsibility. It's excitement and I'm just passionate about being on the touchline."
Scotland are currently at a warm weather camp in La Manga, Spain with a much-changed squad.
Pocognoli has picked a 19-year-old in James Wilson, four 20-year-olds - Findlay Curtis, Ben Gannon-Doak, Lennon Miller and Colby Donovan - and another three aged 22 - Kristi Montgomery, Luke Graham and Robbie Ure.
With Blackburn's Montgomery replacing the injured Kenny McLean, there are now eight uncapped players in the squad.
"It's a lot of new faces, so it's a challenge to find the right balance, to keep the cohesion in the team," Pocognoli said.
- Well-travelled Binks eager to make mark for Scotland 
  - Published19 hours ago
- From leaving Rangers to La Liga - Scotland is next step for Ure 
  - Published5 hours ago
Scotland team 'can be flexible'
The manager says he knows his team and his formation for the Slovenia game but is not wedded to any particular system, although playing three at the back has been a staple of his coaching to this point.
"I always think the players select themselves," he added. "We have four games, so we need to plan. We need to have a periodisation [managing training loads, games and recovery] about the tactical aspect and the physical aspect.
"This team can be flexible. We're ready for the four games in terms of what kind of approach we want to give."
Pocognoli revealed he has had a conversation with his predecessor, Clarke - "a nice meeting on the phone," as he put it.
"He was very kind, very... humble. That was very helpful for me. It just was to let me know that he's behind the team. He was very happy [in his time in the job] but he also felt that it was the right time [to leave]. He wished me all the best.
"I will try to be as successful as the previous staff because we want to play in a big tournament. We want to create this moment for the country."
Asked if his brand of football will involve more risk and adventure than Clarke's, he said: "We have to find the right balance because if you play fantastic football and you don't qualify you get some criticism."
Pocognoli's style is all about aggressive pressing and fast tempo. He says that it might take a while for cohesion to be achieved but there are certain things that he wants to see straight away against Slovenia.
"For me, it's about the personality of the players," he added. "I like a unit team who are just fighting for each other.
"It's a basic principle - attack together and squeeze the pitch. When we need to defend, it's just to defend like brothers. When we lose the ball, it's try to regain the ball as quickly as possible.
"From that, there are a lot of other principles, but that's the base. If you cannot get this, you will never have good principles on the pitch."
Given the condensed nature of the games, there is going to be a fair degree of rotation from Slovenia away, to Switzerland at home, to North Macedonia away and Slovenia at home.
"So good so far," Pocognoli said about what he has seen in La Manga. "But we need to get the response through the games. It's up to them to perform well, but it's up to me to make them perform well."

Meet TWS, the rising K-pop boy group whose debut song became a streaming sensation in South Korea
Ahead of TWS’ first-ever concert in Singapore on Oct 10, the sextet spoke with CNA Lifestyle about their hopes for their maiden show here.
In January 2024, K-pop boy group TWS (pronounced “two us”) made their debut under the label Pledis Entertainment with the extended play Sparkling Blue. By the end of 2024, the album’s single, Plot Twist, became the most-streamed song on South Korea’s Melon chart for the year – a remarkable feat for a rookie group.
Two years on, TWS – which comprises members Shinyu, Dohoon, Youngjae, Hanjin, Jihoon and Kyungmin – continues to make waves in South Korea, consistently releasing crowd-pleasing hits such as Overdrive and You, You.
TWS, whose name is an abbreviation for Twenty Four Seven With Us, have since carved a niche for themselves with their self-coined boyhood pop genre in which the group delves into everyday life and challenges through bright and sentimental music.
After making their mark in South Korea, TWS is following in the footsteps of labelmates Seventeen and other senior groups under South Korean entertainment giant Hybe as they set their sights on the global stage.
The group’s ongoing 24/7: For: You tour marks the first time they’re performing in Singapore and Thailand. Ahead of TWS’ maiden show at Arena @ Expo on Oct 10, CNA Lifestyle spoke with the group about their success and the advice they’ve received from their seniors.
What do you think sets TWS apart from other groups?
Shinyu: I think TWS’ real strength lies in how we honestly capture the emotions and moments of where we are right now, expressing them as “boyhood pop” within our youthful evolution. I believe our biggest charm is that we try to naturally share every step of our growth, rather than presenting a neatly finished story.
Jihoon: I think what sets TWS’ music apart most is how we tailor our sound to tell our honest stories in their truest form. Because our music is a direct reflection of who we are and where we stand today, I feel it’s really special that a single song can share not just TWS’ story, but also the natural energy we carry.
What was it like watching Plot Twist grow from a song you had recorded into such a major hit?
Kyungmin: Honestly, it still feels a bit surreal. Receiving so much love for a debut track is never easy, so I feel immensely proud and overwhelmed with a level of happiness that almost feels like more than we deserve. Even casual listeners who are discovering TWS for the first time often know Plot Twist, which constantly reminds me of just how far that song has reached and how much love it’s received.
You’ve now been K-pop idols for more than two years. What's something you didn’t anticipate before making your debut?
Jihoon: I feel like I’m learning so much about what it truly means to grow as an artiste and what connecting with the audience truly means. I’ve come to realise that it’s not just about doing a good job with what’s right in front of us, but about creating moments across various areas that genuinely move and inspire people. That’s something I want to keep learning and studying.
Hanjin: Since debuting, I’ve realised that the journey of becoming an artiste is ultimately a continuous process of discovering who I am and learning along the way. Things don’t always go as planned on stage or at work, but I’ve learned to use those moments as fuel to do better next time. I want to keep learning and growing through every experience so I can become an even better artiste.
What’s the most memorable advice you’ve received from any of your labelmate seniors, Seventeen?
Youngjae: What stayed with me most was being told not to be afraid of making mistakes on stage, but to just go out there and show everything I want to express. Hearing words of encouragement that I was doing well was also such a reassuring source of strength for me.
TWS have become closely associated with your boyhood pop identity. As you grow older, do you see yourselves evolving or experimenting with a different identity?
Dohoon: I want to build on our distinct identity so that the moment people hear a track, they instantly go, "This is definitely a TWS song." Ultimately, I want to make music that brings comfort and relatable warmth to as many people as possible through our songs.
Kyungmin: I think it’s such a great starting point that people naturally think of TWS when they hear “boyhood pop”. Building on that foundation, we want to broaden our spectrum by weaving various musical colours into the genre moving forward.
Are there any concepts or genres that you’re eager to explore?
Dohoon: I really want to experiment with the “rage” genre. It’s a style I’ve been personally drawn to lately, and a direction I’d definitely love for us to try as TWS.
It will be TWS’ first concert in Singapore. What are you most looking forward to about performing here?
Youngjae: I’m thrilled to finally connect with 42s [TWS’ fandom] in Singapore. As our very first stage in the city, we want to deliver a memorable stage that serves as both a meaningful milestone and a strong starting point for us.
Jihoon: Performing in a new destination for the first time is so exciting! I think I’m mostly curious and eager to see how the local crowd in Singapore will experience our set and connect with our music.
Many of your fellow Hybe seniors like BTS and Le Sserafim have performed in Singapore. What has made you look forward to performing in the country?
Shinyu: Since this is our first concert in Singapore, I’m really looking forward to experiencing the energy of the audience firsthand and seeing how everyone enjoys the show with us.
Kyungmin: First of all, it's such an honor to perform as TWS in a city we’ve never visited before. Just the thought of experiencing the passion and enthusiasm of the local audience in person gets me so excited.
Since this is your first concert in Singapore, have you made any special preparations to make the show memorable for your Singaporean fans?
Youngjae: I’m determined to pour my absolute best into making our first performance in Singapore seamless. By bringing out the diverse layers of TWS through our music so far, my goal is to gift everyone an incredible day – making sure that every step they took to come see us feels deeply rewarding.
Hanjin: Holding our very first concert in Singapore feels especially meaningful for us as well. We’ve prepared fresh song arrangements and unit stages, and with the members directly contributing to songwriting and choreography, I think we’ll be able to showcase a whole new dimension of TWS. I hope this first meeting becomes a cherished memory for both us and everyone who joins us.
What do you hope fans will take away from the concert?
Shinyu: I hope everyone can fully lose themselves in the show and carry the warmth of these moments long after returning home. My wish is that the happiness we shared stays with you as a gentle source of comfort and strength in your daily life.
Dohoon: I hope this concert gives everyone a great boost of positive energy to draw from in their day-to-day lives. If looking back on our time together brings a light smile to your face on a busy day, that’s truly all we could ask for.

Modal Labs in talks to raise funds at $15 billion valuation, Bloomberg News reports
Sept 23 : AI startup Modal Labs is in discussions to raise new financing at a roughly $15 billion valuation, Bloomberg News reported on Wednesday, citing people familiar with the matter.
Modal raised $355 million in May at a valuation of $4.65 billion, Reuters had previously reported.
The startup helps AI companies access the chips they need to run AI tools and has a sandbox product that allows developers to test their code, increasingly created through AI, before embedding it in their products.
Modal Labs did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

The death of an Anna University student at Government Kilpauk Medical College Hospital (KMCH) on Friday (September 18, 2026), due to scrub typhus, has once again brought this bacterial infection to the fore. University authorities have said they have started screening students for scrub typhus as well, along with dengue and leptospirosis
What is scrub typhus?
Scrub typhus is a bacterial infection caused by the bacterium Orientia tsutsugamushi. It is spread by the bite of infected larval mites or chiggers -- it is not a mosquito-borne disease.
Scrub typhus is a major public health burden in South and Southeast Asia. A 2021 systematic review noted that scrub typhus, a common acute febrile illness, is “a grossly under-recognised public health problem in India.” It stated that the proportion of scrub typhus among acute undifferentiated febrile illness (AUFI) studies was 25.3%, and community seroprevalence was 34.2%. The review also noted that the disease causes severe morbidity and accounts for a large number of deaths, with its bueden “underappreciated.”
A 2025 multi-centre study of 587 children with acute encephalitis syndrome (AES) from Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Tamil Nadu revealed that scrub typhus is now the most common infectious cause of AES in southern India.
What are the symptoms?
Symptoms usually begin within 10 days of infection. The United States Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) lists symptoms of scrub typhus as: fever and chills, headache, body aches and muscle pain, a dark, scab-like region at the site of the chigger bite (also known as eschar), mental changes ranging from confusion to coma, enlarged lymph nodes and a rash.
Timely treatment is critical. If left untreated, severe illness from scrub typhus infection can lead to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), shock, meningitis and kidney failure, which can be fatal, notes a research paper, Incidence of Scrub Typhus in Rural South India published in The New England Journal of Medicine last year.
In India, there is a high mortality of scrub typhus, primarily due to late diagnosis and treatment.
How is it diagnosed and treated?
Since the symptoms of scrub typhus are common to those of several other diseases, diagnosis is often delayed. A blood test (IgM ELISA or PCR) can help confirm the diagnosis.
Scrub typhus should be treated with the antibiotics doxycycline or azithromycin. If the treatment is begun in time, it is effective. Results of a trial carried out in seven centres in India, published in 2023, in which patients were randomly assigned to receive a combination therapy of doxycycline and azithromycin, showed faster resolution of complications compared with two other arms where patients were given monotherapy with either doxycycline or azithromycin. The frequencies of respiratory, renal, hepatic, and central nervous system complications were lower in the combination-therapy group than in either of the monotherapy groups.
How can it be prevented?
There is no vaccine as yet for scrub typhus. The infection is not contagious.
Chiggers live in areas with lots of grass, thick vegetation, agricultural fields, plant litter and bare soil across rural areas of Asia, and usually feed on small mammals such as rats and shrews.
Keeping oneself safe from bites through protective clothing, covered footwear and the use of insect repellent may help. Ensuring surroundings are clean and well maintained can also go some way towards reducing mite habitats.
“Early diagnosis and prompt treatment can significantly reduce complications and mortality. Establishing good surveillance and instituting appropriate control measures are urgently needed,” the 2021 review notes.

Here is a story that on the face of it seems so wildly unlikely it can only be true. Indeed, the very concept of a romantic documentary sounds almost oxymoronic, an indication of how much nonfiction films have become synonymous with grim histories full of suffering and injustice. Let’s hope this sweet work, directed by Orlando von Einsiedel (who’s made his share of hardcore, suffering-intensive docs including Oscar-winning short The White Helmets) launches a new trend in nonfiction film-making for stuff that makes you happy-cry.
The basic meet-cute happened in 1975, when PK (played by Chirag Lobo in the film’s extensive re-enactments) met Lotta (Mina Dale) in Delhi. He was a poor street artist, a Dalit, the lowest possible caste, once called Untouchables. The real PK Mahanandia appears on screen to explain how he had left his rural village for Delhi in order to get away from all that caste hierarchy. When he met Lotta he pretty much knew he’d met the woman of his dreams because he’d been carrying a horoscope his father had commissioned for him when he was a baby that prophesised he’d fall in love with a woman whose family owned a jungle. Lotta, a backpacker from Sweden, hailed from a clan back home that owned a forest, so that was good enough for PK to believe he’d met his fate. After a chaste holiday romance bloomed between these two crazy kids, she went back to Sweden and he decided to bicycle the 6,000 miles all the way there from India to prove his love.
As we hear the now elderly young lovers describe what they were thinking at the time, we watch Lobo and Dale act out the journey, with poor PK getting into a few scrapes that set him back a few steps as he plods his way westward. Some of the most touching interludes are the interactions he has with strangers along the way that seem incredibly naturalistic and semi-improvised. Cynics might quibble that one can’t help wondering what darker parts of the story have been left out, and note that the actors chosen to play the lovers are a few notches more conventionally beautiful than the actual people – but every love story has its soft focus, flaw-concealing fudges so we’ll let it slide here.

The Malkajgiri police, in separate operations, seized 730 kg of suspected adulterated ginger-garlic paste, 500 kg of loose paneer and large quantities of skimmed milk powder and other ingredients from food manufacturing units in Hayathnagar, Alwal and Dundigal, on Tuesday.
In the first operation, the M-FAST (Malkajgiri Food Adulteration Surveillance Team), along with the SOT LB Nagar Team and Hayathnagar police, raided Sri Manikanta (SMK) Golden Food Products and Ginger-Garlic Paste Manufacturing Unit at Shiva Shakti Nagar in Hayathnagar. Police apprehended Akula Shivaiah (38) who was manufacturing ginger-garlic paste using low-quality raw material, an unidentified solution and food colour.
The teams seized 13 drums containing 650 kg of ginger-garlic paste, 10 boxes containing 50 kg and 150 boxes containing another 30 kg, taking the total quantity of paste seized to approximately 730 kg. They also seized a 3.5-litre bottle containing an unidentified solution and a box of food colour.
According to M-FAST, the paste was being prepared in unhygienic conditions without following the required food safety and quality standards. The suspected adulterated raw materials and finished products were seized, and a case was registered at Hayathnagar Police Station under Sections 223, 274 and 275 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
In another operation on the same day, the SOT Malkajgiri Team-II of the Cantonment Zone, in coordination with MFAST, raided Natraj Milk and Milk Food Products at Turkapally, Alwal, under Alwal Police Station limits. Police said the unit was preparing paneer by mixing skimmed milk powder. Around 500 kg of loose paneer and two bags containing approximately 50 kg of skimmed milk powder were seized.
The respondent, Japala Natraj (56) was handed over to Alwal Police Station personnel along with the seized material for further legal action. The preparation method and materials found at the premises raised prima facie concerns over compliance with prescribed food safety, quality, composition and manufacturing standards.
The teams also raided M/s Yashoda Sweet and Namkeen at Bowrampet village in Dundigal, where police said the unit was using substantial quantities of skimmed milk powder, oil and dalda or vegetable fat in the preparation of halwa and other sweets.
The teams seized several brands of skimmed milk powder, including approximately 35 bags each of Shreedhi Premium Gold and Ramsons Spray Dried skimmed milk powder, with each bag containing 25 packets of 1 kg. They also seized six 25-kg bags of Dholpur Fresh, four 25-kg bags of Gyan, one 25-kg bag of Lacto Win and one 25-kg bag of Savariya skimmed milk powder.
The operation also resulted in the seizure of 21 kg of prepared and packed Yashoda Sweet Halwa, approximately 100 tins of Freedom Oil and 50 tins of Dalda. The respondent, Pushpendra Baghel, 32, was handed over to Dundigal Police Station along with the seized material for further legal action.

Russians went to the polls. The votes were counted. Russian President Putin's party United Russia won again, and comfortably.
The result itself was hardly the mystery. The more interesting question is why Russia still goes through the elaborate business of elections when the system makes a genuine change of power extremely unlikely.
Because in Russia, an election may not simply be about choosing who governs. It can also tell the Kremlin who is turning up, where support is weakening, which regional leaders can deliver and how well the machinery is working. But first, a simpler question: does a Russian vote actually matter?
Putin's ruling United Russia party won 57.83% of the vote, according to Russia's Central Election Commission, with more than 95% of ballots counted. The result gives United Russia 355 of the 450 seats in the State Duma, preserving its constitutional majority. In the previous parliamentary election in 2021, the party officially received 49.8% of the vote.
The election was also the first parliamentary vote since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Putin had presented it as a test of support for his policies and the war. The Kremlin said the first parliamentary election since Moscow sent troops to Ukraine in 2022 showed Russians were united around Putin, who has been in power since New Year's Eve 1999.
That raises an obvious question: If Russia is widely described as an authoritarian or 'managed' political system, and the Kremlin is not seriously threatened by an opposition party taking power, why bother holding elections at all?
Putin’s United Russia party has won 355 of the 450 seats in the State Duma.
Does a Russian vote actually matter?
It would be too simplistic to say that an individual vote is completely meaningless simply because the ruling party is expected to win. Formally, an individual Russian vote can affect the composition of the Duma in two ways.
Half of the 450 seats are distributed through nationwide party-list proportional representation, with a 5% threshold, while the other 225 are elected from single-member constituencies.
The weight of an individual vote differs between the two.
“In the party-list contest, one vote is a very small part of the national total, although collectively these votes determine 225 seats and can be particularly important when a party is near the 5% threshold,” explained foreign affairs expert Robinder Sachdev. “In a close constituency race, however, a relatively small number of votes can directly determine who wins that seat,” explained foreign expert he added.
The 2026 result illustrates how strongly the constituency component can amplify a party's parliamentary strength.
United Russia won 355 of the 450 seats, up from 343 in the previous Duma and the party's highest total so far.
That gives the party well over the two-thirds threshold in the Duma. It can pass ordinary federal legislation without needing support from other parties and has enough votes for federal constitutional laws and the Duma stage of constitutional amendments.
“So an individual vote has limited weight by itself, but aggregated votes — particularly in single-member constituencies — can have a major effect on the parliamentary balance of power,” Sachdev said.
Does the vote count actually matter?
In the narrowest sense, yes.
Russians cast ballots, those ballots are counted and the resulting numbers determine how parliamentary seats are allocated. United Russia's 57.83% vote share is therefore not simply a number that has no connection whatsoever to voting.
But whether voters have a meaningful opportunity to change who exercises power is a different question.
Russia's political system has placed significant restrictions on genuine electoral competition. Reuters described the 2026 parliamentary election as taking place in a “tightly controlled political system” in which candidates opposed to Moscow's war in Ukraine have largely been excluded.
Several parties besides United Russia are represented in the Duma, but Russia's parliamentary opposition operates within tightly drawn limits, with the major parties generally supporting Putin on key issues, including the war in Ukraine.
According to the Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA), Yabloko, a liberal party that opposed the Ukraine war and called for a ceasefire, was excluded from the federal parliamentary contest. CEPA said Yabloko's support among decided voters had risen to about 6% in the weeks before the election, compared with 1.2% in the 2021 election. Meanwhile, Putin critic Nikolai Bondarenko had already been barred from standing.
Putin has been in power since New Year's Eve 1999.
So should this be called a gimmick?
Not quite.
Even when the broad political outcome is predictable, elections can serve several purposes for an authoritarian political system.
Sachdev said elections provide formal electoral legitimacy while allowing the leadership to demonstrate a measurable level of public participation and support.
“Elections also help manage the political system itself,” Sachdev said, adding that they provide opportunities to renew parliament, accommodate different groups within the governing establishment and assess the performance of regional political organisations and officials.
They also provide information.
“The Kremlin may already have extensive polling and administrative data, but an actual election reveals the geography, intensity and organisational strength of support across the country,” he said.
In other words, the Kremlin does not necessarily need an election to discover who rules Russia. It can use an election to find out how well the political machine is functioning.
1. An election creates a claim of public support
The first and most obvious purpose is legitimacy.
The Kremlin can point to an electoral result and say that millions of Russians participated and that the governing party received a majority of votes.
That does not settle the question of whether the election was free and fair. But politically, the existence of an official vote gives the government a concrete result with which to demonstrate public backing.
This election is particularly significant because it took place during the war in Ukraine. The Kremlin has an interest in demonstrating that the war has not produced a political revolt at home.
Sachdev said the election allows the Russian leadership to “demonstrate a measurable level of public participation and support”, even if the broader political outcome is predictable.
That distinction is important. An election can provide a government with an official measure of participation without necessarily providing an unrestricted contest for political power.
2. It gives the Kremlin a measure of support — even if an imperfect one
This is where the question of whether votes “count” becomes more complicated.
Even in a tightly controlled election, authorities can learn something from participation. How many people turn out? Where is turnout unusually low? Which regions deliver particularly strong support? Where does United Russia perform worse than expected? Are local officials able to mobilise their populations?
These are valuable pieces of information for an authoritarian government.
A 2021 Carnegie analysis described Russian parliamentary elections as functioning less as contests over who would govern and more as a mechanism for measuring and demonstrating support for Putin's system.
Sachdev said an election provides a different kind of information from opinion polls, intelligence reports or administrative data because it “tests behaviour and administrative capacity under real conditions.”
“Turnout, abstention, regional variations and the performance of individual candidates can reveal where support is strong, where enthusiasm is weaker, and how effectively governors and local political organisations are able to mobilise voters,” he said.
Moreover, information moving upwards through a political hierarchy can be filtered, because officials may have incentives to report favourable results to their superiors.
Sachdev said an election can therefore provide an additional dataset against which those reports can be assessed. “Political-science research describes this as a ‘fire alarm’ function of elections,” he said.
So the election does not simply measure public opinion. It gives the Kremlin a regional picture of both political sentiment and the effectiveness of the state and party machinery in mobilising voters.
Does a Russian vote actually matter?
There is another audience for Russian elections that is often overlooked: the people inside the system.
An election allows governors, mayors, party officials and other local power brokers to demonstrate that they can deliver the results expected by Moscow.
Carnegie has described regional elections in Russia as an “initiation ritual” for governors and local elites — an opportunity for them to demonstrate control over their territories.
Sachdev said regional leaders are expected not only to administer their territories but also to maintain political stability and demonstrate an ability to mobilise electoral support.
Research on Russian regional politics has found that United Russia has historically performed better where governors command effective political organisations and local networks, he said.
This means an election can function almost like an internal performance review. If a governor produces the desired result, it demonstrates political control.
If a region suddenly records unexpectedly weak support for the ruling party, that can raise questions in Moscow about the governor's popularity, the effectiveness of the regional administration, the strength of the local party organisation or underlying economic and social dissatisfaction.
An unexpectedly poor result would not automatically lead to a governor's removal. But, Sachdev said, electoral underperformance “can weaken a regional leader's standing with the federal centre” and become one factor in subsequent decisions about appointments, tenure or political advancement.
So even if the Kremlin already knows which party will dominate parliament, the election can tell it how effectively its political network is operating below the national level.
4. It gives voters a controlled way to participate
There is also a social function.
Russia's government does not necessarily want every citizen to become politically disengaged. Voting gives people a formal mechanism for expressing preferences, even if the range of choices is restricted.
The question is not necessarily whether the Kremlin believes Russians are choosing between two equally viable governments.
Rather, elections can allow the system to channel political participation without allowing that participation to threaten the basic distribution of power.
Sachdev said elections also help “renew the composition of parliament” and accommodate different groups within the governing establishment.
This means that even where the election does not pose a serious threat to the ruling political system, it can still play a role in determining which individuals and factions occupy positions within that system.
5. Elections can reveal dissatisfaction — but not necessarily change the government
This is perhaps the most counterintuitive part.
A controlled election can still contain information about dissatisfaction.
People can abstain. They can spoil ballots. They can vote for smaller parties or candidates. They can use whatever limited electoral choices are available to signal disagreement.
Russia's political opposition has previously tried to use elections tactically to weaken United Russia, even when it could not realistically replace the Kremlin.
But the ability to express dissatisfaction and the ability to translate that dissatisfaction into a change of government are two different things which is why the Kremlin may tolerate a certain degree of electoral competition while drawing firm limits around the political system.
So, is the result meaningless?
Not necessarily.
The official vote count is meaningful as a description of what Russia's electoral authorities say happened. But the number cannot be read in isolation as a straightforward measure of Russians' freely expressed political preferences.
The composition of the ballot matters. So does who was permitted to campaign, what political views could be openly expressed, the degree of media access available to competing forces, turnout and the broader electoral environment.
This creates the central paradox of Russia's elections - The votes can be real without the contest being genuinely competitive. A Russian voter can make a choice. But the political system determines, to a significant extent, which choices are available in the first place. That is why the 57.83% figure needs to be read carefully. It is an official electoral result, but it is not equivalent to saying that 57.83% of all Russians freely chose Putin's political system.

Australian man is accused of being Islamic State group propagandist who shared 10,000 files online
Authorities in Melbourne have accused a man of pledging allegiance to the Islamic State group and spreading extremist propaganda online
WELLINGTON, New Zealand -- A man in the Australian city of Melbourne is accused of pledging allegiance to the Islamic State group and spreading thousands of pieces of extremist propaganda online over a period of years, the authorities said on Wednesday.
He was the seventh man to be arrested in Victoria state since May over allegations of possessing or distributing IS content online. Australia's federal police didn't link the latest arrest to the other six and wouldn't say if they believed the man's case was connected.
The 65-year-old Australian citizen, whose name hasn't been released, was due to appear in a Melbourne court later on Wednesday. He's charged with being a member of a terrorist organization and with transmitting violent extremist material in an encrypted messaging app the authorities didn't name.
The maximum penalty for the offenses is 10 years in prison.
The authorities said the man had sent 10,000 files containing extremist content between 2015 and 2020, including material relating to executions, torture and IS propaganda. The federal police allege that he also shared information about avoiding detection from law enforcement and instructional guides on planning and conducting mass casualty attacks, a statement Wednesday said.
Acting Assistant Commissioner Paula Hudson told reporters in Canberra that the scale and distribution of the materials by the man “placed him as a principal distributor of ISIS propaganda within the group.”
“The material glorified acts of violence and terrorism, spreading hateful ideology that is designed to radicalize others,” Hudson said.
An investigation into the man began when border officials examined the man's luggage as he departed Australia for a six-month trip to Egypt in 2020, the authorities said. He wasn't known to have traveled abroad since 2020 and wasn't linked to any attack or plot, Hudson said.
Earlier this month, a 30-year-old Melbourne man was arrested and charged with possessing violent extremist content as he attempted to depart Australia for the Middle East, authorities said. The federal police allege he was part of an online group chat with five other Victoria state men arrested in May, who all face charges relating to possessing extremist material, including IS propaganda.
The Islamic State group is a scattered and considerably weaker group since a 2019 United States-led military intervention drove it out of territory it had seized in Iraq and Syria, but its cells remain active and it has inspired a number of independent attacks, including in western countries. In Australia, a mass shooting at a Hanukkah event in 2025, in which two men are accused of killing 15 Jewish people, was motivated by the shooters' IS affiliations, the authorities allege.
It's thought 200 Australians traveled to Syria and Iraq to join the Islamic State group between 2012 and 2019, according to a website for the country's national security agencies. Dozens more “assisted” IS by supporting those overseas or by planning or carrying out terrorist attacks in Australia, the website says.

Richard Marles says the Department of Defence is examining how F-35 fighter jet parts bound for the US from Australia were unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong.
The acting prime minister said “very much everything that has occurred at the Australian end” will be reviewed, however, he claimed the technology parts were not “sensitive”, as first reported by Politico over the weekend.
The parts, which were being transported by another unknown third party on behalf of manufacturer, Lockheed Martin, still remain unaccounted for months later following their unplanned diversion to Hong Kong.
The last known location of the fighter jet components – in Hong Kong, a special administrative region of China – has sparked concern that some of the program’s technology secrets could have been exposed.
“We are examining [Australia’s involvement], but the point I would make here is that we are confident about the way in which we’ve engaged with the program, and through the US’s prime contractor, Lockheed,” Marles said on Tuesday.
“My understanding is that there is a sense of comfort, and we’re not talking about sensitive equipment here, or sensitive parts.
“Ultimately, though, this is an issue which is going to be managed by the United States and by Lockheed in terms of what has occurred.”
Politico reported sources said the “sensitive” shipment contained on of the jet’s canopies, which reportedly contains stealth technology.
The Guardian has contacted the Pentagon.
While many details have not yet been revealed, Michael Shoebridge, a director for Strategic Analysis Australia who has worked in intelligence agencies, said there were two reasons why China, or another adversary, would want F-35 parts – to reverse engineer them, or to learn how to better exploit and attack them.
Shoebridge added the shipment’s pitstop in Hong Kong was “such an unexpectedly stupid thing” for the manufacturer or Australia to do.
“This is an act of incredible ineptitude and stupidity, and so it’s more the Chinese taking advantage of an incredible stroke of luck brought to them by the stupidity of the people involved,” he said.
Last week, the US State Department announced that the Trump administration would continue with the sale of 48 F-35s to Saudi Arabia, despite reported concerns from the US intelligence community that China could obtain some of the stealth technology.
Australia was one of the early development partners in the F-35. The program spreads the development, supply, management and sustainment of the fighter jets across different countries.
More than 70 Australian companies have production and sustainment contracts with the F-35 program. In excess of 700 of the fighter jet’s “critical pieces” are manufactured in Victoria alone, according to the state government. Australia also hosts a regional distribution hub for F-35 parts in New South Wales.
Australian companies involved in the program’s supply chain have been awarded contracts valued at over $5.2bn, as of September 2025.
Shoebridge said the missing shipment of parts could mean the whole multibillion-dollar fleet is vulnerable to adversaries.
“They’re all now carrying the risk of whatever vulnerabilities this has brought to the to the aircraft,” he said.
“So it’s not just a US-Australia issue. It’s every operator of the F3-5 program [that] has an interest in understanding what happened and what was potentially exposed.”

The story uses screenshots and not the actual viral video in view of its sensitive nature.
A 12-second long video is going viral on social media where a woman is seen bathing in river water while wearing a bikini.
The video was posted on September 15 by X user Barkha Trehan, who describes herself as ‘Activist | Voice Of Men | President, Purush Aayog’. She wrote, “Location : Haridwar. Madam: My Body My Choice. Your take ??” The video garnered over 1 million views. (Archive)
In her X bio, Trehan identifies herself as a “men’s rights activist” and the “president of Purush Aayog”. She also claims to be a TEDx speaker and a “Hindu entrepreneur”; she apparently also “directed a documentary titled The Curse of Manhood”.
Media outlet News 18 Hindi published a report with screenshots from the video pointing out that it had angered social media users. (Archive)
This same video was posted by content creator Piyali Banerjee, where she questioned the “basic decency” and “knowledge of clothing” of the woman.
Other social media users also shared the same video with similar captions, questing the woman for wearing a bikini in Haridwar, with misogynistic comments about her character.
The video is also viral on Instagram.
Fact Check
To verify its authenticity, we ran a reverse image search on a few keyframes from the viral clip. This search led us to a reel posted on Instagram on August 18. The 21-second long reel was uploaded by an account named ‘ishika_pandit’. It showed the same woman bathing at the same spot, but wearing completely different clothes.
This video matched the background of the viral clip with the steel railing on the river and the foundations of a bridge clearly visible in the background. The woman’s hand gestures also mirror the viral video, and the same two men are visible in both videos.
Based on these similarities, it can be concluded that the video uploaded on August 18 is the original footage. The woman in the original video is seen wearing a yellow suit, and not a bikini. Thus, the viral clip is a doctored version of the original video, manipulating the attire of the woman.
Some social media users highlighted the possibility of the viral clip being an AI-generated deepfake, claiming that the woman’s clothes had been purposely changed from a suit to a bikini. (Archive)

Taking a safe bet here that most of you who have heard of Louise Joy Brown have not heard at all of Jean Purdy, or her role in the birth of Baby Brown. Louise Brown was the first baby born of an IVF procedure on July 25, 1978. But this might not have been a joyful story, but for Jean Purdy.
Like all the heroines in this column, Jean Marian Purdy, a clinical embryologist and a critical part of the development of in vitro fertilisation, remained uncredited for a long while. Born in Cambridge, U.K., she went to work with physiologist Robert Edwards and gynaecologist Patrick Steptoe at the Physiological Laboratory in Cambridge. They were working on a high-risk experiment and taking medical science where it had never been before – who would have thought babies could be created in test tubes before the trio managed to show that it is possible.
Purdy trained as a nurse in Addenbrooke Hopsital in Cambridge, and joined Edwards in 1968 as a research nurse and quickly became indispensable to the team. Going back to study the records later, scientists established that it was Purdy who managed the laboratory, prepared and tested culture media, and recorded and organised the data of the early IVF work in the lab. Besides this, the records also put her at the centre of patient care, in this case, supporting women who volunteered their eggs and wombs at a time when public sentiment was entirely against it.
Purdy was the first to recognise and describe the formation of the early human blastocyst – the cluster of cells that forms five or six days after a sperm fertilises an egg, in the culture, a key milestone in pre-implantation development. It represents the early stage of embryonic development, where the embryo implants itself into the wall of the uterus to establish a pregnancy. Purdy was the first to see the embryonic cells successfully dividing in the lab, soon these cells would go on to become on 25 July 1978, she was the first to see the embryonic cells that would become Louise Brown. This moment is significant, because it was the first indication that their pioneering technique had worked.
That was not all; between 1970 and 1985, until her death, she co-authored 26 academic papers with Edwards and others in leading journals, including Nature, documenting methods, outcomes and sophistication that made IVF safe and more reliable.
After NHS funding for IVF was withdrawn following early successes, Purdy helped establish the world’s first dedicated IVF clinic, Bourn Hall Clinic near Cambridge in 1980, and served as its technical director. Again, she helped standardise medical protocols for IVF and scale up treatment, overseeing the birth of more than 500 IVF babies before her death from cancer at just 39 years, in 1985.
In their article The Oldham Notebooks: an analysis of the development of IVF 1969–1978. V. The role of Jean Purdy reassessed, archived in PubMed, Martin H. Johnson and Kay Elder, look at her body of work in early fertility care. The authors pored over the Oldham Notebooks - 21 handwritten laboratory notebooks and loose records kept primarily by Purdy between 1969 and 1978. They concluded that: “Purdy’s interests were clearly focused on the research and development aspects, especially those exploring viable embryo development and improved transfer procedures. For example, in a film made in 1980 (Williams, 1980), she talks about a modification to the transfer cannula that she was trying. Thus, whilst Edwards provided the ideas and the intellectual stimulation and Steptoe the authoritative clinical skills, it is arguable that without Purdy’s systematic approach and dedicated contributions, the project at Oldham may have faltered.”
Despite all this, centuries of sexism weighing in on the scientific community, a classic example of the Matilda Effect, her role was minimised in public memory for decades. Even though Edwards and other colleagues objected to it, Purdy’s name was omitted from a commemorative plaque installed at Oldham Hopsitals, associated with IVF’s breakthrough. Correspondence from Edwards archived at Cambridge later described Purdy as “crucial” to their work, underscoring how her erasure contradicted the team’s own view of her importance. In fact, Edwards’ own records state his growing confidence in her and her essentiality in the team: Purdy was “being ‘particularly good with the patients’, and her ‘cooperation had become crucial. It was no longer just Patrick and me. We had become a threesome’.
However, only Edwards was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for IVF. While recognition for the work that Purdy did, has grown only recently, thanks in good measure to the research of Johnson and Elder, some things cannot be corrected any more. Now, some museums and clinics cite Purdy as the first clinical embryologist, and other institutions have begun naming awards and exhibitions after her. Sidelined again, this time, though her collaborators acknowledged her work, Purdy’s contributions were callously and credit consistently denied.
Though belated, it’s now time to undo the wrongs. It is time to say her name! Say Jean Purdy, shout it out from the rooftops!

The Chinese president, Xi Jinping, has received a red-carpet welcome in India for a summit of Brics developing nations, as regional rivals Beijing and Delhi make a public display of thawing relations while quietly competing to lead at a time of shaky US global dominance.
As Xi stepped off the plane, he was walked past an honour guard of Indian soldiers and traditional dancers in colourful dresses.
The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, and Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, had already been welcomed by the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, who is hosting one of the group’s most closely watched gatherings since its inception.
The summit marks Xi’s first visit to India in seven years and is seen as the biggest step towards reconciliation after a deadly 2020 military clash along the disputed Himalayan border, in which 20 Indian and four Chinese soldiers were killed.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming recently, with flights and high-level contacts gradually being restored. China was “willing” to work with India to properly manage differences and be “good neighbours and friends”, China’s foreign ministry said on Friday.
Leaders and diplomats have been convening in India for the annual gathering of the Brics grouping, named after five of its earliest members – Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa – that was conceived as a counterweight to western dominance.
This summit comes as wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, along with rising US-China tensions, test the bloc’s ability to find common ground.
Since its inception in 2009, Brics has expanded as a forum for major emerging economies to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The group now rivals the US-dominated G7 forum of advanced economies, accounting for half of the global population.
But its growth has also created new fractures and disunity – Iran was bombing Saudi Arabia and the UAE earlier this year, and Brics foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement when they met in Delhi in May.
Reuters reported on Saturday that India’s summit would result in a generic joint declaration that would show unity by condemning unilateral war, but was unlikely to name any single country.
Jiang Shixue, vice-president of the expert committee of the China thinktank Council for BRICs cooperation (China), said the 11 members “cannot speak with one voice on many issues”.
“The only solution is to continuously strengthen political consensus,” he told the South China Morning Post.
Beijing and Delhi have differing views on the role of the group.
China has sought to expand Brics power as a counterweight to the US under Donald Trump’s leadership, which has launched global tariff and trade wars and retreated from multilateral institutions such as the UN, which afforded it international credibility.
India has taken a more cautious approach, seeing Brics as a bridge between the west and the developing world.
Chietigj Bajpaee, a senior research fellow for South Asia in the Asia-Pacific programme at Chatham House, said this week that Delhi had found it hard to maintain its policy of “strategic hedging” during such a disruptive US presidency.
“India’s position can appear out of sync in a forum whose membership includes countries with more overtly anti-western agendas, including China, Russia and Iran. And two other Brics countries, South Africa and Brazil, have suffered high-profile diplomatic disputes with the US,” he wrote.
“The challenge for Delhi is that it wishes to promote this worldview in a way that is non-western but not explicitly anti-western.”
Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

The Best Space Heaters of 2026
Featured in this article
The Best space heaters are winter’s rear guard, the last line of defense against goose bumps and cold feet. Though not a great way to heat a whole home, space heaters can be indispensable for a late-evening movie night, a workbench in a chilly garage, or the home’s odd corners that refuse to heat. And if you live in an apartment building where you don’t control the heat, it may be your only way to feel OK in January.
But safety and reliability are prime concerns, and so is a lot of dodgy and opaque marketing about “Hyperamics,” “Velocity Tuned Heat,” and whatever-wave technology. Whatever the marketing, large space heaters usually aren’t more powerful or more effective than small ones. So I turned down my thermostat and tested dozens of space heaters to find the ones that’ll warm you up as quickly and quietly and safely as possible.
Alongside WIRED’s blessedly balanced and quiet top pick, the Dreo Whole Room Heater 714 ($100), I also sorted out which heaters might best suit specific needs, from the best bathroom heater to a space heater that doubles as an air purifier. For those on a tight budget, the bare-bones Honeywell 360 Surround ($47) often goes on sale.
Looking for more ways to tailor your air? Check out our guide to all things that improve your indoor air quality, as well as our specialized guides to the Best Air Purifiers, Best Humidifiers, Best Fans, and Best Dehumidifiers.
Update September 2026: I tested and added Honeywell’s 2026-model Surround 360 as my new top budget pick, replacing Honeywell’s Uberheat 5. I also tested and added the Heatbit Maxi Pro bitcoin miner and heater; re-added this year’s De’Longhi Dragon as WIRED’s top radiator pick; and removed discontinued products and updated prices, descriptions, and products throughout.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Frequently Asked Questions
Why Large Space Heaters Aren’t More Powerful Than Small Heaters
Nope! It may seem counterintuitive, but large space heaters don’t necessarily heat any better than small ones.
Whatever their physical size, most space heaters in the US and Canada deliver about the same amount of heat. Space heaters top out at 1,500 watts, which is the highest safe operating load for a 15-amp household circuit. And aside from some low-power personal heaters here and there, most space heaters you’ll find on the market are 1,500-watt heaters.
What’s more, electric space heaters are all pretty much 100 percent efficient in converting that electricity to heat. Whether directly or indirectly, nearly all of that energy will eventually become heat.
So if space heaters are the same power and the same efficiency, why are some 1,500-watt heaters advertised for small rooms and some for large rooms? This likely has as much to do with marketing as science. Pretty much every ceramic, electric-coil, or PTC heater has about the same amount of juice and thus the same ability to heat a room … at least eventually.
What differs among heaters is how and where the heat gets distributed and how fast. All other things being equal, the efficacy of a heater is mostly about whether it puts the heat where you want it to go.
What Are the Different Types of Space Heaters?
Basically all electric space heaters do the same thing: They take electricity off the grid, usually 1,500 watts of it if you're in the United States, and turn that power into heat.
The vast majority of space heaters, including ceramic heaters and PTC heaters, are electric resistance heaters. This means they run an electrical current through something that creates resistance: maybe an electric coil or maybe a specially designed ceramic. This quickly turns electricity into heat.
Most space heaters use a fan to disperse this heat out into the world, where we all live. These forced-air convection heaters tend to be the fastest at quickly raising the temperature of the surrounding air. The air then heats you. And so while this variety heats quickly, it can take quite a bit of electricity to heat up a whole room.
Oil-filled radiators, in contrast, heat up oil that circulates inside the device, which then emits heat to the surrounding room. These tend to heat up slower but offer even and lasting heat and are very quiet. These radiators operate on the same principle as steam radiators in buildings with a boiler room. And just like steam radiators, they can get really, really hot to the touch.
Radiant heaters, such as infrared heaters, operate much like the sun or a campfire: Rather than heat the air, they heat objects or people directly by radiating energy toward them. Infrared devices heat the air only indirectly, via the objects it heats—much the same way the sun's heat radiates off baking city streets. The glow is immediately palpable as warmth, but you’ll need to be in the path of the radiation to feel it, and the thermometer might not immediately register the warmth you perceive. Infrared heaters tend to be best at making an individual in front of the heater feel a little warmer without using a lot of energy, making them a more common decision in large and lofty spaces or outside on a patio.
Though they deliver heat differently, both infrared and oil-filled heaters are subject to the same wattage limitations, and have about the same efficiency, as electrical resistance heaters.
The same cannot be said for heat pumps, a newer technology that’s expected to provide the next generation of household heat. Heat pumps don’t use energy to create heat. Instead, they move heat energy from one place to another. Accordingly, they require far less energy than other forms of heater. But household systems cost thousands to install. And while more affordable window and portable heat pumps are ramping up, they’re not yet broadly available.
Are Space Heaters Safe?
Yes, but also definitely no.
Space heaters are much safer than they used to be. Modern space heaters are heavily regulated, especially regarding exposed heating elements and automatic shutoff switches to prevent overheating. But all heating devices require caution, and so do all devices that pull a lot of energy over long periods.
The vast majority of residential heating fires start with actual fire—specifically in fireplaces and fuel burners. But space heaters accounted for more than a thousand fires in the US each year from 2017 to 2019, according to the US Fire Administration. Though this accounted for just 3 percent of heating fires overall, these led to more than 40 percent of fatalities, in part because portable heaters tend to be placed precisely where people are and because the resulting fires are far more likely to be unconfined.
So treat your space heater with the caution and wild skepticism that it deserves. See WIRED's Guide to Space Heater Safety for a full rundown about how not to start fires or cause othr hazards. Our guide follows recommendations from federal experts at the the USFA and the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC), as well as the Association of Home Appliance Manufacturers (AHAM).
But for the short version:
Don’t leave a space heater unattended. "Unattended” includes sleeping, y’all! Might we suggest a wonderful down comforter instead? When possible, safety experts also recommend you don't leave a portable heater running unattended in a room with a baby, nor a person with mobility issues. The risk isn’t just fire but hyperthermia.
Plug your heater directly into the outlet. Don't use extension cords or power strips with space heaters, lest you build up too much electrical load and risk a fire.
Don’t plug another appliance into the same outlet or circuit as the space heater.
Place a space heater only on the floor, on a level surface. Heat rises. You don't need to prop up a heater on an unstable chair or table.
Keep your heater at least 3 feet from flammable objects. This includes bedding, drapes, furniture, clothes, papers, books. All of that.
Keep space heaters away from water and dampness, whether in bathrooms or in moist basements prone to dripping or flooding.
Read the manual. Manufacturers have good advice.
How We Tested and What We Tested
When it comes to testing space heaters, there are a few main questions: How safe is it? How loud is it? How quickly and evenly can it heat a room?
During intensive testing of dozens of space heaters, I lived for weeks in a home with the thermostat set to a chilly 65 degrees Fahrenheit.
I tested how well and quickly each device heated a medium-size room (14 by 14 feet), and also how well it heated a small seating area in a larger, open-format space. To test each heater’s thermostat and also measure the evenness of heating, I placed thermometers at three or more locations in each room, including behind the heater.
I tested the loudness of each device with a decibel meter at 3 feet away and verified power usage with a wattmeter. To see whether the heater’s exhaust put out painful levels of heat, I used an infrared thermometer to gauge precise surface temperatures. When in doubt, I put my own fingers on the line.
Finally, I tested safety features and basic durability. I looked at independent safety certifications, of course. But I also rudely knocked over each device to verify how the device’s tip-over protections functioned, if at all, and verified that the device started working again when set back on its feet.
To test overheat protection, I smothered each device with an old sheet to see whether the device shut itself off or whether it adjusted its power output to keep internal temperature low. After the device shut itself off, I then checked how soon it could turn back on, if it ever did. (Some heaters gave up, in permanent complaint!)
If any device fails the tip-over or overheat tests, we don’t recommend it. If it’s significantly louder than 50 decibels at 3 feet, we don’t recommend it. If the heater breaks during routine operation, we don’t recommend it. Maddening rattles and squeaks are also disqualifying.
We keep on testing our favorites through the cold season and beyond, to see how they hold up over time. And, of course, we continually subject more heaters to our testing regimen to see if other devices can oust our current faves.
More Space Heaters I Recommend
Vornado AVH10: Vornado has an unholy variety of models that look quite similar but have different levels of loudness and different feature sets. Some are built in America, some in China. In general, the models I’ve liked best are the ones that advertise “vortex action,” a fancy name for spinning a fan into a spiral grate oriented opposite to the action of the fan. This leads to a mostly quiet and nigh-undetectable column of warm air, directed out to the back of the room, where it scatters. The TAVH10, which is basically this model but with a timer and remote, is my current favorite, though if you need neither, you can save $30 and get this.
Vornado MVH+ and Vornado VH240+: These two devices are very nearly the same device. And the previous year’s non-digital MVH was my favorite model before getting displaced by a couple newer models of Dreo and Vornado. It remains among the most silent, the most even in its heat, and among the most reasonably priced. However, the TAVH10 got a little quieter and the MVH got a little louder, and the addition of a remote and a timer makes it more attractive. This said, there are reasons to favor an analog device. Because they’re analog, the MVH and VH240 can also be regulated by a temperature-controlled power outlet in order to get the most accurate version of a thermostat.
Lasko Ellipse Ceramic Tabletop Heater: This little ceramic number from Lasko was the space heater I kept reaching for while testing dozens of other space heaters last year. It’s not the most obvious choice: It doesn’t heat a room evenly, its grill surface gets wackily hot, and the thermostat is an inside joke. I’m not sure I’d run it near babies or small dogs. And yet I still kept voting for it with my cold, cold feet. Why? Because this little thing can radically change my whole experience of life within about 15 seconds of being turned on. It brings the heat, as they say, though mostly within an 8-foot radius. Within that manifold, it’s like living inside a hair dryer, which is more pleasant than it sounds. You’re warm and lovely from your heart-cockles to your cankles. This is our previous pick for best foot warmer, and it’s still a good pick. It’s just not as versatile as our new top pick personal heater from Vornado.
Shark TurboBlade Cool + Heat: WIRED reviewer Kat Merck enjoyed the customizable airflow of Shark’s original TurboBlade cooling fan (7/10, WIRED Recommends), which can be angled every which way for optimized airflow and is the perfect height for blasting air onto a bed. On cooling fan settings, these virtues remain true of the new Cool + Heat version. True to its name, the Cool + Heat model also adds a 1,400-watt heater to the equation, with emphasis on “little.” The TurboBlade does not push air through its blade-like “wings” for heating, the way it does for cooling. Rather, it blows hot air only out of the small vent at the center of the device, whose aperture is only somewhat larger than some hair dryers. The versatility of heating and cooling is nice. So is the ability to direct air upward or downward. And especially, I love that this Shark device’s thermostat is actually accurate to within a single degree, and that the Shark automatically modulates its energy output to maintain temperature in a room. This avoids the wild on-off swings of some less sophisticated heaters. But for such a small heater, the TurboBlade is quite big and loud. Even on low settings, the high-pitched jet engine whir never stops. Standing in front of it on high settings, my phone registers 70 decibels. So I’d recommend this for someone who predominantly wants to use the device as a fan. The heater is more of a secondary function.
De’Longhi Slim-Style Portable Panel Heater: This electric panel heater is an interesting hybrid, with dual heat exhausts on each side but also a broad radiant heat panel. This makes for a middle ground between radiators and resistive fan heaters—heating a room much faster than a classic radiator would but still maintaining warm radiant heat over time. This said, it shares a radiator’s main fault, which is that it’s painfully hot to the touch across a large surface—but still issues the same amount of fan noise as a fan heater. Still: It may be your choice if you need to heat up a space quickly and evenly and maintain that heat over time.
Dreo MC706 Fan and Heater: Dreo’s innovative 2-in-1 fan/heater won top marks in our fan guide for its auto-shift positive temperature coefficient (PTC) technology, which moves the heater’s ceramic element aside to allow full fan airflow. Its 1,700 ft/m wind speed is a rarity among tower fans, let alone tower fan/heater combos. It’s not the strongest space heater, but it is sufficient, with five settings, 120-degree oscillation, and tip-over protection. Note that though there is a remote, there are no smart features, and it does not work with Dreo’s app.
Dreo Bathroom Heater: Like Dreo’s smart wall-mounted model I far prefer, this ceramic heater comes with an ALCI plug for safe use near water. I prefer to keep bathroom heaters away from the floor, but not all bathrooms have mountable wall space. This remains a possible, though not ideal alternative, with a somewhat janky thermostat.
Vornado VC-02 Ceramic Heater: Vornado put out two new ceramic heaters at the tail end of 2025. The less expensive, smaller, horizontally oriented VC-01 is WIRED’s top personal heater pick. The VC-02 is a bit like the 01 turned on its end and made into a tower heater. The VC-02 is in most ways a premium model, with more options in terms of power and fan settings. It’s even quieter than its sister model—in fact, it’s one of the quietest heaters I’ve tested, period. It has a thermostat that’s reasonably accurate. It’s also got a remote and the ability to swivel from side to side for full room coverage. (It does not pivot up and down, the way the VC-01 does.) But while I like all these features, its tower-heater shape makes it less optimized than the VC-01 for up-close heating, which is what ceramic heaters do best. At the beginning of the season, this had not yet come back in stock, but I’ll continue monitoring.
Not Recommended
Heatbit Maxi Pro: The Heatbit Maxi Pro (5/10, WIRED Review) is a cool-looking, luxury-styled air purifier and heater with a twist: It offsets its energy use by mining Bitcoin. At the high energy rates and lagging Bitcoin price of 2026, the Bitcoin mining certainly wasn’t profitable. But it did offset the cost of heating with the device by about a third, and made onboarding quite easy for Bitcoin novices. The app and safety features are admirable enough. But the Heatbit is neither a quiet heater nor a great air purifier, and its Bitcoin mining might take most of a decade to make up the $1,500 to $2,000 price tag of the device. In the end, the Heatbit is a conversation item, something to show off to houseguests. But I couldn’t find a way to make it practical.
Boldr Kelvin (Gen 2): The Kelvin is a much different heater than the others on this list: It is a silent white or black panel that slowly heats up over the course of an hour, emitting what the company attests is far-infrared radiation, similar to those mail-order saunas you can find on Wayfair. The standard model tops out at just 450 watts, so the sell isn’t really that it emits a lot of heat: rather, far-infrared feels warmer if you stand in front of it. It operates on the same principle as heat from the sun, warming surfaces (including people) directly rather than heating up the air. In the ideal case, this means you can feel more warmth while using less energy than a traditional heater. Its makers recommend it for those stubborn cold spots in a house. But I struggled with this heater. A wall-anchored heater offers less flexibility, and in the shorter term, a radiant heater provides warmth only directly in the path of the panel, meaning it must be positioned with quite a bit of care to be useful. The Kelvin also uses up quite a bit of wall space, and must be located near an outlet. By design, its front gets quite hot to the touch—near boiling, in fact—and the device projects quite a bit of heat backward into the wall even after a second-generation upgrade to its insulation. It’s an interesting concept, with a smart app to track energy use, but the caveats add up. At $400, it’s hard to make it pencil.
Pelonis 16-Inch Space Heater and Pelonis 23-Inch Space Heater: Both of these towers heated up quite quickly. Both were also enormously hot at the surface of their vents, with relatively little shielding from the visible heating elements. The 23-inch was significantly quieter than the 16-inch, however.
Vornado Velocity Cube 5S: This cube’s outer housing stayed quite cool, and the fan functionality is welcome. But its surface vent got a little hot, and the fan was a bit on the noisy side compared to other Vornados.
Vornado Velocity 5R Whole Room Heater and Vornado VHEAT: The MVH and TAVH line from Vornado are among the quietest space heaters I’ve tested. These were two of the loudest. The 5R topped 70 decibels. The vintage-looking VHEAT is quite lovely, but it’s also a bit of a noisemaker.
Lasko MyHeat Mini: This little thing looked cute, and I thought it would be a nice desktop or under-table personal heater. But even with its low output at 400 watts, the vent got way too hot to want it anywhere near your laptop or papers.
Lasko 22-inch Oscillating Tower With Remote: This one failed our tip-over test when we knocked it over, blasting heat endlessly into the rug until it overheated and sent a burnt-plastic smell into the air. It did restart hours later, meaning this shutoff was a safety feature. But this tower’s a bit too tall and tippable to risk repeating these events often. It’s out of stock on most sites as of February 2026.
Honeywell 2-Position Heater: This compact, simple, analog heater was a nice enough idea, able to rest vertically or on its side. Lord, it’s loud when its fan is in operation, though. As of February 2026, this device is out of stock, but we’ll monitor restocks.
Honeywell Compact Ceramic Tower: This Honeywell performed well in terms of fast heat and safe surface temperature. Its fan wasn’t too loud either. But the one we received had a maddening squeak each time the tower oscillated fully counterclockwise.
Gone but Not Forgotten
Vornado Sensa Cribside Heater: I loved the idea behind this Vornado Sensa Cribside Heater when I tested it: A space heater with an external temperature sensor, with therefore accurate temperature management (hard to find among space heaters!) But it’s disappeared from Vornado’s website, and has dwindled on retail sites. It’s no longer available on Amazon, but if you see it on sale at another site, I still like it.
Also tested but discontinued: Vornado VMHi600, Morento 26-cm Heater, Morento 40-cm Heater, Dyson HP07, many other models of Vornado before the brand’s late-2025 refresh.

An Ahmedabad entrepreneur’s post about an alleged ₹1.5 lakh donation demanded for his two-year-old daughter’s preschool admission has triggered a debate on social media over the rising cost of early education in India. Pritesh Lakhani shared his experience on X while looking for a preschool for his daughter, who recently turned two. According to Lakhani, a parent at one of the schools he was considering told him that paying a ₹1.5 lakh donation was compulsory to secure admission. “1.5 lakh donation to get admission for a 2-year-old kid,” Lakhani wrote on X. The entrepreneur said his family was looking for a preschool where their daughter could continue her education without having to switch schools later. Lakhani said the parent he spoke to claimed that the donation was a mandatory part of the admission process. He alleged that the school could otherwise assess both the child and the parents, and could reject the application or demand a higher amount. He also claimed that the donation for the first year of preschool was ₹1.25 lakh. “Preschool fun should not be this expensive,” Lakhani added. Lakhani’s post led to a discussion on X, with users sharing their views on admission fees, assessments for young children and alternatives to conventional schooling. Some users suggested homeschooling as an option, while others questioned the need for expensive preschool education. “Donation is mandatory in every aspect of education in India now. Hence people chose homeschooling. But that requires a lot of time from parents,” one user wrote. Another user questioned the idea of assessing a two-year-old for preschool admission. “How can they test a 2-year-old for preschool? Clearly, you’ve chosen the wrong school. Like you should see this red flag and move away.” Some users also argued that parents should consider schools that place greater emphasis on practical skills rather than reputation or conventional academic approaches. “These so-called famous schools and pre-schools are actually preparing your kids for a future that will not exist after 2035. It is better you find a school that focuses on preparing your kids for real life skills. As you said, preschool should be fun. Try homeschooling,” the user wrote. Another X user questioned whether preschool itself was necessary, saying, “Preschool as a concept is not necessary and just exists to milk out more money; right games/collaboration with other kids is what any kid should be doing at this age” “homeschool. Something like education is too important to be outsourced to unqualified incompetent twats at inflated prices,” wrote one user. Regarding your editorial (The Guardian view on child marriage: girls should not be wives, 26 August), every year, 12 million girls are married under the age of 18, while more than 70 million more are estimated to be at risk of child marriage between 2025 and 2030. Yet, as international development budgets face unprecedented contractions, traditional field programming alone cannot keep pace.
At current funding levels, international funding for ending child marriage amounts to less than $1 per girl at risk per year – a level of investment that cannot match the scale or urgency of the problem
Ending child marriage requires dismantling the patriarchal norms that perpetuate it. Over eight years of participatory research across Bangladesh, India and Nepal – engaging 350 grassroots partners – our team validated a cost-effective alternative: narrative edutainment. Field-testing a film-driven intervention yielded a striking 49.4 percentage point shift in community attitudes, proving visual storytelling can transform entrenched behaviours where policy alone stalls.
Through our film project, we are establishing a scalable model combining cinema, school toolkits, community screenings and policy briefings to reach 100 million people across south Asia, with a clear blueprint for expansion into sub-Saharan Africa.
Child marriage inflicts a staggering $175bn economic cost worldwide yearly. In an era of scarce global funding, investing in scalable-impact film assets is an urgent necessity. This vital tool can break the cycle of poverty and protect millions of young girls.

The Esports Federation of India (ESFI) has raised concerns over India’s elimination from the quarterfinals of the eFootball competition at the 20th Asian Games 2026 in Japan, alleging that organisational lapses surrounding its fixture against Mongolia and the subsequent qualification calculations denied the team a fair opportunity to pursue a historic esports medal.
Chinmay Sahoo (console) and Danial Patel (mobile), along with Saksham Rattan as coach comprised the Indian team for eFootball at the Asiad
India had begun its Group F campaign with a 0-0 draw against Uzbekistan. Uzbekistan subsequently defeated Mongolia and finished with a substantial positive goal difference. Mongolia failed to report within the stipulated check-in time, resulting in a forfeit in India’s favour.
The match was recorded as a 0-0 win rather than a scoreline carrying a goal difference — a detail that proved decisive and something the Federation raised concerns about.
“ESFI stated that India’s request for a review went unacknowledged and claims that the team was denied the opportunity to lodge a formal protest, despite clarity of rules not being given within the stipulated 15-minute duration as per the rulebook,” a media release from the Federation read.
In its official email to the Asian Games esports organising committee, the federation highlighted a series of technical and scheduling disruptions preceding the forfeit.
“ESFI further stated that Mongolia had not been adequately briefed on the required Call Room reporting time and that its team manager was not permitted by the technical official overseeing the preceding match to leave for the next fixture’s reporting process. The federation has questioned whether these circumstances were adequately considered before the forfeit was declared,” the media release further read.
“In its subsequent review request, India sought clarification from the Olympic Council of Asia (OCA), Esports Organising Committee and competition management on the regulatory basis for recording no goal difference in forfeited matches and using average points and average goal difference to rank second-placed teams.”
The federation said the lack of acknowledgement of India’s review request and the alleged denial of an opportunity to lodge a formal protest had left the team distressed and its concerns unresolved.
Reaffirming its respect for competition rules and technical officials, ESFI has called for a transparent review, a written response to the issues raised and appropriate corrective action under the applicable regulations to uphold fair play and equal sporting opportunity.
