YouTube is getting in on the micro-drama craze, and helping to bring the fast-growing format to TV screens.
On Wednesday, it's releasing a new feature that allows creators to bundle their short videos in a series of episodes or seasons, designed to be viewed sequentially. The tool is available to any Shorts creator, but is particularly helpful for micro-drama studios that make soap-opera-style shows aired in snippets of 1 to 3 minutes.
"Micro-drama studios, even before this tool, are having great success on YouTube, and hopefully it's going to make the viewer experience of their content even better," said Kurt Wilms, senior director of product at YouTube, speaking with reporters at the company's Made on YouTube event on Wednesday.
Micro-drama platforms typically make money via "freemium" models, where viewers can watch a few episodes for free before being asked to pay up. Wilms said studios can mimic that workflow using YouTube's existing memberships product.
He said a studio can offer a few episodes of a series for free, and then "put the rest of them behind the membership table."
YouTube also has in-feed ads that give a share of revenue to creators, offering an alternative way for them to make money.
Serialized short dramas, which often live on dedicated apps like DramaBox or ReelShort, have exploded in popularity in the US over the past few years, captivating and bemusing Hollywood. Despite their zany plot lines around werewolf romances and sordid billionaire affairs, they've become a serious business. Global short-drama revenue is expected to reach $7.8 billion this year, with the US accounting for about 40% of that, per a Deloitte analysis. Streaming platforms like Paramount+ are testing out the format, and YouTube rival TikTok is diving into short dramas at full speed.
Experimenting with a basic micro-drama product will give YouTube a chance to learn more about viewers' appetites and decide if it's worth investing in additional tools.
YouTube is seeing a big increase in micro-drama viewing
YouTube also shared some eye-opening stats on micro-drama viewership:
- In the first half of 2026, the format crossed 6.5 billion views, with watch time growing over 50% year over year
- While micro dramas are a mobile-first format, views on TVs increased by over 90% year over year
"We're seeing both the mini-drama studios as well as creators saying people are watching Shorts on the TV," Wilms said. "People are watching episodic Shorts on the TV, and it's kind of clunky to watch one after the other. And that's why the Shorts tools were made. This is going to hopefully help that use case."
YouTube emphasized that its Shorts series feature isn't just for pure-play micro-drama studios. It identified Kinigra Deon as a creator who was embracing short episodic storytelling, too.
Micro dramas' growth on YouTube in the living room shows in particular how the lines between the video app and traditional TV have been blurring. YouTube has gobbled up a bigger share of the TV viewing pie, and more ad dollars have followed as advertisers differentiate less between the two.
YouTube's massive scale can be a shot in the arm for a new format, as it was for podcasts. In 2025, YouTube said that more than 1 billion people listened to podcasts there every month, helping propel the audio format into a watchable one.
Wilms said he expected the micro-drama category to keep growing as people watch more short-form content — of all kinds — across different screens.
"Micro dramas in particular, they're fast paced, they're action packed," he said. "Overall, we see a lot of success of bite-size content that could be personalized to your taste. There's a little bit of a continuation of short-form content that now applies to episodic content that can engage and retain your viewers."

Asian governments are rushing preparations for the most severe El Niño weather event on record, with hundreds of millions of people bracing for multiple crises at once as extreme heat, heavy rain and food shortages hit the region.
Fuelled by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific – and developing alongside the human-driven climate crisis – El Niño is virtually guaranteed to grow to a very strong intensity towards the end of this year and into 2027.
The World Food Programme has warned that about 50 million people will probably be pushed into acute hunger due to the exceptionally intense weather system, while UN secretary-general António Guterres said this month that El Niño was “being supersized before our eyes”.
Here are the steps countries in Asia are taking to prepare for El Niño:
‘Climate risk maps’ in China
In Hong Kong, authorities have already been forced to revise workplace policies, after the city experienced its hottest day on record on 9 August. During times of extreme heat, companies are expected to reschedule work, provide cooling equipment and rest breaks for their employees.
Employers in the international financial hub could even face prosecution if they fail to provide staff with support at times of sweltering heat.
In mainland China a 100-day campaign has been launched to prepare for extreme weather and help safeguard harvests against the opposing extremes of drought and intense rainfall.
Beijing has plans to upgrade early warning monitoring systems, and in July, it launched a national plan encouraging cities to draw up ‘climate risk maps’ to help identify areas most vulnerable to flooding and severe heat.
Taiwan, meanwhile, is treating the predicted extreme weather as an emergency situation, and preparing using methods similar to what it would do to train for a terrorist attack or earthquake. In early September, the island nation held a mass exercise simulating three consecutive days of temperatures above 40C. Hundreds of people took part in the field exercises, which simulated power and water disruption, rail problems, air conditioner failure and mass heatstroke.
The government has also been testing its “Cool Map” online platform, which helps to direct vulnerable people to airconditioned and cool spaces.
Sri Lanka plans to process salterwater
El Niño is already wreaking havoc across south Asia; in parts of India there has been a shortfall of monsoon rainfall of almost 50% in September, with knock-on effects on key crops such as rice, pulses, cotton and maize. Concerns are mounting that there could be a diminished harvest in the coming months, likely driving up food prices – already crippling for poor and lower middle class families.
The Indian government has taken a hyper-vigilant approach to establish what the agriculture minister, Shivraj Singh Chouhan, described as a “protective shield for farmers”.
In more than 350 vulnerable districts authorities are boosting water conservation infrastructure and water harvesting, and are encouraging farmers to plant low-water, short duration crops – such as pulses and millets.
But the most intense impact of El Niño in the area is in Sri Lanka, where the absence of rainfall and high temperatures have become so severe that the country is experiencing its worst drought in a decade. More than 160,000 people are now facing a drinking water shortage as several key reservoirs run dry.
Officials have been forced to close the tourist areas of the Yala national park, home to leopards, elephants, crocodiles and spotted deer, and have been bringing in tankers of water to fill the ponds to make sure the animals do not die. In Mullaithivu lagoon, in the north-east of Sri Lanka, thousands of fish were found dead due to the lack of fresh water.
The country’s disaster management centre is preparing for a situation in which freshwater supplies could vanish. “If water sources dry up, there will be no alternative means of obtaining water,” an official said. Colombo would then be forced to process salt water from the sea, although relying on the country’s one desalination plant is not considered workable.
Tackling an agriculture crisis in south-east Asia
In south-east Asia, El Niño is compounded by a series of ongoing crises. The Iran war has already disrupted global energy and supply chains and inflated fertiliser costs, disproportionately hitting the region. At the same time, severe haze from seasonal fires across Malaysia and Indonesia has choked cities and is damaging plants and trees.
During the 2023–2024 El Niño, south-east Asian governments successfully cushioned agricultural impacts by adjusting planting calendars and managing water, but those strategies will be insufficient to deal with the scale of the crisis, experts warn. Regional rice yields are already projected to fall by 8 to 10%.
“We can’t just assume that this El Niño is going to be the same as the last because there are so many challenges that have been stacking on top of each other,” says Elyssa Kaur Ludher, a climate and food security expert based in Singapore.
The Philippines, Malaysia and Indonesia are particularly vulnerable to food price changes, says Kaur Ludher, a visiting fellow with the Climate Change for Southeast Asia Programme at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore.
“In Singapore, most of our income is not spent on food. It’s under 10%. But for Indonesians, it can be up to 50% or even more as a proportion of income spent on food. So any price rise affects them disproportionately.”
With the potential for price rises to leave people desperate and angry, Kaur Ludher has argued for food security to be reframed as a national security issue. In Indonesia and the Philippines in particular, she said, social stability depends a lot on food prices. “Rice is a lifeline to this region,” she says.
To prepare, south-east Asian governments and farmer cooperatives are promoting regenerative agriculture and shifting toward biofertilisers.
“We have come to a stage where climate change is putting so much pressure on us – on our existing, already crumbling or structurally unsound, systems,” say Kaur Ludher. “Nature will force us to have a reckoning.”
South Korea overhauls its heatwave alert system
South Korea saw the driest July on record in the country’s south-east. Weeks later came a freak reversal, as a weakening storm system dragged in a deluge that dumped some of the heaviest rainfall ever recorded at a Korean weather station. The heat was so intense that farmers described spoilt potatoes as being “boiled” in the ground.
The country’s weather agency has overhauled its heatwave alert system for the first time in 18 years, adding a top tier that triggers official guidance to stop non-emergency outdoor work once feels-like temperatures hit 38C. Nationwide, phones have buzzed for weeks with government alerts urging people to stay indoors during the hottest hours.
Officials are watching out for a rough autumn, with seas around the Korean peninsula remaining unusually warm for the season and forecasters expecting the north-west Pacific to produce far more powerful storms than usual this year, since a strengthening El Niño is weakening the high pressure that has so far kept them away.
Japan prepares for ‘cruelly’ hot days and typhoons
Japan is also bracing for the arrival of so-called super-typhoons, which experts attribute to a combination of El Niño and human-induced global heating.
El Niño was once associated with slightly cooler summers in Japan. But rising sea surface temperatures mean it is having the opposite effect, blanketing many parts of the country in record-breaking heat and humidity in 2023-4, the last time the weather pattern materialised.
Japan recorded its first official “cruelly hot day” – or kokushobi – in July, just after the start of the current El Niño event. The Japanese term, introduced in April to underscore the threat to health posed by rising temperatures, refers to days when the mercury exceeds 40C.
Now, as the summer heat dissipates, the country is bracing for the arrival of potentially destructive typhoons.
The public is encouraged to take measures to protect themselves and their homes, such as heeding official evacuation warnings and stocking up on food and water. People living in apartments are urged to secure or bring inside flower pots and furniture – anything that could become a dangerous flying object during a storm.
This month the infrastructure ministry said it had identified several high-risk underpasses on national highways that would be closed preemptively during heavy rain. Underpasses – which allow cars to travel beneath other roads or railway lines – became a focus of concern last month after two trapped motorists drowned during record-breaking rain in Chiba prefecture, east of Tokyo.

The festive season has officially arrived, and Indian kitchens are once again coming alive with preparations of laddus, payasam, halwa, burfis, and other traditional sweets. With the rising awareness about the impact of sugar, however, some ingredients in popular sweets are being changed. Refined sugar is increasingly being replaced with jaggery, while some consumers are also experimenting with artificial sweeteners such as stevia, and of late, monk fruit sweetener.
The intention is understandable: enjoy festive food while reducing sugar use. The science behind these sweeteners however, is more nuanced. Not every alternative to sugar is nutritionally equivalent, and ‘natural’ does not automatically mean low-sugar. The important question is not simply what sweetener is being used, but how much sweetness and sugars a person consumes overall.
Jaggery counts as sugar
Jaggery has long been associated with traditional Indian cooking and is often perceived as a healthier alternative to refined sugar because it undergoes less refining and may retain small amounts of minerals. However, it remains a concentrated source of sugar.
This distinction becomes particularly important during festivals, when sweets are rarely eaten in isolation. A person may have a laddu, a serving of payasam/kheer, sweetened beverages and several savoury foods in the same day, or worse in a single meal.
The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that free sugars contribute less than 10% of total daily energy intake, with a further reduction to below 5% providing additional health benefits. For a person consuming around 2,000 calories a day, 5% is roughly 20 to 25 grams, or 4 to 5 teaspoons of sugar.
Therefore, replacing sugar with jaggery does not make a sweet sugar-free. From a doctor’s perspective, portion size and the total amount of free sugar consumed during the day remain far more important than whether the sweetener is brown or white.
Artificial sweeteners
Across the country, many people are now using low-calorie or no-calorie sweeteners. These include artificial sweeteners such as sucralose, saccharin and aspartame, as well as naturally derived sweeteners such as steviol glycosides and monk fruit extract.
Monk fruit extract, the newest addition to sweeteners in the mass market, is particularly interesting because its sweetness comes from compounds called mogrosides. Monk fruit extracts can be approximately 100 to 250 times sweeter than sugar, depending on their mogroside content. The United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has noted that the use of monk fruit extract is ‘generally recognised as safe’ under its intended conditions of use.
Artificial sweeteners work differently. They provide intense sweetness with little or no calories and are commonly used in products marketed as ‘sugar-free’, ‘light’ or ‘diet’. Approved high-intensity sweeteners are considered safe within their specified conditions of use, and several have established acceptable daily intake levels.
However, a ‘safe’ label does not necessarily mean beneficial. The World Health Organization currently advises against relying on non-sugar sweeteners as a strategy for long-term weight control. Its recommendation is conditional and is based on evidence that replacing free sugars with non-sugar sweeteners does not provide a clear long-term benefit for reducing body fat.
This is an important distinction for consumers. A sweetener can be safe to consume and still not be a reason to increase the amount of sweet food in the diet.
A better approach
The biggest misconception is that changing the sweetener automatically changes the nutritional quality of the sweet.
A jaggery laddu is still sweet. A sugar-free dessert can be calorie-dense if it contains large amounts of ghee, nuts, cream or other ingredients. Similarly, replacing sugar with monk fruit does not make an otherwise highly processed dessert a health food.
The more useful approach is for us to look at our entire festive eating pattern. One traditional sweet enjoyed occasionally is very different from consuming several servings every day throughout the season. The goal is not to find a sweetener that allows unlimited sweetness; it should be to reduce excessive sweets while retaining the cultural and social pleasure associated with festivals.
So, if a festival sweet is made with sugar, moderation matters. If it is made with jaggery, moderation still matters. Monk fruit essence or other non-sugar sweeteners do not automatically bestow a license to eat more.
The aim should be not to move from sugar to jaggery or from jaggery to monk fruit. It should be to simply learn to enjoy our favourite sweets alittle less sweet, and a little less often. This also aligns with broader dietary recommendations from the WHO that advise building diets on minimally and unprocessed foods, and restricting free sugars.
There is no need to cut out every single sweet, but do practice portion control and choose wisely. Instead of five laddus, have one and enjoy it mindfully. Keep the overall diet rich in vegetables, fruits, whole grains and fibre, and let sweets remain a small part of the meal.
(Suparna Mukherjee is a dietician with Narayana Health City, Bengaluru. suparna.mukherjee@narayanahealth.org)

For example, GoPro sent a Laowa 7.5-mm lens for me to test with. When HyperSmooth is on, that's the equivalent of shooting with a 23-mm lens on a full-frame camera. With HyperSmooth off, it becomes a 20-mm lens. I bring this up mainly because if you want to go really wide on the ILS, you'll need a very, very wide lens (fisheye lenses are probably your best bet).
Now for the downside to the ILS: There are no electrical contacts, which means lenses that rely on electronic focus or aperture control probably won't work. For example, my all-time favorite MFT lens, Panasonic's original 20-mm pancake, won't work on the ILS because there's no manual aperture ring.
Your best bet is to stick with fully manual lenses that have a mechanical aperture ring. There aren't many, but there are enough with quality glass to cover a good range of focal lengths. GoPro's Abe Kislevitz put together a nice collection of lenses that he has tested with the Mission 1 Pro ILS, along with his recommendations for various shooting scenarios. Be aware that the camera is sold body-only, and so far, we haven't seen any bundles from GoPro or resellers that include a lens.
And yes, you have to manually focus. I could drop some jokes here about kids today not knowing how to do it, but the truth is, I shoot vintage manual-focus lenses all the time on my Sony A7R II. While I've shot sports and wildlife with these lenses and had a pretty high success rate, I struggled to focus on the ILS.
The problem with focusing on the ILS is the small screen. It's hard to see, not just in bright daylight. It's just really small. There is focus peaking, which uses color banding to indicate what's in focus, but it can be hard to see exactly where it ends, and I've learned from my Sony not to fully rely on peaking.
You can zoom in to get very precise focus, which is what I do on the Sony, but again the small screen makes it hard to see. Worse, for filmmakers especially, you have to have the camera at eye level to focus it well, which limits your shooting ability (or you get to contort into all sorts of weird poses). I would love to see the next Mission 1 Pro ILS get a tilting screen; it's not waterproof anyway, so it doesn't seem like there would be a need to reengineer. GoPro no doubt would suggest using the app on my phone, as it does make it considerably easier to focus, but then you need a cage, and then a handle, and at that point most of the Mission 1 Pro ILS' size advantage is gone; you might as well get a Panasonic GH7, which has an even larger sensor.
Ultimately, while focusing on the small screen is challenging, using a phone or other external monitor sidesteps that issue (and is what pro filmmakers do anyway), but the inability to control the lens iris electronically feels like a bigger limitation since it eliminates a significant number of lenses. It would be nice to see a future Mission 1 Pro ILS support at least electronic connectors for aperture and manual focusing on lenses that require it.
Shooting With the Mission 1 Pro ILS
Once you get past the hurdle of manual focusing, there's a lot to love about the ILS footage. Testing it reminded me more than anything of the Blackmagic Pocket Cinema Camera from several years ago. I can't believe this tiny little thing can match the quality of those early Blackmagic cameras.

How Ceuta, football and Israel are shaping Morocco's election
- Published
Disillusioned young voters in Morocco were courted with viral football slogans, promises of one million jobs and anti-Israel rallying calls ahead of Wednesday's parliamentary elections.
Yet, for many young Moroccans, politics remains deeply disconnected from reality.
"I have no hope for this election. I'm ashamed of our political scene. It's a complete circus," Siham Azeroual, 32, an environmental activist who lives in the Atlas region, tells the BBC.
The outcome of the vote will decide the make-up of the next government, just weeks after 60,000 people risked their lives to cross from the North African country to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta - a sign of the lack of opportunities many young people feel they have at home.
Morocco operates as a constitutional monarchy where political parties compete for 395 seats in the House of Representatives, the legislative chamber.
Yet executive power remains closely tied to the crown. King Mohammed VI, the 63-year-old monarch, appoints the prime minister from the political party that comes first in the election, but also presides over the Council of Ministers - the country's most important policy-making body.
The current campaign also follows a wave of Gen Z protests that erupted in September 2025 over unemployment, healthcare and living costs.
Demonstrators chanted slogans like "freedom, dignity, and social justice" which escalated to "get out Akhannouch", a reference to current Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch.
More than 2,400 people faced prosecution following the unrest. Despite the crackdown, some young activists are choosing to enter the political arena.
Hamza El Kharroubi, 29, was briefly arrested during the protests. He is now running for parliament with the little-known Environment and Sustainable Development Party, which has a green agenda.
"As a young person, I don't have much hope. I joined this party because they wanted more Gen Z faces and they are allowing us to speak freely about our demands," El Kharroubi tells the BBC.
He comes from Tetouan, just 34km (21 miles) from Fnideq beach, where the migration wave to Ceuta started in late July.
Some 60,000 people crossed, both Moroccans and other nationalities. At least 100 people died in the largest migration surge to the enclave in recent history.
"We want justice for the families of those who died crossing to Ceuta. We want compensation for their families," El Kharroubi says.
He argues that the crossing was widely linked to economic hardship and unemployment.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates overall unemployment stood at 13% last year, while youth unemployment - between the ages of 15 and 24 - reached 37.3%.
El Kharroubi says his goal is not to compete with established heavyweights - but securing a voice in parliament to build toward 2031.
"As young people, we have to enter the parliament so by 2031 we have strong young politicians who can compete for a seat in the government."
Fouzi Lekjaa, head of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation and a senior politician who works in the finance ministry, has emerged as the kingdom's newest political sensation - and a definite heavyweight.
Credited with helping the Atlas Lions - as the national men's football team is known - become global contenders, Lekjaa joined the centrist Party of Authenticity and Modernity (Pam) in July.
Videos of his campaign rallies have gone viral in the football-mad nation that is jointly hosting the next World Cup along with Spain and Portugal.
The clips show crowds chanting "Sir" which means "Go" in Moroccan Arabic - the iconic catchphrase from Morocco's historic 2022 World Cup run, when it became the first Arab and African side to make it to the semi-finals.
Lekjaa has promised to make Morocco sixth in the world in education and healthcare, to match the Fifa ranking of the men's football team.
Pam is competing against 26 other parties, including Prime Minister Akhannouch's National Rally of Independents (RNI). In its bid for a second term, RNI has renewed a pledge to create one million job opportunities by 2031.
Political expert Rachid Aourraz, from the Moroccan Institute for Policy Analysis (MIPA), remains sceptical about this promise.
"The slogan 'one million jobs' has become an overused electoral slogan. There is also talk of raising the minimum wage, but what is proposed cannot withstand a structural inability to create stable net jobs," Aourraz tells the BBC.
He adds that major parties "do not compete over an alternative model", but rather over how to implement public policies set by a royal vision.
Also seeking a political comeback is the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD) - using anti-Israeli sentiments to woo voters.
Morocco normalised ties with Israel in December 2020 along with several other Arab countries, under the US-brokered Abraham Accords.
Led by populist former Prime Minister Abdelilah Benkirane, the PJD is campaigning heavily on a promise to end diplomatic ties with Israel. He says the normalisation was a "mistake" made by his party which led the government between 2016 and 2021.
Bilateral ties were hit during the Gaza war with weekly protests taking place in the capital, Rabat, against the Israeli diplomatic presence.
During the conflict the Israeli liaison office was closed and direct flights between the two countries were suspended.
Yet despite an outpouring of pro-Palestinian protests, with tens of thousands taking to the streets and setting ablaze the Israeli flag at the height of the war, it was announced earlier this month that Israel and Morocco had agreed to open full embassies in their respective countries.
This followed a meeting between their top diplomats and the US ambassador to the United Nations.
"We have to speak up," Benkirane told supporters at a campaign rally in Marrakesh.
"If we work hard, the king will close the Israeli embassy. The king does not like going against his own people," he added, warning of "the dangers of Israel and Zionism in Morocco".
I think young people should focus on the microscale: rather than running for office, helping build communities and connecting with people and then building up to the top"
More than half of Morocco's total population of roughly 38.8 million is under the age of 35 - though only 4% of the more than 15.8 million registered voters are aged between 18 and 24.
"I am not keeping up much with the campaigns - but I noticed the same faces as usual," says Hiba, a 27-year-old Moroccan living in Canada who preferred not to use her last name.
She lives in Montreal which has a large Moroccan diaspora of about 104,000 people, according to the 2016 census.
Many of last year's Gen Z protests were more vocal outside the country, where young Moroccans were able to express their anger without fear of repercussions.
Hiba, who co-organised several Gen Z protests in Montreal, says she would have considered voting had she been able to find a proxy in Morocco - which is how those in the diaspora can cast their ballot.
"Gen Z protests didn't go in vain. We achieved something. At least now we see more debates with young people on state TV," she says.
Azeroual, the environmental activist, agrees.
But having lived through both the 20 February movement in 2011 that changed the constitution and the recent Gen Z movement, she believes change must come from a multi-faceted approach.
"I think young people should focus on the microscale - rather than running for office, helping build communities and connecting with people and then building up to the top," she says.
Despite not being fully convinced by any political campaign, she says she will be heading to her local polling station to cast her ballot.

SIR row: If decisions were illegal, why didn't ECs approach President? Experts ask
Yogendra Yadav and Rajat Sethi questioned why Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi did not force a full commission meeting over the SIR dispute. The debate sharpened scrutiny of whether internal objections were formally pursued under the Election Commission's own processes.
As questions mount over the Election Commission’s handling of the SIR, political analyst Rajat Sethi and Swaraj India co-founder Yogendra Yadav have turned the spotlight on Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, asking why they did not call a full Commission meeting or approach the President if they believed the poll panel’s decisions were illegal.
Yadav said the continuation of not just Gyanesh Kumar but the other two Election Commissioners was untenable if they believed that illegal decisions were being taken but did not bring the matter before the public.
“Why did the two not requisition a meeting of the Commission? And if they did and the meeting was not held, why did they not approach the President of India?” Yadav asked during a debate on India Today TV.
He questioned why the two commissioners had instead written to the Cabinet Secretary.
“Is Cabinet Secretary the boss of Election Commission of India?” Yadav asked, adding that the entire Election Commission should be held accountable.
Sethi, who has worked on a BJP election campaign in the past, also questioned the conduct of the two commissioners, while stopping short of calling for their removal.
He said the three Election Commissioners should have sat together to deliberate on the issues raised in the internal communications.
“If the two commissioners are on one side on a decision, they could have called the full-fledged meeting of the Election Commission on their own,” Sethi said.
Sethi also questioned why the two commissioners approached the Cabinet Secretary despite the constitutional independence of the Election Commission.
The Election Commission is an independent constitutional body, Sethi said, adding that he did not understand why the two commissioners would show “deference” to a Cabinet Secretary.
“I don't understand the conduct of the two commissioners as well,” Sethi said.
He said the key issue was whether Sandhu and Joshi had jointly opposed particular decisions, thereby forming a majority against them, or whether they had raised objections on separate issues while a majority still supported the decisions.
“Did the two commissioners disagree collectively on a certain topic, making the whole decision illegal, ab initio? Or did the two commissioners disagree on different issues, and the majority was still with the decision that was taken?”
“These details we don't know,” Sethi said, adding that only the Election Commission and the three commissioners collectively could clarify what happened.
He said the available information had led to an assumption that decisions taken by the Election Commission were illegal because there was no majority, if not a consensus. However, he said the records of the deliberations would be needed to establish whether that was actually the case.
Sethi further said that if the two commissioners were together on a particular decision, they had an institutional option to call a full-fledged meeting and potentially annul the decision.
The debate followed reports of internal communications in which the two Election Commissioners had raised concerns over aspects of the SIR process, including changes to electoral forms and the use of centralised electoral-roll software.
Yadav argued that the issue went beyond routine disagreement within the poll panel. He alleged that the Election Commission had authorised its staff to take actions that were the prerogative of electoral registration officers.
He also cited the controversy over changes to Form 6, the statutory application form for inclusion of names in electoral rolls, and said the matter required greater transparency.
Sethi, however, said the central legal question was whether the decisions in question had the required majority under the Election Commission (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.
He said if the two Election Commissioners had jointly opposed a decision and constituted a majority against it, the decision could not have been taken. But he added that the available information did not establish whether their objections amounted to a collective opposition to specific decisions.
“The core legal question” could be answered only by the Election Commission itself, Sethi said.
The debate also saw BJP spokesperson Siddharth Yadav argue that dissent during Election Commission deliberations was provided for under the 2023 law and that the final decisions cited by the poll panel had been unanimous.
He said no formal dissent had been recorded against a final decision and questioned the conclusion that the Election Commissioners had been overruled by the CEC.
The discussion has therefore raised a separate question beyond the allegations against Gyanesh Kumar: if Sandhu and Joshi believed certain actions were unauthorised or illegal, why did they not use the institutional mechanisms available to them to force a full commission meeting or make their objections public?

In September 2026, some Facebook accounts shared a rumor of a chimpanzee saving a person's life by pulling them from a faulty electrical cabinet.
For example, one Facebook page claimed (archived) a chimpanzee left its enclosure to pull a zookeeper away from an electrical cabinet that shocked him and knocked him to the ground. The post included an image of what appeared to be two security camera screenshots showing the chimpanzee pulling the zookeeper away from the cabinet and a rescue team running towards the zookeeper while the chimpanzee watched.
The story as shared by the page read in full:
A chimpanzee pulled a zookeeper away from a faulty electrical cabinet, then sat nearby until the rescue team arrived.
The keeper had entered a service area beside the chimpanzee habitat to inspect a control box that had stopped working. Moments after he opened it, an electrical fault knocked him to the ground.
He was still conscious, but badly disoriented and unable to move away from the cabinet.
A chimpanzee watching from the nearby access doorway immediately became agitated. Instead of retreating, it entered the service yard, grabbed the back of the keeper's jacket and began pulling.
The chimpanzee dragged him several feet across the concrete until they were safely away from the loose cable. Then it released his clothing and moved back toward the habitat entrance.
Other zoo workers noticed the emergency on a security monitor and called the rescue team. Less than a minute later, three responders came running through the service gate with medical equipment.
By then, the keeper had regained enough strength to sit upright. The chimpanzee remained beside the habitat doorway, quietly watching as help approached.
Staff later said the animal had never been trained to perform a rescue. It simply saw someone it knew lying in danger—and did the only thing it could think of.
The rescue team treated the keeper, but the chimpanzee was the one who first pulled him out of harm's way.
The tale was posted to Facebook groups (archived) and also appeared on YouTube (archived). A reader sent Snopes an email asking if the claim was true.
There is no credible evidence supporting the story of the chimpanzee's rescue. The image included in the post was generated using artificial intelligence, and it is likely the story is AI-generated, too. Therefore, we've rated this claim false.
Snopes first looked for evidence supporting the story on various search engines.
We searched for "chimpanzee pulled zookeeper from electrical cabinet" (archived) and "zookeeper saved by chimpanzee" (archived) on Google, and made similar searches (archived) on DuckDuckGo (archived), Bing (archived) and Yahoo (archived). None of the searches yielded any reporting of the incident by credible news organizations, press releases, blog posts from a zoo or any other type of primary evidence of the incident, such as the security footage that allegedly captured it.
Reverse image searches through Google (archived) and TinEye (archived) did not yield any such results either. The few instances of the image the search engines found online were all from Facebook posts retelling the story.
If the story was real, it's very unlikely there would be no reporting, discussion or firsthand accounts available online. The Facebook posts do not identify the people involved, the name of the zoo or the location of the zoo; many fabricated stories are intentionally vague on such details to make it more difficult to debunk them.
The post embedded above, posted by the Facebook page Animal Rescue Stories, appeared to be the original source of the claim. Snopes reached out to the Animal Rescue Stories page over Facebook Messenger to ask whether the page was the source of the story and to request credible evidence supporting the story if it had any. We'll update this story if and when we receive a reply answering our questions.
Evidence of AI generation
The Animal Rescue Stories post also included an "AI content" label. Facebook will automatically apply the "AI content" label when the content was created or modified by Meta AI, or when it detects AI signals within the content (such as hidden watermarks). Facebook users can also add the "AI content" label to their posts themselves.
In this particular case, the label could mean the attached image, the written story or both were generated by artificial intelligence tools.
This label aligns with the about section on Animal Rescue Stories' Facebook page. The about reads:
Emotional stories of animal rescue and hope.
Spreading kindness, protecting wildlife and nature
The stories you are watching are recreated with AI, but the video aims to spread values of compassion, education, and animal protection.
That disclaimer reads as if it only applies to video content, and not to the images or the written stories. Due to this uncertainty, Snopes also asked the Animal Rescue Stories page via Messenger if it generated the story itself using AI. The page didn't reply prior to publishing.
The two screenshots from the security footage have easily identifiable inconsistencies that wouldn't be possible in reality. Although the visible timestamps suggests the screenshots were taken less than a minute apart, there are significantly more objects lining the left wall in the second screenshot than there are in the first. The first screenshot depicts enough space between the right wall and the fence to fit a dumpster and a small vehicle, while the second screenshot depicts significantly less space and different objects in the same area. Even the size of the entrance to the chimpanzee exhibit differs between the two screenshots.
Pangram, a reputable AI text detection tool, determined that the text of the story was 100% AI-generated.
Let us note here: These types of AI detection tools are fallible. Snopes cautions people against using them for definitive answers on media's authenticity without supporting evidence.
The fictional story about the chimpanzee helping the zookeeper resembled glurge, which Dictionary.com defines as "stories, often sent by email, that are supposed to be true and uplifting, but which are often fabricated and sentimental."
This particular story is similar to other AI-generated stories of chimpanzees purportedly saving zookeepers' lives.
For further reading, Snopes fact-checked a similar AI-generated story and image claiming a gorilla cried out for help when its favorite caretaker collapsed.

81-year-old Texas man working to return lost luggage to fund wife’s cancer bills sparks community outpouring
Donald Johnson said he works delivering luggage because nowhere else will hire him

Online donors are rallying around an 81-year-old Texas man who has taken on difficult work — the only job he could land — to help pay for his wife's healthcare needs.
Donald Johnson works as an independent contractor delivering lost luggage to people's homes, and he was doing the grueling work when Erin Howell of The Colony, a suburb near Dallas, saw him struggling with some of the heavier bags.
"The other day, I looked out my door cam and saw an 81-year-old man slowly and painstakingly carrying my heavy luggage that had been lost on a recent flight up a steep flight of stairs," Howell wrote in a GoFundMe entry. "He looked absolutely exhausted, and his steps were heavy with effort."
After talking to him, she learned that Johnson started doing his luggage job three years ago to help pay for his wife, Josephine, who is battling cancer. The couple has been together for 57 years.
Howell asked Johnson why he picked such a physically demanding job, and he reportedly told her that it was the "only job that will hire me."
"The staggering medical bills, continuous treatments, expensive prescription medications, and everyday costs of living have completely overwhelmed them," Howell wrote of Johnson's situation. "At an age when he should be resting and spending every precious single moment by his wife's side, he is out on the road lifting heavy bags just to keep her alive and cared for."
To make matters worse, since Johnson is an independent contractor, he has to use his own car for deliveries. He reportedly has put more than 200,000 miles on his car delivering luggage, and the miles have taken their toll on the vehicle's condition.
Moved by Johnson's struggle and dedication to fight for his wife, Howell started a GoFundMe to help Johnson retire without having to give up on paying for his wife's cancer treatments.
Howell said that all of the money raised will go toward paying for Josephine's medical bills, which will allow Johnson to stop working and focus solely on caring for his wife.
As of Wednesday morning, the fundraiser has raised an impressive $87,000 of its $150,000 goal.
Howell said that she knew Johnson was unlikely to ask for help, so she started to fundraise on her own.
"He is a deeply proud, selfless, and dedicated husband who would never ask for charity himself, which is exactly why I am stepping in as to start this GoFundMe campaign," Howell wrote. "He shouldn't have to carry this crushing financial and physical weight all by himself anymore."

Meesho backer RPS Ventures sold nearly 3.9 Cr shares of ecommerce major Meesho to net ₹899.7 Cr. As per BSE bulk deal data, RPS’ holding entity RPS WOS II LLC offloaded a total of 3.86 Cr equity shares, or around 0.8% of Meesho’s total equity, in a block deal valuing each share at ₹233. The trading price is a 1.4% discount to the stock’s closing price today. The shares that flooded the market were lapped up by the Government of Singapore (1.3 Cr shares), Mirae Asset Mutual Fund (77.2 Lakh shares) and Societe Generale (35.5 Lakh shares). Other major buyers included BNP Paribas Arbitrage, Fidelity, Citigroup, Norway’s pension fund, Ghisallo Capital Management, Morgan Stanley, WhiteOak Capital Mutual Fund, among others. RPS held around 5.4 Cr shares in Meesho or 1.1% stake at the end of the June quarter. With today’s bulk deal, the VC firm has slashed its shareholding by over 71%. RPS Ventures, which is a late-stage VC firm cofounded by ex-Softbank executive Kabir Misra, joined Meesho's cap table in 2018 when it backed the startup's $50 Mn Series C round. The firm did not pare its stake in the ecommerce giant when it made its public markets debut nearly a year ago. However, other investors cashed in 10.6 Cr shares cumulatively as part of the offer for sale component of Meesho’s IPO. Notably, Meesho has seen several major investors offloading stake in bulk over the past few months. Y Combinator dumped 4.85 Cr shares to mint around ₹969.6 Cr around a month ago, while Elevation Capital and Peak XV Partners sold shares worth ₹974.6 Cr each a few weeks prior to that. Earlier, Fidelity also sold almost 6 Cr shares worth ₹988.44 Cr via bulk deals back in June. Meesho’s stock has been on an upward trend in recent months since the company posted strong earnings in the quarter ended June 2026. In Q1 FY27, Meesho managed to slash its consolidated net loss by 54% YoY to ₹132.8 Cr, while its operating revenue surged 48% YoY to ₹3,707 Cr. Shares of Meesho ended the day 1.6% lower at ₹236.35 on the BSE.

Internal Objections In Election Commission Spark Political Storm As Opposition Attacks CEC
A report highlighting repeated objections from two election commissioners over voter roll revisions has triggered a political storm around the Election Commission of India. Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi reportedly raised 14 objections over 10 months concerning the Special Summary Revision exercise, modifications to voter registration Form 6, database centralisation, and digital access issues. Concerns also extended to voter roll processes in West Bengal and software glitches affecting eligible voters in Goa. Key questions surfaced over requirements for parents' and grandparents' details without formal rule amendments. The disclosures have drawn sharp reactions from opposition leaders, including Rahul Gandhi, Mamata Banerjee, Akhilesh Yadav, and Arvind Kejriwal, who demanded strict accountability and targeted Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Rejecting allegations of an internal rift, the Election Commission maintained that internal dissenting notes and diverse viewpoints reflect routine checks and balances within statutory frameworks. The Bharatiya Janata Party defended the poll body, describing internal deliberations and differences of opinion as evidence of a functioning democracy.

Why a new Pakistan-China border pact has irked India
- Published
For decades, India has refused to recognise a Pakistan-China boundary in a disputed part of the Himalayas that Delhi claims as its own.
But last week, Pakistan and China formalised a boundary in a remote part of the mountainous region, drawing a sharp response from Delhi.
The two countries signed the Pakistan-China Boundary Joint Commission, an agreement which Pakistan described as a "significant milestone" that would deepen cooperation on border management, trade and connectivity between India's regional rivals.
Delhi rejected the move as having no legal basis, saying it did not recognise any Pakistan-China boundary located in territory it claims as Indian.
The announcement comes at a particularly sensitive moment.
India and China are seeking to stabilise their relationship after years of military tensions along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the disputed line separating their forces along much of their Himalayan frontier. At the same time, Beijing and Islamabad are deepening cooperation along a neighbouring stretch of the frontier that India also claims.
"There is no boundary between Pakistan and China. We reject the so-called Joint Commission, which is without any legal basis," Indian foreign ministry spokesman Randhir Jaiswal said.
The commission concerns the Pakistan-China frontier, including the Shaksgam Valley, a roughly 5,180 sq km tract that Pakistan ceded to China in 1963 but which India claims as part of its territory in Ladakh.
India says the territory was part of the former princely state of Jammu and Kashmir and was illegally occupied by Pakistan before being ceded to China. The Indian government has never recognised the agreement and considers it illegal and invalid.
This history explains the particular sensitivity of Wednesday's announcement.
"Pakistan has no locus standi to enter into arrangements concerning Indian territory under its illegal and forcible occupation," the Indian foreign ministry said.
Pakistan says Jammu and Kashmir remains a disputed territory, and argues that India therefore has no standing to challenge its 1963 boundary agreement with China. It regards the agreement as valid.
Jabin T Jacob, professor at the Department of International Relations and Governance Studies at Delhi's Shiv Nadar University, said the new development represented the revival of an old mechanism rather than an entirely new arrangement.
"A joint boundary commission is provided for in the 1963 Sino-Pak Agreement, the only issue at hand is the timing of its operationalisation," he told the BBC.
He said there could be several reasons for the timing, including China's broader effort to demarcate its boundaries and a desire to institutionalise exchanges and movement along a frontier at a time when Pakistan's other borders have experienced conflict and instability.
Jacob said India should be "worried" by the development. More importantly, he said, the move appeared to disregard a provision in the 1963 treaty itself.
Article 6 of the agreement provided for its renegotiation once the Kashmir dispute was settled with whichever country ultimately controlled the territory, Jacob said.
For India, Jacob said, the problem is compounded by the international information environment.
"China's relative dominance of the international media and information landscape - [with] CGTN, CRI, presence on social media - relative to India allows it to put forward its narrative and maps globally while India is limited to fulminations that other world capitals are likely to ignore," he said.
That concern is distinct from the practical management of the frontier itself. Pakistan and China already have extensive infrastructure and connectivity links across the region, including the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) and the Karakoram Highway.
Husain Haqqani, former Pakistani ambassador to the US and now a senior fellow at Anwar Gargash Diplomatic Academy and Hudson Institute, said the new commission was both practical and political.
"It is a combination of both," Haqqani told the BBC. "It is a mechanism to enhance border and boundary cooperation, prevent illegal crossings and protect the strategic infrastructure tied to CPEC."
He said it also served as a signal to India that Beijing continued to view Kashmir through the Pakistani prism.
"China has never accepted India's position on Kashmir and China views Gilgit-Baltistan from the Pakistani, not Indian prism," Haqqani said, referring to the region in Pakistan-administered Kashmir that borders China and which India claims as part of its territory.
Haqqani said Islamabad's position had evolved in response to developments in Indian-administered Kashmir.
"Pakistan still maintains that the final status of Jammu and Kashmir is yet to be decided," he said. "But since India has made internal changes - for example, the abrogation of Article 370 - in its part of Kashmir, Pakistan sees no issue with simply institutionalising what has been de facto with China since 1963."
For Beijing, the arrangement also fits into a broader pattern of using its relationships with neighbouring states to manage and signal its position towards India.
Haqqani said reassurance to Pakistan on Kashmir was of both strategic and geopolitical value to Beijing.
"On the strategic front it further deepens ties with Pakistan and on the geo-strategic front it reinforces for India its fear of a two-front threat from China and Pakistan, which pleases Pakistan and benefits China."
The timing of the statement, say experts, is also significant.
"China always plans its decisions months, if not years, in advance so the decision to operationalise a joint boundary commission must have been made some time back," says Haqqani.
"The release of this information was timed for after President Xi Jinping's recent Brics summit trip to send Pakistan a message of reassurance in the strategic partnership, and India a reminder that multilateral engagement does not translate into any change in China's vision for South Asia."
But Jacob cautioned against interpreting every aspect of the development as a direct military move against India.
"There aren't any immediate or apparent implications for the LAC as of now," he said.
That suggests that the significance of last week's announcement may lie less in an immediate change to the disputed Himalayan frontier than in the gradual institutionalisation of arrangements that India has consistently rejected.
India's position, Jaiswal said, remained "clear and consistent": any attempt to legitimise what Delhi considers Pakistan's illegal occupation of Indian territory is unacceptable and has no bearing on India's sovereignty.
But Haqqani believes the dispute goes beyond the legalities of borders.
"The key disagreement between India and China about the border and boundary is geo-strategic, not cartographic," he said. "So there is a limit to what border negotiations and border management mechanisms can achieve."
Pakistan, he added, remained "China's secondary deterrent against India" - and Beijing's engagement with Islamabad would continue to send that message to Delhi.

The US and China have bought themselves more time to negotiate.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Wednesday that the countries had agreed to extend their trade truce from November 10 to January 10. He announced the extension after a meeting in Washington with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, as Chinese leader Xi Jinping arrived for a state visit.
"We will extend what we call the 'Busan Agreement,' the economic detente between the two countries that was scheduled to end on November 10, that is going to be extended until January 10," Bessent told Fox News during a live interview on Wednesday.
The extra two months could lead to a broader deal, Bessent said, and the two sides could also "just roll the current deal" again.
"There are some deliverables that have not been perfect on the Chinese side, so we also want to see, now that we've sat down and told them our expectations, if over the coming months they can be more fulsome in enacting the agreement," Bessent said.
Bessent said Xi's visit could bring announcements on Chinese purchases of American farm products and financial services. US and Chinese officials may also discuss lower tariffs on selected goods and a system for sharing alerts about serious AI-related security incidents.

The Enforcement Directorate (ED) has chargesheeted EaseMyTrip cofounder and chairman Nishant Pitti in the Mahadev online betting app money laundering case, accusing him of facilitating the entry of alleged illegal betting proceeds into the Indian stock market through FPIs. The ED filed its fifth supplementary prosecution complaint before a special PMLA court in Raipur on September 10, according to The Indian Express. This is the sixth chargesheet filed by the agency in the wider money laundering investigation. The agency also provisionally attached demat shares belonging to Pitti worth ₹59.6 Cr under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA). It has sought the court’s permission to confiscate the shares, alleging that they constitute proceeds of crime. Responding to Inc42, Pitti said he was not aware of any chargesheet and had not been summoned by the jurisdictional court. “I have always strived to uphold the highest standards of governance and ethics in my professional and personal dealings,” Pitti said, adding that all his transactions comply with applicable laws and that his assets were acquired through lawful sources of income and formal banking channels. He further said he would contest any contrary allegations before the courts and expressed confidence that the legal process would establish the facts. Pitti also urged against speculation around ongoing judicial proceedings. "I shall submit detailed evidence to establish my bona fide conduct, in accordance with the procedure prescribed by law," he added. Separately, EaseMyTrip said it had not received any formal communication regarding legal proceedings against the company or Pitti. “Easy Trip Planners Limited has not received any formal intimation of legal proceedings against the company or its director, Mr Nishant Pitti,” an EaseMyTrip spokesperson said. Pitti’s name first surfaced in the ED’s investigation last year. In April 2025, the agency conducted searches at multiple locations linked to Pitti and EaseMyTrip across Delhi NCR, Mumbai, Chandigarh, Ahmedabad, Indore, Jaipur, Chennai, and Sambalpur. Pitti was subsequently questioned by the agency. The ED alleged then that Pitti was connected to a network of operators accused of using betting proceeds to manipulate the stock prices of several listed companies. At the time, EaseMyTrip denied any direct or indirect association with the Mahadev betting app or any other betting platform and said it was cooperating with the authorities. ED’s Mahadev Betting Case Probe The latest development comes after Mahadev betting app promoter Sourabh Chandrakar was detained by the Royal Oman Police earlier this year following an Interpol Red Notice issued at the request of the ED and the Chhattisgarh Police. Indian authorities are seeking his extradition or deportation. In March, the ED provisionally attached properties worth ₹1,700 Cr belonging to Chandrakar and entities allegedly linked to him in Dubai and New Delhi. The assets included 18 luxury properties in Dubai, including villas and apartments in Burj Khalifa, Dubai Hills Estate, Business Bay, and SLS Hotel & Residences, besides two properties in New Delhi. The agency alleged that the properties were acquired using proceeds from illegal betting operations and held through entities controlled by Chandrakar and his associates. According to the latest available figures cited in the chargesheet report, the ED has arrested 14 people and attached assets worth ₹1,885 Cr in the case so far. Shares of EaseMyTrip were trading 2.41% higher at ₹5.94 on the BSE at 14:35 IST.

Mum's viral barefoot race sparks debate over India's education crisis
- Published
Despite having no training, or even a pair of running shoes, Ramabai Ranveer sprinted barefoot to victory in her first-ever race in August.
The 47-year-old widow had entered a 3km (1.86-mile) community run with a single goal: winning the prize money to help pay for her two daughters' education.
When she crossed the finish line first, Ramabai from Maharashtra in western India was delighted. The 3,000-rupee ($31; £23) prize would help her buy books and study materials for her daughters.
It was not much money. It would not come close to covering the cost of higher education in India, or even a course at the coaching centre where one of her daughters is preparing for a government recruitment examination.
But videos of her barefoot run spread rapidly on social media and in newspapers, striking a nerve as India's education system faces unusual scrutiny.
"Is it glory or a source of shame for us as a society?" one social media user remarked.
Soon, a woman who had never imagined becoming a runner was being held up as a symbol of something much bigger: the extraordinary lengths some Indian families go to in the hope that education will give their children a better life.
For Ramabai, the decision to run was simple.
"My elder daughter came to me early in the morning and said, 'Mummy, I want to take part in a running race'," she told BBC News Marathi from her home in Beed district.
"I asked her where it was and she said it was nearby. She told me that if she won the prize money, it would help with her education."
Her younger daughter, Arati, lives in Nanded and was struggling to afford books.
"I couldn't send her money to buy books and because of that she didn't speak to me on the phone for eight days," Ramabai said. "So I decided I had to run and win the race."
When her slippers kept slipping off, she removed them, gathered her sari and ran barefoot, pulling ahead to win the women's 30-60 category.
Her elder daughter, Pooja, also won a prize after finishing second in her age group. But she reserved her praise for her mother, describing her as courageous.
Ramabai has been the family's sole provider since her husband died in 2012.
"I did whatever work I could find," she said. "I picked soybeans and chickpeas in other people's fields. I also collected turmeric, processed it and sold it."
She left school when she was 13. Her daughters, she says, should have the opportunities she never had.
"I believe that as long as I am alive, I should do everything I can to give my daughters a good education."
That aspiration is shared by millions of Indian families. But getting a child through the education system and into a secure career can involve years of preparation, intense competition and, for many families, considerable expense.
One of Ramabai's daughters is preparing for police recruitment and the other for the civil services - two fiercely competitive routes into the security and social status associated with a coveted and secure government job.
Millions of young Indians spend years preparing for such examinations, often paying for coaching and study materials. But faith in the system has been shaken by repeated allegations of question-paper leaks and other irregularities.
The controversies have fed a wider sense of frustration among young Indians over education, jobs and the increasingly uncertain promise of a secure future. That frustration has also fuelled student-led protests and youth movements demanding changes to India's education system.
For families such as Ramabai's, education is something they make sacrifices for every day.
After her husband's death, she took whatever work she could find. She now cooks at the coaching centre where one of her daughters prepares for police recruitment.
Ramabai's run also drew the attention of authorities. Earlier this month, Chief Justice of India Surya Kant directed local officials to provide her with financial assistance of 50,000 rupees.
But Sukhadeo Thorat, a former chairman of the University Grants Commission, says the family's story points to broader structural challenges.
"If a woman is compelled to struggle so hard for her daughters' education, it shows that government education schemes are not reaching people adequately," he said. "Both the central and state governments run a variety of schemes. The problem is that implementation remains weak."
For Ramabai, though, the debate is secondary. What matters most is ensuring her daughters have a better future.
"I don't want them to go through the hardships I have faced," she said. "I don't want them to struggle through mud or travel under the scorching sun and rain. Whatever I have suffered, I don't want my daughters to suffer the same."
Additional reporting by Laignee Barron.

Donald Trump has denied claims that administration officials are considering adding the president’s name to Ford’s Theatre, where President Abraham Lincoln was assassinated in 1865 - his latest attempt to add himself to historical landmarks.
Staff members are circulating a list of government sites that could potentially have the president’s name added to them, including Ford’s Theatre, MS NOW reported, citing people familiar with the discussions.
Trump took to Truth Social on Wednesday evening to bash the claim.
“The story that the White House, or me, want to affix my name to Ford’s Theatre, in Washington, D.C., where Abraham Lincoln was assassinated, is a ridiculous lie. It is FAKE NEWS! Who would possibly want a name on such a tragic place?” Trump wrote.
White House officials will apparently pitch renaming buildings after Trump as a way to get on the president’s good side, a former administration official told the outlet.
“They know flattery gets them everything,” the ex-official said.
It was not immediately clear how officials hoped to attach Trump’s name to the Washington, D.C., landmark, which remains operational as a theater and museum and is owned by the Interior Department. An administration official told the outlet that the idea had been discussed, but they didn’t know where it stood.
Administration officials are also looking into buildings and other government sites that they could easily add Trump’s name to without running into legal trouble, according to the report.
It comes as Trump’s long-running legal battle to rename the Kennedy Center after himself hit a boiling point earlier this month, when a federal judge blocked the addition of the president’s name for a second time. A day later, Trump was photographed looking at a poster that apparently addressed the demolition of the historic performing arts venue.
Since returning to office, Trump has slapped his name onto numerous government properties. In addition to the Kennedy Center, Trump officials have added his name to the U.S. Institute of Peace.
They have also affixed his face to a variety of goods — from National Park Service passes to passports and coins. In December, the president announced plans for a fleet of Navy battleships named after him — and last month, CNN reported that the Navy was workiing to rename an aircraft carrier after the president.
Trump has even floated the idea that Congress would rename both New York’s Penn Station in his honor. Republican lawmakers have introduced legislation to rename Dulles International Airport in Virginia after the president.
However, officials still may run into trouble trying to rename the historic theater. The site’s name is set by a federal statute signed by former President Richard Nixon, meaning renaming it would likely require an act of Congress.
Still, this did not stop administration officials from adding Trump’s name to the Institute of Peace or the Kennedy Center, both of which drew emergency legal motions to stop his plans.
The White House denied MS NOW’s reporting, telling The Independent in a statement, “This story is completely false. The reality is that failing MS Now continues to push false and baseless claims from anonymous sources who have no clue what they’re talking about, which is exactly why their credibility is in the toilet. It is embarrassing to watch.”
An Interior Department spokesperson told The Independent, “As we told MS Now, this is not true. “

Peter Byrne, the singer and songwriter for the band Naked Eyes who scored 1980s hits with “Always Something There to Remind Me” and “Promises, Promises,” died peacefully in Los Angeles, California, on Monday, September 14, after a brief illness. He was 74.
His death was announced on the band’s official website.
One of the most popular, if fleeting, British New Wave bands of MTV’s golden era, Naked Eyes was founded in 1982 by Byrne and keyboardist Rob Fisher, who had been college friends in their native Bath, England, and had performed together in a band called Neon from 1979 to 1982. (That band also included Curt Smith and Roland Orzabal, who would go on to form Tears for Fears.)
Within two years Naked Eyes had scored four Top 40 hits on Billboard’s Hot 100. The highest charting was “Always Something There to Remind Me” which peaked at #8 during the summer of 1983. A cover of the 1963 song written by Burt Bacharach and Hal David for Dionne Warwick, the Byrne-Fisher demo of “Always Something There to Remind Me” was strong enough to convince EMI Records to sign the duo that would become Naked Eyes.
The band had three subsequent top 40 hits, the most successful of which was “Promises, Promises,” written by Byrne and Fisher and not to be confused with the Bacharach-David song of the same title that was a hit for Warwick. Both songs were included on the band’s debut 1983 album Burning Bridges, as was a third, less successful single “When the Lights Go Out.”
DEADLINE RELATED VIDEO:
The band’s second album, 1984’s Fuel For The Fire, featured a modest hit “(What) In the Name of Love,” but failed to match the success of the debut album, prompting Naked Eyes to disband (the group never toured). Fisher died in 1999 at the age of 42 following cancer surgery.
Born June 9, 1952, in Bath, Byrne continued writing, recording and touring following Fisher’s death, releasing the solo album The Real Illusion in 2001 under Pete Byrne, followed by two albums under the Naked Eyes name: Fumbling with the Covers in 2007 and Disguise the Limit in 2021. A remaster of the original Naked Eyes self-titled album was release in 2025.
In 2008 Byrne’s Naked Eyes took part in the U.S. “Regeneration” tour with Belinda Carlisle, ABC and the Human League, and in 2024 joined a similarly ’80s themed tour of the U.S. and Canada with Wang Chung, Men Without Hats and The Motels.
Outside of Naked Eyes, Byrne’s work included providing backing vocals on Stevie Wonder’s 1985 hit “Part-Time Lover,” as well as songwriting for film and television. He wrote the song “I Am The Cute One” in 1993 for the Olsen Twins.
Byrne is survived by his siblings Eileen, Sandy, Carol and Steve; children Merlin, Dylan, and Chloe; and ex-wife Elena. A private service will be held for the family.

It was unclear whether the Republicans who voted against House Bill 1505 did so specifically because of the recess provision or for other reasons.
In September 2026, a claim (archived) circulated online that 35 Pennsylvania Republicans voted against a bill that guaranteed daily recess for children in the state.
For example, the pro-Democratic X account @DemzDeliver wrote, "Democrats pass bill guaranteeing recess everyday to Pennsylvania students. 35 Republicans voted no."
The account further spread the claim on Threads and Instagram (archived, archived). It also circulated on another left-leaning Facebook page.
The claim was true. Thirty Pennsylvania Republicans in the House and five in the Senate voted against House Bill 1505, which, alongside other measures, included a section that made recess mandatory from kindergarten through fifth grade.
It was unclear whether the Republicans who voted against House Bill 1505 did so specifically because of the recess provision or for other reasons.
Rep. Scott Barger, who was the only representative to vote against the bill twice, told Snopes via a spokesperson that he voted against the bill because "the overall spending amount of the state budget was too high to be palatable to me, plus the 80 pages don't actually contain meaningful reforms."
House Bill 1505, which Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro announced (archived) that he had signed into law on Sept. 6, 2026, contained a number of changes to the state's Public School Code of 1949.
Shapiro wrote:
Before this year, schools in Pennsylvania weren't required to give students dedicated recess time so they could take a break from learning, get outside, and just be kids. Our latest state budget changes that.
The act added a new section about recess that read, in part (page 49):
Section 1512.2. Recess periods.--(a) a school entity shall provide at least thirty minutes of recess during each school day in full-day kindergarten through grade five and at least fifteen minutes of recess during each school day in half-day kindergarten
The bill went on to say that recess time should be separate from lunch time or physical education. It also specified that recess should be "provided outside" and should not "involve the use of electronic devices."
History of the votes
The Pennsylvania House and Senate voted on the bill three times before it became law.
On July 7, 2026, 202 out of 203 representatives in the state House voted in favor of the bill, sending it on to the state Senate. The lone "nay" vote came from Republican Rep. Scott Barger.
The Senate voted to pass the bill on July 12, 2026. During this vote, five Republicans voted against the bill.
The bill then returned for a concurrence vote in the House on amendments made in the Senate. The House voted, also on July 12, to send the bill to Shapiro for his signature with the amendments from the Senate. Thirty Republicans, including Barger, voted against the bill at this vote, meaning a total of 35 Republicans had voted against the bill in both the House and Senate.
For further reading, Snopes has investigated a series of other rumors about public schools.
